edibleParts.text: Young stems, while they are still tender and no thicker than about 1.5 cm — the fibrous outer skin peels off with a potato peeler. Also the leafy side stalks, young leaves, the flowering heads, and the black seeds. Once the plant has flowered the stems go woody and are not worth the trouble.

habitat.text:
Alexanders is widespread in Britain, where it is frequent in coastal areas in the south, becoming progressively rarer towards the north of Scotland, and absent from Orkney and Shetland. Inland, it is often found close to the sites of medieval monastery gardens and other historical places such as castles.
It is a strictly lowland plant in northern Europe. In Britain, it is recorded no higher than 290 m, at Davidstow Airfield in Cornwall.
In New Zealand: established near deliberate plantings at Takou Bay in Northland, and also coming up in Auckland city with no planting nearby (Ogle et al. 2021, restated).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Smyrnium olusatrum' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Smyrnium olusatrum is a stout, glabrous (hairless) biennial growing to 150 cm tall (exceptionally 180 cm), with a solid stem up to 22 mm in diameter, which becomes hollow and grooved with age. It has a tuberous taproot which can be 60 cm long, as well as fibrous lateral roots.

The stem leaves are arranged in a spiral (although the upper cauline ones are often opposite and sometimes in whorls of 3), with an inflated, purple-striped, fleshy petiole that has papery margins towards the base. The compound leaves are broadly diamond-shaped, 2- or 3-times ternately (sometimes pinnately) divided. Sometimes they are slightly hairy towards the base. The individual leaflets are dark green above, pale green below, flat, lobed and serrated with obtuse teeth that have a tiny white hydathode at the tip.

Inflorescences are terminal or in the leaf axils and consist of a compound umbel of individual umbels, the former 6–7 cm in diameter, with 5–25 penducle rays which are glabrous, ridged and 2–4 cm long. There are 3–4 bracts, which are small, pale and inconspicuous (or absent), and the peduncle is usually longer than its rays. The individual umbels are 1–2 cm across with 10–20 flowers and 1–5 tiny bracteoles. The actinomorphic flowers are small, with 5 yellowish petals and 5 tiny, green sepals, 5 stamens and (if present) 2 styles.
Sometimes there are 4 or 5 peduncles branching from the top of the stem, giving the impression of an umbel of umbels of umbels. Generally, it is only the terminal umbel that has 100% bisexual flowers; the lateral ones have both bisexual and male-only flowers (typically with the male umbellules in the centre), and the tertiary umbels often have only male flowers. This is best seen at maturity, when the male-only flowers wither without producing fruit.

The mature fruit is a black schizocarp 6.5–8 mm long, which splits into two single-seeded mericarps, revealing a stalk (the carpophore) that runs between them. Each mericarp has 3 ridges and numerous vittae (oil tubes), which exude a pungent oil which smells of capsicum or diesel. A single plant may produce between 3,000 and 9,000 seeds in a single year.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock's flowers are white; alexanders' are yellowish. Hemlock's leaves are divided two to four times, finely cut and lacy; alexanders' are divided in threes (sometimes pinnately) into flat, lobed and toothed leaflets. Hemlock's stem is hollow between the joints and usually spotted or blotched purple, most of all towards the base — but not every plant is marked, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Alexanders' stem starts solid but becomes hollow and grooved with age, so a hollow stem does not rule alexanders out. Purple on the leaf stalks does not separate them: alexanders' stalks are purple-striped and hemlock's are purple-blotched when mature. Crushed hemlock gives off a foul, mousy smell. Ripe hemlock fruits are dark brown and 2.5–3 mm long; alexanders' are black and 6.5–8 mm. Both are largely hairless and both can reach about 1.5 m, so neither hairiness nor height helps. If the flowers are white or the leaves finely divided, do not eat it.

preparation.text: Sits between celery, lovage and angelica in flavour — sweet, with a tang that carries. Peel the stems and cook them like celery; the leafy side stalks steam in a few minutes. Leaves are strong enough to treat as a herb rather than a salad green, and the black seeds grind to a peppery, myrrh-scented spice that is best set against citrus or chocolate.

recipes.method: Four large flowering heads, an onion, a parsnip, a handful of wild garlic and a little dulse. Sweat the onion in oil, add the chopped alexanders and the rest, cover with stock and simmer about 10 minutes. Blend smooth and reheat to serve.
recipes.title: Alexanders soup

recipes.method: Take the leafy side stalks and the smaller branching ones. Steam for about 7 minutes, until tender, then toss with butter and season.
recipes.title: Steamed alexanders stalks

recipes.method: 200 g young peeled stems, 100 g golden or brown granulated sugar. Wash, dry and finely chop the stems. Cook in a heavy-based pan over medium-high heat for about 8 minutes, until the liquid they give off has gone. Stir in the sugar and cook a further 10 minutes, until it crystallises around the pieces. Cool in the pan, then store in a dry jar — they keep about 6 months. Makes roughly 120 g.
recipes.title: Candied alexanders stems

recipes.method: 1 heaped tbsp alexander seeds, 500 g white or wholemeal flour (or half of each), a pinch of sea salt, 1 tsp quick yeast, 1 tsp sugar or honey, 400 ml warm water, 15 ml olive oil (optional). Grind or chop the seeds roughly — you want texture, not powder; dry-roasting them at 140 °C for 10–20 minutes first makes them easier to grind, so long as they do not burn. Mix them through the flour and salt. Dissolve the yeast and honey in the warm water, stir into the dry mix and combine well. Knead about 10 minutes, until the dough springs back when pressed. Leave covered somewhere warm until doubled, knock it back, drop it into an oiled tin and prove again until doubled. Bake at 200 °C for 40–45 minutes, until the loaf sounds hollow tapped underneath. Rest 10 minutes in the tin, then cool on a rack before slicing.
recipes.title: Alexander seeded bread

recipes.method: Makes about 25. 100 g salted butter, 40 g demerara sugar, a heaped tsp of orange zest, 1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds, 125 g plain flour, 1/4 tsp baking powder. Heat the oven to 180 °C (160 °C fan) and grease a large tray. Cream the butter and sugar, then beat in the zest and seeds. Mix the flour and baking powder separately and work them in, stopping as soon as it comes together — overworking makes the shortbread tough. Flatten the dough to roughly 20 x 15 cm and cut about 25 rectangles. Lift them onto the tray with a palette knife, at least 1 cm apart, and prick each with a fork. Bake 8–10 minutes, until light brown. Cool 5 minutes before moving them to a rack. They keep a week in an airtight tin.
recipes.title: Alexander and orange shortbread

recipes.method: Built from leftover alexander seed cake. 150 g of the cake (undrizzled), 125 g mascarpone or another soft cream cheese, 120 g dark cooking chocolate, and 1/2–1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds if you want more of them. Crumble the cake into small pieces rather than crumbs and work in the cheese and seeds. Roll into balls about 2.5 cm across on greaseproof paper and chill for an hour. Melt the chocolate in a bowl set over a little simmering water, taking it off the heat when about half has melted and letting the rest come on its own. Dip each ball with a teaspoon until fully coated, return it to the paper, and leave to set hard. They keep several days.
recipes.title: Alexander seed and chocolate truffles

summary.text:
Smyrnium olusatrum, common name alexanders (or alisander), is an edible  flowering plant of the family Apiaceae (Umbelliferae) which grows on waste ground and in hedges around the Mediterranean and Atlantic coastal regions of Europe. In north Africa it is restricted to the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions, including the Canary Islands.

It is recorded as an introduction in New Zealand, Australia and Bermuda.

The conservation status of alexanders in Britain and France is Least Concern, and it is not considered to be threatened in any region, although it is rare in some countries, such as Belgium.
In Ireland it is common around the south and east coasts, but rare inland and to the west. More generally in Europe, it occurs throughout the Mediterranean, where it is recorded in all coastal areas, including the islands, and it extends as far as Crimea and the Black Sea. It is also found along the Atlantic coast of the continent from the Iberian Peninsula northwards through France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and (recently) into Norway; and westwards to the Azores.

habitat.text: Its natural habitat is fields, meadows, roadsides, banks and waste ground. When added to seed mixtures, it seldom persists once the sward has closed up.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Trifolium hybridum' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Growing up to 40 centimetres tall, T. hybridum is a perennial plant with a semi-erect, sparsely branched, grooved stem, hairy in its upper regions. The leaves are alternate and stalked with small stipules. The leaves have three blunt-tipped ovate, unspotted leaflets with finely toothed margins.
From April to October in the Northern Hemisphere, the densely globose inflorescence blooms from a long stalk attached to the leaf axils. The individual florets have a five-lobed calyx and an irregular corolla consisting of five pink petals, one upstanding "standard", two lateral "wings" and the lower two fused to form a "keel". There are ten stamens and a single carpal.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover's flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, whose stipules partly wrap the young head; alsike's heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks longer than the leaves. Red clover's stems are sparsely hairy low down and moderately to densely hairy higher up, and its leaf stalks are usually moderately hairy; the Flora of New Zealand describes alsike's stems and leaves as hairless, though one overseas source says its upper stem can be hairy. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base; alsike's are described as unmarked. Red clover's corolla is 10–16 mm long, alsike's 5–10 mm. Colour is not a safe test: red clover is pink to purple-pink and rarely cream, alsike usually pink. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are hairless or nearly so on stem and leaf, and both hold round heads on stalks that rise above the leaves, so the head settles little: white clover is usually white but occasionally pink to reddish, and alsike is usually pink, so colour overlaps. Follow the stem: white clover creeps and roots at the nodes, while alsike's stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes. White clover's leaflets often carry light or dark markings; alsike's are described as unmarked. With a hand lens, alsike's calyx teeth are usually much longer than the calyx tube, where white clover's are shorter than the tube. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats; alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, alsike clover's 10–35 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes; alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), alsike clover's 10–35 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Its stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes, and its leaflets are c. 10–35 mm long. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 16 mm, so it does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

summary.text:
Trifolium hybridum, the alsike clover, is a species of flowering plant in the pea family, Fabaceae.
Originating in mainland Europe, it has become established as an introduced plant in the British Isles and throughout the temperate regions of the world. It is native to southern Europe and southwestern Asia, especially in mountainous regions.
Because of its wide cultivation and use as forage, its subspecies T. h. hybridum is used and has become naturalised further north in Europe and in other parts of the world.

warnings: The plant can irritate skin if handled.

There is limited evidence of T. hybridum having toxic effects on horses including photosensitization and Alsike clover poisoning. A diet in equestrians of at least 20% T. hybridum over the course of four weeks could lead to poisoning which includes deleterious neurological effects and liver failure.

identification.text:
Amaranth is a herbaceous plant or shrub that is either annual or perennial across the genus. The plant has a primary root with deeper spreading secondary fibrous root structures. Amaranths contain concentric rings of vascular bundles and fix carbon efficiently with a C4 photosynthetic pathway. Amaranth can grow from 1 to 2.5 metres tall with a cylindrical, succulent, fibrous stem that is hollow with grooves and bracteoles when mature varies in flower, leaf, and stem color with a range of striking pigments from the spectrum of maroon to crimson. The leaves are approximately 6.5–15 centimetres and of oval or elliptical shape that are either opposite or alternate across species, although most are whole and simple with entire margins.

Catkin-like cymes of densely packed flowers grow in the summer or fall. The inflorescences are in the form a large panicle that varies from terminal to axial, color, and sex. The tassel of fluorescence is either erect or bent and varies in width and length between species. The flowers are radially symmetric and either bisexual or unisexual with very small, bristly perianth and pointy bracts. The flowers vary interspecifically from the presence of 3 or 5 tepals and stamens, whereas a 7-porate pollen grain structure remains consistent across the family.
Species in this genus are either monoecious (e.g. A. hybridus,) or dioecious (e.g. A. palmeri). The fruits are in the form of capsules referred to as a unilocular pixdio that opens at maturity. The top (operculum) of the capsule releases the urn that contains the seed. The seeds are circular, 1 to 1.5 millimeters in diameter and range in color with a shiny, smooth seed coat. The panicle is harvested 200 days after cultivation with approximately 1,000 to 3,000 seeds harvested per gram.

preparation.text:
This plant is eaten as a vegetable in different places of the world. The water should be discarded after boiling due to the presence of oxalic acid and possibly nitrates. The young shoots and leaves can be eaten raw. The leaves are high in calcium, iron, protein, and phosphorus.

It is among the species consumed as a vegetable in Mexican markets as Quelite quintonil. It is used in the Indian state of Kerala to prepare a popular dish known as thoran by combining the finely cut leaves (cheera) with grated coconut, chili peppers, garlic, turmeric and other ingredients.

identification.text:
Annual up to 1.5 m high, branched or not from base. Stems moderately hairy in younger parts with simple or few-rayed deflexed hairs, becoming ± glabrous and slightly woody toward base when older. Lvs sparsely hairy with mostly simple hairs above and mostly stellate hairs below; lower lvs ovate-triangular to suborbicular, cordate at base, not lobed, crenate, 2–7 cm long; upper lvs shallowly 3–5-palmately lobed or ± entire, crenate; petioles 2–7 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–6 mm long. Fls axillary, solitary; fruiting pedicels 2–10 cm long; epicalyx segments broadly triangular, united for almost entire length, 1/2–3/4 length of calyx, distinctly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; calyx campanulate; calyx teeth ± = tube, triangular to ovate-triangular, acute to acuminate, finely clothed in stellate hairs, ± connivent at fruiting; petals pink or mauve, 20–35 mm long. Mericarps c. 12 per fr., obscured by axis, glabrous, transverse-reticulately veined on back; edges rounded.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4. as Lavatera trimestris  L.]
The mericarps are covered by a disc-like expansion of the central axis which readily distinguishes this sp. from other N.Z. Lavatera. The sp. has been recorded in N.Z. as Althea officinalis.
Petals are usually pinkish but white-flowered variants are frequent in cultivation and have been recorded as an escape.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera, which include Cretan mallow; annual mallow's flowers are single, Cretan mallow's mostly in clusters. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera, which include island mallow. Petal lengths overlap (20–35 mm against 30–40 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Both have an epicalyx that grows larger and spreads in fruit, so that alone does not separate them. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera (tree, island and Cretan mallow); annual mallow's flowers are single, tree mallow's in clusters. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

preparation.text:
The flavour profile of D. muralis leaves evolves significantly with their stage of development. Younger leaves are tender and have a mild, slightly peppery taste, making them ideal for raw preparations like salads or as delicate garnishes. In contrast, mature leaves present a more intense, spicy, and pungent flavour, which enhances their appeal in robust dishes like soups, sauces, or as a garnish for hot meals.
They can also be processed, such as dried or frozen, to extend their shelf life and broaden their applications in different culinary contexts.

The scope of the warning, so it is not read as more than it says. The quoted sentences are about Brassicaceae as a family, not about this species in particular, and the paper makes no claim about roadside plants: its own D. muralis was grown in soil and irrigation water analysed before planting, and those leaves came in below the EU maximum levels for lead, cadmium and mercury (Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915). The warning is on this page because the habitat field above it records the plant growing on waste ground, beside railways and roads and on tips; the inference from one to the other is the reader's to draw and a person's to write, so it is not written here.

months comes from the iNaturalist month-of-year histogram for Diplotaxis muralis in New Zealand (place_id 6803, verifiable records, n=110), read 08/10/2026, taking every month at or above a quarter of the peak month (April, 20 records; threshold 5). That admits ten months and excludes March (4 records) and July (3). Recorded because those two gaps are an artefact of a thin per-month sample rather than a seasonal break — a single observation either way moves them — and because the 34 flowering-annotated records are too few to set a season from. Read it as recorded essentially year round.

summary.text:
Diplotaxis muralis, the annual wall-rocket, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
It is native to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of western Asia.
It is found in North Africa, within Algeria, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia, in addition to Ethiopia in East Africa. Within Asia it is found in the Caucasus, Georgia (country) and Turkey. In middle Europe, it is in Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Switzerland. In southeastern Europe, within Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Malta, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia and Ukraine. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in France, Portugal and Spain.
It has naturalised in the UK since 1778, when it was found in a field of oats raised from imported seeds from a ship wrecked on the Kent coast.

warnings: Brassicaceae plants are known for their tendency to accumulate heavy metals, a trait that makes them valuable for the phytoremediation of contaminated soils. However, this same ability necessitates careful monitoring, as the accumulation of heavy metals can also pose potential health risks.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous, densely hairy perennial with erect, branched stems to  c. 70 cm tall.  Lvs sessile or nearly so, smaller below infl., 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm, broad, usually elliptic, sometimes ovate or oblong-ovate, rugose, crenulate or crenulate-serrate, often grey-tomentose at least below, with oil globules below; base cordate or subcordate and often ± amplexicaul.  Infl. of several narrow elongated terminal spikes, densely hairy, freely branching at base;  central spike to  c. 8 cm long, the others shorter;  fls pedicellate.  Calyx 1.5–2.5 mm long, broad-campanulate, ± green, glandular, hairy;  teeth equal, acuminate, = tube at anthesis.  Corolla 3–3.5 mm long, pale pink or whitish;  lobes ± hairy;  tube exserted.  Stamens exserted or included.  Nutlets  c. 0.8 mm long, ovoid, bluntly angled, reticulate.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character in the Flora of New Zealand separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's leaves are broad, usually elliptic and wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm; spearmint's are lanceolate to ovate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, so leaf sizes overlap. Apple mint is densely hairy and often grey-woolly beneath; spearmint ranges from nearly hairless to densely hairy and grey-woolly beneath, so hairiness alone does not decide it. Both have stalkless or nearly stalkless leaves; apple mint's leaf base is heart-shaped or nearly so and often clasps the stem, spearmint's ranges from tapered to heart-shaped. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish; spearmint's calyx is more or less purple, its corolla mauve or pinkish, and its stems are often tinged red. Apple mint is described as having a fruity, minty flavour, and spearmint a minty, green, cooling, spicy smell, but smell is a clue, not a test. Both are edible.

preparation.text: It is also often used to make a mint tea, as a garnish, or in salads.

recipes.method: A kilo of green cooking apples, quartered but not peeled or cored, simmered with a small bunch of apple mint under water until tender, about 40 minutes. Strain overnight through a jelly bag, stir a cup of cider vinegar into the juice and measure it, then add 500 g sugar for every 500 ml. Dissolve the sugar gently, boil hard to setting point, about 10 minutes, and stir a quarter cup of finely chopped leaves through off the heat before potting into warm sterilised jars.

recipes.method: Five apple mint leaves, a tablespoon of muscovado sugar, two shots of rum, 100 ml soda water, a lime and ice. Squeeze two lime wedges over the sugar in the glass, add the leaves and muddle them into it, pour the rum over, fill with ice, top with soda and stir.

habitat.text: By far the commonest and most widespread wild bamboo in New Zealand: the Volcanic Plateau and most lowland country southwards, thinning out only in the south of the South Island, which roughly tracks where it was planted. Look on roadsides and riverbanks, in and around plantations, in scrub and along forest margins, and especially where a garden boundary meets rough ground — on abandoned sections and in waste places. Spread here is by rhizome and not by seed, so a stand is one clone creeping outwards from something somebody planted.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Medium-sized and forming dense thickets; rhizomes running extensively from periphery. Culm 3–5 m, dark green; banded white just below nodes. Culm-sheath green or greenish purple, eventually very pale, internodes almost all hidden in lower and middle parts of culm; ligule 2–3 mm, broad and prominent, truncate. Branches 1 per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes. Leaf-sheath glabrous, often purplish above. Ligule minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade (1)–3–5–(7) on each branch, to 25–(30) × 3.5–(4) cm, broadly linear or linear-oblong, abaxially upper ⅓ green and lower ⅔ glaucescent, adaxially shining dark green, acuminate. Inflorescence ± purple, at least on exposed side. Spikelets 4–9 cm, flattened; florets to c. 12, distichous. Glumes 2. Lemma 10–13 mm, including short awn, ciliate, obscurely tessellate. Fig. 1.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the lower part of several canes in the stand. On some of fishpole bamboo's canes the lower nodes are crowded together and sometimes zigzag, with swollen, often lopsided internodes; not every cane shows it, so check more than one. Fishpole's canes are green in their first year and yellow afterwards; arrow bamboo's are dark green. Arrow bamboo's cane is round, not notched, with the internodes in its lower and middle parts mostly hidden by sheaths; fishpole bamboo's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches. Arrow bamboo has one branch per node, sometimes two or three at the upper nodes; fishpole usually has two markedly unequal branches with a small or missing third. Arrow bamboo's leaf blades reach 25–30 cm long and 3.5–4 cm wide and are glossy dark green above; fishpole's are usually 5–13 cm long and under 3 cm wide. Height does not separate them (fishpole usually 3–6 m, arrow bamboo 3–5 m), and both have a white band just below the nodes (on fishpole, on young canes). Both have edible young shoots, cooked.
lookalikes.name: Fishpole bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Black bamboo's canes are 4–7 m. In var. nigra they turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year, but the green-caned var. henonis is naturalised here too, so a green stand does not rule it out. Arrow bamboo's canes are 3–5 m and dark green. Both have a white band or waxy ring just below the nodes (on black bamboo, on young canes), so that does not separate them. Black bamboo's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches; arrow bamboo's are round, not notched. Black bamboo usually has 3 branches per node with the middle one small or missing; arrow bamboo has 1 per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes and none at lower ones. Black bamboo's leaf-blades are usually 5–9 cm long (up to 13 cm); arrow bamboo's reach 25 cm (up to 30 cm). Black bamboo's cane sheaths are purple or purple-flushed and fall away; arrow bamboo's are green or greenish purple, fade very pale, and stay on, hiding most of the lower and middle internodes. Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, which must be destroyed by thorough cooking.
lookalikes.name: Black bamboo

preparation.text: The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: The husk is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs, so handle it with that in mind. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. These are the bitter end of the five: cover the core with water, boil it hard, change the water, and keep going in five-minute rounds in fresh water until the flavour comes back mild. Taste between rounds rather than trusting a clock. Cut the shoots when they stand about 8–10 cm above the ground, taking them 5 cm or more below the soil.

Fact restated, not quoted. The page covers six bamboos and names this one, Arrow Bamboo, among them, and its control advice is to remove young shoots in spring while they are soft because running types only shoot in spring. Spring in New Zealand is September to November, which is the whole of this field. This is a weed-control page, so what it dates is when the shoots are soft enough to pull, which is the same moment they are worth eating, but the page has no interest in eating them.

Months, two routes that were NOT used, recorded so they are not retried. Ken Fern's entry (above) has the shoots cut in late spring, but that is the northern hemisphere, and converting it would land on November here by arithmetic rather than by observation. Forest Floor, 'Bamboo for cane production', http://forestfloor.co.nz/ff/bambooshoot.htm, no licence stated, so all rights reserved, retrieved 08/10/2026, has running bamboos in New Zealand shooting spring to early summer, but that page is about growing bamboo for cane and names Phyllostachys aurea and P. nigra, two of this page's lookalikes, not this species. The usual method does not work here either: an iNaturalist NZ month histogram dates the records, and the records are of canes and leaves, which stand all year, so they cannot date the shoots.

NOT YET ON THE PAGE, and it is the owner's to write: the same Auckland Council page states that these six bamboos, this one included, may not be bred, distributed, released, sold or planted in Auckland, with an exception for relocating an existing plant within the same property, and lists the species as Sustained Control across the whole region under the Regional Pest Management Plan. That bears on a forager — taking shoots is fine and is arguably control, but carrying live rhizome home is not — and it is not yet written anywhere on this entry. The council page is all rights reserved, so it cannot be quoted, and a restatement of a legal rule is safety text. Check it against the Regional Pest Management Plan itself rather than the council's summary of it.

summary.text: Pseudosasa japonica, the arrow bamboo (Japanese: metake),  is a species of bamboo in the grass family Poaceae native to Japan and Korea, but planted worldwide as a horticultural plant. The common name "arrow bamboo" results from the Japanese samurai using its hard and stiff canes for their arrows. Introduced to New Zealand as an ornamental and naturalised since 1968, it is the most widespread wild bamboo in the country and is named on DOC's list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

identification.text:
Perennial herb; taproot cylindric, to c. 2 cm diam., often divided; caulorrhiza short and stout, bearing a number of flowering stems. Hairs variable, the longer ones mostly curved or bent near base. Petiole of basal lvs to c. 30 cm long; hairs denser distally and mostly appressed to ascending. Lamina to c. 9 cm diam., reniform to orbicular, lobed to 3/4-⅞ way to midrib; lobes usually 5–7, obovate, sparsely hairy on both sides, obtuse, mucronate, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; median and longer lateral teeth oblong-obovate. Cauline lvs similar to basal but smaller, with few lobes. Flowering stem glabrescent; hairs mostly appressed to ascending; bracteoles ± linear; fls in pairs. Outer sepals 3–3.5 × c. 2.5 mm, ovate-elliptic; inner sepals narrower, with hyaline margins; hairs short and appressed. Petals c. 4.5 × 3 mm, obovate, pale pink. Mericarps hairy; beak to 12 mm long. Seed c. 2 × 1.2 mm, oblong, reddish brown; dorsal alveolae mostly rectangular, rather shallow.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates Australasian cranesbill from Solander's geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in Solander's geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates Australasian cranesbill from turnip-rooted geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in turnip-rooted geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (NZTCS 2023).
lookalikes.name: Turnip-rooted geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from Australasian cranesbill on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Australasian cranesbill, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Australasian cranesbill. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Australasian cranesbill overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them at its first step: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Australasian cranesbill's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Australasian cranesbill under Geranium dissectum (Flora of New Zealand Online cites Allan's 1961 Flora under it as Geranium australe and Geranium dissectum var. glabratum Hook.f.), so older records may use that name. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved cranesbill

identification.text:
Passiflora tarminiana is a high climbing vine with hairy stems and petioles. Where the petioles join the stem it has stipules which are 4–7 by 2–3 mm and are soon deciduous. The leaves are three-lobed and hairy below but usually hairless above. The flowers are solitary and hang downwards. The base of the flower has pale green bracts enclosing a swollen nectary chamber. The floral tube (hypanthium) is 6–8 × 0.7–1 cm and pale green, while the sepals and petals are 3–6 cm long, pink and perpendicular to the floral tube, or reflexed. Fruits taper at both ends, are 10–14 cm long by 3.5–4.5 cm wide and ripen to yellow or light orange. The fruit contain many seeds which are embedded in an edible, orange aril.
Passiflora tarminiana is distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima by a number of features. P. tarminiana has small deciduous stipules while P. tripartita var. mollissima has larger, persistent stipules. The sepals and petals in P. tarminiana are perpendicular to the floral tube or are reflexed, whereas they are never so open in P. tripartita var. mollissima. They are also both much shorter in relation to the length of the floral tube in P. tripartita var. mollissima than in P. tarminiana.

lookalikes.howToTell: The flowers separate them: black passionfruit's petals are white and its corona threads white with a purple base, and it has no conspicuous floral tube; banana passionfruit's flowers are pink, hang down, and sit on a pale green floral tube whose reported length varies by source (up to 6 cm, 6-8 cm, or 6-9.5 cm). Black passionfruit's fruit is dull purple, broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, 5-6.25 cm long and 4.75-5.75 cm across, with black seeds; banana passionfruit's is slender and tapers at both ends, ripening yellow to light orange, with dark red seeds, and reported lengths run from up to 9 cm to 14 cm depending on the source. Black passionfruit has narrow stipules 10-15 mm long; banana passionfruit's are small and soon fall, so mature stems lack them. Both fruits are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are vigorous climbing vines with three-lobed leaves and pink flowers, and both have sweet, edible orange pulp, so leaf outline and flower colour do not separate them. Go to the stipules where the leaf stalk meets the stem: pink-flowered passionfruit's are pinnate — a very narrow central strip fringed almost to its base with dark thread-like segments. Banana passionfruit's are small, about 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and fall early, so a mature stem usually has none. The ripe fruit also helps: pink-flowered passionfruit's is round or slightly flattened, 4–7 cm across, yellow and finely downy; banana passionfruit's is slender and tapers at both ends. Floral-tube length is not a safe test: pink-flowered passionfruit's is about 4–5 cm, and banana passionfruit's is given as anything from up to 6 cm to 9.5 cm depending on the source. Pink-flowered passionfruit's corona threads are violet-blue, but the sources checked do not describe banana passionfruit's corona, so do not use colour there as a comparison. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Pink-flowered passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) has small stipules that soon fall, while P. tripartita's are larger and stay on (Wikipedia; NZPCN). In flower, P. tarminiana's sepals and petals spread flat or bend back, while P. tripartita's never open that far and are much shorter compared with the floral tube (Wikipedia), and P. tripartita's tube is the longer one: 8–10 cm against 6–7 cm in Flora of New Zealand's weed profiles, though Wikipedia's 6–8 cm for P. tarminiana reaches the bottom of that range, so a tube near 8 cm does not decide it. The same profiles describe P. tripartita var. mollissima's leaves as moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface, where P. tarminiana's are usually hairless above. They hybridise (Wikipedia: P. tarminiana 'hybridises with other members of the subgenus Tacsonia'), and iNaturalist New Zealand holds wild records of the hybrid, so an in-between plant may be neither. P. tripartita's other New Zealand variety, var. azuayensis, has leaves hairless or nearly so above (NZPCN, after Heenan & Sykes 2003), so upper-leaf hairs alone do not separate it from P. tarminiana. Both have 3-lobed leaves, pink hanging flowers and edible yellow-orange fruit, so leaf outline, flower colour and fruit colour do not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

recipes.method: 20–30 banana passionfruit, the juice of 2 lemons (6–8 tbsp), and up to 1.1 kg sugar. Halve the fruit and scrape the pulp and seeds into a pot, then drop the empty skins in with them — in the hope they release pectin into the juice; the author notes you might not want to do that if the fruit is not organic. Add just enough water to cover, around 1–1.5 litres, bring to the boil and simmer 30–45 minutes, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the pulp to get all the juice out, and throw away the skins and spent seeds. Return the juice to the pot with the lemon juice and sugar, and boil until it reaches setting point — allow another half hour, longer if it started watery. Pour into clean jars and water-bath 15 minutes to seal. Makes about six half-pint jars. The sugar can come down from 1.1 kg if that is too sweet, but some is needed for the pectin to set.
recipes.title: Banana passionfruit jelly

recipes.method: 12 ripe fruit, 240 ml water, about 300 g sugar, 2 litres milk, 60 ml cream, ice. Halve the fruit and scoop the pulp into a blender with the water, and blend to a cream. Add the milk, the sugar and a little crushed ice and blend at medium speed, then add the cream and blend one minute more. Strain out the seeds if you like, and serve cold.
recipes.title: Curuba milk drink (jugo de curuba en leche)

recipes.method: 8 fruit, 480 ml milk, 4 tablespoons sugar, a 200 g pot of cream, a bar of chocolate. Blend the pulp with 240 ml water and strain out the seeds. Blend the juice again with the sugar, the milk and 6 tablespoons of the cream, with a little ice if you like. Melt the chocolate, coat the inside of each glass and chill to set it. Whip the rest of the cream until firm, pour the sorbete into the glasses and top with the cream.
recipes.title: Curuba sorbete with chocolate

recipes.method: 10 fruit, 600 ml water, about 400 g sugar, 2 cloves, the juice of 1 lemon. Scoop out the pulp, blend it for only about 3 seconds with 120 ml of the water, and strain to keep the liquid. In a large pot put the remaining 480 ml water, the sugar, the cloves and the lemon juice, add the strained liquid and cook over medium-low heat for about 40 minutes, until it thickens. Take out the cloves before it comes off the heat, and let it cool. Good on bread.

summary.text:
Passiflora tarminiana is native to the uplands of tropical South America but the exact native range is uncertain as it has been widely cultivated in this region. It is found in the Colombian highlands and the Venezuelan, Peruvian and southern Ecuadorean Andes where it is cultivated from around 2000 – 3000 metres.
It has naturalised in Australia, Guam, Hawaii, New Zealand and Zimbabwe. In both Hawaii and New Zealand it is regarded as an invasive species. It is widely cultivated throughout the world, including California, Réunion, Mexico, Panama and Papua New Guinea.
Passiflora tripartita var. mollissima and P. tarminiana were until recently considered to be one species, P. mollissima.

warnings: An unwanted organism under the National Pest Plant Accord. It cannot be sold, propagated, distributed or released, and regional rules require control in places — sustained control across the Bay of Plenty, site-led management on Otago Peninsula and around Dunedin's West Harbour.

edibleParts.text:
The pulp surrounding the seeds is eaten. The fruit is yellow-orange when ripe and contains a sweet edible orange-colored pulp with black seeds.
The fruits of this species are a pale yellow colour, the pulp is more aromatic and tart and has a somewhat superior flavour to the flesh of the deep yellow to orange fruits of Passiflora tarminiana.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine; shoots densely hairy, weakly angular when young. Lvs 3-lobed; petioles 1.5–5 cm long, densely hairy, with (4)–6–12 stalked or subsessile glands; stipules 5–10 mm wide (excluding subulate apex when present), subreniform, with glandular teeth; lamina lobes usually 5–14 cm long, extending 1/2-⅔ of the distance in from the margin, usually ± tomentose below, hairy or glabrate above, elliptic or elliptic-ovate, narrow-lanceolate on juvenile shoots, serrate or serrulate, acute; middle lobe largest, 4–9 × 2–5 cm. Fls ☿, solitary. Pedicels > petioles, densely hairy. Bracts 1.5–3.75 cm long, ovate or broad-ovate, ± tomentose outside, entire or slightly toothed, united for lower 1/4–1/2 until anthesis. Hypanthium 8–9.5 cm long, glabrous outside. Sepals 2–3.8 cm long, elliptic, green on reverse, pink or rose inside, rounded and with short horn near apex; petals similar but pink on both sides; corona a ring of purple, white-tipped scales 1–2 mm long. Filaments 1.5–2 cm long, pale, often scarcely > anthers; anthers (7)–10–12 mm long. Ovary white-villous. Fr. (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, ± ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow, puberulent; pulp sweet and orange, edible. Seed 4.5–5.5 mm long, broad-obovoid, dark red to black, alveolate.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Passiflora mollissima (Kunth) L.H.Bailey.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana) has small stipules that soon fall, while P. tripartita's are larger and stay on (Wikipedia; NZPCN). In flower, P. tarminiana's sepals and petals spread flat or bend back, while P. tripartita's never open that far and are much shorter compared with the floral tube (Wikipedia), and P. tripartita's tube is the longer one: 8–10 cm against 6–7 cm in Flora of New Zealand's weed profiles, though Wikipedia's 6–8 cm for P. tarminiana reaches the bottom of that range, so a tube near 8 cm does not decide it. The same profiles describe P. tripartita var. mollissima's leaves as moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface, where P. tarminiana's are usually hairless above. They hybridise (Wikipedia: P. tarminiana 'hybridises with other members of the subgenus Tacsonia'), and iNaturalist New Zealand holds wild records of the hybrid, so an in-between plant may be neither. P. tripartita's other New Zealand variety, var. azuayensis, has leaves hairless or nearly so above (NZPCN, after Heenan & Sykes 2003), so upper-leaf hairs alone do not separate it from P. tarminiana. Both have 3-lobed leaves, pink hanging flowers and edible yellow-orange fruit, so leaf outline, flower colour and fruit colour do not separate them. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Flora of New Zealand's key: pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal (Flora of New Zealand's key; NZPCN). Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Pink-flowered passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tripartita) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's (NZPCN); Flora of New Zealand gives it 5-lobed leaves and calls its pulp 'scanty and inedible'. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and banana passionfruit (P. tripartita)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.

preparation.text: Fruit - eaten raw or used in ice creams, fruit salads, pies, jellies, to make drinks etc.

recipes.method: 20–30 banana passionfruit, the juice of 2 lemons (6–8 tbsp), and up to 1.1 kg sugar. Halve the fruit and scrape the pulp and seeds into a pot, then drop the empty skins in with them — in the hope they release pectin into the juice; the author notes you might not want to do that if the fruit is not organic. Add just enough water to cover, around 1–1.5 litres, bring to the boil and simmer 30–45 minutes, stirring now and then. Strain, pressing the pulp to get all the juice out, and throw away the skins and spent seeds. Return the juice to the pot with the lemon juice and sugar, and boil until it reaches setting point — allow another half hour, longer if it started watery. Pour into clean jars and water-bath 15 minutes to seal. Makes about six half-pint jars. The sugar can come down from 1.1 kg if that is too sweet, but some is needed for the pectin to set.
recipes.title: Banana passionfruit jelly

recipes.method: 12 ripe fruit, 240 ml water, about 300 g sugar, 2 litres milk, 60 ml cream, ice. Halve the fruit and scoop the pulp into a blender with the water, and blend to a cream. Add the milk, the sugar and a little crushed ice and blend at medium speed, then add the cream and blend one minute more. Strain out the seeds if you like, and serve cold.
recipes.title: Curuba milk drink (jugo de curuba en leche)

recipes.method: 8 fruit, 480 ml milk, 4 tablespoons sugar, a 200 g pot of cream, a bar of chocolate. Blend the pulp with 240 ml water and strain out the seeds. Blend the juice again with the sugar, the milk and 6 tablespoons of the cream, with a little ice if you like. Melt the chocolate, coat the inside of each glass and chill to set it. Whip the rest of the cream until firm, pour the sorbete into the glasses and top with the cream.
recipes.title: Curuba sorbete with chocolate

recipes.method: 10 fruit, 600 ml water, about 400 g sugar, 2 cloves, the juice of 1 lemon. Scoop out the pulp, blend it for only about 3 seconds with 120 ml of the water, and strain to keep the liquid. In a large pot put the remaining 480 ml water, the sugar, the cloves and the lemon juice, add the strained liquid and cook over medium-low heat for about 40 minutes, until it thickens. Take out the cloves before it comes off the heat, and let it cool. Good on bread.
recipes.title: Tumbo jam (mermelada de tumbo)

summary.text:
Passiflora tripartita, also called curuba, tumbo, curuba de Castilla, tumbo serrano and poro poro, is a species of Passiflora from Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, and Brazil in areas at elevations of 2000 – 3200 meters. P. tripartita var. mollissima and P. tarminiana were until recently considered to be one species, P. mollissima.
Banana passionfruit is the commonest naturalised sp. of the genus in N.Z. N.; S.: Auckland to Otago Harbour, particularly just N. of Wellington, coastal Marlborough, including the Sounds, and coastal parts of Nelson.
Two varieties grow wild in New Zealand, var. mollissima and var. azuayensis; var. azuayensis has leaves hairless or nearly so on the upper surface.

identification.text:
Glabrous, evergreen or semi-deciduous shrub to c. 7 m high. Shoots terete, grey or yellowish grey; reproductive shoots often pendent. Spines to 2.3 cm long, sometimes single, sometimes 3-partite. Lvs with short petiole to 5 mm long. Lamina mostly 2.5–7.5 × 1–2.5 cm, oblanceolate, elliptic to obovate and often very variable on one plant, entire or spiny serrate (often remotely so), ± shining above and often turning reddish in autumn, reticulate, subcoriaceous, sometimes almost membranous in shadier and moister habitats; base attenuate; apex spiny. Fls foetid, arranged in simple or compound racemes to 6 cm long; bracts 2–3 mm long, lanceolate-acuminate; bracteoles sometimes c. 1/2 way along pedicel, otherwise near base, < bracts. Pedicels 0.6–1.5 mm long. Perianth segments yellow, sometimes the outer red-tinged, 4–7 mm long; outer sepals shorter; inner sepals broadly obovate and petals slightly emarginate, with 2 prominent basal oblong nectaries. Stamens 3–4 mm long. Ovules 4. Berry 7–12 mm long, broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, reddish black, strongly whitish pruinose; juice dark red; fruiting style c. 1 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Barberry's leaves are mostly 2.5–7.5 cm long, entire or spiny-toothed (often only sparsely), and very variable on one plant; Darwin's barberry's are small, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, obovate with two spiny lobes at the tip (shoots that are not flowering sometimes carry extra teeth below). Barberry's flowers are yellow (the outer parts sometimes red-tinged) and smell unpleasant; Darwin's barberry's are orange-yellow. Barberry is hairless, with single or three-parted spines up to 2.3 cm long; Darwin's barberry's shoots are densely brown-hairy and its spines split into five. Barberry's berries are 7–12 mm long and broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, with a style about 1 mm long; Darwin's barberry's are 5–7 mm across and round, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long. An evergreen spiny shrub with dark, white-bloomed berries does not separate them. The garden hybrid B. × stenophylla (Darwin's barberry × B. empetrifolia) has three-parted spines and narrow linear-lanceolate leaves but fruit like Darwin's barberry's, so the spine and leaf tests do not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Barberry's berries are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice; European barberry's are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining and without bloom, oblong, 9–11 mm long. Barberry is evergreen or partly deciduous, its leaves shining above, somewhat leathery (almost thin in shady, moist places) and often turning reddish in autumn; European barberry is plainly deciduous, its leaves thin, dull green above and usually finely toothed. Barberry grows to about 7 m with spines up to 2.3 cm long; European barberry to about 2 m, its spines under 1.5 cm. Leaf size (2.5–7.5 against 2–8 cm long, both 1–2.5 cm wide), yellow flowers in clusters up to about 6 cm, and a place around old homesteads and plantations do not separate them. In New Zealand barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris, even in Allan's 1940 flora (Flora of New Zealand), so a name in print is no guide.

preparation.text: The same forager ate the berries raw, soaked berries that had shrivelled before using them, and scattered them over a cooked vegetable stir-fry at the table.

recipes.method: Written for barberry (Berberis glaucocarpa) by the New Zealand forager who picked it. Soak ½ cup (125 ml) barberries if they have shrivelled, and soak ¾ cup (185 ml) dates. In a food processor, grind ¾ cup (185 ml) almonds and ¼ cup (60 ml) sunflower seeds to crumbs. Add the barberries, dates, ¼ cup (60 ml) dried peaches, a pinch of salt, a pinch of cinnamon, 1 tablespoon carob powder and ¼ cup (60 ml) desiccated coconut, and process until the mixture holds together. Roll into balls and coat them in more coconut. The source leaves out the unit for the almonds, barberries and coconut; cups are assumed here, matching its other lines. Millilitres use the 250 ml metric cup.

summary.text:
Berberis glaucocarpa, sometimes called common barberry or simply barberry, is a species of flowering plant, a barberry, native to the western Himalaya in central Asia, to west central Nepal. It is considered invasive in New Zealand, where it is found in the North and South Island. It has also been introduced to Great Britain. The species is listed as banned in South Africa.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: throughout in modified lowland areas; S.: as far S. as Canterbury and Westland.
Barberry is very commonly cultivated as a hedge in the lowland parts of N.Z. except for colder parts of the South Id. The plants fr. abundantly and the large branches of glaucous-white frs are a characteristic sight on many farms in autumn. In N.Z. barberry or Himalayan barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris although this name should be applied to a very different sp. in another section of the genus. Thus, the short description and diagram in Allan (1940) really refer to B. glaucocarpa. B. glaucocarpa has also occasionally been called B. aristata in N.Z.; this is a related Himalayan sp.
The fruits are spread by birds and mammals, including brush-tailed possums and rodents. The birds which most often spread this plant in New Zealand are themselves exotic frugivores, namely Silvereyes (which self-introduced from Australia), Song Thrush, Common Blackbird, and Common Starling. New Zealand Bellbirds ignore barberry fruits.

preparation.text: The leaves are most often used whole (sometimes in a bouquet garni) and removed before serving (they can be abrasive in the digestive tract). Bay leaves can also be crushed or ground before cooking. Crushed bay leaves impart more fragrance than whole leaves, but are more difficult to remove and thus they are often used in a muslin bag or tea infuser. Ground bay laurel may be substituted for whole leaves and does not need to be removed, but it is much stronger.

recipes.method: Grind 3 small dried bay leaves with 1–2 tbsp of 200 g sugar to a powder, sifting out any stubborn bits. Beat with 454 g soft butter, the rest of the sugar, 1 tsp lemon zest and ⅛ tsp salt, then work in 480 g flour a little at a time to a soft dough. Shape 25 g rounds and bake at 175 °C for 18–20 minutes, until lightly browned at the edges. For the icing, grind 5 small bay leaves with 67 g sugar, then beat with 120 g icing sugar, 1 tbsp meringue powder and 3 tbsp lemon juice at medium speed for 4–5 minutes, until thick but still pourable. Dip the cooled biscuits and leave on racks 12–24 hours to set.

summary.text:
Laurus nobilis  is an aromatic evergreen tree or large shrub with green, glabrous (smooth) leaves.
Laurus nobilis is a widespread relict  of the laurel forests that originally covered much of the Mediterranean Basin when the climate of the region was more humid. With the drying of the Mediterranean during the Pliocene era, the laurel forests gradually retreated, and were replaced by the more drought-tolerant sclerophyll plant communities familiar today. Most of the last remaining laurel forests around the Mediterranean are believed to have disappeared approximately ten thousand years ago, although some remnants still persist in the mountains of southern Turkey, northern Syria, southern Spain, north-central Portugal, northern Morocco, the Canary Islands and in Madeira.

warnings: Some members of the laurel family, as well as the unrelated but visually similar mountain laurel and cherry laurel, have leaves that are poisonous to humans and livestock.

While some visually similar plants have poisonous leaves, bay leaves are not toxic. However, they remain stiff even after cooking and may pose a choking hazard or cause harm to the digestive tract if swallowed whole or in large pieces.

identification.text:
Trailing or lianoid herb or subshrub with terete branching softly woody stems up to ± 3 m. long. Lvs on flattened petioles up to 1 cm. long; lamina fleshy, papillose, (1)–2–3–(5) × 1–3 cm., obtuse, deltoid to broad- ovate to ovate-rhomboid, rather abruptly narrowed to petiole. Fr. 5–7 mm. diam., subglobose, succulent, bright to dark red, not horned; seeds 1–3.
