lookalikes.howToTell: Check the fruit first. Beach spinach's fruit is a round, succulent berry 5–8 mm long, pink to dark red, without horns, holding 1–3 seeds. New Zealand spinach's fruit is typically top-shaped and angled, 8–10(–15) mm long, with 2–4 hardened horns and 4–10 seeds. Without fruit, look at the flowers: beach spinach's sit on slender stalks, about 5 mm long in Allan (1961) and 5–30 mm in NZPCN, while New Zealand spinach's are stalkless or nearly so. Thick, fleshy leaves covered in tiny bumps (papillae), diamond to triangular leaf shapes and yellow flowers are common to both, so none of those separates them.

Hook.f. with biostatus Exotic, its Allan (1961) description being 'as Tetragonia trigyna Banks & Sol. ex Hook.f.' iNaturalist keeps the two apart as species — 2,928 observations of T. trigyna, and no research-grade New Zealand observation of T. implexicoma, checked the same day. Heenan, P.B. 2022, New Zealand Journal of Botany 60(2), https://doi.org/10.1080/0028825X.2021.1955715, is the paper Flora of New Zealand Online cites on the name. https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Tetragonia-trigyna.html

The all-rights-reserved sources also describe T. tetragonioides, and disagree on the blanch: Warndu 10–15 seconds (https://warndu.com/blogs/first-nations-food-guide/get-your-warrigal-greens), ABC Organic Gardener about one minute, ANPSA three to four minutes with the water discarded, calling the oxalic acid high, and ASNSW about three minutes (https://anpsa.org.au/plant_profiles/tetragonia-tetragonioides/). identification.text:
Annual or biennial.  Stems erect or ascending, branching, ribbed to grooved, 15–75–(100) cm tall;  hairs both white, slender, crinkly, subappressed, and red-based, stout, straight, spreading.  Rosette and lower stem lvs thick, petiolate, oblong to oblanceolate, usually deeply runcinately 1–2-pinnatifid, rarely simple and shallowly pinnatifid or toothed, (7)–10–20–(35) × (2)–4–8–(12) cm;  hairs pale, 0.2–0.5 mm long, on both surfaces and margins; lobes slightly recurved, toothed or divided.  Stem lvs similar, deeply pinnatisect to not lobed, toothed, sessile, subauriculate or lobed at base. Capitula campanulate;  buds erect.  Involucral bracts with pale subappressed cobwebby hairs and often dark, spreading glandular hairs on outer surface, and fine appressed straight hairs on inner surface;  outer bracts 6–12, lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate, ?-1/2 length of inner bracts;  inner bracts lanceolate, not keeled, (6)–9–12 mm long, with pale to scarious glabrous margins. Receptacle areoles with raised ciliate margins.  Corolla yellow, sometimes with red stripe on outer face of ligule.  Achenes brown, 10-ribbed, fusiform, scabrid, all long-beaked, 6–9 mm long.  Pappus bristles in 1–(2) rows, fine, white. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: A dandelion's leaves are all in the basal rosette, and its flower stems are hollow and leafless, each carrying a single flower head. Beaked hawksbeard sends up an erect or ascending, ribbed stem, 15–75 cm and sometimes to 100 cm tall, that branches and carries leaves of its own. Before the stems appear, the leaves are similar: both usually have leaves cut into lobes that point back towards the centre, beaked hawksbeard's usually deeply. Beaked hawksbeard's leaves carry short pale hairs on both surfaces and the margins, where a dandelion's are hairless or have only sparse short hairs, mostly on the midrib above — a clue, not a test. Milky sap does not separate them: both belong to the dandelion tribe, the Cichorieae, all of which have milky latex. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Dandelion

lookalikes.howToTell: Leaf shape does not separate them: catsear's leaves are usually shallowly to deeply lobed, rarely simple and toothed, and beaked hawksbeard's are usually deeply lobed with lobes pointing back, rarely simple and shallowly lobed or toothed. Look at the flowering stem. Catsear's leaves are all in the basal rosette, its stems carry only a few tiny bracts, and they are hairless or have a few sparse hairs low down; beaked hawksbeard's stems carry leaves and are hairy, with fine crinkly white hairs and stout, spreading, red-based ones. Under the flower head, catsear's bracts are hairless except for a row of stiff hairs along the midrib; beaked hawksbeard's have pale cobwebby hairs and often dark glandular hairs. Catsear's seed parachute has an inner row of feathery hairs; beaked hawksbeard's is of fine white bristles. Hairy leaves, branched stems and height (catsear 4–60 cm, sometimes to 150 cm; beaked hawksbeard 15–75 cm, sometimes to 100 cm) do not separate them. Catsear has milky sap; sap is not a test.

preparation.text: In Crete, Greece, the leaves of Crepis commutata which are called glykosyrida (γλυκοσυρίδα) are eaten raw, boiled, steamed or browned in salads. Another two species on the same island, Crepis vesicaria, called kokkinogoula (κοκκινογούλα), lekanida (λεκανίδα) or prikousa (πρικούσα) and a local variety called maryies (μαργιές) or pikrouses (πικρούσες) have both its leaves and tender shoots eaten boiled by the locals.

recipes.method: For 4: soak about 450 g of freshly picked young greens in cold water for 10 minutes. Bring about 3.8 L of water and 3 tbsp kosher salt to the boil in a large lidded pot, add the greens, cover and bring back to the boil. Uncover and cook for 60 seconds, stirring until all are wilted, then taste one — some greens take longer — and drain in a colander once tender. Let them drain for a minute, turning them over, then tip into a warmed serving bowl, drizzle with olive oil and serve with lemon wedges and about ½ tsp finishing salt to taste.
recipes.title: Horta (boiled wild greens with olive oil and lemon)

summary.text:
Crepis vesicaria is a European species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae with the common name beaked hawk's-beard.

Crepis vesicaria subsp. taraxacifolia, the beaked hawksbeard, is a subspecies of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to Europe and northwest Africa. It has become naturalized in scattered locations in the United Kingdom, North America, and Oceania.

identification.text:
Perennial herb, apparently acaulous but with underground stolons bearing numerous bulbils near the apex;  contractile roots thick, fleshy, glassy white; bulb to  c. 3 cm long, ovoid;  tunic pale brown, 5–7-nerved.  Lvs 3-foliolate, radical.  Petiole 6–22 cm long, ± hairy;  stipules membranous, glabrous or nearly so.  Lamina sessile (that of terminal leaflet somewhat larger than laterals), 10–32 × 12–35 mm, shallowly to deeply 2-lobed to  c. 1/2 way, glabrous above, ± sericeous and finely reticulate below;  base narrow-cuneate;  lobes oblong to almost obovate;  apex rounded.  Fls (1)–3–18, in pseudoumbels, pendent;  peduncles (7)–15–45 cm long, glabrous to sparsely hairy;  pedicels to 2 cm long, densely clothed in glandular hairs.  Bracts at base of pedicels, c. 2.5 mm long, lanceolate, hairy, with apical calli.  Sepals 5–6.5 mm long, lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate, with glandular hairs mainly towards base, or nearly glabrous;  calli 2, apical, usually orange, sometimes yellow.  Petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, obovate with narrow claw, golden, sometimes red-margined, with appressed hairs outside or almost glabrous.  Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments appendaged below,  c. 7 mm long in the 2 common stylar morphs, 5 mm long in the rare long-style morph.  Styles either < or nearly = lower stamen whorl (short-styled clone), > lower stamen whorl (mid-style clone), or = or > upper stamen whorl (long-style clone), hairy.  Capsule not seen.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

It is a tall robust species (15-30 cm.) that develops numerous bulbils and has bright yellow flowers in an umbel. The leaves are trifoliate, often with purple edges or dots.

lookalikes.howToTell: In flower: white clover packs numerous flowers, each with a corolla 8–12 mm long, usually white and occasionally pink to reddish, into a globe-shaped head. Bermuda buttercup has separate golden flowers with petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, usually 3–18 of them (occasionally 1) hanging from the top of a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long. Out of flower it can be mistaken for clover, and the leaves do not settle it: white clover's leaflets are obovate to elliptic or nearly round with a blunt to notched tip, so they can look notched like Bermuda buttercup's two-lobed leaflets, and the sizes overlap (white clover c. 5–25 mm long, Bermuda buttercup 10–32 mm). Both often carry leaf markings — light or dark on white clover, purple or purplish-brown flecks, dots or edges on Bermuda buttercup. Look instead at how the plant grows: white clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes, while Bermuda buttercup grows upright, its leaves rising from a short vertical stem at the soil surface (or above it in shade or dense growth) over an underground bulb, and its runners, which carry the bulbils, are underground. Season is no help: in New Zealand white clover flowers July to March and Bermuda buttercup is recorded flowering in every month.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three heart-shaped leaflets, and both can have purple in the leaf, so none of those separates them; leaflet sizes overlap too (creeping wood sorrel (2.5)–5–18 mm long, Bermuda buttercup 10–32 mm). Look at how the plant grows: creeping wood sorrel has slender, branched stems up to c. 40 cm long that lie along the ground or rise a little, carry the leaves, and often root at the nodes; Bermuda buttercup is an upright plant from an underground bulb, apparently stemless, its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long. Then the flowers: creeping wood sorrel carries 1–5 on a stalk 1–4 cm long (to 9.5 cm in fruit), with petals 4.5–10–(13) mm long; Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 (occasionally 1), hanging, on a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long, with golden petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long. The petal lengths do not overlap; flower number does. Creeping wood sorrel sets cylindrical capsules, usually hairy, (6)–10–18–(20) mm long; Flora of New Zealand gives Bermuda buttercup's capsule as not seen.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have yellow flowers and three notched leaflets, and both can have purple in the leaf, so none of those separates them. Least yellow sorrel creeps: its stems are more or less thread-like, prostrate or nearly so, root at the nodes and often form mats. Bermuda buttercup appears stemless, with its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long, and grows from a bulb with underground runners that bear many small bulbils. Size helps, but the ranges meet: least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and 1.5–12 mm wide, Bermuda buttercup's 10–32 mm long and 12–35 mm wide; least yellow sorrel's petals are 4.5–9 mm long (up to 13 mm), Bermuda buttercup's golden petals 2–2.8 cm (from 1.5 cm). Least yellow sorrel's flowers are solitary, rarely paired; Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 (occasionally 1), hanging, on a stalk 15–45 cm long (from 7 cm). Least yellow sorrel sets a capsule 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes); Flora of New Zealand records no capsule seen on Bermuda buttercup.

preparation.text: The leaves have a pleasant acid flavour and make a pleasant addition to salads; the flowers make an attractive one. Use the leaves in moderation. In South Africa it is a traditional ingredient in dishes such as waterblommetjiebredie ('water flower stew').

recipes.method: Make the filling first; the pastry needs no resting. Bring 2.5 cm of water to the boil in a large pot, pack in about 680 g of leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed), cover and cook on high for 2 minutes, stir, then cook 2 minutes more until just tender but still bright green. If you use nettles, cover them in boiling water instead and cook about 5 minutes. Drain, refresh in cold water, squeeze as dry as you can, roll in a clean tea towel to press out the rest, and chop roughly. Beat 3 egg yolks and 1 egg with 1 cup crème fraîche or sour cream, ½ cup whipping cream, ¼ tsp salt and plenty of black pepper, then stir in the greens and 3 tbsp chopped Bermuda buttercup stems, adding more salt if needed. For the pastry, stir 2¼ cups plain flour, ¼ tsp salt, ½ cup extra virgin olive oil and ½ cup tepid water together and form a ball. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry into a disc about 30 cm across on an oiled or lined baking tray, turn up and crimp the edge into a lip, spread in the filling and bake 40–45 minutes, until the pastry is crisp and the centre is set.
recipes.title: Leafy green tart with Bermuda buttercup

recipes.method: Cook pasta of your choice as the packet directs, drain and return it to the pot. Stir in olive oil or butter until melted, then add shredded parmesan (or any cheese), a couple of handfuls of Bermuda buttercup flowers and leaves, and salt and pepper to taste. Toss and serve.

summary.text: Oxalis pes-caprae is a species of tristylous yellow-flowering plant in the wood sorrel family Oxalidaceae. Some of the most common names for the plant reference its sour taste owing to oxalic acid present in its tissues. Indigenous to South Africa, the plant has become a pest plant in different parts of the world that is difficult to eradicate because of how it propagates through underground bulbs. In the non-native range the plants largely reproduce vegetatively and many populations have only one style length and the plants never produce seed.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Leccinum scabrum' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Leccinum scabrum is a European species that has been introduced to various areas of the world, mostly appearing in urban areas. In New Zealand, it associates solely with Betula pendula.
It grows in association with birch. It has been found in association with ornamental birch trees planted outside of its native range, such as in California.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Leccinum scabrum' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap is 4–10 cm wide and convex before flattening. The skin of the cap is tan or brownish, usually with a lighter edge; it is smooth, bald, and dry to viscid.
The pores are whitish at a young age, later gray. In older specimens, the pores on the pileus can bulge out, while around the stipe they dent in strongly. The pore covering is easy to remove from the skin of the pileus. The spore print is brown. The spores measure 13–16 by 4–4.5 μm and are elliptical.
The stipe is 5–15 cm long and 1–3.5 cm wide and slim, with white and dark to black flakes; it tapers upward. The basic mycelium is white.
The flesh is whitish, sometimes darkening following exposure. In young specimens, the meat is relatively firm, but it very soon becomes spongy and holds water, especially in rainy weather. When cooked, the meat turns black.


Similar species
Several different species of Leccinum mushrooms are found in mycorrhiza with birches, and can be confused by amateurs and mycologists alike. L. holopus is paler and whitish in all parts. L. alaskanum, common with birch in Alaska, has a dark and light, streaked or mottled cap. L. variicolor has a bluish stipe. L. oxydabile has firmer, pinkish flesh and a different pileus skin structure.

Leccinum scabrum, commonly known as the birch bolete, rough-stemmed bolete, or scaber stalk, is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.
In North America, it can be found from June to September, except on the West Coast, where it appears from September to November.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text: Annual herb to 0.1 m tall. Stems prostrate to decumbent and rooting at nodes, eglandular-pubescent; hairs uniform. Leaf bud indistinct; leaves separating while very small, opposite-decussate, erecto-patent to spreading; lamina thin, ovate to broad ovate, sometimes deltoid, 6–35 mm long, 5–30 mm wide, dull green above, paler beneath, midrib and palmate secondary veins evident; surfaces eglandular-hairy; margin pubescent, serrate; teeth in 3–8 pairs; apex rounded to sub-acute; base truncate; petiole 0.5–7.0 mm long. Inflorescence a terminal raceme, 200–500 mm long; flowers distant, 12–50, all bisexual; bracts alternate, leaf-like; pedicels spreading, 5–15 mm long, up to 40 mm long and incurved at fruiting, with short, antrorse, eglandular hairs and scattered longer eglandular or occasionally glandular hairs. Calyx lobes 4, tapered to narrow obtuse apex, sub-equal, 5–7 mm long, with short, antrorse hairs on margins and a few longer ones on calyx tube. Corolla 8–12 mm diameter; tube white and yellow, c. 1 mm long, much < calyx, eglandular-hairy inside; lobes 4, usually sky-blue, rarely white, erecto-patent to spreading, unequal, orbicular to broadly elliptical, 5–8 mm long, rounded; nectar guides dark blue or purple, rarely absent. Stamen filaments white or pale blue, 2–3 mm long; anthers dark blue. Style glabrous, 1.5–3.0 mm long. Capsules angustiseptate, didymous with prominent veins, diverging obtuse lobes and broad sinus between, eglandular- and glandular-hairy in distal half, 3.5–4.0 mm long, 6–7 mm at widest point. Seeds ellipsoid, smooth and concave on funicle side, wrinkled and convex on back, straw-yellow to brown, 1.5–1.8 mm long.

summary.text:
Veronica persica is a flowering plant in the family Plantaginaceae.
Veronica persica is native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, but it has become widely naturalised elsewhere. It now has a near cosmopolitan distribution, having been introduced to Europe, North Africa, the Americas, East Asia, Australia and New Zealand.
The species was first recorded in Britain in 1825. It rapidly extended its range during the 1800s and was ubiquitous throughout lowland Britain and Ireland by 1960.

habitat.text: Forest and stream margins, scrubland, waste ground, roadsides and gardens.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Open thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm 4–7 m (often much taller in cultivation), green, remaining so or becoming black or heavily blotched black in 2nd year, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes all ± evenly spaced. Culm-sheaths uniformly purple or purple-flushed, sometimes dark blotched above; auricles on main shoots prominent, dark; oral bristles long, caducous; sheath-blade linear, undulate. Branches green or black, spreading widely (giving an open network). Leaf-sheath with very short auricles. Oral bristles present. Leaf-blade usually 5–9–(13)× 0.5–2–(3) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, adaxially moderately shining, acuminate.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Arrow bamboo's canes are 3–5 m and dark green, with a white band just below each node; black bamboo has a white waxy ring there on young canes too, so the band does not separate them. Arrow bamboo's internodes are round, not notched; black bamboo's are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node, though usually round below the lowest branches. Arrow bamboo has 1 branch per node, sometimes 2–3 at upper nodes and none at lower ones; black bamboo usually has 3, with the middle one small or missing. Arrow bamboo's leaf-blades reach 25 cm (up to 30 cm) and are shining dark green above; black bamboo's are usually 5–9 cm (up to 13 cm). Arrow bamboo's cane sheaths stay on and hide most of the lower and middle internodes; black bamboo's fall away. Arrow bamboo forms dense thickets, black bamboo open ones. Arrow bamboo's cooked shoots are recorded as rather bitter.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the lower part of several canes. On some of fishpole bamboo's canes the lower nodes are crowded together and sometimes zigzag, with swollen, often lopsided internodes; black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced. Not every fishpole cane shows the crowding, so check more than one. Fishpole's canes are green in their first year and yellow afterwards; black bamboo's are green and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year. The cane sheaths differ: fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles or bristles; black bamboo's are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots. Height does not separate them (fishpole usually 3–6 m, black bamboo 4–7 m), and both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.

preparation.text: Somewhat acrid when raw, they are prepared for eating by boiling in one change of water, the water being changed after 8 - 10 minutes. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: The husk is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs, so handle it with that in mind. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. Acrid raw, and they come round with less work than most: cover with water, boil, and change the water once after 8–10 minutes, then simmer until tender. The shoots are wide — about 5 cm across — so slice before boiling if you want the leaching to reach the middle. They keep a distinct taste and smell of their own. Cut them at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil.
recipes.title: Preparing fresh shoots

recipes.method: For two: 200 g of shoots already boiled, 1 chicken thigh (about 200 g), 3 snow peas and 15 ml oil; for the seasoning, 15 ml sake, 30 ml mirin, 5 ml sugar, 22.5 ml soy sauce, 2.5 ml granulated dashi and 200 ml water. Cut the tips into 4–5 cm lengths and halve them lengthways; slice the rest 7 mm thick. Cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces and fry it in the oil over a medium heat until it changes colour. Add the seasoning and the shoots, bring to the boil, cover and simmer on a low heat for 10–15 minutes. Top with the snow peas, blanched. Written for hachiku, the green-caned var. henonis, which is naturalised here.
recipes.title: Hachiku simmered with chicken

summary.text: Phyllostachys nigra, commonly known as black bamboo or purple bamboo (Chinese: 紫竹), is a species of bamboo, native to Hunan Province of China, and is widely cultivated elsewhere. Two forms have naturalised in New Zealand: var. nigra since 1991 and the green-caned var. henonis since 1993.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

habitat.text:
Prunus serotina is a pioneer species. In the Midwest, it is seen growing mostly in old fields with other sunlight-loving species, such as black walnut, black locust, and hackberry. Gleason and Cronquist (1991) describe P. serotina as "[f]ormerly a forest tree, now abundant as a weed-tree of roadsides, waste land, and forest-margins". The tree is hardy and can tolerate poor soils and oceanic salt sprays.
In New Zealand: forest, plantations, shrubland, grassland, riparian margins and roadsides (Auckland Council, restated).

identification.text:
a medium-sized tree, up to 15 m high, deciduous, with a tall trunk and erect or spreading branches. its leaves are alternate, thin, green, about 10 cm long, and have toothed margins. its white flowers (about 1 cm across) are spreading and borne in dense terminal racemes.. its fleshy black-purple fruit (up to 1.5 cm long) have a stony centre and resemble a cherry.

The leaves are 5–13 centimetres long, ovate-lanceolate in shape, with finely toothed margins. The fall leaf color is yellow to red. The flowers are small, white and 5-petalled, in racemes 10–15 cm long which contain several dozen flowers. For about its first decade the bark of a black cherry tree is thin, smooth, and banded, resembling a birch. A mature tree has very broken, dark gray to black bark. An almond-like odour is released when a young twig is scratched and held close to the nose, revealing minute amounts of cyanide compounds produced and stored by the plant as a defense mechanism against herbivores.

preparation.text: It must be fully ripe or else it will have a bitter flavour. The fruit can taste sweet or bitter. The better fruits have a thin skin and a juicy flesh with a pleasant vinous flavour. The fruit can also be used as a flavouring in liquors.

recipes.method: Use fully ripe cherries, so dark purple they look black; red ones are under-ripe. If they need cleaning, float 5 cups of cherries in a large pot of cold water, pour off whatever rises, and drain. In a large glass jar (about 7.5 L) crush the raw cherries by hand to break every skin — hands are gentler on the stones than a masher. Add 15 cups cold water, 5 cups raw cane sugar and 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice) and stir until the sugar dissolves; any left will dissolve over the next day. Cover with cheesecloth or a linen towel tied on with string, so it can breathe but fruit flies cannot get in, and keep it in a cool spot out of direct sun, such as a kitchen counter. Stir vigorously with a clean spoon about once every 12 hours (at least once a day) and taste a teaspoon after each stir. After 2–3 days it should be bubbly; fewer days give a sweeter, less fizzy drink, more days a drier, fizzier one — the recipe's authors bottle theirs after 5–7 days. Strain out the stones, skins and pulp, finishing through a fine-mesh strainer, pour into swing-top bottles or jars (not plastic or metal) and refrigerate at once. Never store the bottles at room temperature: the fermentation keeps building pressure and they can burst. It keeps in the fridge for months, and is lightly alcoholic, probably about 1–2.5%.

summary.text: Prunus serotina, commonly called black cherry, wild black cherry, rum cherry, or mountain black cherry, is a New World deciduous tree or shrub in the rose family, Rosaceae. Despite its common names, it is not very closely related to commonly cultivated cherries. The species is widespread and common in North America and Central America. Prunus serotina was widely introduced into Western and Central Europe as an ornamental tree in the mid-20th century, where it has become locally naturalized. It has acted as an invasive species there, negatively affecting forest community biodiversity and regeneration.

warnings: Like apricots and apples, the seeds of black cherries contain cyanogenic glycosides (compounds that can be converted into cyanide), such as amygdalin. These compounds release hydrogen cyanide when the seed is ground or minced, which releases enzymes that break down the compounds.
The foliage, particularly when wilted, also contains cyanogenic glycosides, which convert to hydrogen cyanide if eaten by animals.

The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When injested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

Lvs glabrous to puberulent particularly below, petiolate;  leaflets ovate to elliptic, acute or obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, in 4–10 ± opposite pairs, (10)–20–40–(50) mm long, stipellate;  petiolules 2–5 mm long. summary.text:
Robinia pseudoacacia, commonly known as black locust, is a medium-sized hardwood deciduous tree, belonging to the tribe Robinieae of the legume family.
The genus Robinia is native to North America, although traces of it are found in Eocene and Miocene rocks in Europe.
The species itself is native to the eastern United States, but its exact native range is not accurately known as it has been cultivated and is now found in all 48 lower states, British Columbia, and eastern Canada. The native range is thought to be two separate populations, one centered about the Appalachian Mountains from Pennsylvania to northern Georgia, and a second westward focused around the Ozark Plateau and Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas, Oklahoma and Missouri.
The tree has been naturalized in temperate North America, Eurasia, and Africa. Humans have distributed the tree for landscaping, with its range now including Canada, Southern South America, Europe, temperate regions in Asia (including China, India, and Pakistan), Northern and Southern Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.

lookalikes.howToTell: Poroporo is a hairless, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m; black nightshade is a herb to about 75 cm, usually hairy. Poroporo's flowers are usually 4–5 cm across and violet, though white ones are recorded; black nightshade's are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve. The other native poroporo, Solanum aviculare, has flowers 10–40 mm across in white, lavender or dark blue, so flower size and colour alone do not settle it. Poroporo's berries are 23–30 mm long, egg-shaped to ellipsoid and hanging, usually yellow or pale orange; black nightshade's are 7–10 mm across and round, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Poroporo is poisonous too: NZPCN says its green and yellow berries are poisonous and that ripe orange ones lose much of their toxicity, and Te Papa says the unripe green fruit and the leaves are poisonous but the fruit can be eaten when ripe, orange and with its skin bursting.

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowers or fruit appear, the only character here is the coating: fat hen's leaves may be green or grey-mealy, the meal denser underneath when present, and very rarely a plant is bright green, while Flora of New Zealand describes no mealy coating on black nightshade, whose leaves usually carry scattered short hairs. Leaf shape and toothing overlap and do not separate them. In flower they differ: black nightshade has flowers 10–13 mm across, often star-shaped, usually white (sometimes pale mauve) around a yellow cone of anthers, in small, usually few-flowered clusters, then round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Fat hen's flowers are tiny and green with no petals, usually packed in dense spikes and panicles, and it forms no berry: its fruit stays wrapped in the flower parts around a glossy black seed (1.0–)1.1–1.4(–1.6) mm across.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Solanum nigrum', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanum_nigrum Corroborates the solanine and adds the delay. Symptoms may follow eating raw immature green fruit or mature leaves, with 'typically a delay of 6 to 12 hours after ingestion for symptoms to occur', beginning with fever, sweating, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, confusion and drowsiness; death from large amounts comes through cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory failure, though the plant 'is rarely fatal'. Most suspected poisonings involve leaves or unripe fruit. Solanine is practically insoluble in water and can be destroyed by boiling but not by baking, though 'S. nigrum's leaves may be different from this perspective'; there are ethnobotanical accounts of the young leaves and shoots being boiled as a vegetable with the water discarded and replaced several times. Livestock have also been poisoned by nitrate from grazing the mature leaves and green berries.

The confusion this page does not currently card, and the test for it. Solanum nigrum is sometimes mistaken for the far more toxic deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna, which is a different genus. Two differences: black nightshade berries grow in bunches while deadly nightshade's grow individually, and black nightshade's flowers have white petals. Wikipedia contributors. summary.text: A common garden weed with white star flowers and black berries. Its green parts are poisonous, and it is too easily confused with poroporo and fat hen to treat as food.

warnings: Leaves and green berries contain solanine: vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, and in children worse. Fully ripe berries are eaten in some cuisines, but telling ripe from nearly ripe in the field is not a bet this guide makes.
Keep children away from the black berries — they look like tiny blackcurrants.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine, glabrous except for pistil and stamens.  Shoots slightly angular.  Lvs deeply 3-lobed, but entire on young plants;  petiole 1–3 cm long, with 2 sessile glands near apex;  stipules 10–15 mm long, linear-subulate, entire;  lamina lobes ± elliptic, submembranous, deep shining green above, rounded at base;  middle lobe largest, 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm, serrate or serrulate, obtuse to acute.  Fls ☿, solitary.  Pedicels 4–6 cm long at flowering.  Bracts 1.5–2 cm long, ovate, free, coarsely serrate.  Hypanthium inconspicuous.  Sepals 2.5–3 cm long, oblong, green on reverse, white inside; petals white, similar to sepals;  corona threads 2–2.5 cm long, white with purple base.  Filaments puckered, purple towards base, otherwise white;  anthers 8–10 mm long, > filaments.  Ovary puberulent.  Fr. 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broad-ellipsoid or subglobose, dull purple;  pulp orange, sweet.  Seed  c. 5 mm long, ovate, black, pitted.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. The fruit separates them too: black passionfruit's is dull purple and nearly round; the fruit of banana passionfruit (P. tripartita) is yellow or orange when ripe and elongated. Blue passionflower, which has no entry here, has a flower much like black passionfruit's (NZPCN); Flora of New Zealand gives it 5-lobed leaves and calls its pulp 'scanty and inedible'. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too (Flora of New Zealand: 'entire on young plants'), so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Both are edible.

preparation.text:
The ripe aromatic fruit is allowed to wrinkle and develop its sweetness, it is then eaten raw, juiced, made into a syrup or used in sauces, cakes, ice creams, sherbets etc.
In Australia and New Zealand, it is available commercially both fresh and tinned. It is added to fruit salads, and fresh fruit pulp or passion fruit sauce is commonly used in desserts, including as a topping for pavlova (a regional meringue cake) and ice cream, a flavouring for cheesecake, and in the icing of vanilla slices.

recipes.method: The pulp of about 12 passionfruit (250 ml), 125 g unsalted butter, 165 g caster sugar, 5 eggs and 2 extra yolks. Whisk the pulp to loosen it and push it through a sieve, then stir half the seeds back into the juice. Put the juice, butter and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water, keeping the bowl clear of the water, and stir until the butter melts. Beat the eggs and yolks lightly, whisk them in gently, and keep stirring for 20–25 minutes until it thickens: it is ready when a finger drawn across the curd on the back of a spoon leaves a line that holds. Pour into warm sterilised jars, seal, cool, and keep in the fridge for up to 8 weeks.
recipes.title: Passionfruit curd

recipes.method: 880 g caster sugar, 500 ml water, 250 ml passionfruit pulp, 1 teaspoon citric acid. Put everything in a saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil, take off the heat and let it cool. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 weeks. Serve over crushed ice, topped up with water or soda water. Makes about 1.25 litres.

summary.text:
Passiflora edulis, commonly known as passion fruit, is a vine species of passion flower native to southern Brazil, through Paraguay, and northern Argentina.
This sp. is the black passionfruit of commerce and is widely cultivated in warmer parts of the country. All wild and virtually all cultivated plants in N.Z. belong to f. edulis, and not the less hardy, yellow-fruited f. flavicarpa Degener which is the usual form grown in tropical Polynesia.
N.: N. Auckland (plantations at Waitangi and Silverdale), near Auckland (Waitakere Range), Great Barrier Id; K.: well-established on Raoul Id where it grows so abundantly on and near the forest margin in some places that attempts have been made to eliminate it.

identification.text: Rhizomes erect, forming a woody trunk up to c. 20 m tall, 150–300 mm in diameter, covered in black, hexagonal stipe scars; bearing scales near the apex. Rhizome scales conform, acicular, bearing dark-coloured setae on margins, blackish-brown, shining. Fronds 3000–5000 mm long, arching upwards from the crown; dead fronds usually falling, but up to 5 occasionally persistent. Stipes 160–1650 mm long, 40–95 mm wide and 40–60 mm deep at the base, black, sometimes becoming dark brown distally, weakly tuberculate and slightly rough; blackish-brown or dark brown scales with dark-coloured setae on margins densely covering base of stipe, up to 50 mm long and 2 mm wide, becoming pale brown, smaller and more scattered distally. Laminae deeply 2-pinnate-pinnatifid to 3-pinnate-pinnatifid, elliptic or obovate, 3000–4000 mm long, 600–2000 mm wide, dark green on adaxial surface, pale green on abaxial surface, coriaceous; adaxial surfaces of rachis and primary pinna midribs abundantly covered in fine, acicular, colourless or pale brown hairs up to 1 mm long, more scattered on secondary pinna midribs and tertiary pinnae; abaxial surfaces bearing ovate scales with attenuate apices and dark red marginal and apical setae, up to 2 mm long and 1 mm wide on the pinna midribs, and acicular scales up to 5 mm long and 0.5 mm wide on the rachis; rachis blackish-brown on abaxial surface, becoming yellow-brown or pale brown distally, often yellow-brown or yellow-green or green on adaxial surface especially when young, tuberculate. Primary pinnae in 20–25 pairs, ovate, narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular; the longest at or above the middle, 350–950 mm long, 125–300 mm wide, short to long-stalked, abaxial surfaces of costae tuberculate. Secondary pinnae narrowly ovate or narrowly triangular, the longest 65–185 mm long, 12–37 mm wide, short-stalked or sessile. Longest tertiary pinnae 7–20 mm long, 2–4 mm wide, adnate to decurrent; apices acute; margins serrate or divided up to half way to costa. Sori 0.7–1.1 mm in diameter; paraphyses as long as sporangia; indusia completely covering sori before maturity, splitting irregularly at maturity.

summary.text:
Sphaeropteris medullaris,  synonym Cyathea medullaris, commonly known as mamaku or black tree fern, is a large tree fern up to 20 m tall with a trunk up to 20 cm diameter at breast height.
The species is found across many southwestern Pacific Ocean islands, including New Zealand, Fiji, the Marquesas Islands, Tahiti, the Austral Islands, and Pitcairn Island. It is not present in the Kermadec Islands. In the South Island, its distribution is more localised. In New Zealand it also occurs on the Three Kings Islands in the far north, on Stewart Island / Rakiura in the far south and in the Chatham Islands.

edibleParts.text: Ripe black fruit. Young spring leaf tips make a passable tea.

habitat.text:
Roadsides, riverbanks, gullies, forest margins, abandoned farmland. Forms impenetrable thickets.
Coast and lowlands, especially in high-rainfall country: pasture that is only lightly grazed, orchards and forestry blocks, hedgerows, roadsides and waste ground, scrub, forest edges and clearings, riverbeds, stream banks, swamps, sand dunes and gardens (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: A declared pest plant in most regions. There is no such thing as taking too much.

identification.text: Arching thorny canes, compound leaves of three to five toothed leaflets with a pale underside, white or pink five-petalled flowers, and clustered berries ripening green to red to matte black.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk, where blackberry's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point; raspberry's are densely white-felted underneath. A ripe raspberry comes away from its core when picked and is hollow; a blackberry keeps its core.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the flowers: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while bush lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and bush lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. NZPCN adds that the native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the flowers: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while white-leaved lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and white-leaved lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. NZPCN adds that the native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.
lookalikes.name: Creeping lawyer

preparation.text: Raw, or into jam, crumble, cordial and vinegar. Fully black and pulling away from the plant with no effort means ripe.

recipes.method: Written for blackberries; the page names no species. Makes about 8 jars. 1.8 kg blackberries, 1.5 kg jam sugar (sugar with added pectin), the juice and pips of 1 lemon, and a fingertip-sized knob of butter (optional). The night before, layer the berries and sugar in a very large bowl, cover and leave at room temperature so the sugar starts to dissolve; stir once in the morning. Put a small saucer in the freezer. Tip everything into a preserving pan or a large, wide pan and stir in the lemon juice; tie the lemon pips in muslin or a tea strainer and add them, because they give up pectin and help the set. Warm gently until all the sugar has dissolved, then bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes. Take off the heat and put a little on the cold saucer: once it is cool, push it with a finger, and if it wrinkles it has set. If not, boil 2–3 minutes more and test again, until it wrinkles. Skim, stir in the butter if using, and leave 15 minutes so the fruit settles before ladling into sterilised jars (wash them in hot soapy water and dry them in an oven at 170 °C, 150 °C fan, for at least 10 minutes). Keeps at least 6 months somewhere cool and dark; refrigerate once open.
recipes.title: Blackberry jam

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries. Makes about 200 ml. 350 g blackberries, 115 g caster sugar, 3 strips of pared lemon rind, 2 slices of ginger each about 0.5 cm thick, and 125 ml water. Wash and drain the berries and put them in a non-reactive pan with the sugar, lemon rind and ginger, then pour over the water. Bring gently to the boil and simmer for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the fruit is completely soft and the juice is starting to thicken. Take out the rind and ginger and press the pulp through a sieve with a wooden spoon (or use a mouli) to remove the seeds. Pour into a small sterilised bottle or jar, close it and leave to cool. Keeps up to a month in the fridge. Use it as a cordial with sparkling water, over ice cream, or folded into yoghurt or whipped cream.
recipes.title: Blackberry syrup

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the author notes many roadside patches are sprayed, so pick only where you know they aren't, or use frozen. Serves 10. Dough: 200 g softened butter, 200 g caster sugar, 4 eggs, ½ teaspoon vanilla essence, 400 g plain flour and ¼ teaspoon baking powder. Filling: 4 medium cooking apples (Granny Smith will do), peeled and cored, 200 g blackberries, 80 g caster sugar, the zest of a lemon and 50 g butter, plus caster sugar for sprinkling. Butter a pie dish about 24 cm across and 4 cm deep and swirl caster sugar round to coat it. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla; sift in the flour and baking powder and stir until just combined. Cover and chill for at least an hour. Heat the oven to 190 °C (170 °C fan). Roll two-thirds of the dough between sheets of baking paper and line the base and sides of the dish; roll the rest for the lid and keep it chilled. Cut the apples into thick slices, toss with the 80 g sugar, the blackberries and the lemon zest, and fill the case. Dot with the butter, lay on the lid, press the edges to seal, cut a slit in the top and dust with caster sugar. Bake in the middle of the oven for 40–50 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cool before serving with whipped cream or vanilla ice cream.
recipes.title: Apple and blackberry shortcake

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. 500 g blackberries, 250 g plain or wholemeal flour (or 200 g flour and 50 g rolled oats), 150 g soft brown sugar and 180 g cold unsalted butter, cubed. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan). Put the berries in a lightly buttered ovenproof dish, with a sprinkle of sugar if they are sharp. Rub the flour and butter together with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the sugar (and the oats). Spread the topping evenly over the fruit and bake on the middle shelf for about 30 minutes, until golden. Serve with cream or custard.
recipes.title: Blackberry crumble

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. 250 g blackberries, 50 g caster sugar, 100 ml water and ½ tablespoon vanilla essence. Bring the berries, sugar and water to the boil and simmer until the fruit is mushy. Take off the heat, stir in the vanilla and push through a sieve to remove the seeds. Pour over ice cream, desserts, waffles or French toast, or stir into yoghurt.
recipes.title: Blackberry sauce

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 150 g blackberries, 2 eating apples, 50 g caster sugar plus extra for sprinkling, 2 tablespoons water, 1 beaten egg and 500 g shortcrust pastry. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a baking tray with baking paper. Peel and chop the apples small and cook them with the sugar and water over medium heat for 5 minutes; add the blackberries and cook 5 minutes more on low, then tip into a bowl to cool. Roll the pastry 5 mm thick on a floured surface and cut 12 equal rectangles. Lay 6 on the tray, brush the edges with egg, spoon the fruit into the middle, cover with the other 6 and press the edges firmly with a fork. Cut a few slits in each, brush with egg, sprinkle with sugar and bake for 20 minutes, until golden and bubbling.
recipes.title: Blackberry and apple hand pies

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Makes 12. 100 g blackberries, 250 g jumbo rolled oats, 125 g unsalted butter, 125 g light brown sugar and 2 tablespoons golden syrup. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and line a 20 × 20 cm tin with baking paper. Melt the butter, sugar and syrup in a pan over low heat, stir in the oats until coated, and press the mixture into the tin. Scatter the blackberries on top and press down firmly so it is level. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden, then cool before cutting into 12.
recipes.title: Blackberry flapjacks

recipes.method: Written for wild blackberries; the page names no species. Blackberries alone or mixed with other summer fruit (raspberries, blackcurrants, redcurrants; frozen is fine) — enough to fill your pudding basin one and a half times — plus about 3 tablespoons caster sugar, sliced day-old white bread and a little butter. Butter the basin. Cut the crusts off the bread and line the basin with it, pressed firmly with no gaps, keeping a couple of slices for the lid. Heat the fruit and sugar gently in a pan until it simmers and runs with syrupy juice; taste carefully (it is very hot) and add sugar if it is sharp. Fill the basin with the fruit, keeping back some syrup and fruit. Put on the bread lid, press a plate on top and weigh it down with a can. Once cool, refrigerate overnight so the juice soaks into the bread. Turn out onto a plate, pour over the rest of the syrup and decorate with the leftover fruit.
recipes.title: Summer pudding

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Blackberry' entry.

Its actual legal status, which 'declared pest' summarises. Blackberry is a Sustained Control pest in regional pest management plans rather than an eradication target, because it is too widespread to contain — Hawke's Bay, Bay of Plenty, Auckland and Tasman–Nelson all list it that way, with the occupier responsible for control and rules commonly requiring destruction within 10 m of a boundary where the neighbour is also controlling it. Breeding, distributing, releasing or selling it is an offence under the Biosecurity Act 1993. It is **not** a National Pest Plant Accord species. Hawke's Bay Regional Council, pest hub: 'Blackberry'. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

What it is sprayed with and when, which is what the spray warning is really about. Hawke's Bay Regional Council's guidance for large patches is to spray in summer to autumn, before the leaves go brittle, with metsulfuron-methyl, Tordon Brushkiller or triclopyr 600 EC. Small patches are dug out year-round. Goats control it effectively where they are confined with it. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.hbrc.govt.nz/environment/pest-control/pest-hub/pests/pest/21

Why the scientific name carries 'agg.' — Rubus fruticosus L. is an ambiguous name that has been applied in several ways, which is why the European blackberries are treated as an aggregate rather than a species. The hollow-raspberry test is Wikipedia, 'Rubus idaeus' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1365353396): 'the drupelets separate from the core when picked, leaving a hollow fruit, whereas in blackberries and most other species of Rubus, the drupelets stay attached to the core' — used only on the raspberry–blackberry pair, because 'most other species' does not cover the native lawyers by name. The glandular hairs sentence restates NZPCN's similar-taxa notes for R. australis and R. schmidelioides (ARR); Webb's blackberry key confirms some blackberries lack long-stalked glands. 'Red before it turns black' rests on this catalogue's blackberry identification text ('ripening green to red to matte black', Langlands). No card joins red raspberry and creeping lawyer: Flora of New Zealand puts creeping lawyer only west of the Main Divide from Nelson to South Westland, and lists no raspberry station there. Every number was checked against the saved Flora text. The commonest native lawyers, R. cissoides (bush lawyer, 3,367 wild NZ iNaturalist records on 21/10/2026) and R. squarrosus (leafless lawyer, 541), have no entries, so no card can open them.

identification.text:
Ribes nigrum is a medium-sized shrub, growing to 1.5 by 1.5 metres. The leaves are alternate, simple, 3 to 5 centimetres broad and long with five palmate lobes and a serrated margin. All parts of the plant are strongly aromatic. The flowers are produced in racemes known as "strigs" up to 8 cm long containing 10–20 flowers, each about 8 millimetres in diameter. Each flower has a hairy calyx with yellow glands, the five lobes of which are longer than the inconspicuous petals. There are five stamens surrounding the stigma and style and two fused carpels. The flowers open in succession from the base of the string and are mostly insect pollinated, but some pollen is distributed by the wind. They are somewhat self-pollinating, but produce more fruit when pollinated by another plant of a different variety. A pollen grain landing on a stigma will germinate and send a slender pollen tube down the style to the ovule. In warm weather, this takes about 48 hours, but in cold weather, it may take a week, and by that time, the ovule may have passed the stage where it is receptive. If fewer than about 35 ovules are fertilised, the fruit may not be able to develop and will fall prematurely. Frost can damage both unopened and open flowers when the temperature falls below −1.9 °C. The flowers at the base of the strig are more protected by the foliage and are less likely to be damaged.
In midsummer the strigs of green fruit ripen to edible berries, very dark purple in colour, almost black, with glossy skins and calyxes at the apex (the calyxes being persistent), each containing many seeds. An established bush can produce about 4.5 kilograms of fruit each year.
Plants from Northern Asia are sometimes distinguished as a separate variety, Ribes nigrum var. sibiricum, of which R. cyathiforme is considered a synonym.


Phytochemicals
Polyphenol phytochemicals present in the fruit, seeds, and leaves are being investigated for their potential biological activities. Major anthocyanins in blackcurrant pomace – delphinidin-3-O-glucoside, delphinidin-3-O-rutinoside, cyanidin-3-O-glucoside, and cyanidin-3-O-rutinoside, which are retained in the juice concentrate – are among other polyphenols.

habitat.text:
Macrocystis typically grow forming extensive beds, large "floating canopies", on rocky substrata between the low intertidal. It was harvested by barges which used large blades to harvest up to 300 tons a day along the coast of California.
Macrocystis pyrifera is found in North America (Alaska to California), South America, South Africa, New Zealand, and southern Australia. It thrives in cooler waters where the ocean water temperature remains mostly below 21 °C. The species is also found near Tristan da Cunha in the Mid-South Atlantic Ocean.
Where the bottom is rocky and affords places for it to anchor, giant kelp forms extensive kelp beds with large "floating canopies". When present in large numbers, giant kelp forms kelp forests that are home to many marine species that depend upon the kelp directly for food and shelter, or indirectly as a hunting ground for prey. Both the large size of the kelp and the large number of individuals significantly alter the availability of light, the flow of ocean currents, and the chemistry of the ocean water in the area where they grow.
In high-density populations, giant kelp individuals compete with other individuals of the species for space and resources. Giant kelp may also compete with Pterygophora californica in these circumstances.
Where surface waters are poor in nutrients, nitrogen in the form of amino acids is translocated up the stipe through sieve elements that very much resemble the phloem of vascular plants. Translocation of nutrients along the stipe may be as rapid as 60 cm per hour. Most translocation occurs to move carbon-rich photosynthate, and typically transfers material from mature regions to actively growing regions where the machinery of photosynthesis is not yet fully in place. Translocation also moves nutrients downward from light-exposed surface fronds to sporophylls (reproductive fronds) at the base of the kelp, where there is little light and thus little photosynthesis to produce food.
Recent research has shown that Arctic kelp forests can steadily increase pH levels by 0.15 units over a 10-day period during extended daylight conditions in summer. This pH regulation, driven by sustained photosynthetic activity, helps mitigate the harmful effects of ocean acidification and supports calcifying organisms such as bivalves and sea urchins.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Macrocystis' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Macrocystis is a monospecific genus; the sole species is M. pyrifera. Some individuals are so huge that they may grow to up to 60 m long. The stipes arise from a holdfast and branch three or four times from near the base. Blades develop at irregular intervals along the stipe. M. pyrifera grows to over 45 m long. The stipes are unbranched and each blade has a gas bladder at its base.
Macrocystis pyrifera is the largest of all algae. The stage of the life cycle that is usually seen is the sporophyte, which is perennial and individuals persist for many years. Individuals may grow to up to 50 m long or more. The kelp often grows even longer than the distance from the bottom to the surface as it will grow in a diagonal direction due to the ocean current pushing against the kelp. The stalks arise from a basal meristem, with as many as 60 stalks in older well protected individuals. Blades develop at irregular intervals along the stipe, with a single pneumatocyst (gas bladder) at the base of each blade. At the base of each stalk is a cluster of blades that lack pneumatocysts; instead they develop small sacks on the blade that release the biflagellated zoospores: these are the sporophylls.
The smaller morphs, formerly identified as Macrocystis integrifolia, have deep brown color on flattened rhizomes which are profusely dichotomously branched.  Each is attached by branched root-like structures coming out of the sides of the rhizomes. Slender main stipes (about 1 centimetre wide to 30 metres long) come from the rhizome which is up to 0.1 metres at the widest.  Periodically 5 centimetres wide and 35 centimetres long flattened leaf-like branches derive from the stipe. They have furrowed surfaces and taper gradually, but then have an oval or rounded float where attached to the stipe. The blade-like branches have notched denticulate edges leading to the terminal blade at the tip of the stipe, which is separated by several smaller branches. It grows to only 6 m long. It is found on intertidal rocks or shallow subtidal rocks along the Pacific coast of North America (British Columbia to California) and South America. In New Zealand M. pyrifera is found in the subtidal zone of southern North Island, the South Island, Chatham, Stewart, Bounty, Antipodes, Auckland and Campbell Islands. The species can be found on rock and on sheltered open coasts.

identification.text:
Pileus 30-50 mm in diameter, at first hemispherical, then convex to almost plane, surface dry, velvety, somewhat areolate in age, blackish to dark brown when young, pale brown to ochraceous at maturity with a reddish tint at marginal zone. Flesh whitish to creamy, soft, slightly blueing when injured. Tubes creamy yellow to pale yellow, slightly blueing when bruised. Pores almost concolorous with the tubes to olivaceous yellow, slightly blueing when injured. Taste and smell not distinctive. Stem 3−6.6(−7) × 5−9 mm, cylindrical without a ring, some slightly tapering towards the base, some slightly curved at the base or bulbose, yellow to olivaceous yellow in the upper half, gradually becoming dull red to ocher brown downwards, white fuzzy at the base, Context fibrillose and brittle, blueing when cut or bruised especially towards the base.
Basidia 32–43 × 10–11.5 µm, clavate, 2-4 spored (mainly 4). Basidiospores (10.1−)10.4−12.5(−14.3) × (3.8−)3.9−4.8(−5) µm, subfusiform, thick walled, 1-3 guttulate.
This species may have similar morphological appearance with X. chrysenteron, but the smooth spore surface of X. chrysenteron differs it from this species. Xerocomellus pruinatus also have similar spore ornamentation with X. cisalpinus. But it lacks the ability of blueing.

lookalikes.howToTell: These two are hard to tell apart in the field: macroscopic characters such as colour and cap cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group, both caps often crack, both stain blue, and both have been collected in New Zealand under silver birch. Riverine bolete's cap is described as bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint; bluefoot's is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, but can have a reddish tint or be entirely red. Habitat may help: riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch; about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch.

identification: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. Field characters when fresh and young: the two-toned yellow and red stem, the cap often cracking with reddish tones in the cracks, and in particular an intense blue stain in the stem when scratched. Spores 11.5–15.0 × 4.5–5.7 µm with very faint longitudinal lines. Described in 2003 as a Xerocomus; the epithet means 'on this side of the Alps', after the Italian holotype, and the author calls it a misnomer because the species is common through much of Europe. Usually with Quercus, also other deciduous hosts.

X. cisalpinus, X. ripariellus, X. chrysenteron and X. pruinatus have all been much confused and together formed the composite 'red-cracked bolete' of the older field guides — the same conflation this catalogue's deleted 'Red-pored boletes' entry made.

lookalikes: Kibby, G. (2023). 'Fungal Portrait 96: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and some lookalikes'. Field Mycology 24(4): 111–112, British Mycological Society. In copyright — facts restated, no text reproduced. Separations from the three congeners. X. ripariellus also stains strongly and has striated spores, but has a bright blood-red cracked cap and prefers wetter woodland — pond edges and boggy ground — especially with Salix and Alnus. X. chrysenteron has a more uniformly red stem, flesh that rarely bruises intense blue and is more often dull red in the stem, and spores that are not striated and are broader, 11.8–16.5 × 4.8–6.8 µm. X. pruinatus often does not crack, has a dark plum-red to blackish brown cap with a distinct thin red marginal zone, flesh flushing only slowly pale blue, and prefers Fagus.

identification.text:
Perennial, rarely annual, taprooted herb.  Stems erect, rarely decumbent, glabrous or hairy, (3)–20–40–(100) cm tall.  Lvs glabrous or hairy;  margins toothed.  Rosette lvs petiolate, auriculate at base, deeply pinnatifid to pinnate, (2)–4–7–(10) × 1–3 cm.  Stem lvs similar to rosette lvs, auriculate at base, becoming smaller with narrower lobes above, the uppermost sometimes simple.  Pedicels glabrous or sparsely hispid, erecto-patent at flowering, spreading at fruiting, (2)–4–7 mm long.  Sepals 1.5–2–(2.5) mm long.  Petals yellow, = sepals.  Silicle glabrous, oblong to elliptic, curved, (2)–4–7 × 2–3 mm;  valves not veined;  style 0.5–1 mm long.  Seeds pale brown, c. 0.8 mm long, finely colliculate, in 2 rows per locule.

summary.text:
Rorippa palustris, marsh yellow-cress, bog yellow-cress or common yellow-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
Rorippa palustris is native to, or naturalized across much of the globe.

Native range
AFRICA: in Egypt and Ethiopia.
ASIA and EURASIA: in Afghanistan; Bhutan; the Caucasus (in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Russia) and Ciscaucasia (in Dagestan); much of China and Taiwan; India (in the states of Assam, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and West Bengal); Indonesia (in Papua province, Java, the Lesser Sunda, and Maluku Islands); Japan (in the prefectures of Hokkaido, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku, and the Ryukyu Islands); Kazakhstan; the Korean Peninsula; Kyrgyzstan; Mongolia; Pakistan; Papua New Guinea; eastern and western Siberia; Tajikistan; northeastern Turkey; Turkmenistan; Uzbekistan; and Yemen.
EUROPE: grows natively in most regions.
NORTH AMERICA: in every province and territory (excluding Nunavut) of Canada; Puerto Rico; the District of Columbia and every state (excluding Hawaii) in the United States; Mexico
The CARIBBEAN: in Cuba and Haiti.
AUSTRALASIA: New Zealand

Naturalized range
AUSTRALASIA: Australia and New Zealand
MEZO- and SOUTH AMERICA: in Argentina; Brazil; Chile; Ecuador; Panama; Peru; and Suriname.

summary.text:
Lycium ferocissimum, the African boxthorn or boxthorn, is a shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) indigenous to South Africa.
It has also been recorded in the Free State, but these may represent introductions. It has been widely introduced in South Africa and elsewhere in Africa, as far north as Morocco. It has been recorded in Sardinia, Italy. This shrub is found in other Mediterranean countries such as Tunisia and Spain. There is one record in France from 2020.
It has become naturalised in Australia and New Zealand. It is listed in Australia's Weed of National Significance list and is a declared noxious weed in the United States.

identification.text: A tall coarse fern to 2 m with fronds divided three times into stiff, leathery, triangular blades on a strong dark stalk, forming dense stands rather than single plants. lookalikes.howToTell: Pikopiko (hen and chicken fern) grows from a short, stout, upright rhizome; bracken has long-creeping underground rhizomes and forms extensive stands. Pikopiko's stalks and fronds carry scales, and its fronds lack hairs; bracken's fronds carry hairs and lack scales, and its stalks become woody and chestnut brown at the base. Pikopiko's fronds usually bear small bulbils (plantlets) on the upper surface, and the Flora of New Zealand says it is usually readily recognised by them; bracken's description has none. Habitat helps but is not a test: pikopiko grows in wetter, shaded places on the forest floor, in gullies and on streamsides; bracken grows mostly in the open but also under forest, scrub and pine plantations. The young, unopened fronds of pikopiko are a traditional Māori food.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pteridium_esculentum On the toxin: it contains ptaquiloside, concentrations in New Zealand 'vary greatly, and in a high proportion of stands ptaquiloside is not found', with the higher and very high concentrations in the areas where bovine enzootic haematuria or acute haemorrhagic syndrome was known to occur, and traditional Māori cooking techniques 'may have lessened the content'. It also carries silica structures that ground down teeth — visible in many Māori archaeological sites — and is known to cause constipation.

Aruhe, and why 'were once eaten' undersells it. The rhizome was a staple Māori food, especially for groups away from permanent settlements, and alongside kūmara was often the primary carbohydrate — particularly in the south, where tropical Pacific crops would not grow. Much of the plant's present distribution in New Zealand follows prehistoric deforestation and the deliberate tending of aruhe stands on the richest soils. It was associated with Haumia-tiketike, atua of uncultivated foods, and carried by warriors. The forms are named separately: aruhe the rhizome, roi its roasted product, rauaruhe the fronds, mōkehu the new shoots, and rārahu, rarauhe or rahurahu the whole plant. Wikipedia contributors. Separately, 'were once eaten' undersells aruhe, a staple carbohydrate alongside kumara. Evidence is in this entry's sources; the sentences are a person's to write.

summary.text: The common coarse fern of open country. Its young shoots look like pikopiko and were once eaten, but the plant is carcinogenic and is now left alone.

warnings: Contains ptaquiloside, a proven carcinogen, in every part. Cooking does not remove it.

identification.text:
This siphonous green alga is of two subspecies in Ireland and Great Britain. They are similar, both are dark green in color. It forms long erect finger-like fronds. These grow to 40 cm or more long branching dichotomously. The cortex of the branches is formed by closely packed utricles, these are small cylindrical club-shaped structures formed from a single cell up to 1200 μm (micrometres) long. The rounded tips of these closely packed utricles give the frond a velvety texture. The fronds hang down from rocks during low tide, hence the nickname "dead man's fingers". The "fingers" are branches up to a centimeter wide and sometimes over 30 centimeters long.
Codium fragile occurs in the low intertidal zone, and subtidal on high-energy beaches.
It has no gametophyte stage, and male and female gametes are both produced on separate plants.

identification.text:
Ulva lactuca is a thin flat green alga growing from a discoid holdfast. The margin is somewhat ruffled and often torn. It may reach 18 centimetres or more in length, though generally much less, and up to 30 cm across. The membrane is two cells thick, soft and translucent, and grows attached, without a stipe, to rocks or other algae by a small disc-shaped holdfast.
Green to dark green in colour, this species in the Chlorophyta is formed of two layers of cells irregularly arranged, as seen in cross-section. The chloroplast is cup-shaped in some references but as a parietal plate in others with one to three pyrenoids. There are other species of Ulva which are similar and not always easy to differentiate.


Life cycle
The sporangial and gametangial thalli are morphologically alike. The diploid adult plant produces zoospores by meiosis – making them haploid. These settle and grow to form haploid male and female plants similar to the diploid plants. When these haploid plants release gametes they unite to produce the zygote which germinates, and grows to produce the diploid plant.

Hairy annual or perennial with persistent taproot.  Lvs all radical, rosulate;  petiole ill-defined, with silky tuft of hairs at base.  Lamina (10)–30–120–(200) × 1–5–(10) mm, linear, 1–(2)-pinnatisect, rarely entire, with 1–4 pairs of linear, acute to subulate lobes or teeth, hairy, particularly on the margins, sometimes only sparsely ciliate;  main vein usually 1. Wikipedia contributors. 'Durvillaea antarctica', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durvillaea_antarctica Corroborates the pōhā tradition and adds the te reo name: known as rimurapa, associated in many traditional stories with the entrance to the underworld. Blades are used to make pōhā bags — for carrying and storing food and fresh water, for propagating live shellfish, and for clothing and sports equipment — especially associated with Ngāi Tahu and often used to carry and store muttonbird (tītī) chicks. It was also used to make semi-submersible craft. It has no air bladders and floats on a honeycomb structure instead.

Which species you are actually cutting, because there are two. A 2012 revision split Durvillaea poha out of D. antarctica on genetic, morphological and ecological evidence, and it is the only other species in the genus with the same honeycombed buoyant structure. D. poha occurs only in southern New Zealand and the subantarctic islands, grows higher up or further back on the rock platforms and in more sheltered bays where wave force is weaker, has generally wider and more orange-looking fronds, and — this is the point for this entry — **pōhā are made from both**. In southern New Zealand the two grow together, so a southern blade is as likely to be D. poha. Wikipedia contributors. 'Durvillaea antarctica', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0.
