lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the flowers: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while bush lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and bush lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. NZPCN adds that the native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; bush lawyer's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; bush lawyer is a climbing liane with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Flora of New Zealand's key: bush lawyer's end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, hairless except often on the veins and margins, with fewer than 10 coarse or irregular teeth on each side; white-leaved lawyer's is felted underneath or, if hairless (mostly in the lowland eastern South Island), narrow-lanceolate or linear and coarsely toothed. Juvenile white-leaved lawyer leaflets are much narrower and usually hairless. Their fruit colours overlap, so fruit does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; bush lawyer's have three or more. Creeping lawyer's flowers are relatively large, with stamens and carpels together, where bush lawyer's are small, male and female on separate plants. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.

preparation.text: Eat the ripe fruit raw or cook it. It is edible but bland, so it is better cooked with sugar and spice, as in the recipes here, than eaten by the handful.

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. Somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. For one drink. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

summary.text: Rubus australis, commonly called swamp lawyer, is a climbing plant species found in New Zealand. It is endemic, and grows throughout the North and South Islands (rarely in the drier east) and on Stewart Island.

warnings: Tātaramoa, or “bush lawyer”, has hooked thorns that snag clothing and rip or prick the skin.

edibleParts.text:
The stems and fleshy rhizomes of C. australis are high in natural sugars and were steam-cooked in earth ovens (umu tī, a large type of hāngī) to produce kāuru, a carbohydrate-rich food used to sweeten other foods. The growing tips or leaf hearts were stripped of leaves and eaten raw or cooked as a vegetable, when they were called kōuka—the origin of the Māori name of the tree.
Edible shoots - a cabbage substitute. The leaves are very fibrous even when young, we would not fancy eating them.

habitat.text:
Forest margins, open places, abundant near swamps.
A quote from Philip Simpson sums up the wide range of habitats the cabbage tree occupied in early New Zealand, and how much its abundance and distinctive form shaped the impression travellers received of the country:
"In primeval New Zealand cabbage trees occupied a range of habitats, anywhere open, moist, fertile and warm enough for them to establish and mature: with forest; around the rocky coast; in lowland swamps, around the lakes and along the lower rivers; and perched on isolated rocks. Approaching the land from the sea would have reminded a Polynesian traveller of home, and for a European traveller, conjured up images of the tropical Pacific".
Generally a lowland species, it grows from sea level to about 1,000 metres, reaching its upper limits on the volcanoes of the central North Island, where eruptions have created open spaces for it to exploit, and in the foothills of the Southern Alps in the South Island, where deforestation may have played a part in giving it room to grow.
Cordyline australis is a light-demanding pioneer species, and seedlings die when overtopped by other trees. To grow well, young plants require open space so they are not shaded out by other vegetation. Another requirement is water during the seedling stage. Although adult trees can store water and are drought resistant, seedlings need a good supply of water to survive. This stops the species from growing in sand dunes unless there are wet depressions present, and from hillsides unless there is a seepage area. The fertility of the soil is another factor—settlers in Canterbury used the presence of the species to situate their homesteads and gardens. Another factor is temperature, especially the degree of frost. Young trees are killed by frost, and even old trees can be cut back. This is why C. australis is absent from upland areas and from very frosty inland areas.
Today it is common across farmland, open places, wetlands and scrub in both main islands, but rare on Stewart Island; it likes full sun, so it is scarce inside unbroken forest though common on its edges (DOC, restated). It grows from the coast to montane forest, most of all on alluvial river terraces, and seedlings often come up unbidden in gardens from bird-dropped seed (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need. Cabbage trees should not be cut for exploitation.

identification.text:
Plant to 12–(20) m high; young unbranched stems 5–10 cm diam.; older trees with massive trunk to 1.5m diam., much-branched above. Leaves 30–100 × 3–6 cm, only slightly narrowed above base; midrib indistinct, nerves fine. Panicle lax, 60–150 cm long. Flowers fragrant, white; segments 5–6 mm long. Berry whitish.
[From:  Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: cabbage tree grows to the size of a small tree with a thick trunk and many branches, and its leaf stalk is flat and ill-defined, at least three-quarters as wide as the widest part of the blade; forest cabbage tree rarely approaches tree form and, if tall, usually has several more or less equal main stems, and its leaf stalk is narrow, long (up to a quarter of the blade's length) and deeply channelled, widening rather abruptly into a much wider blade that droops at the tip, with a prominent midrib and several stronger side nerves. Both have white, scented flowers, so flower colour does not separate them. Flora of New Zealand records that where the two overlap at about 300–1,000 ft (90–300 m) on the northern tip of the Tararua Range, about half the plants cannot be put strictly in either species.
lookalikes.name: Forest cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf cabbage tree is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. Hybrids between the two have been described from the far north (C. × matthewsii, Carse 1926), some almost enlarged copies of dwarf cabbage tree, so an in-between plant there may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain cabbage tree grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Cabbage tree (Cordyline australis) grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key puts mountain cabbage tree apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Garden plants sold as 'Cordyline indivisa' or 'Dracaena indivisa' are often young cabbage trees, according to Wikipedia, so a nursery label does not settle it.

preparation.text:
If the spike of unopened leaves and a few outer leaves is gripped firmly at the base and bent, it will snap off. The leaves can be removed, and what remains is like a small artichoke heart that can be steamed, roasted or boiled to make kōuka, a bitter vegetable available at any time of the year. Kōuka is delicious as a relish with fatty foods like eel, muttonbirds, or pigeons, or in modern times, pork, mutton and beef. Different trees were selected for their degree of bitterness, which should be strong for medicinal use, but less so when used as a vegetable.
Johanna Knox (Wild Picnic, 2010) peels back the tough outer leaves of a leaf head until the paler shoot and heart show, stripping too few rather than too many at first; she boils or bakes the heart for 6 minutes or less, depending on its size, and then treats it like an artichoke heart, adding it to a tray of baked vegetables in about the last 10 minutes.
After drying, the harvested stems or rhizomes were steamed for 24 hours or more in the umu tī pit. Steaming converted the carbohydrate fructan in the stems to very sweet fructose. Kāuru could also be dipped in water and chewed and was said to smell and taste like molasses.
Proper kāuru was the side-shoot; "when it was taken the tree did not die, as it did if its root (more-tī) was taken.

summary.text:
Cordyline australis, commonly known as the cabbage tree, or by its Māori name of tī or tī kōuka, is a widely branched monocot tree endemic to New Zealand.
Cordyline australis occurs from North Cape to the very south of the South Island, where it becomes less and less common, until it reaches its southernmost natural limits at Sandy Point (46° 30' S), west of Invercargill near Oreti Beach. It is absent from much of Fiordland, probably because there is no suitable habitat, and is unknown on the subantarctic islands to the south of New Zealand, probably because it is too cold. It occurs on some offshore islands—Poor Knights, Stewart and the Chathams—but was probably introduced by Māori. In the Stewart Island region, it is rare, growing only on certain islands, headlands and former settlement sites where it may have been introduced by muttonbird collectors, while on the Chatham Islands it is also largely "a notable absentee".
Early European explorers of New Zealand described "jungles of cabbage trees" along the banks of streams and rivers, in huge swamps and lowland valleys. Few examples of this former abundance survive today—such areas were the first to be cleared by farmers looking for flat land and fertile soil. In modern New Zealand, cabbage trees usually grow as isolated individuals rather than as parts of a healthy ecosystem.
The cabbage tree's year begins in autumn among the tight spike of unopened leaves projecting from the centre of each tuft of leaves. Some of the growing tips have changed from making leaves to producing inflorescences for the coming spring, and around these, two or three buds begin to produce leaves. The inflorescence and the leaf buds pass the winter protected by the enveloping spike of unopened leaves. Months later in spring or early summer, it bears its flowers on the outside of the tree, exposed to insects and birds.
Flowering takes place over a period of four to six weeks, giving maximum exposure to pollinating insects. The flowers produce a sweet perfume which attracts large numbers of insects. The nectar produced by the flowers contains aromatic compounds, mainly esters and terpenes, which are particularly attractive to moths. Bees use the nectar to produce a light honey to feed their young and increase the size of the hive in the early summer. It takes about two months for the fruit to ripen, and by the end of summer a cabbage tree can have thousands of small fruits available for birds to eat and disperse. The strong framework of the inflorescence can easily bear the weight of heavy birds like the New Zealand pigeon, which was formerly the major disperser of the seeds.
The berries of C. australis are enjoyed by bellbirds, tūī, and kererū. Māori sometimes planted groves of cabbage trees (pā tī) to attract kererū which could be snared when they came to eat the berries. Reminiscing in 1903 about life in New Zealand sixty or more years earlier, George Clarke describes how such a tapu grove of cabbage trees would attract huge numbers of pigeons: "About four miles from our house, there was a great preserve of wood pigeons, that was made as tapu as the native chiefs could devise. At a certain season, the pigeons came in vast flocks to feed on the white berries of the Ti tree (bracœna) [sic] and got so heavy with fat that they could hardly fly from one tree to another. No gun was allowed in the place. The Māoris, with a long slender rod and a slip noose at the end, squatted under the leaves and noiselessly slipped the noose over the necks of the stupid pigeons as they were feeding." As the native birds have vanished from much of New Zealand with the clearing of forests, it is now flocks of starlings which descend upon the fruit.
In the central North Island, it has evolved a much sturdier form (with the Māori name tī manu, meaning "with branches bearing broad, straight upright leaves"). This form resembles that found in the far south of the South Island, suggesting that they are both adapted to cold conditions. The fallen leaves of the tree also help to raise the fertility of the soil when they break down.

identification.text:
Erect or ascending, annual or short-lived perennial herb, sometimes somewhat woody toward base, (10)–15–50 cm tall.  Stems densely clothed in short, erect, glandular hairs, usually becoming glabrous below, much-branched.  Basal and lower cauline lvs sparsely to moderately clothed in simple and glandular hairs, ciliate, usually narrow-obovate, sometimes elliptic or ± orbicular, entire, with few minute scattered marginal teeth, or rarely remotely dentate, obtuse to acute and mucronate, apetiolate and long-cuneate, 6–20 × 1.5–5 cm;  upper cauline lvs similar to lower but becoming smaller, oblong to lanceolate, broad-based and often ± amplexicaul.  Capitula solitary, 35–85 mm diam. Involucral bracts in 2 rows, glandular and ciliate, lanceolate, acuminate, 10–15 mm long, the inner with more conspicuous membranous margins.  Ray florets (20)–40–60, in 1-several rows; ligules usually orange, sometimes pale orange or yellow, clearly exceeding bracts, (8)–12–30 mm long;  disc florets numerous, usually orange, sometimes pale orange or yellow, rarely brownish black.  Achenes glabrous or sparsely hairy, usually of 3 types; outermost achenes strongly incurved, long-beaked, 12–18 mm diam., with small stout spines on back, usually alternating with shorter, short-beaked, broadly 3-winged, tuberculate or smooth-backed achenes;  inner achenes enclosed by outer, tuberculate on back, 4–7 mm diam.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

Calendula officinalis, Mary's gold, common marigold, the pot marigold, Scotch marigold, or ruddles, is a flowering plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae.
It is probably native to southern Europe, though its long history of cultivation makes its precise origin unknown. It is also widely naturalised further north in Europe (as far north as southern England) and elsewhere in warm temperate regions of the world.

Annual or perennial herb.  Habit various, from a tufted rosette to an erect many-stemmed herb with the rosette stage almost completely suppressed.  Stems ribbed, erect, glabrous, 10–30–(40) cm tall.  Lvs much dissected;  petiole > lamina;  lamina to 10 × 10 cm in rosette lvs, usually much smaller in stem lvs.  Pedicels ribbed, 5–10 cm long.  Calyx hood apiculate. habitat.text: It grows in forests, forest edges, and riparian areas. It grows at high elevations of 500–3,000 m in its native region, but may also be found at sea level in Oceania and Pacific islands where it occurs widely in subtropical and warm, temperate conditions. Its latitude range is about 45°S to 60°N, and its altitude range is generally from sea level to 3,000 m.

summary.text:
Physalis peruviana is a South American species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
The species is reportedly native to Chile and Peru. Its center of genetic diversity is in the Andes Mountains of Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, and Peru.
The plant has become invasive in some natural habitats, forming thickets, particularly in Hawaii and on other Pacific islands.
There are believed to be dozens of ecotypes worldwide that differentiated by plant size, calyx shape, and the size, color, and flavor of the fruit. Wild forms are thought to be diploid with 2n = 24 chromosomes, while cultivated forms include varieties with increased ploidy and 32 or 48 chromosomes.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves; flower buds.

habitat.text: Lawns, paddocks, roadsides, dry banks. Often more common than dandelion.

identification.text: A flat rosette like dandelion, but the leaves are rough with stiff hairs and only shallowly lobed, where dandelion's are hairless and jaggedly toothed. Flower stalks are solid, wiry and branch into several yellow flowers; dandelion's are hollow, unbranched and carry one flower each. Sap is clear, not milky.

lookalikes.howToTell: Beaked hawksbeard's flowering stems are ribbed to grooved and carry leaves of their own; catsear's leaves are all in the basal rosette and its stems carry only a few tiny bracts. Beaked hawksbeard's stems are hairy, with fine crinkly white hairs and stout, spreading, red-based ones; catsear's are hairless or have a few sparse hairs low down. Under the flower head, beaked hawksbeard's bracts have pale cobwebby hairs and often dark glandular hairs; catsear's are hairless except for a row of stiff hairs along the midrib. Beaked hawksbeard's seed parachute is of fine white bristles; catsear's is feathery. Leaf shape does not separate them: beaked hawksbeard's leaves are usually deeply lobed with lobes pointing back, and catsear's are usually shallowly to deeply lobed. Hairy leaves, branched stems and height do not separate them either.

identification.text:
Apium graveolens is a stout biennial or monocarpic perennial herb, producing flowers and seeds only once, during its second or a later year. It grows up to 1 m tall, with all parts of the plant having a strong celery odour. The stems are solid with conspicuous grooves on the surface (sulcate). The leaves are bright green to yellowish-green, 1- to 2-pinnate with leaflets that are variously shaped, often rhomboid, up to 6 cm long and 4 cm broad.
The flowers are produced in umbels, mostly with short peduncles, with four to twelve rays. The individual flowers are creamy-white to greenish-white, 2–3 mm across. The fruit is a schizocarp, broadly ovoid to globose, 1–1.5 mm long and wide.

summary.text:
Apium graveolens, commonly known as celery, is an Old World species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae.
Wild celery is native to much of Eurasia, ranging from Ireland in the west, through Europe north to Scotland, Denmark and Poland, and east to the Caucasus and Central Asia, and as far as the western Himalayas, and also through Macaronesia and North Africa to West Asia and the Arabian Peninsula. It is widely naturalised outside this range, including in Scandinavia, North and South America, Africa, India, central, eastern and southern Asia, and New Zealand. The cultivar groups may also be naturalised.

lookalikes.howToTell: Do not decide on the tree. This endemic grows under native beech, but the introduced peppery bolete, usually found with fly agaric under pines and introduced broadleaved trees, also turns up in beech forest where fly agaric has become naturalised. Cap colour helps but the ranges meet at orange. This one's cap is golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. The peppery bolete's is fawn to light brown, brownish orange or cinnamon brown, and slightly slimy when wet. Look at the stem. The peppery bolete's stem is golden yellow at the base, with yellow flesh. This one's stem matches the cap or is reddish, pale yellow at the very top, with pale reddish-brown flesh. A crumb of the peppery bolete, chewed and spat out, is acrid and peppery; this one's taste is not distinctive.

New Zealand Organisms Register, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young' — endemic; basionym Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzor.org.nz/names/169c81df-1fb4-4b19-9e3e-35ac5693f7c6

Conservation, global. IUCN/Global Fungal Red List assessment by J.A. Cooper, 26/07/2019 — Data Deficient, because the population size is uncertain and a decline is possible. Known from 23 records at 13 localities, with only 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the invasive C. piperatus in the same period; an estimate of up to 15,000 mature individuals across roughly 1,000 unrecorded sites. Recorded from both the North and South Islands, in beech forest. Ecology: likely a parasite on indigenous ectomycorrhizal fungi rather than mycorrhizal with the beech itself, host unknown, which may be what restricts it — so habitat prose should not say it partners with Nothofagus, only that it grows under it. Threat: displacement by the introduced C. piperatus and its host Amanita muscaria, which now occupy all but one recorded location of this species. No open licence on the page, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://redlist.info/iucn/species_view/112183/

Biota of New Zealand, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus (McNabb) Pegler & T.W.K. Young 1981' — endemic and present. A third synonym beyond the basionym: Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. 1982. Hosts given as Nothofagus menziesii and N. truncata. Recorded from Buller, Fiordland, Marlborough Sounds, Nelson, Taupo, Wairarapa and Wellington, with historical records from Southland — a much wider range than the Nelson and Southland the NZPCN page gives, so the habitat text should not be written to the narrower claim. Images are under varying copyright and no blanket licence is stated, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/1cb1d0b5-36b9-11d5-9548-00d0592d548c

Landcare Research Fungal Guide, genus Chalciporus — the genus is characterised by reddish pores and bright yellow mycelium at the stipe base, with a viscid cap and a cinnamon to flesh-brown spore print. Two species here: C. aurantiacus, endemic, under native Nothofagus, with a golden yellow, apricot or reddish brown cap and a dull red pore surface; and C. piperatus, exotic, under pines and introduced broadleaves, usually close to Amanita muscaria. That contrast — native beech versus pine, and cap and pore colour — is the axis a person can write the lookalike guidance on. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://fungalguide.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/FG_Genus.aspx?Group=Chalciporus&pk=24737

Queensland Mycological Society, 'Queensland Fungal Record: Chalciporus aff. aurantiacus', P. Leonard, last updated 09/10/2017 — NOT this species. It is an Australian collection growing with Eucalyptus, and the record's own notes say the Queensland material is distinct from the New Zealand fungus: smaller, with pinkish red pores and narrower spores. Its measurements must not be used to describe the endemic. Recorded here only so the next person knows the near-relative exists and why it was set aside. © Queensland Mycological Society. Checked 07/10/2026. https://qldfungi.org.au/wp-content/uploads/FoQs/C-Misc/Chalciporus-aff-aurantiacus.pdf

Wikipedia contributors, 'Chalciporus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — genus of Boletaceae, suborder Boletineae, about 25 species, erected by Frédéric Bataille in 1908. Boletoid fruit bodies with pores in shades of red to pink, stipes lacking reticulation, yellow mycelium and smooth oval spores. C. aurantiacus appears in the species list but the article carries no description of it and does not mention New Zealand at all. The genus prose is openly licensed and could be quoted verbatim as genus context if that is wanted, but there is no species prose here to render. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalciporus

Wikidata, Q10448162 — identifiers, for anyone chasing this further: GBIF 2524866, iNaturalist 409342, Index Fungorum 112183, NZOR 169c81df-1fb4-4b19-9e3e-35ac5693f7c6. Two of its claims are wrong or stale and are recorded here so they are not picked up again. It gives the basionym as Xerocomelus aurantiacus; Index Fungorum and NZOR both give Xerocomus aurantiacus McNabb, which is the one to use, with Boletus aurantiacus (McNabb) G. Stev. an illegitimate later name. And it reports an NZTCS status of Nationally Critical, which is the superseded Hitchmough 2002 listing — see the NZTCS 38 entry below. The four language Wikipedias linked (Cebuano, Swedish, Silesian, Waray-Waray) are bot-generated stubs; there is no English article for the species. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q10448162

Kaimai Bush, 'Chalciporus' — a small bolete, 30–60 mm across, dry, cap yellowish to apricot, pores dull red, yellow mycelium at the stipe base, under native beech. Gives the former name as Xerocomelus aurantiacus, agreeing with Wikidata against NZOR. Sets C. piperatus beside it as the introduced one under Pinus radiata, fawn to light brown, 40–70 mm, dull brown-red pores. No licence statement, so facts only. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.kaimaibush.co.nz/Fungi/C/chalciporus.html

New Zealand Plant Conservation Network, factsheet PDF generated 05/06/2026 — the print version of the species page already cited above, with no facts beyond it. Checked 07/10/2026. https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/site/assets/files/0/20/990/chalciporus-aurantiacus.pdf

Conservation, national — THIS SETTLES IT. Cooper, Buchanan, Leonard, Allison-Cooper, Johnston, Padamsee, McKenzie & Michel, 'Conservation status of selected species of non-lichenised agarics, boletes and russuloid fungi in Aotearoa New Zealand, 2021', New Zealand Threat Classification Series 38, Department of Conservation, October 2022. ISSN 2324-1713, ISBN 978-1-99-116195-6. Licensed CC BY 4.0 — the only openly licensed source on this entry, so its text may be quoted verbatim with credit. Chalciporus aurantiacus is NOT THREATENED, listed with a status change of 'Better': it is one of nine taxa previously assessed as Threatened – Nationally Critical under Hitchmough 2002 whose status improved 'because of a better understanding of their potential distributions'. The Nationally Critical figure that Wikidata still carries is the 2002 listing and is twenty years out of date. Note the national and global assessments disagree in tone and that is not an error: Not Threatened here, Data Deficient globally in 2019. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/nztcs38entire.pdf

MOSTLY RESOLVED, and the resolution favours Cooper: whether this species has yellow mycelium at the stipe base. Cooper's IUCN assessment says C. aurantiacus 'has more persistent orange/red colours and lacks the yellow mycelium at the stipe base', making its absence the separator from C. piperatus. The Landcare Fungal Guide genus page says the genus is characterised by 'the base of the stipe with bright yellow mycelium', and Kaimai Bush gives this species yellow basal mycelium outright. The MycoKeys revision of the subfamily settles the genus-level half of it: across the Chalciporoideae species it describes, basal mycelium is white in five and yellowish in one, so yellow basal mycelium is NOT a genus character and the Fungal Guide's claim is a generalisation from New Zealand's two species. That leaves the specialist who assessed this species against an amateur site repeating a genus page. McNabb's description does not mention basal mycelium at all, so it cannot arbitrate. Cooper is the better authority, but the character has not been checked on a specimen, so the lookalike guidance is safer on cap colour and host tree — which every source agrees on. Checked 07/10/2026.

REJECTED, recorded so it is not used: The Hidden Forest, 'Chalciporus aurantiacus'. It calls the species 'Exotic (Introduced)' and 'Australasian' where NZOR, Biota NZ, the Fungal Guide and the IUCN assessment all have it endemic to New Zealand; gives a season of spring to summer against iNaturalist's January–May records; and gives a cap of 20–60 mm and a stipe of 30–70 mm against McNabb's 3–5.5 cm cap and 2–3.5 cm stipe. Its figures appear to describe something else. Nothing from it is used. It also repeats the yellow-basal-mycelium claim as a key Chalciporus trait, which the MycoKeys revision contradicts. No licence statement either. Checked 07/10/2026. http://hiddenforest.co.nz/fungi/family/boletaceae/bolet03.htm

Zhang, Li, Liang, Mu, Yu, Wu, Chen, Pu & Zeng (2025), 'The subfamily Chalciporoideae (Boletaceae, Boletales) in China', MycoKeys 124: 123–157, DOI 10.3897/mycokeys.124.165901, CC BY 4.0 — openly licensed and quotable, but it does not mention C. aurantiacus anywhere, so there is no description here to use. Two things it does give. Basal mycelium is white in five of the species it describes and yellowish in one, which is the evidence that yellow basal mycelium is not a genus character — see the mycelium note above. And on trophic mode: unlike most Boletaceae, Chalciporoideae species 'may adopt various nutritional strategies, including ectomycorrhizal, saprotrophic, or mycoparasitic modes', with C. piperatus now thought 'more likely a mycoparasitic or saprotrophic fungus' on isotopic and synthesis evidence. That independently supports Cooper's reading of this species as a parasite on other fungi rather than a beech partner. Retrieved 07/10/2026. https://mycokeys.pensoft.net/article/165901/

SEARCH EXHAUSTED for an openly licensed description, 07/10/2026 — recorded so it is not re-searched blind. Checked and came up empty: English Wikipedia (no species article; the CC BY-SA genus article carries no species text and never mentions New Zealand); the new-record-paper route that filled bluefoot-bolete (inapplicable — the species is endemic, so there is no 'first record for X' literature); the CC BY MycoKeys revision of the subfamily (does not include it); GBIF (no description attached to the species in any of its eight checklist datasets); Zenodo and the Biodiversity Literature Repository (no treatments); NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0 but a status assessment, no description). Everything descriptive that exists is all rights reserved — McNabb via the Virtual Mycota, NZPCN, Kaimai Bush — or wrong, as with The Hidden Forest. CONCLUSION: there is no openly licensed description of this species to copy. The summary, habitat and identification have to be written for this guide from the facts above, which README:267 permits with an empty sources array. The protologue itself is McNabb 1968, New Zealand Journal of Botany 6(2): 137–176, DOI 10.1080/0028825X.1968.10429056 — paywalled at Taylor & Francis, and the thing to read if the basal mycelium question is ever worth settling properly.

lookalikes.howToTell: written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, 07/10/2026. It restates facts from two all-rights-reserved sources — the Landcare Fungal Guide genus page (C. aurantiacus endemic under native Nothofagus, golden yellow to apricot or reddish brown cap, dull red pores; C. piperatus exotic under pines and introduced broadleaves, usually near Amanita muscaria) and Kaimai Bush (30–60 mm against 40–70 mm, apricot against fawn to light brown) — with no text reproduced. No openly licensed source separates these two species; the CC BY MycoKeys revision of the subfamily does not mention C. aurantiacus at all. Deliberately NOT written on yellow basal mycelium, which Cooper gives as the separator but the Fungal Guide and Kaimai Bush contradict — see the mycelium note on chalciporus-aurantiacus. Flagged here so it is greppable and reversible.

'unpalatable' follows the trusted NZ source; the owner may prefer 'toxic' as the cautious label. The proposed risk changes the stored value 'unknown' to 'unpalatable'.

Origin checked 20/10/2026 (owner: "find the bio status all shipped species and label them accordingly"), retrieved 20/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Chalciporus aurantiacus' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Chalciporus%20aurantiacus): NZFUNGI biostatus Endemic, Present. Origin 'endemic' stands.
sourcingNote: An endemic species with no openly licensed description. The Virtual Mycota carries McNabb's account and it is in copyright; there is no English Wikipedia article, only a CC BY-SA genus article that never mentions the species or New Zealand; and the one openly licensed source here, NZTCS 38 (CC BY 4.0), is a status assessment with no description in it. So the summary, habitat and identification have to be written, from the facts gathered in the sources above. The conservation question is now settled and it went the permissive way: NZTCS 38 lists this species as Not Threatened, upgraded from the Nationally Critical of 2002 that Wikidata still shows, so harvesting guidance is not ruled out on status grounds. It still has to reckon with the IUCN picture behind that status — 5 confirmed sightings since 2013 against 52 for the introduced bolete that is displacing it, and now present at all but one of this species' recorded sites. The lookalike card to peppery-bolete has the material it needs in cap colour and host tree: apricot to reddish orange under native beech, against fawn under pine. It must NOT be written on yellow basal mycelium, which three sources contradict each other on — see the unresolved note in the sources. Photos are attached, so the only remaining blockers are prose: summary, habitat, identification, a warning or the lookalike card, and the harvesting and tikanga guidance. The lookalike card to the other Chalciporus is the assistant's restatement of the Fungal Guide and Kaimai Bush on the owner's instruction, not the owner's words.

sources: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), 'Malva parviflora'
edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked as a potherb. A mild pleasant flavour, they make a very acceptable alternative to lettuce in salads. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. They are used to make a creamed vegetable soup that resembles pea soup. A few leaves are also added for colouring. The seeds have a pleasant nutty flavour, though they are too small for most people to want to collect in quantity.

Wikipedia, 'Malva parviflora' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Waste land, cultivated land, coastal habitats, river beds.
M. parviflora typically grows on agricultural lands and in disturbed sites such as roadsides.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Malva parviflora' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Malva parviflora' — "(Fig. 84)" omitted

identification.text:
M. parviflora has a decumbent or erect habit, growing up to 50–80 cm in height. The broad leaves have 5–7 shallow lobes. The lobe edges are round-toothed, with varying hairiness. It has small white or pink flowers at the base of leaf stalks. The 2 mm seeds are reddish-brown and kidney-shaped.
Newly sprouted plants have hairless, heart-shaped cotyledons with long stalks. These cotyledons are 3–12 mm long and 3–8 mm wide. Stalks usually do have hairs. The first leaf is rounder and larger than the others. True leaves are round and weakly lobed with wavy, shallow-toothed edges and a red spot at the leaf base. The plant rapidly grows a deep taproot.
M. parviflora has a diploid chromosome count of 42.
M. parviflora is distinguished from M. neglecta by shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx, and reticulately veined mericarps with winged edges.

Annual, procumbent to erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with mostly stellate hairs. Lvs sparsely to densely clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–8 cm diam.; petioles 1.5–10 cm long; stipules ovate-triangular, 2–6 mm long. Fls in axillary clusters of (1)–2–5; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(20) mm long; epicalyx segments linear, somewhat < calyx; calyx teeth ± orbicular with acute apex, glabrous or sparsely clothed in stellate hairs and ciliate, greatly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; petals white, pale mauve or pink towards tips, ± = or only slightly > calyx, 3–5 mm long. Mericarps (9)–10–(11) per fr., glabrous or hairy, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges slightly winged and sometimes toothed.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them; use the petal length, the calyx in fruit and the edges of the fruit segments. Leaf shape and size overlap (cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm across, common mallow 1–15(–20) cm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Flora of New Zealand separates the two by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

preparation.text: Leaves raw in salads or cooked as a potherb; immature seeds raw or cooked, or in a creamed soup. In Jaén, Spain, the little fruits, shaped like bread rolls, have been eaten as a snack (Andújar, Quesada).

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author says little mallow is the kind most eaten in Morocco. Serves 4. About 225 g mallow leaves and stems (about 2 litres, packed), 120 ml olive oil, about 120 ml chopped parsley and/or coriander leaves, 4 cloves garlic, pressed or finely chopped, 1½ tsp paprika, 1½ tsp ground cumin, ¼ tsp salt, ¼ tsp cayenne pepper (optional), 2 tbsp lemon juice, the chopped pulp of 1 preserved lemon, and preserved lemon rind and a handful of red olives to garnish. Wash the mallow thoroughly, drain, chop the leaves and stems and steam over simmering water for 15–20 minutes, until tender; it shrinks a lot and darkens. Press out the extra water against the side of the steamer basket. Meanwhile, fry the oil, garlic, herbs and spices over medium or medium-low heat for several minutes, until the herbs wilt and the garlic smells fragrant, without burning the garlic, then take off the heat. Add the mallow, preserved lemon pulp and lemon juice and cook over medium heat for 5–10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, and serve warm or at room temperature with the olives and preserved lemon rind, usually as a dip with bread. Without preserved lemon, use a little more lemon juice; the same method works with spinach, kale or purslane, with the steaming time adjusted.
recipes.title: Moroccan mallow salad (khoubiza or bakkoula)

recipes.method: Written for cheeseweed, which the author names as Malva parviflora, in the US Southwest. Several handfuls of cheeseweed leaves (about 1 litre once chopped), 1 large onion, diced, cooking oil (the author suggests bacon fat or butter), and salt and pepper, or lemon or vinegar. Strip the leaves from the main stem and wash them; the leaf stalks can stay but chop them small, as they can be tough (chopped stems add a celery-like crunch). Chop the leaves coarsely. Brown the onion in a large frying pan or wok as much as you like (spring onions or garlic chives also work), add the greens and cover with a lid so their own moisture steams them as they shrink. Season and serve as a side dish or on pasta.

summary.text:
Malva parviflora is an annual or perennial herb that is native to Northern Africa, Southern Europe, and Western and Central Asia and is widely naturalized elsewhere. Common names include cheeseweed, cheeseweed mallow, Egyptian mallow, least mallow, little mallow, mallow, marshmallow, small-flowered mallow, small-flowered marshmallow, and smallflower mallow.
Its native range extends from the Mediterranean, through West Asia, and to Central Asia and can be found in Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia, Kuwait, Afghanistan, Cyprus, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Croatia, Italy, Malta, Spain, France, and Portugal. The species is widely naturalized elsewhere, including in North America since the 19th century. It is a naturalized weed in Australia.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, throughout the South Island except Westland and Fiordland, and on the Kermadec Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1883.

warnings: M. parviflora accumulates pollutants such as cadmium and chromium. In nitrogen-rich soils, the plant's leaves and seeds can be toxic to cattle and poultry due to an accumulation of nitrates. If consumed in large amounts, the plant can damage energy homeostasis in horses, possibly due to its cyclopropene fatty acids.
Poisonous (Connor 1977).

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psidium_cattleyanum A small, highly branched tree usually 2–4 m and at most 13 m. Both the thin skin and the juicy interior are soft and edible, though the skin is often removed for a sweeter flavour; it also makes jam and juices, and the leaves can be brewed for tea. The seeds are small, white, high in vitamin C. On how aggressive it is, which is this entry's framing: it is considered the most invasive plant in Hawaii, and is among the worst on Réunion and Madagascar, where it threatens endemic forest — and it was introduced to most of the places it now invades precisely because people wanted the fruit.

On how fast the fruit goes over. Commercial products are not made from it partly for want of a market but also because of the heavy presence of fruit flies, which renders the fruit inedible soon after picking. identification.text: Wild types are large shrubs or small trees reaching 8–12 metres tall, sometimes spiny, with glabrous, ovate deciduous leaves 3–7 cm long. It is one of the first European trees to flower, often before the leaves have opened. The flowers are white or pale pink and about 2 cm across, with five petals and many stamens. The fruit is an edible drupe, 2–3 cm in diameter, ripening to yellow or red. They are self-fertile but can also be pollinated by other Prunus varieties such as the Victoria plum. The plant propagates by seed or by suckering, and is often used as the rootstock for other Prunus species and cultivars.

lookalikes.howToTell: No single test settles it; most of these ranges overlap. Size: a plum is 25–45 mm long, sometimes only 20 mm, and a cherry plum 15–30 mm, sometimes only 10 mm, so a fruit over 30 mm points to the plum, and anything smaller is not settled by size (Flora of North America gives the plum 15–35 mm). Colour overlaps: plums are green, yellow, red or blackish purple, usually bloomed; cherry plums yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, slightly bloomed. Do not use the midrib — cherry plum's can be densely hairy on its lower third underneath. Flora of New Zealand records cherry plum fruiting from November to January and the plum from January to February. Both flower in August and September, and their petals and flower stalks overlap in size.

preparation.text:
The fruits are edible. Some varieties have sweet fruits that can be eaten fresh, while others are sour and better for making jam. Cherry plums are a key ingredient in Georgian cuisine where they are used to produce tkemali sauce, as well as a number of popular dishes, such as kharcho soup and chakapuli stew.
In Middle Asia and Caucasus considerable quantities are processed to preserves, jam, pie and 'lavas' (fruit-flesh dried in thin layers).

recipes.method: 1.8 kg cherry plums, 1.8 kg brown cane sugar and about 285 ml water. Put everything in a large, flat-bottomed pan, stir, and bring to the boil. Boil until the skins start to come off and the fruit comes away from the stones. Pour the mixture into a large piece of muslin and squeeze the pulp through it back into the pan. Keep boiling until it reaches setting point, which can take as long as 30 minutes. To test, chill a couple of saucers in the fridge before you start; drip a little jam onto one, let it cool for a moment, then push it sideways with a finger — it is ready when it wrinkles and feels tacky. Pour into sterilised jars and screw on the lids. Makes about 7 jars.
recipes.title: Cherry plum jam

recipes.method: 1 kg cherry plums, 1 kg white granulated sugar, 2 tbsp freshly squeezed lemon juice and, if you like, 1 tsp vanilla extract or the scraped seeds of half a vanilla bean. Sterilise the jars and let them cool, and count the plums. Put the plums in a large heavy-based pot, stoned or whole (the author prefers to stone them first), and warm over medium heat, stirring often so they do not catch, until they burst and release some juice. Stir in the sugar and lemon juice, bring to the boil, then lower to a hard simmer; if the plums went in whole, press them against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon until the stones come free and sink. Cook to 105 °C, or as high as about 107 °C for a firmer set; the last few degrees can take a long time. Without a thermometer, chill a small plate in the freezer, and once the jam has noticeably thickened put a spoonful on it: if it looks set, it is done; if it is runny, keep cooking and test again every few minutes. Take it off the heat and stir in the vanilla, if using. If the plums were not stoned, strain the jam through a loose colander as needed and count the stones to be sure they are all out. The skins can stay in, or be removed with a colander or food mill. Ladle into the jars leaving 1 cm at the top, stand them in a very large pot of hot water covering them by 4 cm, bring to the boil and boil for 15 minutes, then lift them out very carefully and leave them to cool completely on the bench. Skip the water bath only if the jam will be eaten within a couple of weeks, kept in the fridge. Makes about 1.2 litres, and scales well.
recipes.title: Cherry plum jam with lemon and vanilla

recipes.method: 2.8 kg cherry plums, 1.4 kg sugar, about 4 litres water, 1 sachet wine yeast (any red wine yeast will do), 1 tsp yeast nutrient and 1 tsp pectolase. Boil 1 litre of the water, pour it over the fruit and crush the fruit with the end of a rolling pin until no lumps are left. Leave it a few hours, then add the rest of the water and the pectolase — plums are rich in the pectin that sets jam and also clouds wine. Leave a couple of days, then strain through a fine sieve. Bring the juice quickly to the boil in a saucepan and turn off the heat straight away; the author once skipped this and lost the whole batch to acetobacter. Pour the hot juice over the sugar and stir until it dissolves, cool to room temperature, then add the yeast and yeast nutrient. Top up to 4.5 litres if necessary, funnel into a demijohn and fit an airlock. Rack into a clean demijohn after four to six weeks, and again a few weeks later if you want. Bottle when clear — or, if it will not clear completely, bottle it anyway.
recipes.title: Cherry plum wine

recipes.method: Written for plums in general rather than cherry plums. Makes a 1-litre jar. 250 g granulated sugar, 420 ml apple cider vinegar, ½ tsp crushed coriander, 1 tsp ground cardamom, 750 g plums, stoned and halved, 1 small cinnamon stick, 1 red chilli cut into quarters and 1 star anise. In a large saucepan, bring the sugar, vinegar, coriander and cardamom to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to infuse. Add the plums and cook for about 2 minutes, until just softened but still holding their shape. Put the cinnamon, chilli and star anise in a sterilised 1-litre jar (or two or three smaller ones), scoop in the plums and pack them tightly, leaving about 1.25 cm at the top, then pour the vinegar over until they are completely covered. Seal while still warm, leave to cool at room temperature, then refrigerate for 2 weeks before serving. They should last a couple of weeks in the fridge; for longer storage they can be processed in a water bath. Good on toast with farmhouse cheese, on savoury porridge, in salads, or with pork chops, chicken or turkey.

summary.text:
Prunus cerasifera is a species of plum known by the common names cherry plum and myrobalan plum.
It is native to Southeast Europe and Western Asia, and is naturalised in the British Isles and scattered locations in North America. It is also naturalized in parts of Southeast Australia where it is considered to be a mildly invasive weed of bushland near urban centers.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When injested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

edibleParts.text: Whole aerial plant — leaves, stems, flowers.

habitat.text: Damp shaded garden beds, under hedges, cultivated soil. Grows in dense low mats.

identification.text: Small oval opposite leaves on a weak sprawling stem. The giveaway: a single line of fine hairs running along one side of the stem, switching sides at each node. Tiny white flowers with five deeply split petals that look like ten.

lookalikes.howToTell: Snap a stem: petty spurge bleeds white milky sap, and no milky sap is recorded for chickweed. Spurge sap irritates skin and has caused serious eye inflammation, so keep it away from your face. Petty spurge's stems are hairless, where chickweed's carry a line of hairs down one side; its leaves are alternate, where chickweed's are in opposite pairs; and its small green flower heads have no petals, where chickweed has white petals split almost to the base (rarely none). Both are weeds of gardens and cultivated ground.
lookalikes.name: Petty spurge

lookalikes.howToTell: Scarlet pimpernel's stems are four-angled (square in section) and hairless; chickweed's are round with a single line of hairs. Pimpernel's flowers are orange, orange-red or deep blue, borne singly in the leaf axils on stalks (0.5)–1–2 cm long; chickweed's petals are white and divided almost to the base (rarely absent), in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly dotted with black glands underneath; chickweed's lower leaves have a stalk about as long as the blade. Leaf size and the sprawling habit overlap and do not separate them.

habitat.text: Grown in sunny conditions, it is normally found within coastal dunes and bluffs, margins of estuaries, along roadsides; at elevations from sea level to 100 m along the southern Pacific Coast of North America.

identification.text:
Carpobrotus chilensis sends out prostrate stems that are upwards of 2 metres long; these root at the nodes and can carpet the ground, with fleshy, pointed leaves which are 4–7.5 centimetres long and triangular in cross-section. It is similar to, and often mistaken for, its close relative the "ice plant" (Carpobrotus edulis), which is larger, and grows alongside and sometimes hybridizes with C. chilensis. For comparison, the larger flowers of C. edulis (6.4 to 15.2 cm [2.5 to 6 in] in diameter) are yellow or light pink, whereas C. chilensis flowers are smaller (3.8 to 6.4 cm [1.5 to 2.5 in] in diameter) and deep magenta.
The flowers open in the morning and close at night, and it can bloom and fruit all year round. The fruit has 8–10 chambers.
The plant can easily be propagated by cuttings, which can be planted immediately in soil and will root without the need of rooting hormone or mist.

summary.text:
Carpobrotus chilensis is a species of edible succulent plant known by the common name sea fig.
Usually found in warm temperate and subtropical areas, it is probably native to southern Africa. It is familiar elsewhere, particularly the coastline of western North America, where it is an introduced invasive species that has taken hold and become commonplace. It is also found, and naturalised, in Argentina, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, Australia, Spain, Greece, Southern England and New Zealand.

identification.text:
Large, suckering, spiny shrub up to 3–(4) m high when mature and several m diam.;  stems brownish olive, smooth, shining and glabrous when young, often forming dense thickets.  Lvs distributed along length of first-year, non-flowering stems, and in fascicles on short shoots on older flowering stems;  petiole 6–12 mm long, green or red-tinged, glabrous; blade obovate to elliptic, finely serrate to crenate, (30)–50–80–(100) × 20–50 mm, acute and often curled at tip, attenuate to petiole at base, glabrous, ± shining and deep green on upper surface, paler below;  lvs of short shoots on flowering stems similar but smaller;  stipules prominent, reniform, up to 12 × 20 mm, crenate.  Fls in fascicles of (3)–4–5, 25–35 mm diam., ± sessile.  Sepals fused at base;  lobes broadly ovate to oblong, 3–5 mm long, green, glabrous, with hyaline ciliate margins. Petals 5, ± overlapping, suberect or spreading, broad-ovate to orbicular, 12–20 mm diam., shortly clawed;  limb white to bright pink to scarlet. Stamens < petals; filaments coloured as in petals.  Fr. up to 60 mm diam., ± broadly ovoid to subglobose but often misshapen, yellowish and often brown-speckled, indented at base and apex.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
In the most common variety, the fruit is roughly pear-shaped, somewhat flattened and with coarse wrinkles, ranging from 10–25 cm long, with thin green skin fused with green to white flesh, and a single, large, flattened stone. This seed or stone can be up to 10 cm long by 7 cm wide. Some varieties have spiny fruits. Depending on the variety, a single fruit can weigh up to 1.2 kg. The flesh has a very watery but complex taste and the texture is described as a cross between a potato and a cucumber. Natives describe the spiny varieties as being more flavorful than the spineless ones.
The chayote vine can be grown on the ground, but as a climbing plant, it will grow onto anything, and can easily rise as high as 12 m when support is provided. It has heart-shaped leaves, 10–25 cm wide and tendrils on the stem. The plant bears male flowers in clusters and solitary female flowers.

identification.text:
Perennial herb, with slender or sometimes fairly stout caulorrhiza. Hairs soft, retrorse or antrorse, generally appressed and often short, sometimes spreading. Stems slender, prostrate or spreading, with ± retrorse hairs; branches usually many. Basal lvs rarely persistent through growing season; petioles to 12–(19) cm long; hairs retrorse and dense. Lamina usually to 3–(4) cm diam., reniform to orbicular or broadly ovate, lobed 3/4-⅞ way to midrib; lobes (3)–5, narrowly to broadly obovate-cuneate, obovate-elliptic, obovate-oblong, or oblong, with appressed hairs on both sides or glabrous above, rounded to acute or mucronate at apex; larger lobes usually with 2 ± oblong or elliptic secondary lobes. Cauline lvs smaller, with fewer lobes. Peduncles (with pedicels) usually 1–3–(4) cm long, filiform, with dense, retrorse hairs; bracteoles subulate or linear-subulate; fls 1–(2). Sepals 3–5–(6) × 1–2.5 mm, lanceolate to elliptic, broadly elliptic or ± ovate, usually with green margin, sometimes completely purple; hairs ± spreading, often very short and antrorse towards apex, sometimes few. Petals 4–5 × 2–2.5 mm, broadly obovate, pink. Mericarps 2–3 mm long, with ± dense hairs; beak (6)–7–10 mm long. Seed 1.5–1.9 mm long, oblong, distinctly alveolate.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from Solander's geranium on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from turnip-rooted geranium on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in turnip-rooted geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in turnip-rooted geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (NZTCS 2023).

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from Australasian cranesbill on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Australasian cranesbill, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Australasian cranesbill. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Australasian cranesbill overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga).

summary.text:
Geranium potentilloides, belongs to the family Geraniaceae, and is a small prostrate perennial herb that can grow up to 60cm high. The species is commonly referred to as Soft Cranesbill or Cinquefoil geranium.
Geranium potentilloides is native to the south-east of Australia, New Zealand and Indonesia.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Auckland southwards, widespread and common; S.: Nelson, Marlborough, and collected once between Akatore and Glenledi (S. Otago).

edibleParts.text: Young shoots and tips before flowering.

habitat.text: Hedges, garden edges, fence lines, damp waste ground; scrambles over anything nearby.

identification.text: Long, weak, square stems that cling to skin and clothing with tiny hooked hairs. Leaves in whorls of six to eight narrow blades around the stem. Tiny white four-petalled flowers, then small round burrs that stick to everything.

identification.text:
Climbing or scrambling, dioecious or monoecious perennial with tuberous woody rootstock; stems to  c. 3 m long, glabrous, flexuous.  Lvs all similar. Petioles slender, = or often > lamina.  Lamina 3–8 × 2–6 cm,  ± triangular or hastate with 2 long basal lobes at 45° to petiole, otherwise entire, slightly puberulent on main veins below when young;  sinus broad and rounded;  apex acuminate to cuspidate.  Panicle pyramidal, with small lvs in the lower axils only.  Pedicels filiform, long, glabrous.  Perianth 1.5–2 mm long, green; outer segments ± ovate-oblong, becoming strongly reflexed in ♀ fls.  Fr. valves (4)–6–9–(9.5) mm diam., orbicular, entire, prominently reticulate, cordate, yellow, pink to crimson;  tubercles 0. Nuts  c. 3 mm long, glossy light brown;  keels almost winged.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Rumex sagittatus, synonym Acetosa sagittata, commonly known as turkey rhubarb or rambling dock or potato vine, is a herbaceous perennial plant native to southern Africa, which has become a weed in Australia and New Zealand.
The plant is native to southern Africa, where it occurs from Malawi and Zambia south to South Africa. It has become naturalised in many parts of Australia near urban areas, from Queensland to eastern Tasmania, and warmer locales in New Zealand.
It spreads by seed or by resprouting from the tuber. The seeds float on water and hence may be conveyed far from the parent plant. Tubers may be broken up by tractors or road graders and each fragment may be able to regrow; they can also be difficult to find with removal of plants by hand. Rumex sagittatus may grow and smother other plants it covers.
