habitat.text: Lactarius glyciosmus is a common mushroom and is found under broad-leaved trees, particularly birch—often inside of sphagnum moss. It grows in soil individually or in scattered groups.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lactarius glyciosmus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Lactarius glyciosmus is a small to medium-sized agaric, which typically has a convex cap measuring between 2 and 6 centimetres, with a small central depression developing with age. Sometimes there is a central pimple, and the cap is typically coloured a greyish lilac, sometimes varying to a pale buff. It is thin fleshed, with an incurved margin in younger specimens. The stem measures between 25 and 65 millimetres in height, with a width between 4 and 12 mm. The cylindrical stem is typically widest at the bottom becoming narrower towards the top, or sometimes club shaped. The stem is concolorous with the cap, but sometimes is a little paler or with a yellowish hue. The stem is particularly soft and easily broken, and can become hollow. The flesh is buff. The gills are decurrent and crowded, and vary in colour from a pale yellowish to a pale flesh, turning to a greyish lilac with age. The milk is white with an initially mild, later hot and acrid taste. The mushroom has a strong smell of coconuts.
The spore print is a creamy white colour, and the spores themselves are broadly elliptic in shape, and covered with small warts. The warts are connected by thin ridges in an incomplete network. The spores measure between 8 and 9 by between 5 and 6 micrometres.


Similar species
It is similar to L. vietus, the grey milk cap, but is differentiated by the fact L. vietus milk dries grey, while L. glyciosmus milk dries white. It can also be confused with L. cocosiolens, which also smells of coconuts, but L. cocosiolens has a slimy brown or orange cap and is not found among birch.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

Season: iNaturalist NZ observations of 'Lactarius glyciosmus' in New Zealand by month of year — 45 research-grade records, March to May carrying every month at or above a quarter of the April peak. The 'late summer and autumn' of the description is the northern season, not this one. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/382879

Edibility, and the sources hedge. Wikipedia calls it 'a semi-edible mushroom' and, separately, 'considered edible, but is not recommended by some mycologists', noting it is sold in rural markets in Yunnan. Its own description gives the milk as 'initially mild, later hot and acrid'. Wikipedia contributors. 'Lactarius glyciosmus', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactarius_glyciosmus

Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius glyciosmus' — the New Zealand record, with the description attributed to McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66. McNabb's text is in copyright, so the facts below are restated and nothing is quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5181 Biostatus 'Present in region - Exotic'. On New Zealand material: cap 3–6 cm, typically umbonate when young and usually centrally papillate at maturity, dry and azonate, greyish lilac to pale greyish brown with faint lilac tints or brownish grey with leaden tints; gills pale pinkish buff; latex rather watery, white, unchanging; stem 2–5 cm by 0.7–1.1 cm and solid; spores 7.5–10 × 6.5–8 µm; taste mild at first, becoming slightly acrid. McNabb notes it is introduced and typically associated with broadleaved trees, particularly Betula.

First Nature, 'Lactarius glyciosmus' (coconut milkcap) — © First Nature / Pat O'Reilly, all rights reserved, so facts only and nothing quoted beyond the short phrases marked. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-glyciosmus.php Cap 2–5.5 cm, greyish lilac to dull buff, thin-fleshed, sometimes with a small central pimple; gills pale yellow becoming lilaceous grey with age; stem fragile and often hollow when old; spore print creamy white; taste mild at first, then slightly hot and bitter. Mycorrhizal mainly with birch, sometimes alder and other broadleaves. Rated edible but rarely gathered, because it fruits in too small a quantity to interest a forager. On separating it: 'No other pale milkcaps have such a distinctive coconut scent.'

MushroomExpert.Com, 'Lactarius glyciosmus' — cap 2–7 cm, thin and fragile, dry, bald, finely roughened, pinkish buff; gills whitish to yellowish and not bruising or discolouring; latex white, often scanty, unchanging, not staining the tissues; odour 'strongly of coconuts'; taste slightly acrid; KOH yellowish on the cap surface; spore print cream. Mycorrhizal with birch and possibly alder. Cannot settle edibility by design: 'This site contains no information about the edibility or toxicity of mushrooms.' © MushroomExpert.Com, so facts only. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.mushroomexpert.com/lactarius_glyciosmus.html

How strong the coconut smell is, and the sources disagree — which matters, because the smell is this entry's identifying feature. Wikipedia: 'a strong smell of coconuts'. MushroomExpert: 'strongly of coconuts'. First Nature calls the scent distinctive. But McNabb, describing New Zealand material, records it as 'faintly of coconut'. The sources also split on the stem: solid (McNabb) against fragile and often hollow when old (First Nature, Wikipedia). The sources do not agree on how strong the scent is, and this entry does not pick between them. Checked 06/10/2026.

identification.text:
It is a strongly aromatic shrub growing as high as 1 to 2 metres tall. The leaves are evergreen,  2–6 centimetres long, and 4–6 millimetres broad. The flowers are typically purple (lavender-coloured), produced on spikes 2–8 cm long at the top of slender, leafless stems 10–30 cm long.
Members of sect. Spica Ging., lacking any enlarged terminal bracts but with bracteoles present, are very common cultigens in many colder parts of N.Z.; they are mostly selections or hybrids of L. angustifolia Miller (L. spica L. pro parte.) and L. latifolia Villars. These hybrids are collectively called L. × intermedia Lois., a few being valued as a source of oil of lavender. L. angustifolia is often known as English lavender.

lookalikes.howToTell: Common lavender's flower spike has no enlarged bracts at its tip, and has bracteoles; French lavender's spike is crowned by mauve-blue sterile bracts 7–10 mm long, and has no bracteoles. French lavender's leaves are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped. A strong aromatic smell and flower spikes held on long stalks do not separate them. The bract test does not separate common lavender from the lavandins (L. × intermedia), its hybrids with spike lavender, which are very common in gardens in many colder parts of New Zealand and also lack enlarged terminal bracts.
lookalikes.name: French lavender

lookalikes.howToTell: Common lavender's flower spike has no enlarged bracts at its tip, and has bracteoles; topped lavender's spike is crowned by a plume of mauve sterile bracts 1–2 cm long, and has no bracteoles. Common lavender's spikes, 2–8 cm long, sit on slender leafless stalks 10–30 cm long; topped lavender's stalk is only about as long as its spike. Narrow leaves, a strong aromatic smell and purple flowers do not separate them. The bract test does not separate common lavender from the lavandins (L. × intermedia), its hybrids with spike lavender, which are very common in gardens in many colder parts of New Zealand and also lack enlarged terminal bracts.

preparation.text:
The fresh or dried flowers are used as a tea. The fresh flowers are also crystallized or added to jams, ice-creams, vinegars etc as a flavouring.
The flowers are also used as a culinary herb, most often as part of the North American version of the French herb blend called herbes de Provence.

recipes.method: Written for English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) — the author names it and bakes with 'Hidcote'. Cream 115 g butter (or vegan margarine) with 50 g caster sugar until pale and fluffy. Stir in 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, 1 tablespoon dried lavender flowers (or 2 tablespoons fresh), 175 g plain flour and 2 tablespoons plant-based milk, and bring it together into a ball. Wrap and chill for 20 minutes. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the dough out on a lightly floured board, cut out biscuits and bake on a tray for about 10 minutes, until golden. Cool for 5 minutes on the tray, then on a rack. Serve sprinkled with sugar.
recipes.title: Lavender biscuits

recipes.method: Written for English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) by a lavender farm that grows it; the author uses 'Hidcote' for the deepest colour. Pick a handful of flowers just as they open. Heat about 600 ml (2½ cups) milk gently with the flowers; do not let it boil. Strain out the flowers and, while the milk is still hot, stir in about 200 g (1 cup) sugar and ¼ teaspoon salt. Stir in 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and about 950 ml (4 cups) light cream, and chill for at least 2 hours. Churn in an ice-cream maker, or freeze in a steel bowl and whisk every 15 minutes until thick. Scatter in a few fresh florets in the last minutes. With dried flowers instead, use 3 tablespoons, steep them in the hot milk for 5 minutes and strain at once; steeping longer makes it bitter and grey. Metric amounts are converted from the source's cups.
recipes.title: Fresh lavender ice cream

recipes.method: From Lynda Dowling's Herbal Adventures, on the recipe page of a lavender farm that asks for English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia). Sterilise five 1-cup (about 250 ml) jars. Bring about 780 ml (3¼ cups) water to the boil, add about 360 ml (1½ cups) fresh lavender flowers, cover, simmer for 5 minutes and take off the heat. Without lifting the lid, steep for at least 20 minutes, or overnight. Strain, and measure about 720 ml (3 cups) of the infusion into a deep pan. Whisk in one box of powdered pectin and 1 tablespoon white wine vinegar, bring to the boil and whisk in about 800 g (4 cups) sugar. Keep it at a rolling boil that cannot be stirred down for about 1 minute. Take it off the heat, let it stand for 5 minutes, skim, then pour into the jars and seal before it sets. The author lets it age for a month. The source does not give the size of the pectin box. Metric amounts are converted from the source's cups.

summary.text:
Lavandula angustifolia, formerly L. officinalis, is a flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin. Its common names include lavender, true lavender and English lavender (though it is not native to England); also garden lavender, common lavender and narrow-leaved lavender.
In New Zealand it is recorded as casual rather than fully naturalised (Flora of New Zealand Online); NZPCN gives 1994 as its year naturalised, and says it rarely sets seed here.

warnings: NC State Extension rates English lavender as a low-severity poison: its flowers, leaves and stems contain linalool and linalyl acetate, and the symptoms it lists are nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite. It flags the plant as a problem for dogs, cats and horses.

identification.text:
Stoloniferous rosette perennial.  Basal lvs cuneately narrowed to a petiole ± = lamina, mostly spathulate, obovate or elliptic-oblong, crenate-serrate with 2–6 pairs of teeth or remote denticles, almost glabrous to moderately hairy on both surfaces, often more hairy on lower, with 1 main vein, (10)–20–60–(80) × (4)–8–20–(25) mm.  Peduncle moderately to densely hairy, leafless, 3–15–(25) cm long.  Capitula 15–25 mm diam. at anthesis; receptacle conic.  Involucral bracts ovate- to elliptic-oblong, usually obtuse, rarely subacute, sparsely to moderately hairy.  Ray florets in 1–(5) rows; ligules linear, white, often tinged pink to reddish purple on lower surface or at apex, rarely wholly pink to reddish purple, 5–8–(11) mm long.  Disc florets yellow.  Achenes hairy, brown with pale ribs, 1–1.3–(1.6) mm long;  pappus 0. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Bellis perennis ( BEL-iss pə-REN-iss), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
Bellis perennis is native to western, central and northern Europe, including remote islands such as the Faroe Islands, but has become widely naturalised in most temperate regions, including the Americas and Australasia.

The young leaves also make a very acceptable substitute for lettuce in a salad. Immature seed - raw. Used as a nibble, the seeds have a nice nutty flavour. Flowers - raw. Added to salads or used as a garnish.

identification.text:
Common mallow is a herbaceous perennial with an erect or decumbent branched stem up to 1.5 metres tall. The minutely ridged stems are covered with fine soft hairs, sometimes with a slightly bulbous base. The leaves are alternate, with a petiole up to 20 centimetres long, simple but palmate, with stellate hairs (i.e. several strands radiating from a common center) and prominent veins on the underside. 

The flowers are reddish-purple with dark stripes and occur in axillary clusters along the main stem with the flowers at the base opening first. There are 5 petals, and 5 sepals, 3–6 mm long, which are fused in the lower half, and have broadly triangular lobes. There is also an epicalyx (or false calyx) with oblong segments, two-thirds as long as calyx lobes (2–3 mm long x 1.5 mm wide).


Fruits
Nutlets strongly reticulate (usually without hair, with sharp angle between dorsal and lateral surfaces, 5–6 mm in diameter.


Seeds
Also called 'cheeses', the seeds are brown to brownish green when ripe, about 2.5 mm long and wide.


Chemistry
M. sylvestris contains malvin and malonylmalvin. It also contains the naphthoquinone malvone A, which is also a phytoalexin.

The large-flowered mallow is very variable in size, particularly of the fls, and petals may vary in colour from pale pink through to a deep bluish purple. Small-flowered plants appear similar to M. nicaeensis but are distinguished by the slightly longer petals, longer fruiting pedicels, and the presence of hairs at the base of the calyx tube.

Perennial, ascending to erect herb. Stems glabrous to densely hairy with simple and stellate hairs. Lvs ± glabrous to densely hairy, reniform to suborbicular, obtuse to cordate at base, shallowly or moderately 3–5–(7)-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–15–(20) cm diam.; petioles 1–15–(30) cm long; stipules narrowly to broadly ovate with acute apex, 3–10 mm long. Fls 2–10 in axillary clusters or irregular racemes; fruiting pedicels 10–45 mm long; epicalyx segments narrow-oblong to elliptic-ovate, somewhat < calyx; calyx teeth broadly ovate with acute apex, sparsely to densely hairy with stellate or simple hairs and ciliate, not enlarged at fruiting; petals from deep pink to reddish or bluish purple with darker markings, 2–5× as long as calyx, 12–30 mm long. Mericarps 8–12–(15) per fr., usually glabrous, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them; use the petal length, the calyx in fruit and the edges of the fruit segments. Leaf shape and size overlap (cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm across, common mallow 1–15(–20) cm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand says Cretan mallow is often confused with forms of common mallow whose epicalyx segments are slightly joined at the base, and separates it by its round-edged, more or less smooth-backed fruit segments (net-veined and sharply angled in common mallow), its long-pointed calyx teeth (acute in common mallow) and its generally broader epicalyx segments. Petal colour and length overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Petal lengths overlap between 12 and 15 mm, and common mallow can have pale pink flowers, so on a pale, mid-sized flower use the fruit: hairy and smooth-backed in dwarf mallow, usually hairless and strongly net-veined in common mallow. Dwarf mallow lies flat or ascends and common mallow ascends or stands upright, so an ascending plant fits both. Leaf shape and size overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates French mallow from small forms of common mallow by the hairless base of the calyx tube (hairy in common mallow), and notes common mallow's slightly longer petals and longer fruiting stalks. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow's petals (30–40 mm) and common mallow's (12–30 mm) only meet at 30 mm, and both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, so the flower colour does not separate them; check the calyx, long and tube-shaped in island mallow, and the fruit, smooth with one low rib against strongly net-veined. Leaf size overlaps. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the upper stem leaves (cut almost to the base in musk mallow, shallowly lobed in common mallow) and the fruit (densely hairy and smooth-backed against usually hairless and net-veined). Petal lengths overlap ((15–)20–30 mm against 12–30 mm), so the flower does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. The flowers overlap: both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, and tree mallow's 15–20 mm petals sit inside common mallow's 12–30 mm range. Use the epicalyx, which is longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow but shorter than the calyx in common mallow (whose epicalyx segments may be somewhat joined at the base, so joining alone is not a test), and the fruit, ribbed crosswise against net-veined. Both have lobed leaves that can reach 20 cm across. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: In Morocco, Tunisia and Palestine, Malva leaves are steamed with garlic and tomatoes, and eaten as an appetizer or salad. In Egypt, the leaves are made into a stew-like vegetable dish, known as khobeiza, which is similar to Molokheia. In Spain the tender leaves are eaten fresh in salads, alone or with other plants (Alt Empordà, Córdoba), or blanched (Alt Empordà, central Valencia, Mallorca); they have also been eaten fried, and in Cabo de Gata stewed alone or with other greens. In Albanchez de Mágina (Jaén) they are boiled and then sautéed. More rarely the petals are eaten raw in salads. The flowers are infused as a cooling drink (La Garrotxa), and flowers and fruits go into homemade ratafia liqueurs in Catalonia. The commonest use is the fruits, eaten on the spot as a snack, slightly unripe or ripe, even as they start to dry on the plant; their shape gives them names such as panecillos (little bread rolls) and quesitos (little cheeses). In Mancha Real (Jaén) people said the fruits are very constipating.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. Serves 2. 450 g mallow leaves, 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil, 1 medium onion, diced, and 1 medium lemon. Pull the leaves off the stems and soak them in water with a small pinch of salt, then rinse well under running water to remove any dirt or grit and drain completely. Fry the onion in the oil until soft and translucent, then lift it out. In the same pan, cook the leaves with a splash of water over medium heat, stirring now and then, until they wilt and shrink. Once they are tender, stir the onion back in, tip onto a plate and finish with lemon juice, to taste, and a drizzle of olive oil. Young leaves are best; older ones are tougher and have less flavour. Good with vermicelli rice or fresh pita bread.
recipes.title: Sautéed mallow with onions (khobeizeh)

recipes.method: Written for Malva sylvestris. 6 large eggs (or more, to fill the tray), 3 tbsp milk, grated Parmigiano Reggiano, salt and freshly ground nutmeg to taste, and freshly picked mallow leaves (the page gives no amount). Heat the oven to 180 °C. Cook the leaves in boiling water for a few minutes, rinse, and blend to a purée. Whisk the eggs, milk, cheese, salt and nutmeg in a small bowl, stir in the mallow purée, and pour into a prepared muffin tray. Bake until cooked through and golden, 30–35 minutes. Leave to cool, then keep in a container in the fridge until eaten.
recipes.title: Egg muffins with mallow

recipes.method: Written for common mallow (Malva sylvestris) picked in Andalusia, as a mallow version of the Granada tapa of spinach with chickpeas. A bag of mallow leaves, a large jar of chickpeas (drained), 4 tsp (20 ml) cumin seeds, half a bulb of garlic (crushed), the juice of 1 lemon, olive oil and salt. Rinse the leaves, roll them into a tight bunch and slice roughly at about 1 cm. Steam them gently, covered, over low heat with a small cup of water until wilted, then set aside; mallow goes dry if only fried, so steam it first. Dry-toast the cumin seeds in a large frying pan until lightly browned and grind them. Fry the cumin in olive oil over medium heat for a minute, add the garlic and stir for about two minutes, then stir in the chickpeas to coat them, and then the mallow. Cover and simmer gently for 10–15 minutes, adding a little water if it dries out. Season with salt and lemon juice. Serve on its own or with bread.
recipes.title: Mallow with chickpeas (espinacas con garbanzos style)

recipes.method: Written for common mallow, used in place of jute mallow in an adaptation of the Egyptian green soup molokhia. Serves 4. 200 g mallow leaves (plus a few flowers to decorate), 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil, 1 small onion, finely chopped, salt, 4 garlic cloves, chopped, 2 tsp (10 ml) ground coriander, 500 ml well-flavoured stock and 4 tbsp (60 ml) natural yoghurt. For the dukkah: 2 tbsp (30 ml) hazelnuts, 1 tbsp (15 ml) sunflower seeds, 2 tsp (10 ml) sesame seeds, 1 tsp (5 ml) each of cumin, fennel, nigella and coriander seeds, and ½ tsp (2.5 ml) sweet paprika. Strip and rinse the leaves and chop roughly. Soften the onion with a pinch of salt in the oil over low heat for 5 minutes, add the garlic until lightly golden, then the coriander until fragrant, then the stock, and bring to the boil. For the dukkah, roast the hazelnuts at 160 °C for 10 minutes, rub off their skins in a tea towel, toast the seeds for 5–10 minutes until lightly browned, then crush everything roughly in a mortar and mix in the paprika. Add the leaves to the boiling stock and cook about 5 minutes, until tender but still bright green, then purée and season. Serve with a spoonful of yoghurt, the dukkah and the flowers, with rice or flatbread.
recipes.title: Mallow soup with hazelnut dukkah

recipes.method: Written for common mallow (Malva sylvestris), cooked to a molokhia recipe. 800 g common mallow leaves, 6–8 garlic cloves, crushed, about 1 litre of chicken broth, 1 tbsp (15 ml) vegetable or olive oil, ½ tsp (2.5 ml) salt and a pinch of black pepper. Bring the broth to the boil, add the washed leaves, return to a mild boil, then simmer gently without boiling, stirring now and then, until the leaves have melted (15–20 minutes); simmer about 5 minutes more and take off the heat. Fry the garlic in the oil over medium heat until golden, without burning it, add the pepper, then ladle soup into the pan a little at a time — it should sizzle — until it is all mixed in. Salt to taste and eat as it is, or poured over rice and toasted pita.
recipes.title: Garlic mallow soup (molokhia style)

summary.text:
Malva sylvestris is a species of the mallow genus Malva, of which it is the type species. Known as common mallow to English-speaking Europeans, it acquired the common names of cheeses, high mallow and tall mallow (mauve des bois by the French) as it migrated from its native home in Western Europe, North Africa and Asia through the English-speaking world.
One of the major areas that it grows in is northeast and central Iran. It is also found in North Africa and grows as a biennial in the Mediterranean; it grows as a perennial elsewhere. It has been introduced to and has become naturalised in eastern Australia, in the United States, Canada, and Mexico as an invasive species.
Palearctic:
Macaronesia: Azores, Madeira Islands
Northern Africa: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco
Arabian Peninsula: Saudi Arabia
Western Asia: Afghanistan, Sinai, Iran, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey
Caucasus: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Ciscaucasia, Dagestan, Georgia
Soviet Middle Asia: Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan
Mongolia: Mongolia
China: Xinjiang
Indian Subcontinent: Bhutan, India, Pakistan
Northern Europe: Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom
Middle Europe: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia, Switzerland
East Europe: Belarus, Central Russia, Central Black Earth, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Northern Russia, North Caucasus, Northwestern Russia, Volga, Urals, Volga-Vyatka, Ukraine
Southeastern Europe: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Macedonia, Montenegro, Sardinia, Serbia, Sicily, Slovenia, Romania, Cyprus
Southwestern Europe: Balearic Islands, Corsica, France, Portugal, Spain
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island except Taranaki, in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and Otago, and on the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1870.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are cultivated inorganically), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.

In northern Europe, it grows from sea level up to 1,850 m altitude, while in China it grows at 1,400–3,200 m altitude.

Great mullein most frequently grows as a colonist of bare and disturbed soil, usually on sandy or chalky ones. It grows best in dry, sandy, or gravelly soils, although it can grow in a variety of habitats, including banksides, meadows, roadsides, forest clearings, and pastures. This ability to grow in a wide range of habitats has been linked to strong phenotype variation rather than adaptation capacities.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial, with greyish or white tomentum of stellate hairs;  stems to  c. 1 m tall, usually simple, sometimes with a few branches from near base. Rosette lvs shortly petiolate, 7–20 × 3.5–10 cm, elliptic-ovate to elliptic-obovate, crenulate;  base attenuate;  apex obtuse to acute.  Cauline lvs sessile, often more elongated, oblong, to  c. 30 cm long;  base decurrent. Infl. dense, woolly, to  c. 80 cm high, simple or sometimes with 1–2 branches. Bracts lanceolate, acuminate.  Fls subsessile or very shortly pedicellate, 1-several in each axil.  Calyx 8–12 mm long, deeply lobed;  lobes triangular-acuminate.  Corolla 1.5–2.5–(3) cm diam., yellow, hairy;  lobes rounded.  Stamens 5;  upper 3 stamens with white-villous filaments;  lower 2 stamens glabrous or nearly so, and with anthers decurrent.  Capsule 8–10 mm long, broad-ovoid, exserted from calyx.  Seeds cylindric-oblong, rugose;  apex truncate.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Verbascum thapsus, the great mullein, greater mullein or common mullein, is a species of mullein native to Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, and introduced in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand.
V. thapsus has a wide native range including Europe, northern Africa, and Asia, from the Azores and Canary Islands east to western China, north to the British Isles, Scandinavia, and Siberia, Kashmir and south to the Himalayas.
It has been introduced throughout the temperate world, and is established as a weed in Australia, New Zealand, tropical Asia, La Réunion, North America, Hawaii, Chile, Hispaniola, and Argentina. It has also been reported in Japan.
In the United States, it was imported very early in the 18th century and cultivated for its medicinal and piscicide properties. By 1818, it had begun spreading so much that Amos Eaton thought it was a native plant. In 1839, it was already reported in Michigan and in 1876, in California. It is now found commonly in all the states. In Canada, it is most common in the Maritime Provinces and southern Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia, with scattered populations in between.

Medium-sized to tall tree with rough shallowly fissured, dark grey bark,  c. 6–12 m high (to  c. 15 m in cultivation); branches erect when young but later spreading.  Young shoots shining brown or reddish brown, becoming glabrous, sometimes with branch spines on older shoots.  Lvs very variable and mostly crowded on short shoots;  petiole 15–65–(80) mm long;  glabrate to pilose;  blade broadly ovate, elliptic, broad-elliptic, or  suborbicular, (25)–35–80–(100) × (20)–30–60–(80) mm, apiculate to acuminate, rounded at base, bright green, glossy and glabrous above when mature, paler below and sometimes pilose when young, crenulate-serrate; stipules attenuate.  Infl. of usually 5–10 fls;  pedicels 18–30 mm long, glabrate or softly pilose.  Sepals triangular, brown- or grey-tomentose, recurved.  Petals broadly obovate or obovate-oblong, 14–22 × 10–18 mm, concave, white;  apex rounded.  Anthers ± purple.  Fr. usually pyriform or broadly obovoid, less commonly subglobose or globose, usually 40–80 mm long (longer in some cultivated plants), sweet, with a gritty texture when ripe;  skin green to yellow, sometimes brown.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

habitat.text: Cow parsley grows in sunny to semi-shaded locations in meadows and at the edges of hedgerows and woodland. It is a particularly common sight by the roadside and with its frothy early-flowering white blooms is regarded as the most important springtime landscape wildflower in Britain.

identification.text:
Cow parsley is an upright herbaceous (non-woody) perennial, growing to 60–170 centimetres tall. The stems are hollow, striate (striped with parallel, longitudinal lines), furrowed, and green in colour with flushes of purple, with a diameter up to 1.5 cm. It has tiny hairs on the stem, rachis, and leaf stalks which are difficult to see but can easily be detected by touch. The petioles clasp the stem around the base and are broad and flattened with a downy margin. The rachis has a deeply grooved channel.
The leaves are triangular, 2–3 pinnate, roughly 30 cm wide and 45 cm long, green, and fern-like or feathery in appearance with hair on the underside. The lowest primary division is much smaller than the rest of the leaf.
The flowers are arranged in compound umbels on short pedicels (<1 cm) with a ring of short, stout hairs at the apex. There are downy oval bractioles with red pointy tips on the umblets, arranged on 4–10 rays 1.5–3 cm long. The rays are glabrous (smooth and hairless), with no bract present. Peduncles are similar in length to rays, more or less glabrous and furrowed. Each flower has 5 white petals, 2 stamens and 2 styles with an enlarged base forming a swelling at the apex of the ovary (stylopodium).
The main stem meets the roots in a single primary taproot which can branch further below the surface. From the roots lateral rhizomes can form.  Flowering time in the UK is April to early June.

summary.text:
Anthriscus sylvestris, known as cow parsley, wild chervil, Queen Anne's lace or keck, is a herbaceous biennial or short-lived perennial plant in the family Apiaceae (Umbelliferae).
However, the plant is also sufficiently common and fast-growing to be considered a nuisance weed in gardens.  Cow parsley's ability to spread rapidly by means of rhizomes and to produce large quantities of seeds in a single growing season has made it an invasive species in many areas of the United States. Vermont has listed cow parsley on its "Watch List" of invasive species, while Massachusetts has banned the sale of the plant. It is classed as a Class B Noxious Weed in the State of Washington since 1989, where its sale is also banned. In Iceland, where cow parsley is now commonly seen overgrowing lupine fields, it has been classified as an alien invasive species.

identification.text:
Low-growing shrub;  creeping stems up to 1 m long, rooting at nodes, terete, glabrous;  armature of small prickles restricted to young stems. Lvs reduced to a single leaflet;  leaflet lamina coriaceous, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20)–25–90 × 5–22 mm, sometimes with a pair of obscure lobes near base, glabrous on both surfaces or with sparse scattered hairs on midrib, veins and margins, bronze-green on upper surface, paler on lower, sharply serrate-dentate. Infl. a few-flowered panicle or fls solitary.  Petals white.  Drupelets red.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
R. parvus has relatively large ⚥ fls whereas the other indigenous spp. have small fls and are dioecious.
The sterile hybrid R. ×barkeri is often sold as this species; it has three-leaflet leaves and does not flower (NZPCN).

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet, where blackberry's have (3–)5(–7); creeping lawyer creeps along the ground, blackberry arches and scrambles. Ripe creeping lawyer fruit is red, but blackberry is red too before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; bush lawyer's have three or more. Creeping lawyer's flowers are relatively large, with stamens and carpels together, where bush lawyer's are small, male and female on separate plants. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; white-leaved lawyer's have three or more. Creeping lawyer's flowers are relatively large, with stamens and carpels together, where white-leaved lawyer's are small, male and female on separate plants. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. Somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. For one drink. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.

identification.text:
Much-branched, prostrate, spreading to suberect, ± farinose annual monoecious herb.  Stems ± slender;  ribs and nodes often purplish or dark red. Petiole of lower lvs usually 1–2.5 cm long, slender;  lamina of lower lvs 1–9 × 0.75–8 cm, mostly narrowly to broadly triangular-hastate, sometimes ± ovate or rhombic-ovate, green, glaucous or sometimes reddish, sparsely to prominently and deeply dentate above basal lobes;  base usually truncate, sometimes broad- cuneate or sagittate;  apex acute or subacute.  Infl. lvs smaller and more often ovate to lanceolate.  Infl. of long reddish or brownish spikes;  fls in glomerules.  ♂ fls:  perianth 0.5–0.8 mm long with margins hyaline. ♀ fls:  bracteoles 1–2 mm long at anthesis, sessile, triangular-hastate, broad-ovate or rhombic-ovate, usually dentate, less commonly entire, generally with appendages.  Fruiting bracteoles to 9 × 6.5 mm, sometimes unequal, almost free or shortly united.  Fr. enclosed by bracteoles, 1–2.5 mm long, ± circular, laterally flattened;  pericarp easily removed;  larger-fruited plants with bracteoles often larger and lacking appendages.  Testa shining black or deep brown, smooth.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
A perennial with a slender main root and no bulbs. Its slender, weak, branched stems, up to about 40 cm long, lie along the ground or rise a little, are covered in spreading hairs and often root at the nodes. Each leaf has three equal, broadly heart-shaped leaflets, (2.5–)5–18 mm long, notched up to halfway down, on a hairy stalk (0.5–)1–7 cm long. The leaves are green or purple.

The flowers are yellow, with petals 4.5–10(–13) mm long, in clusters of 1 to 5 on a stalk 1–4 cm long (up to 9.5 cm in fruit). The fruit is an upright, cylindrical capsule (6–)10–18(–20) mm long, usually densely hairy, which bursts to throw out its seeds.

In New Zealand two forms are told apart: the typical form, with green leaves and stems, and var. atropurpurea, with purple-green leaves and stems, purple flower stalks and sepals, and a thicker taproot.

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel spreads on slender, branched stems up to c. 40 cm long that lie along the ground or rise a little, carry the leaves, and often root at the nodes. Bermuda buttercup is an upright plant from an underground bulb with no leafy stem above ground; its leaves all rise from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long. Its flower stalks are (7)–15–45 cm long, against creeping wood sorrel's 1–4 cm in flower (to 9.5 cm in fruit), and usually carry 3–18 hanging flowers (occasionally 1) with golden petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long; creeping wood sorrel carries 1–5 flowers with petals 4.5–10–(13) mm long, so petal length separates them where flower number does not. Creeping wood sorrel sets cylindrical capsules, usually hairy, (6)–10–18–(20) mm long; Flora of New Zealand gives Bermuda buttercup's capsule as not seen. Yellow flowers, heart-shaped leaflets, leaflet size and purple in the leaf do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel looks like a smaller creeping wood sorrel, with much the same leaves, creeping stems and yellow flowers, so size and flower count are the tests, and size changes with growing conditions. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its leaves typically under 10 mm across; creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm) and its leaves normally about 20 mm across. Count the flowers on a stalk: least yellow sorrel's are solitary, rarely paired; creeping wood sorrel carries 1 to 5, usually at least two. Least yellow sorrel's capsule is mostly 7–10 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's mostly 10–18 mm, though the ranges meet. Least yellow sorrel is more often in lawns, creeping wood sorrel in garden beds and nurseries. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover's leaflets are 5–25 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes; creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes. Red clover's leaflets are 15–40 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes; creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes. Alsike clover's leaflets are 10–35 mm long, creeping wood sorrel's 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm). Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

preparation.text: Add the leaves to salads, cook them as a pot herb with milder greens, or use them to give a sour taste to other food. For a drink, steep the leaves in hot water for about 10 minutes, sweeten and chill. The leaves are very small and fiddly to pick.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. Use it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: About 950 ml (1 US quart) water, 125 ml (½ cup) wood sorrel leaves, stems, flowers and seed pods, 15 ml (1 tbsp) agave nectar or honey, and a dash of salt. Mix everything in a blender. If you can, leave it in the fridge overnight before drinking.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel cooler

recipes.method: Fresh wood sorrel leaves and boiling water, one part leaves to three parts water. Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

Card to/from Bermuda buttercup, rewritten 11/10/2026 after the owner required every claim to rest on a trusted source. Creeping wood sorrel's stems (prostrate to suberect, to c. 40 cm, slender, branched, often rooting at nodes), leaves green or purple, leaflets (2.5)–5–18 mm long and obcordate, inflorescence 1–5-flowered on a peduncle 1–4 cm (to 9.5 cm in fruit), petals 4.5–10–(13) mm, capsule (6)–10–18–(20) mm, cylindric, usually hairy: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 11/10/2026, https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-corniculata.html. Capsules erect and bursting to expel the seeds; Bermuda buttercup upright, with a single short vertical stem mostly underground and a loose basal rosette: UC IPM Pest Notes 7444, 'Creeping Woodsorrel and Bermuda Buttercup' (LeStrange, Cudney & Elmore, 06/2010; © Regents of the University of California, facts only), https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7444.html. Bermuda buttercup's flowers, leaflets and 'Capsule not seen': Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 11/10/2026. CONFLICT: this page's identification text (Wikipedia) says a plant can carry over 20 flowers; Flora of New Zealand gives 1–5 per inflorescence, and UC IPM 2 to 5. The card follows Flora of New Zealand. Risk edible because the Bermuda buttercup page says the plant is palatable and eaten, with an oxalate warning.

Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes.

Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026).

Fixed 15/10/2026 (owner: "do a web search and fix this one"). Identification rewritten from Flora of New Zealand Online, 'Oxalis corniculata' factsheet (Webb, Sykes & Garnock-Jones 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV; © Landcare Research, CC BY 3.0 NZ), https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-corniculata.html, retrieved 15/10/2026 — stems, leaves, petiole, leaflets, inflorescence, peduncle, petals and capsule as given there; 'no bulbs' and the two New Zealand forms (var. atropurpurea purple-green foliage and stems, purple peduncle and calyx, thicker tap root) from NZPCN, 'Oxalis corniculata subsp. corniculata' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-corniculata-subsp-corniculata/) and 'Oxalis corniculata subsp. corniculata var. atropurpurea' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-corniculata-subsp-corniculata-var-atropurpurea/), retrieved 15/10/2026, facts only; 'upright' capsule that bursts from UC IPM Pest Notes 7444 (cited above). Replaced the Wikipedia description because it conflicted with Flora of New Zealand: it said a plant can carry over 20 flowers (Flora NZ: 1–5 per inflorescence; that sentence has no citation) and called the leaflets rounded (Flora NZ: broadly obcordate, notched up to half their length). Not used from Flora NZ: seed 'cm long' (evidently mm; NZPCN gives 1.0–1.3 mm), sepals, bracts, stamens and styles. Wikipedia's 'flowers close when the plant is not within direct sunlight' and pollen size dropped (uncited).

Habitat, paraphrased: the garden sites for each form from the two NZPCN factsheets above ('Gardens, mostly in deeper soils and more shaded sites than var. atropurpurea'; var. atropurpurea 'Gardens, most commonly in sunny sites with shallow soils such as rock gardens, around the bases of potted plants and gravel paths and driveways'); 'lawns and farmland' from Wikipedia ('often regarded as a weed in gardens, agricultural fields, and lawns', cited to Hackney 1992 and UC IPM) — a worldwide statement, not New Zealand-specific. NZPCN also gives year naturalised 1944 and wetland rating FACU (usually in uplands). Not used: PGG Wrightson / NZ Lifestyle Block 'Pasture Weed Watch: Oxalis' (Milton Munro, 2014), whose 'Across New Zealand, in gardens, paddocks and lawns' is about Oxalis as a whole, not this species.

Edible parts, preparation and warning: Wikipedia, 'Oxalis corniculata', Uses section (revision 1368886676, 11/08/2026; CC BY-SA 4.0), cited there to Lee Allen Peterson, Edible Wild Plants (Houghton Mifflin, 1977), p. 104 — leaves edible with a tangy lemon taste; drink of leaves infused in hot water about 10 minutes, sweetened and chilled; 'Any woodsorrel is safe in low dosages, but if eaten in large quantities over a length of time can inhibit calcium absorption'. Useful Tropical Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis corniculata', https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Oxalis+corniculata, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 15/10/2026 — leaves raw or cooked, flowers raw; added to salads, cooked as a potherb with milder greens or used to sour other foods; 'very small and fiddly to harvest'; Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses): not to be eaten in large amounts since oxalic acid can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. This replaces the OWED warnings line written when the recipes were added; those recipe pages' warnings agree with it. Not used from Useful Tropical Plants: medicinal uses, nutrient and oxalate percentages, cultivation (RHS/Flora Europaea dry habitats are not New Zealand).

Months emptied (year-round) 15/10/2026: the previous [6, 7, 8] had no source line. Flora of New Zealand gives 'Flowering: Jan.–Dec.' (Phenology), and Useful Tropical Plants says the leaves are available all year round unless the winter is very cold; leaves and flowers are the parts eaten.

The gratin and potato salad recipes were copied 16/10/2026 from pale-pink-wood-sorrel (owner, 16/10/2026: "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"); they were written for Oxalis incarnata, not this species. Their provenance, as recorded there: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Origin checked 20/10/2026 (owner: "find the bio status all shipped species and label them accordingly"), retrieved 20/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Oxalis corniculata' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Oxalis%20corniculata): NZFLORA biostatus Exotic, Present. Origin 'introduced' stands. Kept introduced, not pest: not on DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340, https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf), not in Wildland Consultants' table of weed taxa in every regional pest management plan (2021, Contract Report 5396 for the PCE, Appendix 2, https://pce.parliament.nz/media/fx4pjock/hutchison-et-al-review-of-weed-management-programmes-pdf-6mb.pdf), and no Unwanted Organism or Pest Plant Accord listing.

summary.text:
Oxalis corniculata, the creeping woodsorrel, procumbent yellow sorrel or sleeping beauty, is a somewhat delicate-appearing, low-growing herbaceous plant in the family Oxalidaceae.
This species probably comes from southeastern Asia. It was first described by Linnaeus in 1753 using specimens from Italy, and it seems to have been introduced to Italy from the east before 1500. It is now cosmopolitan in its distribution and is often regarded as a weed in gardens, agricultural fields, and lawns.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Glabrous perennial rhizomatous herb.  Stems erect, often flexuous, 30–70 cm tall.  Lvs variable in shape;  margins toothed.  Rosette lvs petiolate, auriculate at base, deeply pinnatifid, 4–10–(25) × 2–4 cm. Middle and upper lvs smaller, 1–2-pinnatifid, linear to ovate;  lobes narrow-lanceolate to linear, entire or toothed;  basal auricles present.  Pedicels erecto-patent at flowering, spreading at fruiting, 5–15 mm long.  Sepals 2–2.5 mm long.  Petals yellow, (3)–4–5 mm long.  Silique glabrous, linear, curved, 10–15 × 1–1.5  mm, but often not or poorly developed;  valves with median vein weak or 0;  style c. 0.5 mm long. Seeds brown, c. 0.6 mm long, finely colliculate, in 2 rows per locule.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

edibleParts.text: Recorded as eaten in Spain and Morocco. In Spain the small fruits have been eaten as a snack, especially by children, who call them panecillos ("little bread rolls"), the same way as common mallow's, and in Petra, Mallorca, the round leaves are eaten steamed.
