identification.text:
Stout annual to biennial up to 2 m high but frequently smaller, often branched from base.  Stems densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming ± glabrous and often woody at base when older.  Lvs densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming sparsely so when older, suborbicular, cordate to obtuse at base, shallowly 3–5-palmately lobed and crenate or serrate, 1–15 cm diam.;  petioles 1–15 cm long;  stipules ovate-triangular, 3–6 mm long.  Fls in axillary clusters of (1)–2–6–(8);  fruiting pedicels 5–25 mm long;  epicalyx segments ovate to broadly ovate, united for lower 1/4, c. ⅔-4/5 length of calyx, unchanged at fruiting;  calyx shallowly campanulate;  calyx teeth ± = tube, ovate, acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, usually ± connivent at fruiting;  petals lilac or pink with darker veins, (8)–10–18 mm long.  Mericarps 8–10 per fr., glabrous, ± smooth or faintly ribbed on back and with a single low longitudinal rib;  edges usually rounded, rarely ± sharply angled.
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera cretica L.]
L. cretica is often confused with the forms of Malva sylvestris in which the bases of the epicalyx segments are slightly fused. L. cretica can be distinguished by the round-edged, ± smooth-backed mericarps, the acuminate calyx teeth, and generally broader epicalyx segments.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera, which include Cretan mallow; annual mallow's flowers are single, Cretan mallow's mostly in clusters. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Flora of New Zealand says Cretan mallow is often confused with forms of common mallow whose epicalyx segments are slightly joined at the base, and separates it by its round-edged, more or less smooth-backed fruit segments (net-veined and sharply angled in common mallow), its long-pointed calyx teeth (acute in common mallow) and its generally broader epicalyx segments. Petal colour and length overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

summary.text:
Malva multiflora (previously known as Lavatera cretica) is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family known by the common names Cornish mallow and Cretan hollyhock. It is native to western Europe, North Africa, and the Mediterranean Basin, and it is naturalized in areas with a Mediterranean climate, such as parts of Australia, South Africa, and California.
In New Zealand it grows in Auckland City, Waikato, Coromandel, Napier and from Palmerston North to Wellington, and in Nelson, lowland Canterbury and North Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1940.

identification.text:
Hairy, annual, taprooted herb, with large basal lf rosette and ± ascending branches to c. 50 cm long. Stems ± densely hairy with the hairs ± retrorse. Petioles to c. 20 cm long, longest in rosette lvs, with hairs as on stems. Lamina 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, orbicular or suborbicular, with appressed hairs, especially on veins below; lobes 5–7, extending almost to the petiole, again pinnately lobed or 3-lobed, especially in rosette lvs; ultimate segments linear or narrow-oblong, acute. Fls usually in pairs; peduncles usually > pedicels, both densely hairy with eglandular and often pink-tipped glandular hairs. Sepals 5–8 mm long (excluding awn), ovate, densely clothed in long, white, eglandular and short glandular hairs, aristate with awn (1)–2–3 mm long. Petals 3.5–5 mm long, obovate, pink or rose, emarginate; claw short. Filaments whitish; anthers blue. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, with white, patent hairs. Seeds prominently isobilaterally alveolate.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the fruit: dove's-foot cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairless on the outer face and ridged, cut-leaved cranesbill's hairy and smooth. Without fruit, use the leaves: cut-leaved cranesbill's are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, dove's-foot cranesbill's to about 3/4 of the way into broader lobes. The anthers differ too (blue against mauve). Both are hairy annuals with a basal rosette and small, notched pink petals, and both have glandular hairs in the flower clusters, so none of those separates them. Dove's-foot cranesbill's fruits are recorded as eaten by young people in Spain as a nibble (CONECT-e).
lookalikes.name: Dove's-foot cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them at its first step: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Solander's geranium is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Solander's geranium's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Solander's geranium under Geranium dissectum (NZPCN lists Geranium dissectum var. pilosum Hook.f. and var. australe Benth. among its synonyms), so older records may use that name. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them at its first step: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Australasian cranesbill's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Australasian cranesbill under Geranium dissectum (Flora of New Zealand Online cites Allan's 1961 Flora under it as Geranium australe and Geranium dissectum var. glabratum Hook.f.), so older records may use that name. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga).
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the leaves and stamens: cut-leaved cranesbill's lower leaves are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, its sepals end in an awn and all 10 stamens are fertile; small-flowered cranesbill's are divided to about 3/4 of the way into oblong to ovate segments, its sepals end in a point under 0.5 mm, and 4–5 of its 10 stamens lack anthers. Both have hairy fruit segments (mericarps), so the fruit alone does not separate them, though cut-leaved cranesbill's hairs spread and small-flowered cranesbill's are pressed flat. Its petals are pink or rose and 3.5–5 mm long against small-flowered cranesbill's pale mauve 2.5–3.5 mm, and its anthers blue against mauvish brown. No source read records small-flowered cranesbill as food (Plants For A Future and Useful Temperate Plants: none known).

summary.text:
Geranium dissectum or cut-leaved crane's-bill is a plant species of the genus Geranium. It is native to Europe.
It can be found on other continents as well, in some instances as an introduced species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: commonest from Taranaki northwards; S.: Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (at least S. to Ashburton); K. (Raoul, but not collected recently), Ch. G. dissectum has recently become a prominent weed of arable land in N. and E. South Id.

habitat.text: Lawns, verges, pasture, waste ground.

identification.text: Flat rosette of jagged backward-pointing lobed leaves. A single flower per hollow, leafless stem. Every part bleeds white milky sap. No branching stem — this is the key check.

lookalikes.howToTell: Catsear's leaves carry moderately dense, stiff pale hairs; a dandelion's are hairless or only sparsely hairy. Catsear's flower stems are usually branched, solid and almost leafless, with only a few tiny bracts, and can carry several flower heads; a dandelion's are hollow, unbranched and leafless, with one flower head each. Both have a rosette of leaves, yellow flower heads and milky sap, so none of those separates them. Catsear is edible: its young leaves are bland and can be eaten raw or cooked, though older leaves can be tough.

lookalikes.howToTell: Beaked hawksbeard's stem branches and carries leaves, and stands 15–75 cm tall, sometimes to 100 cm; a dandelion's flower stem is hollow, leafless and unbranched, with a single flower head — the same check as for catsear. The rosettes alone do not separate them: both usually have leaves with backward-pointing lobes, and both have milky sap.

identification.text:
Evergreen shrub to c. 4 m high.  Shoots densely clothed in brown hairs, terete or nearly so.  Spines palmately 5-partite, hairy.  Lvs subsessile or nearly so.  Lamina 1–3–(3.5) × 0.5–1.5–(2) cm, obovate with 2 spiny apical lobes (lvs of vegetative shoots sometimes with additional spiny teeth below), glabrous, glossy dark green above;  base cuneate.  Infl. usually a simple pendulous raceme to c. 7 cm long, occasionally slightly paniculate.  Bracts lanceolate, reddish, much < pedicels.  Pedicels 5–15 mm long at anthesis, reddish.  Perianth segments 5–8.5 mm long except in the much shorter outermost whorl, orange-yellow except for reddish flush on outermost segments, usually oblong or oblong-obovate; innermost whorl (petals) slightly emarginate.  Nectaries inconspicuous. Stamens slightly < petals.  Ovules up to 8.  Style = or > ovary at anthesis.  Berry 5–7 mm diam., subglobose or globose, black or nearly so, ± pruinose;  fruiting style conspicuous, 1.5–3 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry's leaves are small, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, obovate with two spiny lobes at the tip (shoots that are not flowering sometimes carry extra teeth below); barberry's are mostly 2.5–7.5 cm long, entire or spiny-toothed (often only sparsely), and very variable on one plant. Darwin's barberry's flowers are orange-yellow, barberry's yellow. Darwin's barberry's shoots are densely clothed in brown hairs and its spines split into five like a hand; barberry is hairless, its spines single or three-parted and up to 2.3 cm long. Its berries are 5–7 mm across and round, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long left at the tip; barberry's are 7–12 mm long, broadly ellipsoid to nearly round, with a style about 1 mm long. Dark berries with a whitish bloom, an evergreen habit and a tall spiny shrub do not separate them. The garden hybrid B. × stenophylla (Darwin's barberry × B. empetrifolia) has three-parted spines and narrow linear-lanceolate leaves but fruit like Darwin's barberry's, so the spine and leaf tests do not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry is evergreen and its berries are black or nearly so, with a whitish bloom, 5–7 mm across and round; European barberry is deciduous and its berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining, without bloom, oblong and 9–11 mm long. Darwin's barberry's leaves are glossy dark green above, with spiny lobes, up to about 3.5 cm long; European barberry's are thin, dull green, usually finely toothed and 2–8 cm long. Darwin's barberry's spines split into five; European barberry's are mostly three-parted and under 1.5 cm long. Spiny stems and yellowish flowers in clusters do not separate them. Red berries alone do not mark European barberry: the Flora of New Zealand records the deciduous B. wilsonae (red, round berries without bloom; adult leaves entire) wild at three sites, and garden B. thunbergii also has scarlet berries.
lookalikes.name: European barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Darwin's barberry has simple leaves, 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long, in clusters on stems armed with five-parted spines; Oregon grape's leaves are compound, up to about 25 cm long, of 3–7 pairs of holly-like leaflets 5–9.5 cm long plus one at the tip, and its stems carry no spines (the Flora of New Zealand: in Mahonia the leaves are never modified to form spines). Darwin's barberry's berries are 5–7 mm across with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long left at the tip; Oregon grape's are about 10 mm across. Glossy, spiny-edged, holly-like foliage, dark berries with a bloom and yellow to orange flowers do not separate them.

recipes.method: Written for Darwin's barberry (Berberis darwinii) by the horticulturist who grew it. Simmer 900 g ripe berries in 2 litres of water until soft. Push the fruit and liquid through a sieve to hold back the skins and most of the seeds, then squeeze the pulp through muslin to get as much juice as you can. Heat the juice with the juice of one lemon, stirring in about 400 g (2 cups) sugar a cupful at a time as it warms. Boil hard for about 25 minutes, until it starts to set, then spoon into sterilised jars and cover. The author got two good-sized jars. The source calls its strained liquid both '3 cups' and '1.5 L', which do not agree, so measure your own. Metric sugar is converted from the source's cups.

summary.text:
Berberis darwinii, Darwin's barberry, is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is native to southern Chile and Argentina and naturalized elsewhere. Regional vernacular names include michay, calafate, and quelung. Growing to 3–4 m tall, it is an evergreen thorny shrub.
Berberis darwinii was first described in 1835 by Charles Darwin during the voyage of the Beagle. It was one of many named in honour of Darwin. The berries of this species are known to have been consumed by prehistoric native peoples in the Patagonian region over millennia.
Berberis darwinii is regarded as an invasive plant pest in New Zealand that escaped from gardens into indigenous plant communities via its bird-dispersed seeds. It is considered a serious threat to indigenous ecosystems throughout New Zealand and is listed on the National Pest Plant Accord.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: locally common in Wellington and the Wairarapa; S.: extensively naturalised from C. Canterbury to Foveaux Strait; St.: Halfmoon Bay, very common.
B. darwinii is a variable sp. with several described vars; N.Z. material can be referred to the type var. One New Zealand collection represents the commonly cultivated hybrid B. × stenophylla Lindley (B. darwinii × B. empetrifolia Lam.). This has long arching branches, 3-parted spines and linear-lanceolate lvs. It has frs similar to B. darwinii and sets viable seed.
Brought to New Zealand as an ornamental, it was naturalised in 1946 (NZPCN) and is now common from the central North Island to Stewart Island (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research). Birds and possums eat the berries and spread the seed; soil and water movement occasionally carry it too (NZPCN, Weedbusters). Two weevils were approved in 2012 for its biological control: one destroys the flower buds, the other damages the fruit and seeds. The fruit-and-seed weevil was first released in 2015 and is established at a number of sites in Southland and Wellington (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text: Smooth greenish, yellowish or bronze cap, often with a faint radial sheen. Gills WHITE and free of the stem at every age. White stem with a skirt-like ring, and — the critical feature — a membranous cup (volva) around the swollen base, frequently hidden below the leaf litter. Spore print white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Field mushroom's gills are deep pink at first and turn chocolate brown to almost black; it has no volva, and its thin ring often disappears. Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink or green tint, as it ages, but not the deep pink then chocolate-brown of a field mushroom. Its stem has a skirt-like ring, and the swollen base sits in a white, sack-like volva that is sometimes underground. Cap colour does not separate them. Death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but young caps can be almost white and an all-white form occurs. In a closed button a white veil hides a field mushroom's gills, so never judge a button. Dig up the whole base of every mushroom and check the gills of every one, every time. A spore print confirms it: field mushroom deep chocolate brown, death cap white.
lookalikes.name: Field mushroom

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow from a sac (volva) at the stem base, and their buttons look alike. The straw mushroom is usually picked and eaten at the button stage, and overseas death caps have reportedly been mistaken for straw mushrooms, with fatal results. Death cap has a skirt-like ring on the stem that usually persists but is sometimes lost, a white volva and white gills, and its spore print is white. Straw mushroom has no ring, a volva that is brownish grey to nearly black above and whitish below, gills that start white and turn pink, and a pink to brownish-pink spore print. Because young straw mushroom gills are also white, gill colour and spore print only separate mature mushrooms - not the buttons.
lookalikes.name: Straw mushroom / paddy straw

summary.text: Listed so you can recognise it. Established in New Zealand, and responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide.

warnings: Symptoms are delayed six to twenty-four hours, and there is often a deceptive period of apparent recovery before liver failure. By the time you feel ill, damage is underway.
If ingestion is even suspected, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately. Do not wait for symptoms.
Keep children and dogs away from mushrooms under oak trees in autumn.

identification.text:
Clump-forming, fountain-like; rhizomes not running. Culms initially erect and wand-like, later arching over, 2–2.5 m, glaucous-white when young, becoming medium to deep green. Culm-sheath uniformly green or purplish green; ligule 1–5 mm, puberulent; auricles and bristles 0; sheath-blades linear-subulate. Branches many at each node, small, densely tufted. Leaf-sheath green or purplish, glabrous excepting margins sometimes ciliate. Ligule prominent, oblong, minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade usually 4–12–(15) × 0.4–0.8–(1.3) cm, narrow lanceolate or linear-lanceolate, long acuminate. Panicles large and diffuse. Spikelets 8–12 mm, often purple or strongly flushed purple. Glumes < florets, unequal, minutely puberulent; lower ¾ - ⅚ length of upper. Lodicules c. 2 × 2 mm, ciliate. Caryopsis 6–7 mm, blackish.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

Glabrous, short-lived, tap-rooted perennial;  stems rather thin, wiry, flexuous, spreading, green to dark red, to  c. 1 m tall.  Petioles of basal lvs often very long, particularly in subaquatic plants.  Lamina of lower lvs (3)–7–20–(23) × (1)–1.5–3.5 cm, oblong or ovate-oblong, ± membranous; margin often undulate and crisped;  base broad-cuneate, rounded or cordate; apex acute or subacute.  Stem lvs progressively smaller and extending  c. ⅔ along infl. branches.  Infl. many-branched, spreading and flexuous, becoming twisted.  Whorls all distant;  fls probably protandrous, ☿, small, dense.  Pedicels slender, reddish.  Perianth (0.7)–1–5 mm long;  outer segments ovate, obtuse, not reflexing at fruiting;  inner segments greatly enlarging at fruiting.  Fruiting valves 2–2.8–(3.2) mm long, ovate, reticulate, entire, rounded at apex, generally becoming dark red, each with a large tubercle occupying ?-3/4 valve width.  Nut 1.5–2 mm long, dark glossy brown or reddish brown, acutely angled.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
Douglas-firs are medium-sized to extremely large trees, 20–100 metres tall (although only coast Douglas-firs reach heights near 100 m) and commonly reach 2.4 m in diameter, although trees with diameters of almost 5 m exist. The largest coast Douglas-firs regularly live over 500 years, with the oldest specimens living for over 1,300 years. Rocky Mountain Douglas-firs, found further to the east, are less long-lived, usually not exceeding 400 years in age.
There are records of former coast Douglas-firs exceeding 120 m in height, which if alive today would make it the tallest tree species on Earth. Particular historical specimens with heights exceeding 120 m include the Lynn Valley Tree and the Nooksack Giant.
The leaves are flat, soft, linear needles 1.5–4 cm long, generally resembling those of the firs, occurring singly rather than in fascicles; they completely encircle the branches, which can be useful in recognizing the species. As the trees grow taller in denser forest, they lose their lower branches, such that the foliage may start as high as 34 m off the ground. Douglas-firs in environments with more light may have branches much closer to the ground.
The bark on young trees is thin, smooth, and gray, and contains numerous resin blisters. On mature trees, usually exceeding 80 years, it is very thick and corky, growing up to 36 cm thick with distinctive, deep vertical fissures caused by the gradual expansion of the growing tree. Some of the mature bark is brown, while other parts are lighter colored with a cork-like texture; these develop in multiple layers. This thick bark makes the Douglas-fir one of the most fire-resistant tree native to the Pacific Northwest.
The male cones are yellowish red, 5–12 mm long. The female cones are green when young, maturing to reddish-brown or gray, 6–10 cm long; they are pendulous, with persistent scales, unlike those of true firs. They have distinctive long, trifid (three-pointed) bracts which protrude prominently above each scale and are said to resemble the back half of a mouse, with two feet and a tail. The seeds are 5 mm long, with a longer wing.
The massive genome of Douglas-fir was sequenced in 2017 by the large PineRefSeq consortium, revealing a specialized photosynthetic apparatus in the light-harvesting complex of genes.

summary.text:
The Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) is a conifer species in the pine family, Pinaceae.
Pseudotsuga menziesii var. menziesii, the coast Douglas-fir, grows in the coastal regions from west-central British Columbia southward to Central California. In Oregon and Washington, its range is continuous from the eastern edge of the Cascades west to the Pacific Coast Ranges and Pacific Ocean. In California, it is found in the Klamath and California Coast Ranges as far south as the Santa Lucia Range, with a small stand as far south as the Purisima Hills in Santa Barbara County. One of the last remaining old growth stands of conifers is in the Mattole Watershed, and is under threat of logging. In the Sierra Nevada, it ranges as far south as the Yosemite region.
Another variety exists further inland, Pseudotsuga menziesii var. glauca, the Rocky Mountain Douglas-fir or interior Douglas-fir. Interior Douglas-fir intergrades with coast Douglas-fir in the Cascades of northern Washington and southern British Columbia, and from there ranges northward to central British Columbia and southeastward to the Mexican border, becoming increasingly disjunct as latitude decreases and altitude increases. Mexican Douglas-fir (P. lindleyana), which ranges as far south as Oaxaca, is often considered a variety of P. menziesii.
Fossils (wood, pollen) of Pseudotsuga are recorded from the Miocene and Pliocene of Europe (Siebengebirge, Gleiwitz, Austria).
It is also naturalised throughout Europe, Argentina and Chile (called Pino Oregón). In New Zealand it is considered to be an invasive species, called a wilding conifer, and is subject to control measures.
The species was introduced in the 20th century for its wood.

identification.text:
Taprooted, annual herb, with basal rosette of lvs, densely covered in short or long hairs.  Stems decumbent or ± ascending, pinkish, to  c. 50 cm long. Petiole of rosette and lower cauline lvs to 14 cm long, densely covered in patent white hairs.  Lamina palmately lobed, 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, reniform to orbicular, densely covered in long white hairs;  lobes 5–9, extending to  c. 3/4 way to petiole, usually with 3 oblong to obovate, obtuse to rounded, secondary lobes towards apex.  Upper lvs smaller and simpler with shorter petioles.  Fls numerous, usually paired;  peduncles with dense, long, white, eglandular and short glandular hairs;  pedicels similar but often < peduncles and curving upwards after flowering.  Sepals 2–3.5 mm long, ovate, with hairs as on pedicels, mucronate.  Petals (3)–4–6 mm long, obovate, rosy pink or pink, deeply emarginate; claw very short.  Filaments whitish;  anthers mauve. Mericarps  c. 1.5 mm long, broad, glabrous, with prominent pale transverse ridges.  Seeds smooth.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the fruit: dove's-foot cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairless on the outer face and ridged, cut-leaved cranesbill's hairy and smooth. Without fruit, use the leaves: cut-leaved cranesbill's are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, dove's-foot cranesbill's to about 3/4 of the way into broader lobes. The anthers differ too (blue against mauve). Both are hairy annuals with a basal rosette and small, notched pink petals, and both have glandular hairs in the flower clusters, so none of those separates them. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Cut-leaved cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Flora of New Zealand says the two are similar in habit but can always be told apart by the fruit: small-flowered cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairy but otherwise smooth, dove's-foot cranesbill's hairless with cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill also has only 5–6 fertile anthers where dove's-foot cranesbill's 10 stamens all carry one (NatureGate), is usually less hairy, and generally has smaller petals (2.5–3.5 mm against (3)–4–6 mm). Both are hairy annuals with round leaves cut about 3/4 of the way into 5–9 lobes, so the leaves do not separate them. No source read records small-flowered cranesbill as food (Plants For A Future and Useful Temperate Plants: none known).

summary.text:
Geranium molle, the dove's-foot crane's-bill or dovesfoot geranium, is an annual herbaceous plant of the family Geraniaceae.
It is native to the Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean areas, but has naturalized in other parts of Europe, in southwestern and central Asia and in North Africa, though it may have already been in those parts and areas, just not properly identified. It is considered an introduced species in North America, where it is known as Dovefoot Geranium or Awnless Geranium. Although non-native in parts of its range, this species poses little threat to native ecosystems.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.; St.; K., Ch., C.: a common weed throughout, but not collected recently from K. and C.
In New Zealand it has been recorded as naturalised since 1852 (NZPCN); Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and growing wild, from 53 databased New Zealand collections, 30 of them from Canterbury. NatureGate says it now spreads mostly as a contaminant of clover seed, and has travelled from Western Europe, the Mediterranean and the Near East to most of Europe, the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and the Far East (restated).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lactarius pubescens' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap is 2.5–10 cm wide, obtuse to convex, becoming broadly convex with a depressed center. The margin (cap edge) is rolled inward and bearded with coarse white hairs when young. The cap surface is dry and fibrillose except for the center, which is sticky and smooth when fresh, azonate, white to cream, becoming reddish-orange to vinaceous (red wine-colored) on the disc with age. The gills are attached to slightly decurrent, crowded, seldom forked, whitish to pale yellow with pinkish tinges, slowly staining brownish ochraceous when bruised.
The stem is 2–6.5 cm long, 6–13 mm thick, nearly equal or tapered downward, silky, becoming hollow with age, whitish when young, becoming ochraceous from the base up when older, apex usually tinged pinkish, often with a white basal mycelium. The flesh is firm and whitish; the odor is faintly like geraniums or sometimes pungent, and taste is acrid. The latex is white upon exposure, unchanging, not staining tissues, taste acrid. The spore print is cream with a pinkish tint. The edibility of Lactarius pubescens has been described as unknown, poisonous, and even edible.
The spores are 6–8.5 by 5–6.5 μm, elliptic, ornamented with warts and ridges that sometimes form a partial reticulum, prominences up to 1.5 μm high, hyaline (translucent), and amyloid. The cap cuticle is a layer of thin-walled hyphae.


Varieties
Lactarius pubescens var. betulae (A.H. Sm.) Hesler & A.H. Sm. 1979
Lactarius pubescens var. betularum (Bon) Bon 1985
Lactarius pubescens var. scoticus (Berk. & Broome) Krieglst. 1991


Ectomycorrhizae
The ectomycorrhizae that L. pubescens forms in association with Betula pendula and Populus tremuloides has been grown in pure culture and described scientifically.


Similar species
Lactarius scoticus Berk. & Broome is a small morphological mimic of L. pubescens, growing in arctic-alpine birch. L. pubescens is often mistaken for L. torminosus which has larger spores (7–10 by 6–8 μm). Certain identification may require microscopic or genetic analysis.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Downy milk cap's milk is white and does not change colour or stain the flesh. Downy milk cap's cap margin is rolled in and bearded with coarse white hairs when young, and the cap is white to cream, reddening at the centre with age; saffron milk cap's cap is orange to salmon. The trees differ too: in New Zealand and Australia downy milk cap grows with birch, saffron milk cap only with pine.

Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-pubescens.php Cap 5–15 cm, buff and pale pink, woolly especially at the inrolled margin, with faint pinkish concentric bands and a pinkish-brown centre; gills shortly decurrent, crowded, white with a faint salmon-pink tinge, exuding white unchanging latex; stem 3–6 cm by 10–23 mm; spores 6.5–8 × 5.5–6.5 µm; spore print pale ivory; a slight turpentine or Pelargonium odour; taste hot and acrid. Ectomycorrhizal under birch, including birches less than five years old, in lawns, parks and heathland. Edibility, flatly: poisonous, and 'should not be gathered to eat', though unlikely to kill or cause long-term illness. Lactarius torminosus differs in a salmon-pink, more obviously zoned woolly cap and larger spores.

Edibility: the contradiction resolved one way. The entry's warning records that authorities split between unknown, poisonous and edible. First Nature is unambiguous — poisonous, do not gather — and no source consulted calls it good eating. The warning stands as written; this is the strongest single verdict behind it. summary.text:
Lactarius pubescens, commonly known as the downy milk cap, is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

The fungus is common all over temperate Europe and has been reported from eastern North America, the Pacific Northwest, Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, and western Canada; its frequency of appearance is occasional. It is also found in Greenland, and was reported for the first time in Rome, Italy, in 1997.

warnings: Edibility is recorded as unknown, poisonous and edible by different authorities, and the taste is acrid — contradictory sources on a mushroom are a reason not to eat it, not a reason to pick which one to believe.

identification.text: Cordyline pumilio is a plant rarely exceeding 2 metres tall. It is a very narrow-leaved species, and does not develop into the large tree-like form of C. australis. It often flowers while its short stem is leafy to the ground. In older plants the bare part of stem is up to 1 metre long and 1.5 cm wide, and not usually very erect. The leaves are 30 cm to 1 metre long and 1 to 2 cm wide, and may narrow above the base into a channelled petiole. The midrib is prominent abaxially, or at least proximally and the leaf margins are slightly recurved. The flower spike or panicle appears in November or December and is up to 60 by 30 cm, very open with slender axes, branched to the second order, with small white or bluish-white flowers irregularly scattered along the branches. The bracts are often small and inconspicuous. The tepals are narrow, recurved and have three nerves. The stigma is short and trifid.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. Hybrids between the two have been described from the far north (C. × matthewsii, Carse 1926), some almost enlarged copies of dwarf cabbage tree, so an in-between plant there may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Dwarf cabbage tree (Cordyline pumilio) is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.

preparation.text:
Young seedlings were carefully selected and planted out, and after perhaps three years the roots were dug up, stacked in small piles, and dried in the sun. As they dried, the fibrous roots were burned off, and then the roots were scraped and baked slowly in an umu or hāngī, requiring twelve to eighteen hours to cook. The cooked roots were chewed, or pounded and washed and squeezed to extract the sugar, which was eaten with fern root as a relish.
Roots tied separately for baking in bundles of hangehange, Geniostoma rupestre. (Colenso 1868a).
Roots dug up and dried, sometimes eaten raw (Colenso 1880)

summary.text:
Cordyline pumilio, commonly known as the dwarf cabbage tree, pygmy cabbage tree or by its Māori names tī koraha or tī rauriki, is a narrow-leaved monocot shrub endemic to the North Island of New Zealand.
It has long leaves and can easily be mistaken for a grass or a sedge. C. pumilio grows in the north of the North Island from North Cape at 34°S to Kawhia and Ōpōtiki at about 38°S, generally under light forest and scrub.

edibleParts.text: This plant is often consumed as a food, with its leaves, stalks and seed all being considered edible. Leaves and young shoots - raw or cooked. They can be added in quantity to salads, and make an excellent lettuce substitute, they can also be cooked as greens. Some people find this mucilaginous texture unpleasant, especially if the leaves are cooked. Immature seeds - raw or cooked. The seeds can be eaten raw or cooked and have a nutty flavor. Mature seeds can be cooked like rice or grains.

identification.text:
Dwarf mallow is a prostrate, downy, herbaceous plant, growing to approximately 60 cm.
The leaves are alternate with long, strongly channeled petioles, up to 12 cm, and narrowly triangular stipules.
It is a broadleaf winter annual that also persists through a biennial or perennial life cycle if environmental conditions are favorable.
Each leaf is reniform or with 5–7 shallow lobes, the basal leaves are 3–7 cm.
It grows a tough taproot.
The flowers are single-stalked and occur in clusters of 2–5 in the leaf axils.
The flower stalks are shorter than the leaf stalks, with the leaves partially obscuring the flowers.
The fruits are schizocarps, which split into mericarps (nutlets) and are smooth and hairy.
In addition to daily phototropic movements, leaves show epinasty, geotropism and sleeping behaviors. Leaves joined to the stem on the east side of the plant bend abaxially and leaves on the west side of the plant bend adaxially, while leaves on the north and south sides turn sideways. Overnight, leaves were observed returning to their morning position.

The smooth-backed mericarps clothed in short hairs distinguish this sp. It has often been recorded in N.Z. as M. rotundifolia.

Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent to ascending herb. Stems sparsely to densely clothed in stellate hairs. Lvs sparsely to moderately clothed in mostly stellate hairs above, densely hairy below, reniform to orbicular, cordate, shallowly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–7–(8) cm diam.; petioles (2)–4–20 cm long; stipules triangular, 3–6 mm long. Fls in axillary clusters of 2–5; fruiting pedicels 1–8 cm long; epicalyx segments linear to narrowly ovate-oblong, < calyx; calyx teeth ovate-triangular, acuminate, with stellate hairs and ciliate, not enlarged at fruiting; petals white to lilac, often with lilac to pink veins, usually at least twice as long as calyx, (7)–8–15 mm long. Mericarps 12–15 per fr., hairy, rarely sparsely so, smooth or faintly reticulate on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates the two by cheeseweed mallow's shorter petals, enlarged fruiting calyx and net-veined fruit segments with winged edges. Both are low herbs with round to kidney-shaped, lobed leaves of overlapping size (1–8 cm and 1–7(–8) cm across) and flowers in clusters in the leaf joints, so the leaves do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Petal lengths overlap between 12 and 15 mm, and common mallow can have pale pink flowers, so on a pale, mid-sized flower use the fruit: hairy and smooth-backed in dwarf mallow, usually hairless and strongly net-veined in common mallow. Dwarf mallow lies flat or ascends and common mallow ascends or stands upright, so an ascending plant fits both. Leaf shape and size overlap. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the fruit: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

preparation.text: In culinary applications, it is cooked similar to spinach, or used for thickening soups, as the leaves release a thickening agent similar to okra which is also in the mallow family. In Morocco leaves are known as Bakola or Khobiza, braised as a side dish (called salad, but cooked) or used as a sauce over couscous. The root can be ground and used as a meringue substitute by boiling in water, simmering until thickened, and then whisked like egg whites. In Spain the unripe fruits are eaten raw as a treat (Arraia-Maeztu, Álava), and in Cazorla and Santiago-Pontones (Jaén) people eat the little fruits, called panecillos.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the author gives khobiza as Malva neglecta or Malva parviflora. Serves 2. ½ tbsp olive oil, 1 small onion, thinly sliced, about 500 ml roughly chopped mallow leaves, a pinch of salt and black pepper, and a squeeze of lemon. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion for 2–3 minutes. Add the mallow, toss, and season with salt and pepper. Add the lemon and serve straight away. Keep leftovers in the fridge for a couple of days only.
recipes.title: Palestinian sautéed mallow (khobiza)

recipes.method: Written for mallow (Malva neglecta and other species) by herbalist Erin Smith. 2–3 large handfuls of mallow leaves, 2 tbsp (30 g) butter, 1 large or 2 small onions, finely sliced, 1 large carrot, chopped, 2 celery sticks, chopped, 1 large garlic clove, crushed, about 1 litre of good chicken or vegetable stock, 1 medium potato, 2 tbsp (30 ml) yoghurt or crème fraîche (optional), a pinch of grated nutmeg, salt and black pepper. Soften the onion, carrot, celery and garlic in the butter without browning. Add the stock (and the potato, chopped — the page lists it but does not say when it goes in), bring to the boil and simmer until the potato and carrot mash with a fork. Add the mallow leaves and simmer 5–10 minutes. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg, purée with a hand blender, return to the pan, stir in the cream and warm through. Serve with a little yoghurt or cream and chopped herbs (chives, parsley, rosemary or thyme).
recipes.title: Blended mallow soup

summary.text:
Malva neglecta is a species of plant of the family Malvaceae, native to most of the Old World except sub-Saharan Africa. It is known as common mallow in the United States and also as buttonweed, cheeseplant, cheeseweed, dwarf mallow, and roundleaf mallow.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island, in eastern areas of the South Island from the Marlborough Sounds to Southland, where it is common, and on the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1867.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are inorganic), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.
It has a high nitrate content, similar to that of arugula.

identification.text:
Shallowly taprooted, erect monoecious annual, moderately clothed in short-stalked stinging hairs, otherwise sparsely to densely hairy.  Stem with lateral branches usually present, up to 60 cm high.  Lvs ovate or elliptic, acute, obtuse to truncate at base, coarsely serrate, (1)–2–8–(10) cm long. Petiole c. ⅔ as long as lamina.  Stipules 4 per node, entire, 1–3 mm long. Racemes with numerous ♂ and ♀ fls, up to 1.5–(3) cm long.  Perianth segments of ♀ fls extremely unequal, glabrous to hairy;  margins ciliate. Achene ovoid, light brown, 1.5–2 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Urtica urens, commonly known as annual nettle, dwarf nettle, small nettle, dog nettle,  burning nettle, or bush nettle  is a herbaceous annual flowering plant species in the nettle family Urticaceae.
The native distribution of Urtica urens includes most of Europe except the British Isles, northern Asia, north and northwest Africa.
In the British Isles, Urtica urens is an archaeophyte, an ancient introduction. It has been introduced to all other continents of the world except Antarctica.

identification.text:
Annual herb.  Stems erect, softly hairy, to 1 m tall.  Lvs sparsely to densely hairy.  Rosette and lower stem lvs lyrate-pinnatifid or pinnatifid to almost lyrate-pinnate, 5–10–(30) × (1)–2–8–(15) cm;  terminal lobe ovate to triangular to hastate;  lateral lobes in 1–5 pairs, narrow-lanceolate or triangular, entire, sinuate or coarsely toothed.  Upper stem lvs usually smaller with narrower, but not linear-filiform lobes, or hastate, or ovate and not lobed.  Racemes often flexuous, ebracteate, glabrous or sparsely hairy, 20–40–(60) cm long.  Pedicels 3–5 mm long, elongating to c. 10 mm long at fruiting, sparsely hairy.  Sepals usually hairy, 3–5 mm long, not horned.  Petals yellow, 6–10 mm long.  Anthers 1–1.5 mm long;  filaments > sepals.  Silique glabrous or hairy, spreading, linear-cylindric, (40)–60–100 × 1–1.5 mm;  style 0.5–2 mm long.  Seeds oblong, brown, c. 1 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text:
Glabrous, deciduous shrub to c. 2 m high. Shoots angled. Spines generally 3-partite, < 1.5 cm long on adult shoots. Petiole to 1 cm long; lamina 2–8 × 1–2.5 cm (often some very small lvs on flowering spurs), elliptic to obovate, membranous, dull green above, usually serrulate, sometimes entire; base attenuate; apex obtuse. Fls in racemes to c. 6 cm long at anthesis. Bracts 1–2 mm long, ovate or lanceolate-ovate. Pedicels 5–10 mm long. Perianth segments medium yellow, those of outermost whorl smaller, ovate; innermost sepals c. 5 mm long, obovate; petals c. 5 mm long, obovate, ± rounded at apex. Nectaries c. 1 mm long, prominent, orange. Stamens 2–3 mm long. Ovules 2. Stigma sessile. Berry 9–11 mm long, oblong, scarlet or crimson-scarlet, shining.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry is deciduous and its berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining, without bloom, oblong and 9–11 mm long; Darwin's barberry is evergreen and its berries are black or nearly so, with a whitish bloom, round and 5–7 mm across. European barberry's leaves are thin, dull green, usually finely toothed and 2–8 cm long; Darwin's barberry's are glossy dark green above, with spiny lobes, up to about 3.5 cm. European barberry's spines are mostly three-parted and under 1.5 cm long; Darwin's barberry's split into five. Spiny stems and yellowish flowers in clusters do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: European barberry's berries are scarlet to crimson-scarlet, shining and without bloom, oblong, 9–11 mm long; barberry's are reddish black under a heavy whitish bloom, with dark red juice. European barberry is plainly deciduous, its leaves thin, dull green above and usually finely toothed; barberry is evergreen or partly deciduous, its leaves shining above, somewhat leathery (almost thin in shady, moist places) and often turning reddish in autumn. European barberry grows to about 2 m with spines under 1.5 cm; barberry to about 7 m with spines up to 2.3 cm. Leaf size, yellow flowers in clusters up to about 6 cm, and old homestead and plantation sites do not separate them. In New Zealand barberry has usually been called B. vulgaris, even in Allan's 1940 flora (Flora of New Zealand), so a name in print is no guide.

preparation.text:
The dried fruit is still often used as a condiment, it is very popular in Uzbekistan, for example, where it is used to make the national dish known as 'Plov'.
A refreshing lemon-like drink can be made from the fruit.
The dried young leaves and shoot tips make a refreshing tea.
In Europe, the berries have been traditionally used as an ingredient in making jam. The berries are high in pectin which makes the jam congeal as it cools after having been boiled. In southwestern Asia, especially Iran, the berries are used for cooking, as well as for jam-making. In Iran, barberries are commonly used as a currant in rice pilaf.
Eaten raw, European barberries are usually flavoured with something, because they can be very sour; cooking or drying mellows the sourness (MasterClass).
Wear gloves to pick them, as the shrubs are very thorny, and strip the berries from their stalks indoors. The seeds are large for the size of the berry: for jam, cook the berries until soft and press them through a fine sieve to hold back the seeds, stalk bits and the small black flower remains at the tip of each berry (Creative Canning).

recipes.method: From a German herbal page about the common barberry (Berberis vulgaris). Bring 1 kg washed berries to the boil with 500 ml water and simmer for about 20 minutes. Pour through a sieve and catch the juice. Mix the juice with 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind (Gelierzucker 2:1, sugar with added pectin for twice its weight of fruit), bring back to the boil, boil hard for about 4 minutes and pour into sterilised jars.
recipes.title: Barberry jelly

recipes.method: Written for European barberry (Berberis vulgaris) by a forager who picks it wild from hedgerows in Vermont. Put 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups) in a saucepan with 250 ml water and simmer gently for about 5 minutes, mashing, until the berries fall apart and release their juice. Press through a fine sieve to remove the seeds, stalk bits and black flower remains; sieve again through a finer sieve or muslin for a smoother jam. Expect about 375 ml of pulp. Return it to a clean pan with the same volume of sugar (about 375 ml for 375 ml of pulp), bring to a rolling boil over high heat and boil, stirring all the time, for 2 to 3 minutes, until it starts to gel; test on a plate chilled in the freezer. It sets soft and spoonable. Ladle into two hot, sterilised 250 ml jars, leaving 6 mm headspace. Keep in the fridge or freezer, or process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes (15 minutes above about 1,800 m) and leave undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours before checking the seals. Sealed jars keep 12 to 18 months; once opened, refrigerate and use within 2 to 3 weeks.

summary.text:
Berberis vulgaris, also known as common barberry, European barberry or simply barberry, is a shrub in the genus Berberis native to the Old World. It produces edible but sharply acidic berries, which people in many countries eat as a tart and refreshing fruit.
The shrub is native to central and southern Europe, southern England, northwest Africa and western Asia; it is also naturalised in northern Europe and North America. In the United States and Canada, it has become established in the wild over an area from Nova Scotia to Nebraska, with additional populations in Colorado, Idaho, Washington state, Montana, and British Columbia. It is also cultivated in many countries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): S.: Canterbury, Otago, especially inland.
European barberry was introduced to N.Z. in the early period of European settlement, and seems to have been mainly planted in the South Id.
B. vulgaris is the alternate host species of the wheat stem rust fungus (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici), a grass-infecting rust fungus that is a serious fungal disease of wheat and related grains.
In New Zealand, where it has been naturalised since 1875, it spreads both by seed and by suckering; it sets a great deal of seed, which birds and people carry (NZPCN).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text:
Deciduous, generally small tree up to  c. 6–(9) m high when mature, sometimes forming thickets, not or sparsely armed;  trunk short to fairly tall;  secondary branches erect to spreading.  Lf petiole (10)–15–30 mm long, pilose at least when young;  blade moderately thin, obovate to broadly elliptic or suborbicular, 30–70–(120) × 15–45–(60) mm, acute or short-apiculate at apex, cuneate at base, glabrous and ± slightly shining above, duller below, hairy at first and usually with at least some hairs remaining on major veins and lower part of margins, otherwise glabrous, serrulate, almost 2-serrate or crenate, sometimes with teeth glandular; stipules short, oblong-triangular, deciduous.  Fls 1–2–(4), in fascicles on short shoots, not fragrant;  pedicels (5)–10–25–(30) mm long, pendent or spreading, glabrous or hairy, greenish.  Hypanthium broad;  sepals oblong-lanceolate,  c. 3 mm long, obtuse, glabrous or glabrate except on inner face, mostly green, often becoming reflexed, with or without marginal, stalked glands.  Petals 5, spreading, ± orbicular or elliptic-obovate, (8)–10–15 mm long, rounded, ± undulate, white or greenish white.  Stamens < petals;  filaments whitish.   Fr. (20)–25–45 mm long (to  c. 60 mm in cultivation), globose, subglobose, broadly ellipsoid or broadly ovoid-oblong, sulcate, glabrous, green, yellow, red or blackish purple in flesh and skin, usually pruinose, somewhat sweet to dry or slightly bitter;  stone smooth.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: No single test settles it; most of these ranges overlap. Size: a cherry plum is 15–30 mm long, sometimes only 10 mm, and a plum 25–45 mm, sometimes only 20 mm, so a fruit over 30 mm points to the plum, and anything smaller is not settled by size (Flora of North America gives the plum 15–35 mm). Colour overlaps: cherry plums are yellow to orange-red or scarlet, sometimes dark crimson, and only slightly bloomed; plums green, yellow, red or blackish purple, usually bloomed. The midrib does not help, because cherry plum's can be densely hairy on its lower third underneath. Flora of New Zealand records cherry plum fruiting from November to January and the plum from January to February. Both flower in August and September.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prunus_domestica The pulp is edible and usually sweet, though some varieties are sour enough to need cooking with sugar. On the hybrid sign in the scientific name: the parentage was long held to be Prunus spinosa with P. cerasifera, but recent cytogenetic evidence seems to implicate P. cerasifera as the sole wild stock from which the cultivated plant could have evolved. Greengages and damsons are subspecies of the same plant, and Wikipedia says (without citation) that the subspecies cross easily.

The kernels, and the chemistry behind the warning. Plum kernels contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that releases hydrogen cyanide when broken down in the small intestine — the same compound as in apple seeds and peach kernels. summary.text: Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae. A deciduous tree, it includes many varieties of the fruit trees known as plums in English, though not all plums belong to this species. The greengages and damsons also belong to subspecies of P. domestica.

warnings: Never eat the stones or kernels — they contain cyanogenic compounds.

habitat.text:
Marasmius oreades grows extensively throughout North America, especially the east where they are also more diverse, and Europe in the summer and autumn (May–November in the UK), or year-round in warmer climates. It appears in grassy areas such as lawns, meadows, and even dunes in coastal areas.
It grows gregariously in troops, arcs, or rings (type II, which causes the grass to grow and become greener).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Marasmius oreades' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap is 1–5 centimetres across; it is bell-shaped with a somewhat inrolled margin at first, becoming broadly convex with an even or uplifted margin. It usually retains a slight central bump and is dry, smooth, pale tan or buff (occasionally white), or reddish tan; it usually changes color markedly as it dries out; the margin is sometimes faintly lined.
The bare, pallid, and tough stem grows up to about 2–6 cm tall and 2–6 mm in diameter.
The gills are attached to the stem or free from it, fairly thick and spaced apart, and white or pale tan, with a cyanide-like odor and producing a white spore print. The spores measure 7–10 μm × 4–6 μm; they are smooth, elliptical, and inamyloid. Cystidia are absent. The pileipellis is without broom cells.


Similar species
It can resemble M. nigrodiscus.
This mushroom can be mistaken for the toxic Clitocybe dealbata or C. rivulosa, which have closely spaced decurrent gills. The latter lacks an umbo and is white to grey in color.
Some species of the Collybia, Marasmiellus, Micromphale, and Strobilurus genera are also similar, sometimes requiring microscopic analysis to differentiate.
