summary.text: Marasmius oreades, also known as the fairy ring mushroom, fairy ring champignon or Scotch bonnet, is a mushroom native to North America and Europe.

edibleParts.text: Young leaves and growing tips. Seeds can be eaten but need care to process.

habitat.text: Cultivated and disturbed ground: vegetable gardens, compost heaps, paddock edges, building sites. Anywhere the soil has been turned.

identification.text: Upright, 30 cm to 1.5 m, with a stem often streaked red or purple. Leaves are roughly diamond- or goosefoot-shaped with wavy teeth, and the young leaves and growing tips are coated in a white, mealy bloom that rubs off. Flowers are tiny, green and clustered, without petals.

lookalikes.howToTell: Before flowers or fruit appear, no reliable field test is recorded. Fat hen is green or grey-mealy, the mealy coating, when present, denser underneath, and very rarely the leaf is bright green; Flora of New Zealand describes no mealy coating on black nightshade, whose leaves usually carry scattered short hairs. Leaf shape and toothing overlap and do not separate them. In flower and fruit: black nightshade has flowers 10–13 mm across, often star-shaped, usually white (sometimes pale mauve) around a yellow cone of anthers, in small few-flowered clusters, then round berries 7–10 mm across, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow. Fat hen's flowers are tiny and green with no petals, packed in dense spikes and panicles, and it forms no berry: its fruit stays wrapped in the flower parts around a glossy black seed 1.1–1.4 mm across.

preparation.text: Cook like spinach — steam or wilt. Do not eat raw in quantity.

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

Savage, G.P. & Vanhanen, L. 2018, 'Oxalate Contents of Raw, Boiled, Wok-Fried and Pesto and Juice Made from Fat Hen (Chenopodium album) Leaves', Foods 8(1): 2 (Lincoln University, New Zealand). https://doi.org/10.3390/foods8010002 — measures what cooking actually does to the oxalate, and it is the reason this entry's preparation note now says to boil and tip the water away. Raw leaves held 1112.4 mg total oxalate per 100 g dry matter; boiling dropped that to 682.8 and wok-frying to 883.6. The soluble fraction is the one that matters for kidney stones, and it stayed at about three-quarters of the total in both raw and boiled leaves while falling to 53.4% in wok-fried ones. Making the cooked leaves into pesto, or juicing them, significantly reduced both total and soluble oxalate. Checked 06/10/2026.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Chenopodium album', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chenopodium_album On eating it: young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked, leaves are preferably cooked, and the flower buds and flowers can also be eaten cooked. A 100 g serving of cooked leaves is high in vitamin C (96% of the daily value), vitamin A (73%), riboflavin (37%), manganese (37%), calcium (31%) and vitamin B6 (21%). It is a close relative of quinoa, which is grown for the same kind of seed.

Nitrate accumulation, which is the entry's second warning. Fat hen is a known nitrate accumulator; drought, fertilisation and nutrient deficiency all drive nitrate up in the tissues, concentrations are generally highest in the stems, and animal metabolism converts nitrate to nitrite, which is the toxic form. Nitrate poisoning of cattle fed Chenopodium album hay is on record. Oxalate is highest in the fastest-growing plants and much higher in the leaves than the seeds or stems, and older foliage also carries saponins. Oregon State University Extension, 'Nitrate and Oxalate Poisoning'. Checked 06/10/2026. https://extension.oregonstate.edu/sites/extd8/files/documents/1/ppnitrateoxalatepoisoning0.pdf

summary.text: Not wild so much as unclaimed — every second suburban street has a tree dropping more than anyone can eat.

warnings: Fruit fallen onto a berm is usually fair game; fruit on the tree is not. Ask.

edibleParts.text: Cap and stem.

habitat.text: Open grazed pasture and paddocks, especially after autumn rain. Not in woodland.

harvestEthics.text: Pasture is almost always private land, and often recently sprayed or fertilised. Ask the farmer.

identification.text: White cap, sometimes with fine scales. Gills start pink and mature to chocolate brown — never white at maturity. Stem is short with a thin ring and NO sac or bulb at the base. Flesh may bruise faintly pinkish, never bright yellow. Pleasant mushroom smell.

lookalikes.howToTell: Death cap's gills are white, turning cream, sometimes with a faint pink or green tint, as it ages, but not the deep pink then chocolate-brown of a field mushroom. Its stem base sits in a white, sack-like volva that is sometimes underground, so you must dig up the whole base to see it. It has a skirt-like ring that usually stays; a field mushroom's thin ring often disappears. Cap colour does not separate them. Death caps are usually yellow-green, olive or bronze, but young caps can be almost white and an all-white form occurs. In a closed button a white veil hides a field mushroom's gills, so never judge a button. Death cap grows with trees, especially oak (in New Zealand it is thought to have arrived with introduced trees such as oak or spruce), and field mushrooms are often found in fields bordered by trees that death cap can be associated with, so open grass is no guarantee. Half a mature cap is reportedly a lethal dose for an adult. Always dig up the whole mushroom and always check gill colour. A spore print confirms it: field mushroom deep chocolate brown, death cap white.
lookalikes.name: Death cap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut through the base of the stem, or scratch the cap edge. Yellow stainer turns bright chrome yellow almost at once, most strongly at the stem base (the change is most marked in young, fresh mushrooms), and smells of ink, phenol or iodine, especially at the cut base. Field mushroom does not turn yellow: its flesh reddens when cut and it smells pleasant. Field mushroom's stem narrows towards the base; yellow stainer's base is bulbous. White caps and pink-then-brown gills are shared, both can grow on lawns, and a spore print will not help - both drop dark brown. Check every stem base.

summary.text: Familiar and delicious — and the species whose lookalikes include the deadliest fungus on earth.

warnings: Dig up the entire base of every single mushroom. A buried volva is the difference between dinner and a liver transplant.
Never harvest a white-gilled mushroom. If the gills are white, put it down.
Amanita phalloides is established in New Zealand and is associated with oak, birch and other introduced trees.
Never eat a wild mushroom you have not confirmed with an experienced identifier. Photos are not identification.

habitat.text: Brassica rapa is an early-season nectar and pollen source for a wide range of insects. Numerous pollinators are attracted to its bright yellow flowers, including bees, flies, and butterflies. A common visitor, the small white butterfly (Pieris rapae) uses the plant both as a nectar source and as a host for larval feeding. Conversely, insect pollination is also very important to the plant; insect pollination of B. rapa leads to 30% more yield when compared to self-fertilizing controls. Furthermore, B. rapa can undergo rapid genomic adaptations when selected on by bumblebees.

identification.text:
Annual with lax rosette.  Stems erect or ascending, glabrous, to 1.5 m tall, sometimes becoming subwoody below.  Lower lvs petiolate, lyrate-pinnatifid with large terminal and 1–3 pairs of lateral lobes, bright green, bristly, 15–25–(30) × 5–10 cm;  margins sinuate, toothed. Upper lvs becoming amplexicaul, glaucous, not lobed, sessile, glabrous, narrowly triangular, entire, 2–10 × 1–2 cm.  Racemes to 40 cm long;  open fls overtopping buds.  Sepals narrow-oblong, (4)–5–7 × 1–1.5 mm.  Petals bright yellow, 6–10 × 3–4 mm.  Lateral stamens spreading.  Silique terete, glabrous, linear-lanceolate, slightly constricted between seeds, (30)–40–60 × 2–5 mm;  gynophore 0;  valves with prominent median and weaker lateral veins;  beak tapering, seedless, 6–10 mm long.  Seeds reddish brown, 1–1.5 mm diam.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

sources: Wikipedia, 'Stachys arvensis' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Field woundwort is an annual herb with branched, square stems up to 45 cm long, growing with a sprawling or erect habit. The stems are pale green and covered with patent, sparsely glandular hairs up to 2 mm long. Plants are easily uprooted to reveal a mass of short, white, fibrous roots at the base of the plant and sometimes along any horizontal stems close to the base. The leaves are arranged in opposite, decussate pairs, with no stipules, and petioles of up to 4 cm long; the blade is simple and oval, up to 4 cm long, with a truncate base and between 7 and 12 rounded teeth per side. They are dull, medium green on the upper surface and paler beneath, hairy on both sides.
The inflorescence consists of a terminal spike with up to 8 false whorls (actually two opposite clusters that look like a whorl) of 4 to 7 flowers, each with a short pedicel of up to 1.5 mm. The whorls are subtended by a pair of leaf-like bracts which are stalked at the base of the inflorescence, becoming sessile towards the top of the plant. There is also one tiny bracteole at the base of each cluster of flowers. The lower whorls are widely spaced, but the upper ones are more crowded towards the tip of the plant. The flowers are zygomorphic with 
a 5 lobed calyx tube 5 to 7 mm long, and two lipped corolla 6 to 8 mm. The upper lip is entire and the lower lip is three lobed, with the central lobe much larger. It can be white, pink or purple.

identification.text:
The common forms of P. aurea are easily identified by their characteristic compressed internodes in the lower part of the canes which have a tortoise shell-like appearance.
Fairly dense thicket-forming with rhizomes running extensively. Culm usually 3–6 m (often taller in cultivation), glaucous when young, green during the first year, yellow afterwards, erect, with white waxy ring beneath nodes when young; nodes on some shoots congested and sometimes zigzag towards base; internodes swollen and often asymmetric. Culm-sheath light mauve-brown or pinkish brown, mottled dark purplish, especially towards apex; auricles and oral bristles 0; sheath-blade narrow linear, flat, often with greenish pink marginal band. Branches spreading widely to give an open network. Leaf-sheath with long oral bristles. Auricles 0. Ligule minutely puberulent. Leaf-blade usually 5–13–(15) × 0.7–2–(2.7) cm, lanceolate, abaxially glaucescent, acuminate.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Check the leaves: arrow bamboo's blades reach 25–30 cm long and 3.5–4 cm wide, glossy dark green above, against fishpole's usually 5–13 cm and under 3 cm wide. Arrow bamboo has one branch per node, sometimes two or three at the upper nodes, where fishpole usually has two markedly unequal branches. Its canes are round, not notched, and dark green; fishpole's internodes are flattened or grooved on alternate sides above each node (usually round below the lowest branches), and its canes turn yellow after the first year, with crowded nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base of some canes. Height does not separate them (arrow bamboo 3–5 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), and both have a white band below the nodes (on fishpole, on young canes). Arrow bamboo's young shoots are edible cooked, with a rather bitter flavour.
lookalikes.name: Arrow bamboo

lookalikes.howToTell: Black bamboo's canes are green at first and either stay green or turn black or heavily black-blotched in their second year; fishpole's turn yellow after their first. Because some naturalised black bamboo stays green, a green stand does not rule it out — look at the nodes and sheaths instead. Black bamboo's nodes are all more or less evenly spaced; some of fishpole's canes have crowded, sometimes zigzag nodes and swollen, often lopsided internodes near the base. Black bamboo's cane sheaths are uniformly purple or purple-flushed, with prominent dark auricles on the main shoots; fishpole's are light mauve-brown or pinkish brown mottled dark purple, with no auricles. Both have a white waxy ring below the nodes on young canes, and their heights overlap (black bamboo 4–7 m, fishpole usually 3–6 m), so neither helps. Both have edible young shoots, cooked.

preparation.text: The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways. The shoots of some species contain cyanide that must be leached or boiled out before they can be eaten safely. Slicing the bamboo shoots thinly assists in this leaching.

recipes.method: The husk is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs, so handle it with that in mind. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base. The sweetest shoots of the genus, with very little bitterness, and reported edible raw — but the warning on this page stands, so cook them unless you have reason to trust that claim. Cover with water, boil, change the water once, and simmer until tender; they need far less of this than the others. The canes are slender, about 15 mm, thicker in their native China. Cut them at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil.

summary.text: Phyllostachys aurea is a species of bamboo, and is of the 'running bamboo' type, belonging to the diverse Bambuseae tribe. Brought here from south-eastern China as an ornamental and naturalised since 1977, it is named on DOC's list of environmental weeds.

warnings: Raw bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides, natural toxins also contained in cassava. The toxins must be destroyed by thorough cooking, and for this reason, fresh bamboo shoots are boiled before being used in other ways.

identification.text:
It is a deciduous shrub growing to 3 metres tall and broad. It is naturally multi-stemmed with an upright-arching to rounded habit, although it can be grown in tree form. The bark is dark brownish-grey with prominent paler brown lenticels.
The leaves are alternately arranged, simple, 2–7 centimetres long and broad, palmately lobed with five lobes. When young in spring, they have a strong resinous scent.
The flowers are produced in early spring at the same time as the leaves emerge, on dangling racemes 3–7 cm long of 5–30 flowers; each flower is 5–10 millimetres in diameter, with five red, pink, or white petals.
The fruit is a dark purple oval berry about 1 cm long; it has an insipid taste.

summary.text:
Ribes sanguineum, the flowering currant, redflower currant, red-flowering currant, or red currant is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Grossulariaceae.
It is native to the western United States, Canada and Mexico. In western British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon, it is distributed widely in the moist regions west of the Cascades. In California it is restricted to areas near the coast, and can be found as far south as Santa Barbara County. In Mexico, it is only found on the Pacific island of Guadalupe, where it may be extirpated. Although its conservation status is secure across the rest of its range, in Idaho it is critically imperiled and is found only rarely in Bonner, Kootenai, Benewah, and Adams counties.
It is widely cultivated and naturalized throughout temperate Europe and Australasia.

habitat.text:
Forest margins.
Cordyline banksii tolerates a wide variety of habitats. It is common in coastal, lowland, and lower montane forests in the North Island, widespread in the northern half of the South Island and Westland as far south as Haast. It also occasionally occurs in subalpine regions in the South Island. In shrublands it occurs with Cordyline pumilio and may form hybrids with it.

identification.text: Tī ngahere is a sparingly-branched cabbage tree up to 4 metres tall. The leaves are lanceolate (somewhat paddle-shaped), up to 2 metres long and from 40–80 millimetres wide. The leaves are broad in the mid portion and droop from there. A prominent flat midrib runs the whole length of the leaf. The fruiting panicle is up to 2 metres in length. The flowers are white and pleasantly perfumed. The globe-shaped fruit are up to 5 millimetres in diameter, and are white, bluish-white, or blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: cabbage tree grows to the size of a small tree with a thick trunk and many branches, and its leaf stalk is flat and ill-defined, at least three-quarters as wide as the widest part of the blade; forest cabbage tree rarely approaches tree form and, if tall, usually has several more or less equal main stems, and its leaf stalk is narrow, long (up to a quarter of the blade's length) and deeply channelled, widening rather abruptly into a much wider blade that droops at the tip, with a prominent midrib and several stronger side nerves. Both have white, scented flowers, so flower colour does not separate them. Flora of New Zealand records that where the two overlap at about 300–1,000 ft (90–300 m) on the northern tip of the Tararua Range, about half the plants cannot be put strictly in either species.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf cabbage tree is rarely more than 2 m tall and often flowers while its short stem is still leafy to the ground; its leaves are 30–60–(100) × 1–2 cm, more or less narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk, with the midrib prominent underneath at least near the base; its panicle is very open, up to about 60 cm long, with slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers that are whitish or pink outside, and its berries are bluish or flecked with blue, 4–5 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key: dwarf cabbage tree is usually no more than 1–(2) m tall with a main stem 1–2 cm across and leaves rarely over 2 cm wide, its flower cluster large for the plant but with very slender branches and small, widely spaced flowers; forest cabbage tree's main stem soon exceeds 2 cm across even on a young plant, and its leaves are mostly over 2 cm wide. A hybrid between the two has been described (C. × gibbingsae, Carse 1929) that looks like a small, stemless forest cabbage tree, so an in-between plant may be neither.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain cabbage tree grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Forest cabbage tree (Cordyline banksii) grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key puts mountain cabbage tree apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Kirk (1874) listed 'dubious forms' among New Zealand cabbage trees, some intermediate between these two.

habitat.text: G. monspessulana and related plants are common in European shrublands. French broom was originally distributed throughout Mediterranean Europe and northwest Africa, the Azores, and the Canary Islands. Due to its lower tolerance for frost than other broom species, it is common in warmer, lower elevation areas. It is found on coastal strips and in sunny inland areas, and does best with plentiful rainfall and sandy soils.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Genista monspessulana' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
G. monspessulana grows to 1–2.5 metres tall, with slender green branches. Stems generally ridged or angled and green when young. The leaves are evergreen, trifoliate with three narrow obovate leaflets, 1–2 centimetres long. The flowers are yellow, grouped 3–9 together in short racemes. Like other legumes, it develops its seeds within a pod. The pods are 2–3 cm long, tough and hard, covered all over with hairs, and are transported easily by flowing water and animals. They burst open with force, dispersing the seeds several metres. The plant begins seed production once it reaches a height of approximately 40 cm, and each plant can live for 10–20 years. One mature plant can produce 10,000 seeds per season. The generous seed production and the plant's ability to re-sprout after cutting or burning help it to invade new habitat vigorously when introduced.
It is related to the common broom and Spanish broom.

identification.text:
Bushy shrub to  c. 1 m high, often grey and with stellate tomentum, strongly aromatic.  Lvs sessile, linear to narrow-oblong, sometimes revolute, mostly 2–3 cm long, pinnate with obtuse leaflets to pinnatifid or crenulate, with scattered simple hairs in the stellate tomentum.  Peduncle to 30 cm long, much > spike;  spike 3–4.5 cm long, broad-cylindric, dense.  Fertile bracts 7–11 mm long, broad-ovate, apiculate, purplish;  sterile apical bracts 7–10 mm long, ovate, ovate-lanceolate, to nearly elliptic, mauve-blue.  Calyx 5–7 mm long, tubular, ± tomentose outside;  dorsal appendage broadly reniform to suborbicular, ± mucronate.  Corolla 8–10 mm long;  tube > calyx by  c.  2 mm;  limb mauve, somewhat irregular;  lobes 1.5–2.5 mm long.  Nutlets  c. 1.5 mm long, oblong, not mucilaginous when wet.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is distinguished from all other spp. in sect. Stoechas by its pinnate or toothed lvs.

lookalikes.howToTell: French lavender's leaves are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped; topped lavender's leaves are entire. French lavender's flowers are mauve; topped lavender's are dark purple. French lavender's flower stalk, up to 30 cm, is much longer than its spike; topped lavender's is about as long as its spike. The sterile bracts crowning the spike are 7–10 mm long in French lavender, 1–2 cm in topped lavender. Wetted, topped lavender's nutlets turn mucilaginous; French lavender's do not. Leaves that are often grey with star-shaped hairs, a strong aromatic smell and a crown of sterile bracts on the spike do not separate them: both belong to the same section of the genus.
lookalikes.name: Topped lavender

lookalikes.howToTell: French lavender's flower spike is crowned by mauve-blue sterile bracts 7–10 mm long, and has no bracteoles; common lavender's spike has no enlarged bracts at its tip, and has bracteoles. French lavender's leaves are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped. A strong aromatic smell and flower spikes held on long stalks do not separate them. Lavandins (L. × intermedia), common lavender's hybrids with spike lavender, are very common in gardens in many colder parts of New Zealand and, like common lavender, lack enlarged terminal bracts.

summary.text:
Lavandula dentata, the fringed lavender or French lavender, is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Yemen, and the Arabian Peninsula.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: naturalised around old house sites in 2 former settlements on Rangitoto Id. Toothed lavender is a very common cultigen in lowland areas of the North Id and northern parts of the South Id. The common name French lavender is sometimes wrongly applied to this sp.; it should be reserved for L. stoechas.
Other names: toothed lavender (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN); fringed lavender (Wikipedia).

edibleParts.text: The leaves and stems are edible, and are widely collected for food. Leaves - raw or cooked. A very mild flavour with a mucilaginous texture, they make a very acceptable part of a mixed salad, or a good filling for a salad sandwich, though they are somewhat boring on their own. The cooked leaf has a rather slimy texture. Seed - raw. Best used before it is fully mature, the seed has a pleasant nutty taste but it is rather small and fiddly to harvest.

identification.text:
Annual or short-lived perennial, procumbent, ascending or erect herb. Stems sparsely to moderately hairy with usually simple hairs. Lvs glabrous to sparsely hairy with usually simple hairs and rarely stellate hairs above, sparsely to moderately hairy below, reniform to orbicular, obtuse to cordate at base, shallowly or moderately 5–7-palmately lobed and crenate, 1–10–(15) cm diam.; petioles 1–20–(30) cm long; stipules broadly ovate with acute apex, 2–8 mm long. Fls in axillary clusters of (1)–2–6; fruiting pedicels 2–10–(15) mm long; epicalyx segments narrowly ovate-oblong to broadly ovate, ± = calyx at flowering; calyx teeth broadly ovate-triangular, sparsely hairy with simple or stellate hairs and ciliate on teeth but lower tube ± glabrous, slightly enlarged at fruiting; petals pale lilac or pink with darker veins and tips, about 2× length of calyx, 6–10 mm long. Mericarps 8–9–(10) per fr., often hairy when immature but usually becoming glabrous, strongly reticulately veined on back; edges sharply angled but not winged.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
N.Z. material has petals < the 10–12 mm given in European Floras, possibly indicating that plants have come from the E. part of the sp. range. M. nicaeensis is distinguished from small forms of M. sylvestris by the glabrous base of the calyx tube, from M. neglecta by the strongly reticulately veined mericarps, and from M. parviflora by the squared edges of the mericarps and longer petals.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the edges of the fruit segments (squared in French mallow, slightly winged in cheeseweed mallow) and French mallow's longer petals. Both have strongly net-veined fruit, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates French mallow from small forms of common mallow by the hairless base of the calyx tube (hairy in common mallow), and notes common mallow's slightly longer petals and longer fruiting stalks. Both have strongly net-veined fruit segments, so the veining does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the fruit: strongly net-veined on the back in French mallow, smooth or faintly veined (and hairy) in dwarf mallow. Petal lengths overlap (6–10 mm against (7–)8–15 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

preparation.text: They make an excellent garnish when chopped and fried in olive-oil with onions and spices. A particularly famous preparation are the Khubeza patties. In Villarino de los Aires (Salamanca, Spain) the green, unripe fruits are eaten raw.

recipes.method: Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. The author was told by Turkish cooks that large mallow leaves are used as wrappers for dolma, and went looking for the biggest-leaved mallows they could find. Serves 8. Large mallow leaves, about 240 ml short- or medium-grain rice (not long-grain, which sets hard when cold), ½ onion, finely chopped, about 225 g fresh mushrooms, finely chopped, about 80 ml pesto, 3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil, and salt. Prepare the leaves as you would grape leaves: boil them in salted water for a minute or two, cool them in iced water, and let them drip dry. Heat a large frying pan over high heat, add the mushrooms and shake the pan often until they give up their water. When most of it has gone, add the onion, oil and a little salt and fry until the onion starts to colour. Add the rice, toast it for a minute, then add about 240 ml water and a little salt, turn the heat to medium and cook until the water is absorbed. Take off the heat, let the rice cool, and stir in the pesto (with a little more oil if the pesto is dry). Lay a leaf smooth side down, base towards you, and put about a tablespoon of filling in a short log across the bottom, leaving at least 1 cm clear at each side. Fold the bottom up once, fold in the sides and roll up; leaves vary in size, so adjust the filling to suit. Pack the rolls seam side down and snug together in a steamer insert or on the bottom of a large pot, up to three layers deep; mallow rolls do not need weighing down. Add water to just below the rolls, cover, bring to the boil and steam gently for 40 minutes to an hour, until the rice is no longer crunchy. Serve warm or at room temperature; they keep a week in the fridge.

summary.text:
Malva nicaeensis is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family known by the common names bull mallow and French mallow. It grows in the Middle East, where it has variously served as food.
In New Zealand it grows throughout the North Island and in Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury and North Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1957, though Flora of New Zealand says it was present much longer and had been confused with other mallows.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Monstera deliciosa' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: Monstera deliciosa is native to humid tropical forests, in lowlands and on lower mountains, in the south of Mexico and also in Costa Rica, Guatemala and Panama. The seeds fall to the ground, then the seedlings crawl (negative phototropism) until they meet a tree on which to attach. The many adjacent roots thus allow the plant to anchor against its new support and reach the canopy light (although it rarely grows in full sun and prefers a light dimmed by the foliage).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Monstera deliciosa' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
This member of the arum family (Araceae) is a hemiepiphyte with aerial roots. It is able to grow up to 20 m high in the wild, with large, leathery, glossy, pinnate, heart-shaped leaves 25–90 cm long by 25–75 cm broad. The leaves on young plants are smaller and entire with no lobes or holes, but soon produce lobed and fenestrate leaves as they grow. Although it can grow very tall in nature, it only measures between 2 and 3 m when grown indoors. The older the plant, the more the leaves are covered with its familiar large perforations. The exact purpose of the fenestrations remains unclear, but three main theories have been brought forth: increasing water absorption, limiting the damage done by the wind and reducing the impact of herbivores. 
Wild seedlings grow towards the darkest area they can grow until they find a tree trunk, then start to grow up towards the light, creeping up the tree.
The inflorescence is adorned with a cream-white spathe of uniform, velvety appearance, covering, like a hood, a yellowish white spadix 10 to 15 cm high and about 3 cm in diameter. Flowers are bisexual, containing both androecium and gynoecium, though protogynous development reduces self-pollination; in the wild they are pollinated mainly by nitidulid beetles.


Fruit

The fruit of Monstera deliciosa is up to 25 cm long and 3–5 cm diameter, and it looks like a green ear of maize covered with hexagonal scales. As the fruit ripens, these scales or platelets fall off the fruit, releasing a strong and sweet scent. The smell has been compared to a combination of pineapples and bananas. The fruit is edible and safe for humans.
Fruits of plants of the Araceae (Arum family) often contain raphides and trichosclereids – needle-like structures of calcium oxalate. In M. deliciosa, unripe fruit containing these needle-like crystalline structures can cause irritation of the mouth.
It takes longer than a year for fruits to reach maturity. The fruit first shows signs of ripening by the yellowing of its lowest scales. As it ripens, the starch that was stored in the green fruit is converted to sugar, giving it its sweet flavor. This mechanism is comparable to how banana fruits ripen. The strong odor the fruit produces becomes noticeable when it is half-ripe. As time passes and the fruit continues to ripen, the odor becomes stronger. After it becomes fully ripe, however, the scent deteriorates quickly.

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Fruit-salad plant' entry.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Atriplex hortensis' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Atriplex hortensis is a hardy annual plant, with an erect, branching stem. It varies in height from two to six feet, according to the variety and soil. The leaves are variously shaped, but somewhat oblong, comparatively thin, and slightly acidic to the taste. There are varieties with red, white and green leaves. The flowers are small and obscure, greenish or reddish, corresponding to a degree with the color of the foliage of the plant. They can be male, female or hermaphrodite. The fruits are often overhanging because of their weight. The seeds retain their viability for three years. The yellow-brown seeds with a diameter of 3 to 4 millimeters and a more translucent seed shell are immediately germable. The black seeds with a diameter of only 1.5 to 2 millimeters and smooth, thick, leathery seed shell germinate only after two years.
The pollination is carried out by self-pollination, wind pollination, or insects.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Parsley' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Garden parsley is a bright green, biennial plant in temperate climates, or an annual herb in subtropical and tropical areas.
Where it grows as a biennial, in the first year, it forms a rosette of tripinnate leaves 10–25 cm long with numerous 1–3 cm leaflets, and a taproot used as a food store over the winter. In the second year, it grows a flowering stem to 75 cm tall with sparser leaves and flat-topped 3–10 cm diameter umbels with numerous 2 mm diameter yellow to yellowish-green flowers.
The seeds are ovoid, 2–3 mm long, with prominent style remnants at the apex. One of the compounds of the essential oil is apiole. The plant normally dies after seed maturation.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Matricaria chamomilla' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Matricaria chamomilla is a member of the Asteraceae family, native to southern and eastern Europe. It can be found on all continents, has a branched, erect and smooth stem, and grows to a height of 15–60 cm. The long and narrow leaves are bipinnate or tripinnate. The flowers are borne in paniculate flower heads (capitula). The white ray florets are furnished with a ligule, while the disc florets are yellow. The hollow receptacle is swollen and lacks scales. This property distinguishes German chamomile from Anthemis arvensis (corn chamomile), which has a receptacle with scales. The flowers bloom in early to midsummer and are fragrant.
The essential oil of the flowers gives them a characteristic smell and has interesting properties. The blue color of the oil, attributable to the chamazulene it contains, explains why the plant is also known by the common name blue chamomile. The fruit is a yellowish-brown achene.

habitat.text: The giant puffball is commonly found in meadows, fields, and deciduous forests in late summer and autumn. It is found in temperate areas throughout the world.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Calvatia gigantea' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Calvatia gigantea grows up to 10–50 centimetres wide and high. It can grow to 80 cm diameter and weigh several kilograms. A specimen weighing over 23 kg was recorded in Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada.
The interior of an immature puffball is white, while that of a mature specimen is greenish brown. The fruiting body of a puffball mushroom develops within a few weeks and soon begins to decompose and rot, at which point it becomes dangerous to eat. Unlike most mushrooms, all the spores of the giant puffball are created inside the fruiting body; large specimens can easily contain several trillion. The spores are yellowish, smooth, and 3–6 μm in size. They produce a white spore print when young, while it is olive with an unpleasant smell in age. Prof. John Lindley has calculated that C. gigantea grows at a rate of sixty million new cells per minute on its way to making seven quintillion  (7 × 1018) spores.


Similar species
Identification techniques make it relatively easy to distinguish from others of its genus.
Giant puffballs resemble the poisonous common earthball (Scleroderma citrinum). The latter species is distinguished by a much firmer, elastic fruiting body, and having an interior that becomes dark purplish-black with white reticulation early in development.
Immature gilled species, including various Amanita species, can look similar to puffballs while still contained within their universal veil. Many such species are poisonous, or even deadly, such as the destroying angel. To distinguish puffballs, they are cut open; edible puffballs have a solid white interior with no gills or other irregularities. If the inside of the puffball looks gelatinous, it may be a stinkhorn fungus and should not be consumed.

identification.text:
Hairy or occasionally glabrous short-lived perennial herb with stout caudex and many large adventitious roots, occasionally with persistent, well-developed primary roots.  Lvs all radical, rosulate;  petiole 1–20–(30) cm long, broadened at base, channelled.  Lamina to 21 × 16 cm, ovate to suborbicular (somewhat narrower in small-leaved plants), generally puberulent, at least on the main veins beneath, sometimes glabrate or glabrous, entire or remotely dentate;  main veins 5–7;  base truncate to cordate in more typical  large-leaved plants but often cuneate to attenuate in smaller, and especially narrower-leaved forms;  apex rounded to obtuse.  Scapes  c. 5–80 cm long, not ribbed, generally hairy, at least towards base, sometimes glabrous or nearly so. Spikes dense, 1.5- c. 30 cm long, narrow-cylindric.  Bracts ovate, > calyx, herbaceous and keeled, glabrous, sometimes with membranous margin.  Sepals 1.5–2.1 mm long, broad-ovate;  keel green and herbaceous, otherwise sepal scarious.  Corolla tube = or slightly < calyx;  lobes 1–1.3 mm long, ovate to elliptic-ovate, reflexing.  Stamens glabrous, long-exserted.  Style long-exserted, puberulent.  Capsule usually 2.5–4 mm long, broad-ellipsoid, 6–16-seeded.  Seeds 1–1.8 mm long, slightly trigonous but also rather irregular, rugose, dark red, brown, dark brown or black.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Plantago major, the greater plantain, is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
Greater plantain is native to almost all of Europe (Iceland excepted), northern and central Asia, and northern and southern Africa. and has become widely naturalised elsewhere in the world.
The ability of greater plantain to survive frequent trampling and colonise compacted soils makes it important for soil rehabilitation. Its roots break up hardpan surfaces, while simultaneously holding together the soil to prevent erosion. The seeds are a common contaminant in cereal grain and other crop seeds. As a result, it now has a nearly worldwide distribution.
As a result of its wide occurrence, Plantago major has many vernacular names. In addition to greater plantain, other recorded vernacular names include broadleaf plantain, common plantain, broad-leaved plantain, cart track plant, dooryard plantain, greater plantago, healing blade, hen plant, lambs foot, roadweed, roundleaf plantain, snakeroot, waybread, wayside plantain, and white man's footprint. Plantago major is believed to be one of the first plants to reach North America after European colonisation. Reportedly brought to the Americas by Puritan colonists, greater plantain was known among some Native American peoples by the name "white man's footprint", because it thrived in the disturbed and damaged ecosystems surrounding European settlements.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Annual loose tufts or solitary shoots, (18)–25–65–(90) cm. Leaf-sheath papery, glabrous, finely ribbed, light green, light brown or purplish. Ligule 2–4–(5) mm, glabrous, denticulate, centrally tapered. Leaf-blade (2.2)–5–23 cm × 2–8 mm, thin, flat, finely ribbed, gradually tapered to fine acicular tip, abaxially occasionally sparsely prickle-toothed on ribs, adaxially ribs usually finely scaberulous; margins finely scaberulous. Culm (12)–20–50 cm, erect or geniculate at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle (2.2)–4–13–(16) cm, secund, nodding, of 1–12, rarely to 18, papery spikelets; branches few, sparsely scabrid, pedicels filiform, 0.5–2–(3) cm. Spikelets 1–2–(2.5) × 0.6–1.5 cm, 8–15-flowered, silvery, light green to golden-brown, often dark purplish at base. Glumes subequal, 5–6–(6.6) mm, (5)–7–9-nerved, spreading, firmly membranous, concave, suborbicular, smooth, often purplish. Lemma 6.5–8.5 mm, 7–9–(11)-nerved, centrally hardened and concave, glabrous, base cordate, sometimes with minute glandular hairs especially on auricle-like extensions, and appressed fine hairs on broad, firmly membranous margins, apex subacute. Palea 3–4 mm, to ⅔ length of lemma, orbicular, keels finely winged and densely short-ciliate, interkeel glabrous. Lodicules (1)–2–3 mm, lanceolate, obtuse. Anthers 1.5–2 mm. Gynoecium: ovary c. 1 mm; stigma-styles 2 mm. Caryopsis 2.5–3 × 1.5–2 mm; embryo 0.7–1 mm; hilum linear, 1.2–1.5 mm.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

summary.text:
Glechoma hederacea is an aromatic, perennial, evergreen creeper of the mint family Lamiaceae.
European settlers carried it around the world, and it has become a well-established introduced and naturalized plant in a wide variety of localities. It is also considered an aggressive invasive weed of woodlands and lawns in some parts of North America, being considered a non-native plant in the United States, and invasive in some U.S. states. It has invaded wild areas, sometimes choking out native wildflowers.

habitat.text: It is commonly found in damp, recently disturbed soil, open ground, turf and waste places and native to Europe, the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, North Africa, Central Africa, and the Horn of Africa.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Cardamine hirsuta' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Depending on the climate C. hirsuta may complete two generations in a year, one in the spring and one in the fall; also depending on the climate, the seeds may germinate in the fall and the plants may remain green throughout the winter before flowering in the spring. It often grows a rosette of leaves at the base of the stem, while there may be leaves on the upright stem, most of the leaves will be part of the basal rosette. The leaves in this rosette are pinnately divided into 8–15 leaflets which have short stems connecting them to the petiole. These basal leaves are often 3.5–15 cm long. The leaflets are round to ovate in shape and may have smooth or dentate edges. The leaflet at the tip of the leaf (terminal leaflet) will be larger than the other leaflets and round to reniform in shape. The cauline (attached to the upright stem) leaves are also pinnately divided, with fewer leaflets, and generally smaller than the basal leaves; these leaves will be borne on a petiole and are 1.2–5.5 cm long. The stems, petioles, and upper surfaces of the cauline leaves are sparsely hairy.

Plants of this species are usually erect and grow to no more than about 30 centimetres from a stem which is either unbranched or branched near the base. The small white flowers are borne in a raceme without any bracts, soon followed by the seeds and often continuing to flower as the first seeds ripen. The flowers have 4 white petals (which may be lacking but are mostly present) which are 1.5–4.5 mm long and spatulate shaped. The flowers also have 4 stamens of equal height instead of the 6 which are found in most closely related plants. Pollen grains are elongated, approximately 32 microns in length.

Below the flowers there are 4 sepals which are oblong shaped and 1.5–2.5 mm long and .3–.7 mm wide. The seeds are borne in upright pointing siliquae which are straight and 1.5–2.5 cm long and 1–1.4 mm in diameter. When the fruit is ripe the valves on the siliquae will coil tightly from the bottom to the top after being touched and burst explosively, sending the seeds flying far from the parent plant. This seed dispersal strategy is referred to as ballochory and is a type of rapid plant movement.

Hairy bittercress is very similar to Cardamine flexuosa. Some differences are that C. hirsuta stems are hairless and the leaves do not clasp the stems, as in C. flexuosa. It usually has only 4 stamens, while C. flexuosa has 6 stamens, and the fruits of C. hirsuta overtop the flowers whereas in C. flexuosa the fruits do not overtop the younger flowers. The fruits grow in a thin pod arranged as a single row.
Cardamine hirsuta has a chromosome number of 2n = 16.

summary.text:
Cardamine hirsuta, commonly called hairy bittercress, popping cress, common bittercress, hoary bittercress, hairy wood-cress, small bittercress, pepperweed, shotweed, or snapweed, is an annual or biennial species of plant in the family Brassicaceae, and is edible as a salad green.
These conditions are prevalent in nursery or garden centre plants, and hairy bittercress seeds may be introduced with those plants. Once established, it is difficult to eradicate. The tiny flowers are attractive to a few early butterflies, including (in the United States) spring azure (Celastrina ladon) and falcate orange-tip (Anthocharis midea).
Cardamine hirsuta has been introduced in many countries across the world. Its range includes but is not limited to: Argentina, Australia, Canada, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Gabon, Great Britain, India, Japan, Laos, Madagascar, Mexico, Pakistan, Panama, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Turkmenistan, United States, Venezuela, and Vietnam.
The 1889 book The Useful Native Plants of Australia records that it was also called "Lady's Smock" and that "This and other species afford excellent pot-herbs when luxuriant and flaccid. The present one is a common weed almost throughout the world."

Wikipedia contributors. 'Crataegus monogyna', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crataegus_monogyna Corroborates the edible parts and the reason for cooking: the haws are sometimes called edible raw but are too dry to be of interest, and are commonly made into jellies, jams, syrups or wine, or used to flavour brandy; the young leaves are tender enough for salads and the petals are edible too. Each haw contains a single stone-encased seed. Hawthorn petals appear in the medieval English dish spinee, recorded in The Forme of Cury around 1390.

The stones, and how much the risk actually is. The seed contains amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that releases hydrogen cyanide when broken down in the small intestine — the same chemistry as apple pips and cherry stones. The practical risk is dose-dependent and low: poisoning is rare because a large quantity of seed would have to be eaten, and one or two swallowed whole will not hurt an adult, though a child is more exposed. The intact stone is the barrier, which is exactly why crushing, grinding or blending whole haws is the thing not to do — de-stone first, or cook whole and pass through a sieve, discarding the stones. Separately, hawthorn is used in herbal medicine to lower blood pressure and may interact with beta-blockers, blood-pressure medication and digoxin. Checked 06/10/2026.

identification.text:
Annual herb.  Stem erect, hairy, to 1 m tall.  Lvs and petioles with fine stiff hairs.  Rosette lvs deeply lyrate-pinnatifid to lyrate-pinnate, (3)–7–25–(30) × (1.5)–2–9–(12) cm;  terminal leaflet not lobed or 2–3-lobed, broadly toothed, ovate to reniform;  lateral leaflets in 2–6 pairs, ± deflexed, triangular.  Upper stem lvs smaller, deeply lyrate-pinnatifid to lyrate-pinnate;  terminal leaflet narrow-oblong; lateral leaflets in 1–2 pairs, spreading or ± deflexed.  Uppermost stem lvs becoming simple and hastate to narrow-triangular.  Racemes ebracteate, suberect to spreading, hairy, (10)–20–30–(40) cm long.  Pedicels c. 3 mm long, hairy.  Sepals hairy, c. 2 mm long, not horned.  Petals yellow, 3–4 mm long.  Anthers c. 0.5 mm long;  filaments > sepals.  Silique hairy or glabrous, appressed to stem, tapering evenly from base, 10–15–(20) × 1–2 mm; style c. 0.5 mm long.  Seeds oblong, brown, c. 1 mm long.

Rhizomatous, strongly aromatic or foetid perennial herb, to 80–(100) cm tall, densely hirsute, with many glandular hairs, also with sessile, white, glandular scales.  Petioles to 7 cm long in lower lvs, often much less in upper lvs.  Lamina 5–10 × 3–6 cm, usually ovate, sometimes oblong-ovate, deeply crenate-serrate and teeth often mucronulate;  base cordate;  apex acute. Corolla 12–16 mm long, reddish purple with whitish markings on the downward curved, spathulate, lower lip;  tube exserted from calyx;  upper lip hooded, with dense simple and glandular hairs outside;  lower lip c. 9 mm long × 8 mm across lateral lobes, > upper lip. summary.text:
Stachys sylvatica, commonly known as hedge woundwort, whitespot, or sometimes as hedge nettle, is a perennial herbaceous plant growing to 80 cm tall in woodland and unmanaged grassland.
Hedge woundwort is native to Europe and central and western Asia.
It has been introduced into New York state, Ontario, and New Zealand.

edibleParts.text: None.

habitat.text: Roadsides, stream banks, waste ground, paddock margins and the edges of gardens — the same damp, disturbed ground as wild fennel and sea celery, and often growing right through them.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text: A hairless plant 1–2.5 m tall. The stem is smooth, hollow and ridged, and marked with purple-red blotches and streaks, heaviest near the base — no edible umbellifer in this guide has them. Leaves are finely divided, glossy and fern-like, like an oversized parsley. Flowers are small and white in loose, flat-topped umbels in late spring and summer. Crush a leaf: the smell is musty and mousy, nothing like aniseed or celery.

lookalikes.howToTell: Fennel's leaves are divided into thread-fine segments, its flowers are yellow, the plant is aromatic and its leaves smell of aniseed, and its leaf stalks extend into a thin ribbed sheath along their whole length; there are no bracts under its umbels. Hemlock's leaf segments are broader — narrowly to broadly ovate or triangular, toothed or cut — its flowers are white, it has a few narrow, down-turned bracts under each umbel, and it smells foetid or musty when crushed. Hemlock's stem is usually spotted or blotched purple, especially toward the base, but not always, so an unspotted stem does not prove fennel. Both are hairless, so a smooth stem does not separate them. Check every one of these on every plant.
lookalikes.name: Wild fennel

lookalikes.howToTell: Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; sea celery usually has none, occasionally a single bract that falls early. Hemlock is erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems usually spotted or blotched purple; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its sprawling stems 0.3–1.2 m long. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided and sea celery's three-parted to 1–2 times divided with lobed, toothed segments that are narrow in some plants, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Hemlock smells foetid or musty when crushed and sea celery has a celery-like aroma, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, and hemlock grows in damp waste ground and riverbeds, so place does not rule hemlock out. Flora of New Zealand gives both white flowers in compound umbels; NZPCN gives sea celery's flower colour as cream or yellow.
lookalikes.name: Sea celery / Māori celery

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild carrot's stem is bristly-hairy and more or less solid, up to 120 cm tall, and sometimes tinged purple; hemlock's is hairless and hollow, up to 2 m (rarely 3 m), and usually spotted or blotched purple — but sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Wild carrot's leaves are sparsely to moderately hairy; hemlock is hairless throughout. Under the umbel, wild carrot has numerous bracts divided into narrow linear segments; hemlock has about 4–8 narrow-triangular bracts that bend back. A few central flowers of a wild carrot umbel are sometimes red or purple. Wild carrot's root smells of carrot; crushed hemlock smells foetid and musty. Every one of these must agree before you treat a plant as wild carrot.
lookalikes.name: Wild carrot

lookalikes.howToTell: Alexanders has yellowish flowers and leaves divided in threes into flat, shiny, lobed and toothed leaflets. Hemlock has white flowers and leaves divided two to four times into finely divided segments. Hemlock's stem is hollow and usually spotted or blotched purple, sometimes tinged purplish or pink, particularly toward the base, but an unmarked stem does not rule it out. Alexanders' stem starts solid but becomes hollow and grooved with age, so a hollow stem does not separate them either. Purple on the leaf stalks is no help: alexanders' are purple-striped, and hemlock's are purple-blotched when mature. Crushed hemlock smells foul and mousy. Ripe hemlock fruits are dark brown, 2.5–3 mm; alexanders' are black, 6.5–8 mm. Check every character on every plant, and if the flowers are white or the leaves finely divided, do not eat it.
lookalikes.name: Alexanders

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conium_maculatum Puts a number on the lethal dose, which is the most useful thing a deterrence page can carry: 'Ingesting more than 150–300 milligrams of coniine, approximately equivalent to six to eight hemlock leaves, can be fatal for adult humans.' The toxic alkaloids are coniine and γ-coniceine; coniine resembles nicotine in structure and acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system. Two facts that cut against assuming a given plant is mild: the alkaloids are volatile and drying loses a large part of them, but plants grown in sunny conditions can be twice as poisonous as those from wet, cloudy ground. Poisoning is recorded across pigs, cattle, turkeys, horses, rabbits, cats and dogs.

summary.text: The tall, purple-blotched umbellifer that kills people who think they have found fennel, parsley or wild carrot. Every part is lethal.

warnings: Every part — leaf, stem, root, seed — is lethal. Death is by respiratory paralysis, typically within a few hours.
Do not handle it and then eat with unwashed hands. Do not let children pick the hollow stems for whistles or blowpipes.
If you suspect any contact with food, call the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 immediately.

habitat.text: It is found growing in open areas, gardens, fields and meadows, and widely in uncultivated areas in urban habitats. It propagates freely by seed, where it becomes a key part of a meadow ecosystem; sometimes entire fields will be reddish-purple with its flowers before spring ploughing.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lamium amplexicaule' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
It is a low-growing annual plant growing to 10–25 cm (rarely to 40 cm) tall, thinly pubescent with soft, finely hairy stems. The leaves are opposite, rounded to kidney-shaped, 2–3 cm diameter, with a lobed margin, and often with long internodes. The lower leaves are stalked and the upper ones stalkless, often fused, and clasping the stems. The flowers are pink to purple, relatively large, 1.5–2 cm long, and form a few-flowered terminal spike with axillary whorls. The calyx is regular with five lobes and closes up after flowering. The corolla is purplish-red, fused into a usually erect tube 15 to 20 mm long. The upper lip is convex, 3 to 5 mm long and the lower lip has three lobes, two small side ones and a larger central one 1.5 to 2.5 mm long. There are four stamens, two long and two short. The gynoecium has two fused carpels and the fruit is a four-chambered schizocarp.
This plant flowers very early in the spring even in northern areas, and for most of the winter and early spring in warmer locations such as the Mediterranean region. At times of year when there are not many pollinating insects, the flowers self-pollinate.
It is often found alongside Lamium purpureum (red dead-nettle), for which it is easily mistaken, because the two species bear not only similar leaves, but also similar bright pink to purple flowers. They can, however, be distinguished from one another by the form of the leaves on their respective flowering stems; those of red dead-nettle are petiolate, while those of henbit dead-nettle are sessile.

summary.text:
Lamium amplexicaule, commonly known as henbit dead-nettle, is a species of Lamium native to most of Europe, Asia and northern Africa.
Henbit dead-nettle is native to most of Europe, Asia and North Africa, and has since been spread around the world by human activity.
It is widely naturalised in eastern North and South America, New Zealand, South Africa and Tasmania. Its attractive appearance, edibility, and readiness to grow in many climates often mean it is permitted to grow when other weeds are not.
Its status in Great Britain and Ireland is disputed; some sources give it as native, while others cite it as an archaeophyte.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, fresh or as a tea; leaves and flowers, dried for tea. The Woodland Trust says the leaves are edible and some people use them to make tea; Edible Wild Food says the fresh leaves can be eaten or steeped as a tea, and the leaves and flowers dried and kept for tea or added to salads. Neither page cites a source for this, and Plants For A Future and Useful Temperate Plants list no edible use.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial hairy taprooted herb, with a characteristic scent.  Stems decumbent to spreading, to  c. 50 cm long, lax, often red where exposed to strong light, sometimes with base thickened;  internodes short and lvs rosette-like. Petioles long and slender on lower lvs, often reddish, glabrous or hairy. Lamina palmate, to  c. 9 × 10 cm, broad- or triangular-ovate, usually becoming red with age;  lobes 3–5, at least the terminal petiolulate, pinnately divided to varying degrees, ± appressed-hairy;  ultimate segments usually mucronulate. Infl. very diffuse;  fls paired;  peduncles usually > pedicels; peduncles and pedicels with long- and short-stalked glands.  Sepals (at anthesis) 6.5–8 mm long including apical awn, ovate, prominently 3-nerved, with hairs as on pedicels.  Petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long, obovate-oblanceolate, pink or rose except for white margin of claw;  limb = claw;  apex rounded. Filaments pinkish;  anthers orange.  Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, glabrous or hairy, with 4–6 transverse ridges.  Seed smooth.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Small herb Robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems are sprawling to nearly upright and reach about 30 cm; its leaves are 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, cut very deeply into 5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink to rose petals 6–9 mm long; its anthers are yellow; its fruit segments are 2.5–3 mm long, with many close cross-ridges on their upper two-thirds. Herb robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems reach about 50 cm; its leaves reach about 9 × 10 cm, with 3–5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink or rose petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long; its anthers are orange; its fruit segments (mericarps) are 2.5–3 mm long, with 4–6 cross-ridges. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the petals, usually 10–11.5 mm in herb robert and 6–9 mm in small herb Robert, and the anthers, orange in herb robert and yellow in small herb Robert. Its note on small herb Robert says the two have sometimes been confused, and gives small petals, yellow pollen and more, closer ridges on the fruit segments together as the signs of small herb Robert, which is also generally more upright, with smaller leaves. No single sign settles it: herb robert's petals can be as short as 7.5 mm, inside small herb Robert's range, and Wikipedia says both species have yellow pollen, so anther colour alone can be hard to read. Both are scented, both have paired pink flowers and deeply divided leaves that turn red, and their fruit segments are the same length. No source read records small herb Robert as food (Useful Temperate Plants has no page for it; CONECT-e has no traditional-use record).

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are put in a mug of hot water as a tea, or the leaves and flowers dried for tea in winter (Edible Wild Food).

recipes.method: Blend 30 g herb robert leaves, 30 g basil leaves and 1 crushed garlic clove with enough olive oil to make a loose purée. Stir in 40 g finely grated Parmesan or Pecorino and the juice of half a lemon, then season with salt and black pepper to taste. Freezes well in ice-cube trays.

summary.text:
Geranium robertianum, commonly known as herb-robert or, in North America, as Robert's geranium, is a species of cranesbill that is widespread throughout the northern hemisphere and introduced to some countries in the southern.
The main areas of distribution of herb-robert are throughout Europe northwards to the Baltic and eastwards as far as Russia. It also occurs in north Africa and it is considered also to be native in north America, although in some western states it is regarded as a weed.
The IUCN has not assessed the threat status of this species, but in some countries it is classified as Least Concern.
It grows at altitudes from sea level to 700 m at Great Dun Fell in England and up to 2,400 m in Kashmir.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.: widely naturalised but commonest in the North Id. It has been recorded as naturalised since 1878 (NZPCN).

warnings: In Cantabria, Spain, people interviewed for two ethnobotanical studies called herb robert poisonous and warned that it should be handled with care (CONECT-e, citing Pardo de Santayana 2004 and 2008); no case or toxic compound is named.
Its safety has not been established in pregnancy or while breastfeeding (Herbal Reality).

identification.text:
Shrub to 2–(3) m high;  stems hollow, glabrous, green, glaucous at first. Petiole 0.5–2–(5) cm long, purplish, with hairy groove on upper side.  Lamina 4–14–(24) × 1.5–8–(12) cm, ovate or broad-ovate, mostly entire, sometimes 5–9-lobed (rarely divided almost to midrib) with rounded sinuses, becoming glabrous except for midrib and bases of main veins;  base rounded to cordate; apex long-acuminate.  Infl. 3–8 cm long at flowering.  Bracts mostly 1–3 cm long, sessile, broad-ovate, aristate-acuminate, ± glandular-hairy, usually deep reddish purple.  Calyx small, hidden by bracts;  lobes very unequal. Corolla  c. 1.5 cm long, funnelform, white;  lobes rounded at apex, much < tube, with glandular-hairy margins.  Stamens shortly exserted.  Style > stamens.  Berry 7–10 mm diam., subglobose, dark brownish purple, glandular-hairy. Seed 1.1–1.5 mm long, obovoid-ellipsoid, shining brown, minutely white-dotted. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Leycesteria formosa, the pheasant berry, is a deciduous shrub in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to the Himalayas and southwestern China.
L. formosa includes within its wide range of distribution the areas of all the other known species of the genus. From the North-West Frontier Province and the Punjab it ranges the whole length of the Himalaya eastwards to south-eastern Yunnan, where it was collected by Henry near Mengtze, and north-eastwards to Szechuan and eastern Tibet, where Rehder's var. stenosepala appears to replace very largely the typical form.
A Revision of the Genus Leycesteria
— H.K. Airy-Shaw

The species is native to Pakistan, India, Nepal, East and West Himalaya,  Southwestern China (Sichuan, Yunnan and Guizhou), Tibet and Myanmar.

habitat.text: It is found sparsely in grassy fields and open land generally. It inhabits an elevation range from coastal to alpine, within a range of sea level to 1,400 metres.

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Mentha cunninghamii' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Mentha cunninghamii shares a mint odor with other species within the Mentha (mint) genus, but in appearance is very distinct from many other mints. It has been suggested that it may actually be more closely related to members of the Micromeria genus.
It is a slender, wiry, prostrate perennial plant, with a creeping rhizome. The plant is much branched, often matted, with numerous stems arising from the rhizome, diffusely branched, pubescent, growing from two to twelve inches long. Its leaves are shortly petiolate or nearly sessile, 1/6 to 1/2 inches long, broadly ovate or almost orbicular, obtuse, entire or with an obscure notch on each side, and glandular-dotted. Its flowers are small, white, axillary, usually solitary but sometimes with two to three in each axil. Its peduncles are slender and variable in length. Its calyx are about 1/8 inches long, tubular-campanulate in shape, densely hairy, with teeth villous within. Its corolla-lobes are almost equal, flat and spreading, with the upper one shortly bifid. Its stamens protrude equally with the corolla or are slightly exserted.

summary.text:
Mentha cunninghamii, known commonly as New Zealand mint or Māori mint, is a species within the Mentha (mint) genus, endemic to New Zealand.
Mentha cunninghamii is endemic to the four islands of North Island, South Island, Chatham Island and Stewart Island in New Zealand.
Sources variously describe its flowering season as beginning in the Southern Hemisphere in either September or November, ending in April.
As of 2018, New Zealand's Department of Conservation's New Zealand Threat Classification System (NZTCS) assesses Mentha cunninghamii's conservation status as "At Risk: Declining." The system uses the Declining status to indicate populations that currently possess large populations, but are experiencing declines that could eventually lead to a listing as "Threatened."

Lunaria annua, commonly called honesty or annual honesty, is a species of flowering plant in the cabbage and mustard family Brassicaceae.
Lunaria annua is native to southern Europe from Spain to Romania, and has been introduced to many other parts of the world with temperate climates.

identification.text:
It was originally described as Armillariella novae-zelandiae by Greta Stevenson: "Pileus 3-8 cm diam., olive-buff to olive-brown, sprinkled at centre with very small dull brown scales, convex at first with a strongly down-rolled margin, becoming plane to shallow concave, moist when fresh with a conspicuously striate margin, drying matt; flesh creamy white. Gills decurrent to a most sinuate, creamy white becoming dull fawn, moderately crowded with many short members. Stipe 4–7 x 0.4–0.8 cm, fawn above evanescent ring, brown to dark purplish brown below, smooth or striate, tough, solid, bases swollen and united. Spores 8–9 x 5.5–6.5μm, non-amyloid rather thick-walled (Fig. 24). Spore print white".
The pileus of A. novae-zelandiae can sometimes be bioluminescent.

summary.text:
Armillaria novae-zelandiae is a species of mushroom-forming fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.
Armillaria novae-zelandiae is found in Australasia (New Zealand including the Chatham Islands, Tasmania, Eastern Australia, and Papua New Guinea), South America (Argentina and Chile), and Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia and Amami-Oshimi islands of Japan). Isolates from New Zealand and Australia are reciprocally monophyletic but considered conspecific by virtue of their similar basidiocarp morphology, vegetative growth characteristics and sexual compatibility. The South American lineage is sister to the Australasian clade, while isolates from Asia are a basal monophyletic lineage within A. novae-zelandiae.

identification.text:
Dioecious or monoecious climber, with extensive roots.  Stems striate, up to 10 m long and clothed in rough deflexed hairs.  Lvs broadly ovate, not lobed or deeply 3–5-lobed;  lobes acute to acuminate, serrate, ± glabrous to sparsely hairy above, ± glabrous to moderately hairy with yellow glandular hairs below. Petiole usually ± = lf blade.  Stipules 2 per node and 2-fid or 4 per node and entire.  Bracts of ♀ fls triangular, hairy, green, elongating and becoming yellowish at fruiting to form a cylindric-ovoid infructescence (the hop) with yellow glandular hairs especially at base of bracts.  Calyx of ♂ fls ovate-triangular, green, hairy.  Achene ovate-ellipsoid, covered by glandular calyx.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
