identification.text: A large tree with big compound leaves of five to seven leaflets spread like fingers from one stalk. Upright cones of white flowers in spring. The nuts sit one or two to a thick green husk with a few short, widely spaced spikes, and are large, glossy and rounded with one pale patch. Sweet chestnut husks are densely bristly like a hedgehog and hold two or three flattened nuts with a pointed tuft.

lookalikes.howToTell: Look at the leaves first. Sweet chestnut's are single, long (about 15–32 cm), oblong and boldly toothed; horse chestnut's are hand-shaped, with five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk. Horse chestnut's leaflets are toothed too, so teeth alone do not separate them. Both cases are spiny; sweet chestnut's is reportedly covered in many fine spines, horse chestnut's in short spikes. Sweet chestnut's case usually holds two or more nuts with a tufted tip; horse chestnut's usually holds one round, glossy, dark brown conker with a large pale scar, sometimes two. Some grafted sweet chestnut varieties bear a single large nut, so nut count alone does not decide it. Sweet chestnut is edible.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesculus_hippocastanum Corroborates the toxin and adds to it: raw seed, leaf, bark and flower are toxic through aesculin and should not be ingested; the glycoside and saponin constituents are also considered toxic; young fresh seeds contain alkaloid saponins and glucosides. The US Food and Drug Administration classifies horse chestnut seed as an unsafe herb. Not dangerous to handle — which is why conkers are a children's game — but they cause sickness when eaten, and in horses tremors and loss of coordination. There is a kidney risk: in cardiac-surgery patients given escin intravenously, 340 µg/kg altered nothing, 360 µg/kg mildly impaired kidney function, and 510 µg/kg caused acute kidney injury.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Agaricus arvensis' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
It is one of the largest white Agaricus species in Britain (where it appears during July–November), West Asia (Iran), and North America.
Frequently found near stables, as well as in meadows, it may form fairy rings. The mushroom is often found growing with nettles (a plant that also likes nutrient-rich soil). It is associated with cypress on the North American West Coast and spruce to the east.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Agaricus arvensis' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap is 7–20 cm across, whitish, smooth, and dry; it stains yellow, particularly when young. The gills are pale pink to white at first, later passing through grey and brown to become dull chocolate. A large, spreading ring has white above, but sometimes with yellowish scales underneath. Viewed from below, on a closed-cap specimen, the twin-layered ring has a well-developed "cogwheel" pattern around the stipe. This is the lower part of the double ring. The stalk is 5–12 cm long and 1–3 cm wide.
The spores are brown and smooth, producing a dark brown spore print. Its odor is similar to that of almond extract or marzipan, due to the presence of benzaldehyde. It tends to stain yellow on bruising.


Similar species
In addition to its similarity to other related species, this fungus can be confused with deadly species of Amanita.
Agaricus osecanus is rare and lacks the almond smell. Agaricus xanthodermus, the yellow stainer, can cause stomach upsets.

identification.text:
Erect annual or biennial herb, up to 2–(2.5) m tall.  Stems ridged, moderately to densely softly hairy, often becoming sparsely hairy below. Cauline lvs usually obovate to narrow-oblanceolate, rarely linear, ± flat, apetiolate and cuneate, acute, often shallowly 1-pinnatifid or remotely serrate, sometimes entire especially above, sparsely to densely scaberulous, ciliate, (20)–35–120–(250) × 4–20–(45) mm;  uppermost lvs smaller, usually narrow-oblanceolate or narrow-elliptic.  Infl. a leafy pyramidal panicle with dominant main axis.  Capitula 1.5–2 mm diam.;  receptacle usually with distinct flanges between pits, sometimes with short flanges or ± smooth.  Inner involucral bracts lanceolate, green, usually hairy at least toward apex, 4–5.5–(6) mm long;  outer bracts moderately to densely hairy.  Outer florets filiform, cream, usually becoming reddish.  Achenes obovoid, sparsely hairy, 1–1.2–(1.4) mm long;  pappus hairs fawn or dirty white.  
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Conyza albida Spreng.]

summary.text:
Erigeron sumatrensis (syn. Conyza sumatrensis) is an annual herb probably native to South America, but widely naturalised in tropical and subtropical regions, and regarded as an invasive weed in many places.It is a perennial in the Western Cape of South Africa.
It probably originates from South America, but is now naturalised in North America, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australasia. It poses a significant threat to wildlife conservation areas and other reserves. In Britain, of the non-native former Conyza species, it is the second most abundant (after Erigeron canadensis) and is typically found in London and the South East of England. It was first recorded in London by Brian Wurzell in 1984,
and noted in France at Saint-Sozy (Dordogne) in 2006.

Wikipedia, 'Zealandia pustulata' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: Zealandia pustulata is widespread and commonly described as both a lithophyte and epiphyte. They are evident across a range of wet sclerophyll forest and rainforest, as well as more open, subalpine environments, with preferred growing conditions being in ferneries or gullies in partial- to full shade. Within these forested environments, the species is described as a middle-storey inhabitant, but is able to grow anywhere from the forest floor to the canopy.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Zealandia pustulata' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text: This epiphytic fern species seems to climb onto suitable substrates (fallen logs, rocks, growing plants etc.) via long, creeping grey-green rhizomes. The rhizomes have clathrate, ovate scales which are 3-7 mm long and 1-2 mm wide. Generally, the species exhibits 1-9 pairs of lobed, glossy-green fronds which are erect to pendant and can range from 5-50 cm in length. The texture of the fronds is leathery, and they have thick, wavy margins. They have distinct, relatively large (approximately 3-4 mm wide) circular sori on their abaxial surface. The spores themselves are 45–62.5 μm long, 20–32.5 μm wide, pale, with wart-like protuberances. The species can grow to a maximum height of approximately 30 cm and a maximum width of approximately 120 cm.

summary.text:
Zealandia pustulata is a species of fern native to eastern Australia and New Zealand.
Zealandia pustulata ranges from southeastern Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria on the Australian mainland, and to Tasmania, Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island,  New Zealand's North and South Islands, and the Chatham, Kermadec, and Antipodes islands.
There are two subspecies, Zealandia pustulata ssp. pustulata, the type species which is present across the plant's mainland and insular ranges; Z. pustulata ssp. howensis is uniquely endemic to Lord Howe Island.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Coprosma foetidissima' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
NZ Plant Conservation Network, 'Coprosma foetidissima' — smell (paraphrased)
identification.text:
C. foetidissima grows as a small open branched tree or shrub, typically up to 3 m tall, but in the Auckland Islands reaching heights of 6 m, with a trunk up to 45 cm in diameter. The bark is dark brown, and the branchlets are glabrous (lacking hairs). The interpetiolar stipules are shorter than those of many other coprosma species and taper to a conspicuous tooth fringed by fine short hairs and with uneven tufts of hairs at the tips. Leaves are thin, 30-50 mm long, 14-20 mm wide, somewhat leathery-textured, and shaped obovate to oblong to broadly ovate. Leaf tips may be rounded or have a small tapered point. The leaves lie in a single plane on the branchlet. The leaves of C. foetidissima (and many other species of Rubiaceae) have domatia, small indentations on the underside that may be occupied by potentially beneficial insects such as mites and other arthropods.
C. foetidissima is dioecious, meaning that male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. Flowering occurs between October and November. The flowers are solitary and occur on the ends of branchlets. The calyx of male flowers is  cup-like with four or five teeth; the corolla is bell-shaped, 4 or 8 lobed to the middle; and anthers are large, elongate-oblong in shape, and as long as the corolla. Female flowers have a short, narrowly ovoid, tubular, and toothed calyx and the corolla is a curved tube with 4 or 5 splits extending one-third to halfway down. The styles are long and substantial. Fruiting occurs between March and July. The drupes are 7–10 mm in length with an oblong shape. They are yellow to orange-red in colour, and are dispersed primarily by birds.
Crushed leaves smell strongly of dung.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Hūpiro's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. summary.text:
Coprosma foetidissima, commonly known as stinkwood or hūpiro (Māori), is a species of flowering plant in the family Rubiaceae, native to mainland New Zealand as well as Stewart Island and the Auckland Islands.
C. foetidissima is endemic to New Zealand and found from the Coromandel Peninsula southwards to Stewart Island, and on the Auckland Islands.

The only record found is a 2022 tasting by a West Coast Agroforestry grower, of plants growing outside in Christchurch: the leaves were slightly crunchy, without fibres and very good to eat, possibly even a little sweet; the flower was chewier and not good. No other source found records this species as food.

identification.text:
Woody shrub up to 2–(4) m high, much-branched from base.  Stems clothed in very fine stellate hairs when young, becoming ± glabrous when older.  Lvs densely clothed in fine stellate hairs, triangular to suborbicular, cordate to obtuse at base, (3)–5–7-palmately lobed to  c. 1/2 radius, coarsely crenate, 2–15–(20) cm diam.;  petioles 3–15 cm long;  stipules triangular, 3–5 mm long, deciduous.  Fls in axillary clusters of 1–4–(5);  fruiting pedicels 20–50 mm long;  epicalyx segments ovate-triangular, united for lower ⅓, usually c. 1/2 as long as calyx, unchanged at fruiting;  calyx long-tubular; calyx teeth much < tube, triangular, acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, somewhat recurved at fruiting;  petals magenta with darker veins, 30–40 mm long.  Mericarps 7–9 per fr., glabrous or sparsely to moderately hairy, smooth on back, but a single low longitudinal rib usually present;  edges sharply angled or slightly rounded.  
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera assurgentiflora Kellogg]
The sp. is distinguished by the long-tubular calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera, which include island mallow. Petal lengths overlap (20–35 mm against 30–40 mm). Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, cheeseweed mallow 1–8 cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Island mallow's petals (30–40 mm) and common mallow's (12–30 mm) only meet at 30 mm, and both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, so the flower colour does not separate them; check the calyx, long and tube-shaped in island mallow, and the fruit, smooth with one low rib against strongly net-veined. Leaf size overlaps. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Both have palmately lobed, toothed leaves whose sizes overlap (island mallow 2–15(–20) cm across, dwarf mallow 1–7(–8) cm), so use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Tree mallow

Edible parts (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, 19/10/2026 (owner pasted the page's link a second time after being told it was not enough on its own)): restates the tasting in West Coast Agroforestry (NZ nursery, all rights reserved), 'Plant Detective Case 1: Malva assurgentiflora', Jon Colyer, posted 13/07/2022, https://agroforestry.co.nz/plant-detective-case-1-malva-assurgentiflora/, retrieved 19/10/2026: "The flower was the first thing I tasted… definitely not that good"; "The leaf was far tastier than the flower, being slightly crunchy… with a distinct lack of fibres… They tasted very nice and were possibly even a little sweet." 'Raw' is our reading: the author tasted the plants where they grew. The author's confidence rested on "Pretty much every Malva species is edible, so that’s a given" — a genus generalisation, NOT used. Searched 19/10/2026 for any other record: Useful Temperate Plants' 'Malva assurgentiflora' page lists no edible use ("Known Hazards: None known"); Wikipedia records only ornamental and windbreak use; Langlands' 'Island mallow' entry has not been read. One grower's tasting is the whole evidence, and the field says so. Card risk into this entry stays `unknown` (a card may be less certain than the page, not more).

Card risks: `edible` into cheeseweed, dwarf, common and tree mallow (Useful Temperate Plants and Wikipedia record their leaves and seeds as eaten); `unknown` into island mallow (no openly licensed or authoritative record of it being eaten). UNRESOLVED: cheeseweed mallow is `edible` although Webb 1988 notes "Poisonous (Connor 1977)" — Connor's text has not been read, so whether it concerns people or livestock is not known; tree mallow is `edible` although NZ Flora lists Connor 1977 in its bibliography [as Lavatera arborea] without saying what it records.
Habitat tags 19/10/2026: classify_habitats on the habitat text → coastal, disturbed (before: coastal, urban).

Months: left empty (= year-round), 19/10/2026 — the part eaten is the leaves of a long-lived shrub (Webb 1988: woody shrub; West Coast Agroforestry: "a longer term perennial"). Flowering, Webb 1988: Jan–Dec. iNaturalist NZ research-grade records: 44, in every month but none-to-few in some.

Also from the same page, not written into the entry: the two Christchurch patches "were very near to older cultivated gardens" with only 3 seedlings found (agrees with Webb 1988's "persists at old house sites"), and Malva arborea self-seeding profusely beside them.

Not changed (same as taupata).

summary.text:
Malva assurgentiflora, formerly classified as Lavatera assurgentiflora, the island mallow,  mission mallow, royal mallow, malva rosa island mallow, island tree mallow or malva rosa ('pink mallow') in Spanish, is a species of flowering plant in the mallow family.
It is endemic to southern California, where it is native only to the Channel Islands. It can also be found growing as an escapee from cultivation in localised spots in coastal mainland California and Baja California, as well as sparingly in locations in Guatemala, cooler regions in mountainous or Mediterranean areas in western South America, New Zealand and Australia.
In New Zealand it is locally established on the east coast of the South Island from Marlborough to Otago. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1940.

summary.text:
Cymbalaria muralis, commonly called ivy-leaved toadflax, is a low, spreading, trailing plant with small purple flowers, native to rocky habitats in southern Europe.
POWO regards the native range for this species to be limited to southern Europe, in Austria, France, Italy, Switzerland, and the former Yugoslavia, with the nominate subspecies Cymbalaria muralis subsp. muralis also occurring throughout this range. Similarly the World Plants database records it as native to the same areas, but more specifically to Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia & Hercegovina, Serbia, and Kosovo in the former Yugoslavia and to the small state of San Marino on the Italian peninsula. It also shows it as native to additional areas north east of the Alps such as the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Liechtenstein, and many Atlantic Ocean islands such as the Azores, Madeira, the Canary Islands, and the Cape Verde Islands.
Cymbalaria muralis subsp. visianii recorded by POWO as growing in the southeastern part of the species' range, only in Italy and the former Yugoslavia. The World Plants database largely agrees listing it as native to the central and southern parts of Italy and to Croatia, but also listing it as introduced in Germany; it has also been recorded as naturalised in Britain since 1970.

From this original range it spread to much of Europe and to the rest of the world as either an accidental introduction or because of its use as an ornamental plant. Its first record outside of cultivation in Great Britain is from 1640. A frequently repeated story is that the plants were introduced accidentally as part of a shipment of statuary to Oxford. However, this is unlikely since it was recorded growing in an English garden in 1617 in Droxford. Thereafter it became a popular ornamental plant that was widely planted in the United Kingdom through the 19th century. Regardless of its status it is recorded from Ireland and Portugal in the west in every country as far east as Ukraine, Poland, and Sweden, and according to POWO it may also be found in the Baltic States, northwestern Russia, and the North Caucasus with World Plants recording it in Belarus and Georgia.
In Africa it grows in Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia in the north and in South Africa it grows in the Cape Provinces and the Northern Provinces floristic areas. In Asia it is now found in Turkey, Jordan, North Korea, South Korea, and the eastern Himalayas.
In North America Cymbalaria muralis has been recorded growing outside cultivation in Bermuda, Canada, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, and the United States. In the USA it is generally agreed that it grows in much of the Midwest, north-east, and New England as far south as South Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas and as far west as Wisconsin, Illinois, and Missouri with the exception of Maine and New Hampshire. It is also found on the west coast in California, Oregon, and Washington State. It is more scattered in the interior states, listed as growing in Colorado, Nebraska, South Dakota, and Utah, with the last of these recorded by USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service PLANTS database (PLANTS) and World Plants, but not POWO. In Canada it agreed that it grows in five provinces, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, and Québec. However PLANTS and World Plants also record it in Nova Scotia while POWO alone records it on the island of Newfoundland.
In South America it has been observed in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru in the north. It has also been recorded in the south and southeast of Brazil, Uruguay, Bolivia, and the north of Argentina. In mainland Chile it has been reported from Valparaíso, in Santiago, the Maule Region, and the Biobío Region.
On oceanic islands it has been introduced to Maui in Hawaii, both the North and South Island of New Zealand, Bermuda, Mauritius, St. Helena, and the Juan Fernández Islands. It is also found in six Australian states, Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, the south of Queensland, and the island state of Tasmania.

identification.text: Cryptomeria is a very large coniferous tree, reaching up to 60 m tall and 4 m trunk diameter, with red-brown bark which peels in vertical strips. The leaves are arranged spirally, needle-like, 0.5–1 cm long; and the seed cones globular, 1–2 cm diameter with about 20–40 scales. It is superficially similar to the related giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum), from which it can be differentiated by the longer leaves (under 0.5 cm in the giant sequoia) and smaller cones (4–6 cm in the giant sequoia), and the harder bark on the trunk (thick, soft and spongy in giant sequoia). Prior to 1916, the sylvics expert E.H.Wilson measured a sugi at the village called "Sugi", Tosa Prefecture, Shikoku Island, Japan, which measured 50 m in height, and 25 m in girth at breast height.

identification.text:
Deciduous, spreading to erect tree, 4–12–(15) m high when mature, not armed;  trunk tall.  Lf petiole (14)–20–32–(40) mm long, glabrous or occasionally with sparse hairs;  blade usually thin, usually broadly ovate to broadly elliptic, occasionally oblong or narrowly obovate, (70)–80–130–(155) × (40)–45–60–(65) mm, acuminate to long-acuminate at apex, usually rounded to subcordate or occasionally cuneate at base, glabrous above and below, with lower surface slightly paler, serrate with teeth aristate and often gland-tipped;  stipules long-triangular, early deciduous.  Infl. a corymbose cluster of (2)–3–4–(6) fls, on short lateral shoots, sometimes clustered near branchlet tips, up to 45–(80) mm long, ± pendent;  fls not fragrant;  pedicels (10)–14–(35) mm long, glabrous, subtended by serrate bracts.  Hypanthium narrowly campanulate; sepals 4–7–(8) mm long, lanceolate or subulate, acuminate, glabrous, greenish to magenta, erect to spreading or occasionally reflexed.  Petals 5 or many, ± spreading at anthesis, broadly obovate to orbicular, (12)–14–18–(20) × 9–14 mm, undulate and notched, white or pink-flushed to rose.  Stamens < petals;  filaments whitish or flushed pale pink. Fr. < 15 mm diam., globose, glabrous, black-purple, bitter;  stone smooth.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Taiwan cherry's flowers are deep pink to rose-magenta and more or less bell-shaped, the lower part of each petal staying semi-erect while the upper part eventually spreads, with magenta to dark deep red sepals; Japanese cherry's petals are white or pink-flushed to rose and more or less spread open, and its sepals are greenish to magenta. Weedbusters names the bell-shaped flower as what sets Taiwan cherry apart from Japanese hill cherry. Fruit: Taiwan cherry's is glossy scarlet and egg-shaped to ellipsoid, up to 12 × 10 mm; Japanese cherry's is round, black-purple and bitter, under 15 mm across — but Auckland Council describes Japanese cherry fruit as red or black, so a red fruit does not settle it. Leaf teeth: Japanese cherry's end in a bristle and are often gland-tipped; Taiwan cherry's are pointed. Flowering overlaps: Flora of New Zealand gives Taiwan cherry July to September and Japanese cherry August to October. Leaf size, leaf-stalk length and flower-stalk length overlap, and neither has spines.

preparation.text: Owing to their bitter taste, the raw sakuranbo is unpalatable and rarely eaten; instead, the seed inside is removed and the fleshy part preserved.

recipes.method: About 50 g cherry blossoms (around 5 very loosely packed cups), 2 tsp flaky or fine sea salt, 240 ml rice vinegar and, if you have it, 2 tsp umezu (Japanese plum vinegar). Pick from an unsprayed tree, choosing flowers that are just starting to open. Soak them gently in clean water, stirring lightly with your hands, then lay them out to dry or give them a quick, gentle spin in a salad spinner. Layer the flowers in a small jar, sprinkling each layer with salt, and refrigerate for 3 days. Cover with the vinegar and refrigerate for another 3 days. To keep them as a pickle, simply leave the flowers in the vinegar in the fridge; they keep 6 months or more but fade. To dry them, drain off and keep the vinegar, then spread the flowers on a tray lined with a soft cloth in a warm, dry place out of direct sun, checking once a day — about three days on average — or dry them in a dehydrator at about 35 °C for 6–8 hours. Keep the heat low, or they turn brown. Flowers left a little moist can be tossed with a further 5 g (1 tsp) sea salt. Dried blossoms keep at room temperature, out of direct sun, for about a year; the pink sakura vinegar keeps in the fridge for 6 months or more and is salty, so use it like a seasoned vinegar, for example in sushi rice. Makes about 1 cup of flowers and 240 ml of vinegar.
recipes.title: Preserved cherry blossoms (sakura no shiozuke) and sakura vinegar

recipes.method: A handful of clean, fresh cherry blossoms with the stalks removed, water and white sugar. Put the blossoms in a dish, pour over enough water just off the boil to cover them, cover the dish and leave to infuse for 24 hours. Strain the liquid through a fine sieve, muslin or a paper filter into a small pan and add the same quantity of sugar — 500 g sugar to 500 ml of liquid. Heat gently until the sugar dissolves, bring to the boil and simmer for 3 to 5 minutes. Funnel into a sterilised bottle and seal. Once opened, keep it in the fridge and use within 2 months. Use it as you would a subtle orgeat or maraschino, in drinks.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom syrup

recipes.method: About 200 g (1 cup) sugar, 240 ml (1 cup) water and 1 cup of fresh cherry blossoms. Rinse the blossoms, put everything in a pan, bring to a boil and stir for 10–15 minutes, until it turns syrupy. Strain out the blossoms and pour the syrup into a jar. The blossoms turn green in heat, so the syrup comes out light green; the author suggests taking every bit of green stem off the petals if you mind the colour. Good in iced or hot tea, drizzled over yoghurt, or soaked into a cake.
recipes.title: Quick cherry blossom syrup

recipes.method: About 2 cups of fresh cherry blossoms and about 475 ml raw apple cider vinegar. Pick flower buds and open blooms from a tree you know has not been sprayed or contaminated, leaving the leaves behind — the author advises against harvesting leaves with the flowers. Fill a glass jar about two-thirds full of flowers and top up with the vinegar. If the jar has a metal lid, put a piece of parchment or wax paper between jar and lid so the vinegar does not eat the metal. Leave to infuse for at least 2–4 weeks; pink blossoms turn it a golden fuchsia. Strain, and use it in salad dressings, marinades, soda water or cocktails.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom vinegar

recipes.method: First infuse a handful of clean, fresh cherry blossoms in vodka for a couple of days, then fine-strain. For one drink: 75 ml sake, 15 ml dry gin, 15 ml of the cherry blossom vodka, 1 tsp cherry blossom syrup and a salted cherry blossom (or a small pinch of salt). Stir with ice, strain, and garnish with a fresh or salted cherry blossom.
recipes.title: Sakura martini

recipes.method: Cherry blossoms and good mirin. Put the blossoms in a jar, cover them with mirin and leave for four days, then strain out the flowers and keep the mirin in the fridge. The author drizzles it over mild, crunchy salads and spoons it over silken tofu as a dessert.
recipes.title: Cherry blossom mirin

recipes.method: 1 Japanese or 5 Persian cucumbers, 1 tbsp (15 ml) sesame seeds toasted in a pan, 3 tbsp (45 ml) cherry blossom mirin (above), 2 tsp (10 ml) rice vinegar, ¼ tsp sea salt, and cherry blossoms to scatter. Crush the cucumbers lightly with the back of a knife or a rolling pin, break them into chunks and put them in a bowl. Roughly crush the sesame seeds in a mortar. Whisk the mirin, vinegar and salt together in a small bowl, add them to the cucumber with the sesame seeds and toss well. Turn onto a serving dish, scatter over the blossoms and serve at once. The salad can be left to macerate in the mirin mixture for an hour to develop its flavour, but add the sesame seeds and blossoms just before serving.
recipes.title: Cucumber and cherry blossom salad

identification.text: Castanea crenata is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree growing to 10–15 m tall. The leaves are similar to those of the sweet chestnut, though usually a little smaller, 8–19 cm long and 3–5 cm broad. The flowers of both sexes are borne in 7–20 cm long, upright catkins, the male flowers in the upper part and female flowers in the lower part. They appear in summer, and by autumn, the female flowers develop into spiny cupules containing 3–7 brownish nuts that are shed during October.

identification.text:
Vigorous climber, evergreen, or semi-evergreen in cold districts.  Stems mostly purplish and hirsute when young.  Lvs dimorphic:  those produced in colder weather in early spring sinuate to deeply lobed;  summer lvs and those on reproductive shoots entire.  Petiole to 1.3 cm long, densely hirsute.  Lamina of entire lvs 2.5–12 × 1.5–6 cm, ovate-oblong, ovate or ovate-elliptic, usually deep ± shining green or sometimes yellowish green above, lighter green below, sometimes mottled yellow, densely hairy to glabrous on veins beneath;  midrib above glabrous or hairy;  base rounded, truncate or subcordate;  apex obtuse to acute;  lvs subtending fls similar but smaller, all free.  Fls in axillary pairs, fragrant;  peduncles 0.5–2.5 cm long, densely hirsute.  Bracteoles ± oblong-obovate, much < ovaries.  Calyx lobes very small, ± narrow-triangular, fringed with long hairs.  Corolla 2–4.5–(5) cm long, usually white, becoming yellow after anthesis, often flushed pink on reverse, glandular-hairy outside;  tube 1–3 cm long, cylindric;  limb 2-lipped;  single linear lobe of lower lip recurving; upper lip 4-toothed.  Stamens and style < to = corolla limb.  Ovaries separate.  Berry (4)–5–7 mm diam., broad- ovate to suborbicular, glossy black.  Seed  c. 2 mm diam.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Lonicera japonica, known as Japanese honeysuckle and golden-and-silver honeysuckle, is a species of honeysuckle native to East Asia, including many parts of China.
The flowers can also be a significant source of food for deer, rabbits, hummingbirds, and other wildlife.
Japanese honeysuckle has become naturalized in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, and much of the United States, including Hawaii, as well as a number of Pacific and Caribbean islands. It is classified as a noxious weed in 46 states, being prohibited to be bought and sold in Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, and Vermont, and banned in Indiana and New Hampshire. It is on the New Hampshire invasive species list.
Lonicera japonica was initially brought to the U.S. from Japan in the early 1800s as an ornamental plant. It is still deliberately planted in the U.S. for reasons such as erosion control or forage for deer, but has become invasive in many areas.
Once it has invaded an area, Lonicera japonica grows rapidly and outcompetes native plants for sunlight and nutrients. It proliferates using both sexual and vegetative reproduction, producing seeds that are spread by animals and expanding locally via rhizomes. Eventually, it will form a dense thicket which prevents other plant species from germinating in that area. Due to its suppression of germination in the understory, Lonicera japonica also prevents the regeneration of trees.
Management of invasive Lonicera japonica has been achieved through a variety of means. Small patches can be removed by hand, or using simple digging tools, but all plant parts including roots and rhizomes must be removed to prevent resprouting. Larger patches can be removed through repeated mowing, but application of herbicide is also recommended to prevent regrowth. There has been some study of using controlled burns to remove L. japonica, but the underground portion of the plant is usually able to survive and resprout, limiting the effectiveness of this method. Browsing by herbivores may limit its growth, but is unlikely to eliminate it.

Biological control
The EPA of New Zealand approved the release of Limenitis glorifica butterflies in 2013 as a biological control for Lonicera japonica. This butterfly is host specific for Japanese honeysuckle, but it may incidentally feed on other closely related plants, including Himalayan honeysuckle Leycesteria formosa. Oberea shirahatai is a Japanese honeysuckle host-specific beetle that feeds on the stems and leaves of Japanese honeysuckle. It was released in New Zealand in 2018 as another L. japonica-specialist biological control.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Reynoutria japonica' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The flowers are small, cream or white, produced in erect racemes 6–15 cm long in late summer and early autumn. Japanese knotweed has hollow stems with distinct raised nodes that give it the appearance of bamboo, though it is not related. While stems may reach a maximum height of 3–4 m each growing season, it is typical to see much smaller plants in places where they sprout through cracks in the pavement or are repeatedly cut down. The leaves are broad oval with a truncated base, 7–14 cm long and 5–12 cm broad, with an entire margin. New leaves of Reynoutria japonica are dark red and 1 to 4 cm long; young leaves are green and rolled back with dark red veins; leaves are green and shaped like a heart flattened at the base, or a shield, and are usually around 12 cm long.
Mature R. japonica forms 2-to-3-metre-tall, dense thickets. Leaves shoot from the stem nodes alternately in a zigzag pattern. Plants that are immature or affected by mowing and other restrictions have much thinner and shorter stems than mature stands, and are not hollow. The below-ground rhizome network acts as a long-lived storage system; it is often concentrated in the upper metre of the soil profile, but may extend well beyond the visible stand.


Similar species
Japanese knotweed may be confused with other plants suspected of being knotweed owing to the similar appearance of leaves and stems. Dogwood, lilac, houttuynia (Houttuynia cordata), ornamental bistorts such as red bistort (Persicaria amplexicaulis), lesser knotweed (Koenigia campanulata), Himalayan balsam (Impatiens glandulifera), broad-leaved dock (Rumex obtusifolius), bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), bamboo, Himalayan honeysuckle (Leycesteria formosa), and Russian vine (Fallopia baldschuanica) have been suspected of being Reynoutria japonica.

summary.text:
Reynoutria japonica, synonyms Fallopia japonica and Polygonum cuspidatum, is a species of herbaceous perennial plant in the knotweed and buckwheat family Polygonaceae.
It is native to East Asia in Japan, China and Korea. In North America and Europe, the species has successfully established itself in numerous habitats, and is classified as a pest and invasive species in several countries. Spread in invaded ranges is mainly vegetative, through rhizome pieces, stem fragments and soil contaminated with plant material; waterways, construction activity and garden waste can move these propagules over longer distances. Many introduced populations are dominated by male-sterile clonal plants, but seed set, hybridisation with giant knotweed and the production of viable seed by Bohemian knotweed have also been reported.

identification.text:
Arborescent shrub to c. 3 m high; stems few and with terminal crown of lvs. Lvs to c. 40 cm long, sessile, composed of 5–9 pairs of sessile (except the terminal) leaflets, the basal pair smaller and stipule-like, the terminal leaflet largest. Leaflets of main pairs 4–7.5 × 2–3.5 cm, ovate, rigidly coriaceous, with 2–5 spiny teeth on margins; apex spiny. Racemes lax and spreading, to c. 20 cm long; basal scales to 1.5 cm long, broadly ovate, membranous, dark brown. Bracts ovate, slightly < pedicels at anthesis. Perianth segments to 9 mm long, ovate, imbricate except for short outermost whorl. Stamens included, < inner perianth segments; filaments entire. Style very short. Berry 8–10 mm long, ± broadly obovoid, blue-black and pruinose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Mahonia japonica (Thunb.) DC.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves are stalkless, and their lowest pair of leaflets is small and stipule-like; Oregon grape's leaves have no such pair and usually sit on a dark red stalk up to 4 cm long (the Flora of New Zealand's key). Japanese mahonia has few stems to about 3 m, each crowned with leaves; Oregon grape is many-stemmed and suckering, usually about 1 m. Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax, spreading and up to about 20 cm; Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Japanese mahonia's berries are broadly egg-shaped, 8–10 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leaflet counts overlap (5–9 pairs against 3–7), and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading (Flora of New Zealand); leatherleaf mahonia's stand upright, 7–26 cm long (Flora of China). Japanese mahonia's main leaflets are 4–7.5 cm long and 2–3.5 cm wide; leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider (Wikipedia), 2–6 cm (Flora of China), so only a wide leaflet tells. Japanese mahonia's berries are 8–10 mm long; leatherleaf mahonia's up to 15 mm. Leaflet counts (5–9 pairs against 4–10), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them. The two have long been confused: leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'), so a garden label does not settle it. Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) adds that the two have hybridised in gardens and that many seedlings are hybrids, so intermediate plants are fairly common. Missouri Botanical Garden, though, describes plants grown under the name leatherleaf mahonia in the United States with loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese mahonia's leaves carry 5–9 pairs of ovate leaflets with 2–5 spiny teeth; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones (14–20 pairs of broad-lanceolate leaflets is the Flora of New Zealand's test between the two). Japanese mahonia's flower clusters are lax and spreading; mountain grape's dense and upright (Auckland Council). Blue-black berries with a bloom do not separate them, and neither test settles the garden hybrid B. × hortensis ('Charity', 'Winter Sun'), whose parents are these two species.
lookalikes.name: Mountain grape

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia picked in Victoria, British Columbia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm square tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Berberis japonica is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae, native to Taiwan. Despite the name, it is not native to Japan, though it has been known in cultivation there for centuries.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): S.: known from 2 sites only, Botanical Hill (Nelson), just north of Clarence Bridge (coastal Marlborough).
M. japonica is fairly common in old gardens throughout N.Z. and persists for a long time without cultivation. Wild plants are presumably the result of dispersal of the fr. by birds.
Berberis bealei, native to mainland China and also widely cultivated, is usually treated as a separate species, but in the past has been listed as a cultivar of Berberis japonica. Its most obvious differences from B. japonica are in shorter, upright flowering racemes and wider leaflets.
Where it grows wild is not settled. Kew's Plants of the World Online gives Taiwan; the NZPCN says the origin is uncertain, probably southern China or northern Taiwan; Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) doubts the Taiwan record, which rests on treating the Taiwanese M. tikushiensis as the same species; and Useful Temperate Plants suggests it may be known only in cultivation.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

identification.text:
It is a deciduous tree growing to 20 m tall, rarely 30 m, and 40–80 centimetres stem diameter, with light grey bark. The leaves are pinnate, 50–90 cm long, with 11–17 leaflets, each leaflet 7–16 cm long and 3–5 cm broad. The whole leaf is downy-pubescent, and a somewhat brighter, yellower green than many other tree leaves.
The male flowers are inconspicuous yellow-green catkins produced in spring at the same time as the new leaves appear. The female flowers have pink/red pistils. The fruit is a nut, produced in bunches of 4–10 together; the nut is spherical, 3–5 cm long and broad, surrounded by a green husk before maturity in mid-autumn.

habitat.text: It inhabits mostly lowland forests between 0–600 m above sea level, though may in rare cases reach montane areas. It used to dominate a swamp forest type that now exists almost only on the South Westland region of the South Island. Kahikatea prefers flooded or alluvial soils with low levels of drainage, which in Westland occur from post glaciation events.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Dacrycarpus dacrydioides' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Kahikatea is a coniferous tree reaching a height of 50–65 m, making it the tallest New Zealand tree, with a trunk 1–2 m through. It has a 600 year life span and gains maturity after between 250 and 450 years. Near the base of the tree, the roots are typically buttressed and grooved. Adult trees that grow in clusters develop interlocking root islands that may help prevent individual trees from falling during high winds. The wood itself is odourless and white. The majority of the trunk is branchless—in adults around three quarters—and has grey or dark grey coloured bark which falls off thickly in flakes. Young adults have no branches in a third to a half of the trunk and have a conic shape.
In juveniles the leaves are 3–7 (reaching 4 mm in young adults) by 0.5–1 mm and a dark green to red colour that come to a marked point. They are narrow, arranged in almost opposite pairs spreading away from a wider base, and curved like a scythe. In adulthood the leaves change dramatically and are a brown-green colour and just 1–2 mm long, waxy, and grow overlapping one another tightly.

As a conifer, kahikatea has no flowers and instead has cones. Male cones, which occur on different trees to female ones, are 1 cm long and rectangular. The pollen is a pale yellow colour and has a three-pored or trisaccate shape that is distinctive in the New Zealand flora and so can be identified easily. The fruit is highly modified with a yellow-orange fleshy receptacle that is 2.5–6.5 mm long. The purple-black seed is roughly spherical and 4–6 mm in diameter. Both the seed and the ovary are covered with a thin layer of wax. Kahikatea has a diploid chromosome count of 20.


Phytochemistry
Several different glycosides have been isolated from the leaves; the tricetin 3',5'-di-O-/β-glucopyranoside and 3'-0-β-xylopyranoside have been found only in kahikatea. The receptacles and seeds have been found to contain anthocyanins, rare in gymnosperms, which it was suggested in one 1988 paper make the fruit as a whole more attractive to prospective animal dispersers.

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Kahikatea' entry.

summary.text:
Dacrycarpus dacrydioides, commonly known as kahikatea (from Māori) and white pine, is a large coniferous tree in the family Podocarpaceae, endemic to New Zealand.
Kahikatea is endemic to the North, South, and Stewart Islands of New Zealand, and is the only member of the genus Dacrycarpus found in the country.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to c. 6 m. tall; trunk slender (not always developed); branches and branchlets rather stout, glab. Lvs on petioles ± 2–5 cm. long. Stipules tapering from rather broad base to 2 conspicuous denticles, glab. Lamina membr. to subcoriac., subglossy green above, paler below, broadly elliptic to obovate; apex subacute, sts apiculate; rather gradually narrowed to petiole; (10)–15–20 × (5)–7–10 cm.; margins sts waved, sts ± crenulate. Reticulations close, conspicuous or evident on both surfaces. Fls in clusters on trichotomously branched peduncles up to c. 6 cm. long. ♂ with 4–5-toothed cupular calyx; corolla narrow-funnelform, lobes us. 5, acute, < tube; stamens us. 5. ♀ us. with small stipulate bracts at axils of branches; calyx-teeth us. 5, small, acute; corolla tubular, lobes 5, narrow-triangular, acute, ± = tube. Drupe reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm. long.
[From:  Allan  (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Coprosma australis (A.Rich.) Robinson]

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. The Flora's key separates them by leaf thickness: shining karamū's are thick, kanono's rather thin. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text: Coprosma autumnalis or C. grandifolia according to earlier Colenso authority,  (In Māori: kanono, raurēkau or kawariki) is a native forest shrub of New Zealand. It is widespread in both the North Island and in the northern South Island, and has the largest leaves of any New Zealand coprosma. The name kawariki was applied after its leaves resembling those of the tropical Terminalia catappa which was once planted as shade for noble chiefs (ariki).

identification.text:
Kunzea ericoides is a spreading shrub or tree, sometimes growing to a height of 18 m with bark which peels in long strips and young branches which tend to droop. The leaves are variable in shape from linear to narrow elliptic or lance-shaped, 6.5–25 mm long and 1–5 mm wide with a petiole up to 1 mm long. The flowers are white or pale pink, crowded on side branches or in the axils of upper leaves. The floral cup is covered with soft, downy hairs and is on a pedicel 3–6 mm long. There are five triangular sepals about 1 mm long and five petals about 2 mm long. There are up to 25 stamens which are 1–4 mm, mostly longer than the petals. Flowering occurs between October and February and is followed by fruit which is a cup-shaped capsule 2–4 mm long and wide. The capsule usually opens to release its seed when mature.
Kunzea ericoides is very similar to the Australian endemics K. leptospermoides and K. peduncularis which were formerly included in K. ericoides. The new status of K. ericoides follows the publication of a paper entitled "A revision of the New Zealand Kunzea ericoides (Myrtaceae) complex" by the New Zealand botanist Peter de Lange.

summary.text:
Kunzea ericoides, commonly known as kānuka or white tea-tree, is a tree or shrub in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae and is endemic to New Zealand.
Kānuka (or mānuka, as it was mostly known until the 1930s) is only known from the north of the South Island. It is found north of the Buller and Wairau Rivers, and is most common near Nelson. Members of the kānuka complex are found throughout New Zealand occurring on the Three Kings Islands, Aotea (Great Barrier Island), from Te Paki (on the Aupōuri Peninsula) at the northern tip of the North Island to as far south as Dunedin and Central Otago in the South Island, and Stewart Island. Within this range kānuka is widespread ranging from coastal scrub and sand dunes (where it may form a distinct forest type) through lowland and montane forest, with one member of the complex reaching elevations of 2000 metres above sea level.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corynocarpus_laevigatus Names the toxin class and describes the processing this entry tells the reader not to attempt. The seeds 'contain highly toxic glucosides of 3-nitropropionic acid, such as karakin'; initial symptoms are diarrhoea, nausea and restlessness, developing into more severe gastrointestinal and neurological problems. The traditional process: seeds dropped each autumn were collected into open-weave kete, washed in water to remove the outer pulp, then baked and sun-dried, which removed the toxicity. It was one of the most grown pre-European Māori food crops, alongside kūmara and aruhe — the bracken rhizome, which has its own entry here — and in Māori tradition the tree came from Hawaiki. The flesh tastes sickly sweet, of apricots or dates, and the fruit is a valuable food for kererū and the Chatham Islands pigeon.

summary.text: Listed so you can recognise it and leave it alone. The kernel is severely poisonous without traditional processing.

warnings: No part is edible without the traditional multi-day steeping and cooking. Do not attempt it yourself: the raw kernel causes convulsions and permanent paralysis.
The kernel contains karakin. Poisoning causes violent convulsions and can result in permanent limb contractures and paralysis. There is no simple home antidote.
The orange flesh is not the hazard — the kernel inside is, and separating them reliably is not a beginner's task.
Fallen karaka fruit is a recognised poisoning risk for children and dogs. Learn the tree so you can steer them away from it.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 6 m. tall; branches and branchlets spreading, stout, glab. Lvs opp. on rather stout petioles ± 10–20 mm. long. Stipules connate towards base, obtuse, glab., crowned by 1–2 prominent sharp denticles. Lamina coriac., dullish dark green above, paler below, glab.; elliptic to elliptic-oblong to broad-ovate, acute or obtuse, ± mucronate, gradually narrowed to petiole, ± 7–12 × 3–4–(5) cm.; reticulated veins us. conspicuous on both surfaces. ♂ in axillary many-fld glomerules on short peduncles, glomerules again divided into dense clusters. Calyx-teeth minute; corolla subcampanulate, lobes triangular, acute, < tube. ♀ in compound clusters on trichotomously branched axillary peduncles 10–15 mm. long. Calyx minute, truncate, sts with 1–2 teeth; corolla c. 5 mm. long, narrow-funnelform, lobes acute or obtuse, oblong-triangular, < tube. Drupe dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrow-ovoid, 8–9 × 4–5 mm.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. The Flora's key separates them by leaf shape and stipule: shining karamū's leaves are widest above the middle and its stipules acute; karamū's are elliptic to ovate with tapering, long-pointed (acuminate) stipules. Shining karamū's leaf is glossy, karamū's rather dull. Wikipedia adds that shining karamū's roots and inner bark are yellow, karamū's dull brown, and that shining karamū lacks karamū's foul smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. The Flora's key separates them by leaf width and fruit length: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; Karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text:
Coprosma robusta, commonly known as karamū, is a flowering plant in the family Rubiaceae that is endemic to New Zealand.
Karamū is endemic to New Zealand. However, it is gradually becoming naturalised in areas of the south-east coast of Australia such as Victoria and Tasmania and has been rated as a weed threat there.
It is widely distributed across New Zealand in both the North and South Islands. On the Chatham Islands between Waitangi and Owenga, there is a small area where karamū has become naturalised.
Judging from the distribution map on New Zealand Plant Observation, the distribution of karamū increases with the differentiation in lower altitude which means more karamū in the North Island.
In Canterbury, karamū is found on Banks Peninsula in fragments of regenerating native bush and bush remnants. Additionally it is also found in forest margins and edges of the montane and lowland forests in the southern alps at the start of the Canterbury plains.

edibleParts.text: The soft new shoot tips, while they still snap.

habitat.text: Lowland and hill forest throughout the North Island and the wetter parts of the South Island, looping between trees in dense, dark tangles.

harvestEthics.text: A native of the forest interior, so almost always on conservation land — a DOC permit is required, and the vine is a food and rongoā plant for mana whenua. Take a few tips from a large tangle, not every tip from one plant, and never cut the vine.

identification.text: Thick, smooth, dark brown to black woody vines that loop and tangle through the understorey. In spring the growing tips are soft, pale green to reddish shoots the thickness of a pencil that snap cleanly when bent. Leaves are glossy, oval and opposite, on the older growth. Berries are bright red.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripogonum_scandens Endemic to New Zealand, across the North and South Islands and some offshore islands. Corrects this entry's line about the fruit: the red globe-shaped fruits are edible, and are eaten and dispersed by birds — but most of each fruit is seed, and the botanist and horticulturalist Lawrie Metcalf described them as 'quite tasteless'. The newly formed shoots at the ends of the vines are the part worth having: an important traditional food, nicknamed bush asparagus, tasting of green beans. Māori also used the vine for traps for crayfish, eels, kōkopu and kiore, and the roots medicinally.

harvestEthics.text: Karengo is a taonga species with deep customary significance, and specific beds are managed by hapū. Check for rāhui before harvesting, cut rather than tear so the holdfast survives, and take only what you will use. Some areas are subject to customary management under the Fisheries Act — ask locally.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyropia Supports the 'native nori' description and explains the double genus name on this entry. Pyropia is a genus of red algae of intertidal zones and shallow water worldwide, and several of its species are what nori is made from — a two-billion-dollar industry centred on China, Korea and Japan — with nori carrying substantial vitamin B12. Many species now in Pyropia sat in Porphyra until recently, and New Zealand material drove some of that: 2013 research on New Zealand plants moved Pyropia plicata out of Porphyra. Both names are therefore in circulation for the same seaweeds, which is why this entry lists both.

identification.text:
Woody but brittle perennial climber attached by roots to trunks of forest trees or in large masses on ground. Stems c. 4 cm. diam., branched, marked with scars of old lvs. Lvs ± tufted towards ends of stems, spirally arranged, to c. 150 × 2–2.5 cm.; sheathing bases pale; tips long-attenuate, triangular in T.S.; margins, and midrib abaxially, minutely and distantly spinulose. Spadices simple and solitary in axils of several ± foliaceous bracts at stem apex; bracts thick and succulent towards base, white to purplish. Peduncle 1–4 cm. long, glab., whitish; spadix at fl. c. 7 × 1.5 cm., cylindrical or slightly flattened, the axis quite hidden by tightly packed fls. ♂ of several stamens each with a long filament, ovate anther and cop. ± confluent pollen surrounding a small rudimentary ovary; limits of individual fls not easily determined. ♀ with 6–12 purplish staminodes at base of flattened, vertically elongated ovary c. 2–4 × 1 mm. × 2 mm. tall, the long sides grooved between the staminodes; stigmas c. 6–12, sessile, arranged around a long groove; locule narrow, placentae forming ridges projecting into it. Infructescence to c. 15 × 3 cm. on stiff woody peduncle. Individual frs (phalanges) c. 8 × 2 × 10 mm., compressed laterally, thin-walled proximally, broadest c. ⅓ from base and almost woody towards top. Seed c. 1 mm. long, narrow, on long, slender funicle.
[From:  Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]

identification.text:
Rhizomes short-creeping, up to 100 m long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales narrowly ovate, 5–21 mm long, 1–2 mm wide, chestnut-brown, concolorous or occasionally slightly bicolorous with paler margins. Fronds strongly dimorphic; fertile and sterile fronds with similar habit, arching upwards or outwards; sterile fronds 185–2780 mm; fertile fronds on same plant equalling or shorter than the sterile, 210–2250 mm long. Sterile fronds. Stipes 35–1150 mm long, sometimes black-brown at extreme base but mostly yellow-brown, bearing narrowly ovate chestnut-brown concolorous scales and bicolorous scales with a conspicuous dark spot around the point of attachment. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, scaly. Laminae 150–2125 mm long, 65–740 mm wide, 1-pinnate, elliptic to obovate, with an undivided apical segment, bright green, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, coriaceous; scales on abaxial pinna costae with a dark spot around the point of attachment, but becoming concolorous towards the pinna apices and on the distal pinnae. Pinnae in 7–53 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong, straight or slightly falcate, markedly reduced to small, rounded lobes at the lamina base; the longest pinnae above the middle, 32–400 mm long, 9–30 mm wide, apices acuminate, margins shallowly crenate, bases auricled, short-stalked; the basal pinnae opposite. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 100–900 mm long. Laminae 135–1350 mm long, 65–280 mm wide. Pinnae in 8–45 pairs, linear, straight or curled basiscopically, 48–320 mm long, 2–6 mm wide; short, sterile, proximal flanges present on the middle pinnae; 2–9 pairs of pinnae at the base of the lamina replaced by short, rounded, sterile lobes. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along most of the length of the pinna except for the proximal sterile flanges.
Note: Measurements given above are from herbarium specimens. Larger fronds are known to occur in the wild. CHR 199087, from Moumoukai, South Auckland, comprises parts of a frond said to measure 3000 mm long.
