identification.text:
Vigorous, dioecious, high-climbing vine, glabrous except for slightly hairy young stems.  Lvs simple;  petioles (0.8)–1–2 cm long, eglandular;  stipules minute or 0;  lamina (4)–5–12–(14) × (1.8)–2–4–(5.5) cm, lanceolate to narrow-ovate or elliptic, coriaceous, dark glossy green above, entire, acute to acuminate.  Fls (1)–3–4 in cymes, fragrant.  Pedicels 5–15 mm long.  Bracts ± subulate, caducous.  Hypanthium 0.  Perianth 4-merous;  segments 5–6 mm long, ± oblong, yellowish green;  corona threads 2.5–3.5 mm long.  ♂ fls with 4 stamens;  filaments 5–6 mm long forming a short androphore bearing an abortive ovary.  ♀ fls with short staminodes.  Ovary glabrous;  styles (2)–3,  c. 2 mm long.  Fr. (2)–2.5–3 cm diam., subglobose or broad-ellipsoid, orange;  pulp reddish, sparse.  Seeds 3–7 mm long, flattened, wrinkled.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and banana passionfruit (P. tripartita)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and banana passionfruit (P. tarminiana)'s leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Black passionfruit is hairless except in the flower; its leaves are deeply 3-lobed (undivided on young plants) and deep shining green above, the middle lobe 6–10 × 3–5.5 cm; its stipules are narrow, 10–15 mm long; its flowers stand on stalks 4–6 cm long, are white with white corona threads purple at the base, and have no obvious floral tube; its fruit is 5–6.25 × 4.75–5.75 cm, broadly ellipsoid or nearly round, dull purple, with black seeds. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and black passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. A young black passionfruit's leaves are undivided too (Flora of New Zealand: 'entire on young plants'), so on a young plant go by texture: kōhia's are leathery, black passionfruit's thin. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Black passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and pink-flowered passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. Lookalike cards among the five Passiflora entries (written by the assistant on the owner's instruction (owner, 22/10/2026: /goal "find all you can about Passiflora and fill in following the rules")): each card restates the two species' descriptions and Flora of New Zealand's Passiflora key — Webb, C.J. et al. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/0e0cc34b-28b7-4b4a-8a94-9b059b1af976 — couplet 1 'Hypanthium cylindric and strongly elongated' against 'Hypanthium 0 or saucer-shaped and inconspicuous'; couplet 2 'Stipules pinnate with filiform segments; fr. ± globose' (pinnatistipula) against 'Stipules simple, ovate and toothed or subulate and entire; fr. ellipsoid'; couplet 3 '× rosea' 'Stipules with lanceolate rachis; stamens abnormal and ± petaloid'; couplet 6 'Lvs entire, coriaceous; perianth < 2 cm diam. when fresh' (tetrandra) against 'Lvs lobed, membranous or submembranous; perianth > 4 cm diam. when fresh'. Descriptions: Webb 1988 for P. edulis, P. pinnatistipula, P. tetrandra and P. mollissima (= P. tripartita var. mollissima; Flora of New Zealand Online files Webb's P. mollissima description under that name); for P. tarminiana, which Webb did not separate, Wikipedia 'Passiflora tarminiana' (revision 1352787405, CC BY-SA 4.0), NZPCN's P. tarminiana page (all rights reserved; facts restated) and Flora of New Zealand Online's weed profiles (CC BY 3.0 NZ: tube '6-7 cm' for P. tarminiana, '8-10 cm' and leaves 'moderately to densely hairy on the upper surface' for P. tripartita var. mollissima). The tarminiana–tripartita test follows Wikipedia's 'distinguished from P. tripartita var. mollissima' paragraph and NZPCN ('Can be distinguished from P. tarminiana by the large persistent stipules, and the long hypanthium'); var. azuayensis 'leaves glabrous to glabrate on upper surface' is NZPCN after Heenan & Sykes 2003; the hybrid is iNaturalist taxon 1645626, Passiflora tarminiana × tripartita (43 wild New Zealand records on 22/10/2026). Blue passionflower: NZPCN 'Most similar to P. caerulea in flower'; Webb 1988 'Lvs 5-lobed almost to base', 'pulp scanty and inedible'. × rosea: Webb's key and NZPCN's P. pinnatistipula page. Kōhia's fruit only on female plants: Wikipedia 'Passiflora tetrandra' (revision 1324332696). Risk `edible` every way, because every page carries a food record. Not carded: black passionfruit ↔ pink-flowered passionfruit — Webb gives black passionfruit 'N.: N. Auckland … Great Barrier Id; K.' and pink-flowered 'S.: Banks Peninsula (widespread), Otago (Palmerston)', so their wild ranges do not meet in the Flora. Blue passionflower, P. × rosea, P. mixta and P. antioquiensis have no entries (owner, 22/10/2026: blue passionflower 'Skip it').

summary.text:
Passiflora tetrandra (Māori: kōhia), also known as New Zealand passionflower, New Zealand passionfruit, or kohe, is a climbing vine found in New Zealand. Of the c. 500 species of passionflower, this is the sole species native to New Zealand.
It occurs throughout the North Island and in parts of the South Island as far south as Banks Peninsula.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Barbarea verna' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Annual or biennial, winter green, herbaceous plant in the Brassicaceae. The seeds typically germinate in the autumn to form an over-wintering rosette. The following spring, it grows a main stem up to about 90 cm, sometimes up to 130 cm, which is pale green, grooved (sulcate) and occasionally branched. The leaves are alternate and pinnate with clasping auricles at the base and between 4 and 11 pairs of sub-opposite lobes. The upper leaves have much narrower lobes than those found lower down. The whole plant is almost entirely glabrous.
The flowers appear in early spring.  The inflorescence is a terminal raceme, or lateral raceme arising from the leaf axils, with 6 to 25 flowers on short 3-8mm pedicels. There are four yellowy green sepals, 5mm long and four bright yellow petals each 8mm long. Six stamens and one style with a capitate stigma at the tip.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Morchella importuna' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: A saprobic fungus, Morchella importuna fruit bodies grow in wood chips, gardens, fire pits, planters, and almost any disturbed ground in urban areas. Kuo suggests that it has mycorrhizal tendencies when grown in an environment with trees. Known primarily from northern California and the Pacific Northwest region of the United States, it has been reported from British Columbia (Canada), California, Washington, Nevada, and Oregon, although there have been a few isolated reports of the morel from the Midwestern United States and from eastern North America. Fruiting occurs in the spring, from March until May. Identified as phylogenetic species "Mel-10", Morchella importuna has also been found in Turkey and China, but it remains unclear whether dispersal between these distant locations occurred naturally or through accidental introduction by humans.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Morchella importuna' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The fruit bodies of M. importuna are 6–20 cm high. The cap is 3–15 cm high and measures 2–9 cm wide at its widest point. It is conical to widely conical or occasionally egg-shaped. Its surface has pits and ridges, with 12–20 primary vertical ridges and numerous transecting horizontal ridges, creating a laddered appearance. The cap is attached to stipe with a sinus about 2–5 mm both deep and wide. The ridges are smooth or finely velvety and colored pale to dark gray when young, becoming dark grayish brown to nearly black in age. They are bluntly rounded when young, but later become sharpened or eroded. Pits are vertically elongated in all stages of development. They have a smooth or finely velvety texture. The pits open and deepen with development, progressing from gray to dark gray when immature to grayish brown, grayish olive or brownish yellow at maturity. The stipe measures 3–10 cm high and 2–6 cm wide, and is often somewhat thicker near the base. Its whitish to pale brownish surface is smooth or finely mealy with whitish granules. It develops longitudinal ridges and grooves (particularly near the base) as the fruit body matures. The flesh is whitish to watery tan, measuring 1–3 mm thick in the hollow cap; in the stipe, this tissue is sometimes arranged as chambers or layers. The sterile inner surface of the cap is whitish and pubescent (covered with short soft "hair").

The ascospores are elliptical, smooth, and measure 18–24 by 10–13 μm. The cylindrical, hyaline (translucent), asci are eight-spored, measuring 220–300 by 12–25 μm. Paraphyses are septate, measuring 150–250 by 7–15 μm. They are cylindrical with variably shaped tips: rounded to roughly club-shaped, pointy, or fuse-shaped. Elements on the sterile ridges are septate and measure 25–300 by 10–30 μm. Terminal cells are cylindrical with a rounded tip that is variably shaped similar to the paraphyses. Both the paraphyses and the terminal cells are hyaline or brownish in dilute (2%) potassium hydroxide.
As a member of the Morchella elata group of black morels, M. importuna is sought after as a choice edible mushroom. Raw morels are poisonous and should always be cooked.


Similar species
The rare Pacific Northwest morel Morchella hotsonii, known only from its type collection, is quite similar in appearance to M. importuna. The former species is distinguished by its finely velvety surface.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Larix decidua' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
The seeds are an important food for some birds, notably siskin, redpoll, and citril finch, while the buds and immature cones are eaten by capercaillie.
Larch needles (including L. decidua and L. sibirica) are the only known food for caterpillars of the case-bearer moth Coleophora sibiricella; its cone scales are used as food by the caterpillars of the tortrix moth Cydia illutana.
It is susceptible to larch canker Lachnellula willkommii.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Larix decidua' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Larix decidua is a medium-size to large deciduous coniferous tree reaching 25–45 metres tall, with a trunk up to 1.5 metres diameter (exceptionally, to 53.8 metres and 11.20 m girth (3.56 m diameter). The crown is conic when young, becoming broad and often irregular with age; the main branches are level to upswept, with the side branches often pendulous. The shoots are dimorphic, with growth divided into long shoots (typically 10–50 cm long) and bearing several buds, and short shoots only 1–2 mm long with only a single bud. The leaves are needle-like, light green, 2–4 centimetres long which turn bright yellow before they fall in the autumn, leaving the pale yellow-buff shoots bare until the next spring.
The cones are erect, ovoid-conic, 2–6 centimetres long, with 10-90 erect or slightly incurved (not reflexed) seed scales; they are bright pinkish-red at pollination, then green variably flushed red to purplish when immature, and turn brown and opening to release the seeds when mature, 4–6 months after pollination. The old cones commonly remain on the tree for many years, turning dull grey-black.
It is very cold tolerant, able to survive winter temperatures down to at least −50 °C, and is among the tree line trees in the Alps, reaching 2,400 m altitude, though most abundant from 1,000–2,000 m. It only grows on well-drained soils, avoiding waterlogged ground and is not shade tolerant.
It is closely related to Siberian larch Larix sibirica and similar in morphology; the two are best distinguished by the dense pubescence on the cone scales of L. sibirica, compared to the glabrous or only thinly pubescent cone scales of L. decidua.

habitat.text: It grows only under larch trees. Widespread in North America and Europe (July–November). In Asia, it has been recorded from Taiwan.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Suillus grevillei' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Suillus grevillei is a mushroom with a 5–10 cm cap colored from citrus yellow to burnt orange, that is at first hemispherical, then bell-shaped, and finally flattened. It has a sticky skin, often with veil remnants on the edge, short tubes of yellow (possibly staining brownish) which descend down to the bottom of its cylindrical stalk (6–10 x 1–2 cm), which is yellowish above the ring area with streaks of reddish brown below. The flesh is yellow, staining brown.
Taste mild to slightly astringent to bitterish; odor none to somewhat metallic.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 5–(10) m. tall; branches and branchlets stout, glab. Lvs on stout petioles ± 12–25 mm. long. Stipules connate into broad membr. sheath tipped by long sharp denticle. Lamina subcoriac., broad- to elliptic-ovate, obtuse or subacute to mucronulate, ± 9–13 × 4–8 cm. Midrib prominent, secondary veins and reticulations evident. ♂ in compound glomerules on axillary peduncles 10–15 mm. long; calyx-teeth minute; corolla c. 9 mm. long, subcampanulate, lobes ovate-triangular, acute, < tube. ♀ 2–5 together, on simple or branched peduncles 20–70 mm. long; calyx-teeth acute; corolla tubular, widening above, lobes acute, < tube. Drupe orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm. long.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. The Flora's key separates them by leaf width and fruit length: karamū's leaves about 35–42 mm wide with fruit 8–9 mm long; large-seeded coprosma's about 40–80 mm wide with fruit 10–25 mm long. Widths meet at about 40 mm, so take both tests together. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Shining karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; large-seeded coprosma's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. identification.text:
Large, narrow-pyramidal tree;  branches usually present to near ground and ± drooping towards the apex.  Bark thick, fibrous, reddish brown, fissured.  Branchlets in horizontal sprays, green or, less commonly ± glaucous (mostly glaucous in cultivation), aromatic when bruised.  Sapling quickly passing into adult condition.  Scale lvs appressed;  facial pairs on lateral shoot systems (excluding 1–3 year terminal brown shoots) mostly 1–2 mm long, broad-ovate, subacute, with gland on back elongated and appearing as a translucent dot in transmitted light;  lateral pairs similar but mostly 1.5–2.5 mm long, with whitish stomatal lines on lower side ± evident when fresh.  ♂ strobili 2–5 mm long;  pollen sacs deep pink to crimson.  ♀ cones blue when young, brownish with bluish bloom and 6–9 mm diam. when mature;  scales 8; umbo a small ridge.  Seeds 2–4 on each scale, with conspicuous resin tubercles; wing narrower than or = to seed. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

habitat.text: Lawns and other open turf, typically dry and poor but also wet or rich ground, and urban areas; also disturbed or regenerating native vegetation, often on track edges, rarely in dense forest. Coast to subalpine (to 1100 m), mostly lowland.

harvestEthics.text: This species is abundant, nevertheless collect it mindfully.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Perennial;  primary root slender to stout, occasionally to  c. 10 mm thick. Stems glabrous to densely hairy (hairs usually antrorse, occasionally dense and patent), ± filiform, creeping, prostrate or nearly so, rooting at nodes, much-branched and often mat-forming.  Lvs 3-foliolate.  Petiole 5–40 mm long, with patent or antrorse hairs, these sparse to dense;  stipules adnate, truncate or rounded at apex.  Petiolules very short.  Lamina of leaflets equal, 1–9 × 1.5–12 mm, obcordate, sometimes broadly so, with width > length, with narrow to broad sinus and rounded lobes, glabrous or hairy above, glabrate or with appressed hairs beneath, ciliate or eciliate, often purplish below;  calli 0.  Fls solitary, rarely paired;  peduncle glabrate to densely clothed in antrorse hairs, generally geniculate at apex;  pedicel (4)–8–25 mm long. Bracts 1–3 mm long, ± linear-subulate, hairy, situated at base or at middle of pedicels;  calli 0.  Sepals 2.3–3.5–(4) mm long, oblong-lanceolate, oblong, or ovate-elliptic, glabrate or with antrorse hairs;  calli 0.  Petals 4.5–9–(13) mm long, ± oblong-obovate, yellow, often pink-flushed outside, glabrous.  Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous or nearly so;  filaments united at base, those of longer whorl  c. 1.5 mm long.  Styles < or > longer stamens, densely hairy.  Capsule (3)–7–10–(13) mm long excluding styles, broadly cylindric, cylindric-ovoid or conic, glabrous to densely hairy; hairs short, patent or retrorse, sometimes glandular.  Seed 1–1.3–(1.5) mm long, broad-ellipsoid;  transverse ridges 7–13, subacute, sometimes white-topped; grooves deep.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel creeps: its stems are more or less thread-like, prostrate or nearly so, root at the nodes and often form mats. Bermuda buttercup appears stemless, with its leaves all rising from the base on stalks 6–22 cm long, and grows from a bulb with underground runners that bear many small bulbils. Measure a leaflet and a petal, remembering the ranges almost meet: least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its petals 4.5–9 mm (up to 13 mm); Bermuda buttercup's leaflets are 10–32 mm long and its golden petals 2–2.8 cm (from 1.5 cm). Least yellow sorrel's flowers are solitary, rarely paired, and it sets a capsule 7–10 mm long (3–13 mm at the extremes); Bermuda buttercup usually carries 3–18 flowers (occasionally 1) hanging on a stalk 15–45 cm long (from 7 cm), and Flora of New Zealand records no capsule seen on it. Yellow flowers, notched leaflets and purple in the leaf do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel looks like a larger least yellow sorrel, with much the same leaves, creeping stems and yellow flowers, so size and flower count are the tests, and size changes with growing conditions. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm) and up to 23 mm wide, and its leaves are normally about 20 mm across; least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long and its leaves typically under 10 mm across. Count the flowers on a stalk: creeping wood sorrel carries 1 to 5, usually at least two; least yellow sorrel's are solitary, rarely paired. Creeping wood sorrel's capsule is mostly 10–18 mm long, least yellow sorrel's mostly 7–10 mm, though the ranges meet. Creeping wood sorrel is more often in garden beds and nurseries, least yellow sorrel in lawns. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover's leaflets are 5–25 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Red clover's leaflets are 15–40 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Alsike clover's hairless stems stand erect or rise from the base and do not root at the nodes; least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats. Alsike clover's leaflets are 10–35 mm long, least yellow sorrel's 1–9 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

preparation.text: Add the leaves to salads, cook them as a pot herb with milder greens, or use them to give a sour taste to other food. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads. The leaves are very small and fiddly to pick.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. Use it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: About 950 ml (1 US quart) water, 125 ml (½ cup) wood sorrel leaves, stems, flowers and seed pods, 15 ml (1 tbsp) agave nectar or honey, and a dash of salt. Mix everything in a blender. If you can, leave it in the fridge overnight before drinking.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel cooler

recipes.method: Fresh wood sorrel leaves and boiling water, one part leaves to three parts water. Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis exilis: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. This page records no edible parts of its own; the recipes rest on the owner's word that wood sorrel recipes are interchangeable. Provenance as recorded on creeping-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). Gratin and potato salad, as recorded on pale-pink-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

summary.text: Oxalis exilis, the least yellow sorrel or shady woodsorrel, is a small herbaceous plant found in Australia and New Zealand.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

In New Zealand: native and exotic forest, forest margins and shrubland, most likely near gardens or historic sites (Environment Canterbury, for the four mahonias growing wild here); recorded growing wild in the Christchurch Botanic Gardens.

identification.text:
Berberis bealei is a multi-stemmed, evergreen shrub or small tree with irregular, strong upright stems that have limited branching. It grows up to 8 metres tall, is upright, and is scarcely branching. The leaves are up to 50 centimetres long, with 4–10 pairs of leaflets, plus a much larger terminal leaflet. The sessile leaflets have spines and the terminal leaflets are larger than others.
The flowers are borne in an erect raceme up to 30 cm long. The berries are blue or dark purple colored egg-shaped berries, up to 15 millimetres long, that turn bluish black with a grayish bloom. Fruits hang in grapelike clusters and are glaucous, covered with a white waxy coating. The erect stems are stiff and unbranched.

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves are up to about 50 cm long with 4–10 pairs of leaflets and a much larger terminal one; Oregon grape's are up to about 25 cm with 3–7 pairs. Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long (Flora of China); Oregon grape's reach 6–7 cm. Its berries are egg-shaped and up to 15 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Leatherleaf mahonia has stiff upright stems and can reach 8 m; Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m. Leaflet counts overlap at 4–7 pairs, and dark bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. NC State Extension, though, describes leatherleaf mahonia's berries as globose, so shape alone does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's flower clusters stand upright, 7–26 cm long (Flora of China); Japanese mahonia's are lax and spreading (Flora of New Zealand). Leatherleaf mahonia's leaflets are wider (Wikipedia), 2–6 cm (Flora of China), against Japanese mahonia's 2–3.5 cm, so only a wide leaflet tells. Leatherleaf mahonia's berries reach 15 mm long; Japanese mahonia's are 8–10 mm. Leaflet counts (4–10 pairs against 5–9), a small lowest pair, spiny teeth and blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them, and leatherleaf mahonia has been listed as a form of B. japonica ('Bealei'). Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) adds that the two have hybridised in gardens and that many seedlings are hybrids, so intermediate plants are fairly common. Missouri Botanical Garden, though, describes plants grown under the name leatherleaf mahonia in the United States with loose, spreading to hanging flower clusters and narrow leaflets, so on a planted or escaped shrub neither trait settles it.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Leatherleaf mahonia's leaves carry 4–10 pairs of broad leaflets, roundish to ovate and 2–6 cm wide; mountain grape's carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones, 1–2.5 cm wide (Flora of China). Leatherleaf mahonia's berries are up to 15 mm long; mountain grape's up to 8 mm. Upright flower clusters, a tall habit and dark blue bloomed berries do not separate them, and the garden hybrid 'Arthur Menzies' has both as parents.

preparation.text: The berries can be eaten raw but the seed to pulp ratio is large so most of these berries are boiled and strained.

recipes.method: Written for the berries of Japanese and leatherleaf mahonia picked in Victoria, British Columbia. Base: 375 ml flour, 440 ml rolled oats, 125 ml chopped walnuts, 250 ml packed dark brown or coconut sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp fine salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 250 ml melted butter. Topping: 625 ml mahonia berries, 250 ml sugar, 2 tsp grated orange or lemon zest and two lavender buds. Heat the oven to 180°C and line a 20–23 cm square tin with baking paper, leaving it overhanging the sides. Stir the dry ingredients together, then work in the melted butter until crumbly. Press three-quarters of it firmly into the tin and bake for 10 minutes. Cook the berries with the sugar, zest and lavender over low heat for 15 minutes, until they pop open; cool for 5 minutes and take out the lavender. Pour over the base, scatter the rest of the crumble on top and bake for 30–40 minutes, until golden. Cool completely in the tin, lift out by the paper and cut into 12 large bars or 24 squares.

summary.text:
Berberis bealei, also known as leatherleaf mahonia, Beale's barberry, is a species of evergreen shrub native to mainland China. The species has been regarded as the same species as Berberis japonica, native to Taiwan, but the two differ consistently in certain floral and leaf characters. Both species are widely cultivated in many countries as ornamentals.
Berberis bealei is one of approximately 70 species that were once classified in genus Mahonia. Thus, older sources refer to this species as Mahonia bealei or M. Japonica.
In New Zealand: Flora of New Zealand Online and NZPCN list it as exotic, as Berberis bealei with the synonym Mahonia bealei; neither describes it.
Biota of New Zealand records it as a casual exotic (growing wild but not naturalised), after Heenan, de Lange et al. (2004). In the south-eastern United States it has escaped gardens and naturalised, and North Carolina lists it as invasive; it spreads by seed and by suckers, which can form a colony, and birds eat the fruit.

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

NC State Extension says the berries contain berberine, which can upset the stomach, especially in children, and that eating the poisonous parts (bark, leaves, roots and sap) can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Rhizomatous, lemon-scented herb with branched puberulent stems ascending to c. 60 cm.  Lvs and bracts petiolate.  Lamina 2–8.5 × 1–7 cm, elliptic to broad-ovate, hairy, sometimes only sparsely hairy above, prominently crenate-serrate;  base ± truncate in larger lower lvs, cuneate in upper smaller lvs and bracts. Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Melissa officinalis is native to south-central Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, Central Asia and Iran, but is now naturalized in the Americas and elsewhere around the world.

habitat.text:
Pittosporum eugenioides is found throughout the South Island and North Island in low lying forests. It is found in forest clearings and along forest margins up to 600 m above sea level.

Pittosporum eugenioides can be found in a cooler, mature, lowland and subalpine forest climate zone throughout New Zealand. The species can be found in regenerating areas of forest, both young and old. It has proved to be a great plant for establishing a quick canopy.

At home in the garden, P. eugenioides prefers a sunny to part shade position, does not mind the wind, and thrives in soil with good drainage.

identification.text:
Polygamodioec. tree with spreading branches, up to 12 m. tall, trunk up to 6 dm. diam., bark pale. Lvs alt., often approximate, 5–10–(15) × 2.5–4 cm., on rather slender petioles 1–2 cm. long. Lamina subcoriac., glossy, scented, elliptic to elliptic-oblong, acute to subacute, narrowed to petiole; margins us. undulate, midrib pale. Fls fragrant, in terminal compound umbels, subcorymbosely arranged. Peduncles and pedicels with scattered hairs; peduncles 1–2 cm. long, pedicels c. 5 mm. long. Sepals ovate to narrow-ovate, pale, membr., c. 2 mm. long; petals narrow-oblong, yellowish, 5–7 mm. long. Capsules glab., finely granulate, ovoid to elliptic in outline, 5–6 mm. long; valves 2 or sts 3; seeds immersed in viscid pulp, remaining ± covered by papery endocarp at dehiscence.

summary.text:
Pittosporum eugenioides, commonly known as tarata or lemonwood, is a species of evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand.
Pittosporum eugenioides is endemic to New Zealand. There are "about 200 trees and shrubs" in the genus located in neighbouring parts of the world. Places where the genus is found include Africa, Australia, some Pacific islands, southern and eastern Asia, and New Zealand.
A reason for this endemic occurrence is due to the isolation of New Zealand over a long period of time.
This species, along with other Pittosporum, are making their way in to the average household gardens. Nurseries and garden centres are stocking this native because it is suited to New Zealand conditions where it naturally grew many years ago.

habitat.text: Pasture, meadows, lawns and rough grassland on rich, acidic soil, most often where sheep or cattle have been grazing. It feeds on decaying grass roots, not on the dung itself, so look in the sward rather than on a pat. Fruits in autumn, singly or in scattered troops.

identification.text:
Cap 5–25 mm across and about as tall, sharply conical to bell-shaped, and almost always tipped with a small distinct nipple. Colour shifts with moisture: chestnut to olive-brown when damp, with the gill lines showing through the margin, fading to pale buff as it dries. A damp cap is tacky, with a gelatinous skin that peels away if you bend the margin back — the most useful confirming test in the field.
Gills are narrow and crowded, pale brown at first, darkening to purple-brown with paler edges. The stipe is 4.5–14 cm long but only 1–3.5 mm thick, slender, often wavy, and has no ring. Spore print is dark purple-brown.
Any part handled or bruised stains blue-green. A conical, nipple-tipped grassland cap that bruises blue and gives a purple-brown print is this species.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both grow in grass, so habitat does not separate them. Cap shape is the first check but not a certain one. A liberty cap is sharply conical to bell-shaped, often tipped with a small nipple, and keeps that shape as it ages. A mower's mushroom is conical or bell-shaped when young but opens out to broadly convex and lacks the liberty cap's point. A liberty cap stains bluish where it is handled or bruised, and its stem is sometimes blue towards the base. The mower's mushroom's flesh does not change colour when cut. Bend back a piece of a damp liberty cap and a thin gelatinous skin peels away (not once the cap has dried out); the mower's mushroom is not described as having this skin. Mower's mushroom gills are broad and often go mottled as the spores ripen. A liberty cap's gills are narrow and moderately crowded, darkening to dark grey or purple-brown. Both can have paler gill edges, so the edges do not separate them. The spore print will not decide it either: liberty cap very dark purple-brown, mower's mushroom dark brown, sometimes purplish to nearly black.

The legal claims on this page, checked against the Act rather than a summary of it. Schedule 1 (Class A controlled drugs) lists Psilocine, Psilotsin and Psilocybine by name and formula. Section 7(1)(a) makes it an offence to procure, possess, consume, smoke or otherwise use a controlled drug, and section 7(2)(a) sets the penalty at 'imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to both where a Class A controlled drug was the controlled drug' — which is what this entry's warning says. Note that section 7(2) applies 'without prejudice to any liability under section 6', the dealing provision, which carries life imprisonment for a Class A drug: the same handful of mushrooms can be charged either way depending on quantity and circumstance. Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, read on legislation.govt.nz 06/10/2026. https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/DLM436100.html

The fungus itself is a prohibited plant, which is a second offence this page did not mention. Section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 defines 'prohibited plant' to include 'any fungus of the genera Conocybe, Panaeolus, or Psilocybe from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug' — so cultivating it is an offence under section 9, separately from possessing it under section 7. Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, read on legislation.govt.nz 06/10/2026. https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/DLM436100.html

The card introduces no fact that was not already on one of the two pages: the nipple, the peelable gelatinous skin and the blue-green bruising come from this entry’s identification, and the convex nippleless cap, the absence of a peelable skin, the mottled gills and the absence of blueing come from mowers-mushroom.identification. It also records that the spore print does not separate them, because that entry gives a deep brown print with a purplish cast against the dark purple-brown given here. A note on the risk level of that card. It is set to unpalatable, not toxic, because that is what the mower’s mushroom entry itself says — its only warning is that the mushroom is unpalatable. No claim about psilocybin in Panaeolus foenisecii is made on either page, in either direction, because nothing cited on either page settles it. Note separately that section 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, quoted above, names Panaeolus alongside Psilocybe, but it reaches only a fungus of that genus ‘from which a controlled drug can be produced or which contains a controlled drug’, so the Act does not itself decide the question for this species and neither does this guide.

Correction to the two lookalike cards, 08/10/2026, same day they were written, after re-reading them against the pages they draw on. Four claims were stronger or looser than their source. (1) Both cards stated the liberty cap's nipple flatly, where liberty-cap.identification says 'almost always tipped with a small distinct nipple' — the hedge is restored on both, because a nippleless liberty cap is precisely the specimen a hardened card fails to warn about, and it is the first character a reader checks. Both cards now give each species' gills as its own page gives them. (3) 'sometimes' was restored to the mower's mushroom's purplish spore-print cast. (4) 'their seasons overlap through autumn' was replaced by the actual overlap of the two months arrays, April to June, which runs past autumn. summary.text: A small, sharply conical grassland mushroom with a nipple-tipped cap that bruises blue. It contains psilocybin, which makes it a Class A controlled drug in New Zealand.

warnings: Psilocybine and psilocine are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and New Zealand Police list magic mushrooms as Class A. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

The plant is originally from China, where related species can be found growing in the wild. It grows in places where suitable winter temperatures are generally above -12°C, such as Georgia, Argentina, Armenia, Afghanistan, Australia, Azerbaijan, Bermuda, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Greece, Kenya, Syria, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Türkiye, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, South Africa, the whole Mediterranean Basin, Pakistan, New Zealand, Réunion, Tonga, Central America, Mexico, South America and warmer parts of the United States such as Hawaii, California, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, with a maximal range comprising coastal Oregon and Washington, southern Tennessee, and most of North Carolina, in places with a favorable humid subtropical climate with relatively mild winters. 
China is the largest producer worldwide (400,000 t annually), with Spain being the second with 41,487 t annually, half of which is destined for export markets.

identification.text:
Pseudowintera axillaris is one of four Winteraceae species endemic to New Zealand.
It has many distinguishing features that can identify it from other Winteraceae species. Growing up to 8 metres tall and a trunk up to 10 cm in diameter this small shrub-like tree, prefers damper, cold, tree shaded locations found in New Zealand forests in the North Island and the northern parts of the South Island. Distinguishing features of this plant include its dark green coloured leaves, and natural glossy wax that gives the underside a pale to glaucous but not white; midvein pale appearance. These leaves have smooth margins and unlike many other plant species, P. axillaris usually has no red or brown blotches or discolouration. Adult leaves can grow up to 6–10 cm long by 3–6 cm wide and have red leaf stalks, with yellowish midribs, and smooth margins. Juvenile leaves have distinctive, white, net-like secondary veins on the upper surface. Another known feature of the P. axillaris is the peppery taste it upholds when chewing. P. colorata is known for its extremely spicy peppery taste compared to that of a chilly, whereas P. axillaris has a slight, pleasant peppery taste, known to keep plant grazing insects away. P. axillaris has very dark red – black branches, with the branchlets usually becoming more black in colour toward the leaves. It is considered to be a very primitive flowering plant, and is one of the more common of the four Pseudowintera species, after P. colorata. The flowers are small in size, 10mm across, [bisexual] on quite long stalks, and greenish yellow in colour. They occur in clusters in the leaf axils or in the scars of fallen leaves. Petal numbers vary between 4-7 free petals, and calyx cup shaped. The petals are 5-6mm long, narrow-oblong to narrow-obovate, apex obtuse. Other parts of the flower are symmetrical apex obtuse, carpels 1–6, stigma apical very short stamens but many (6-20) crowded around a few short ovaries Pseudowintera axillaris fruits are berries, one from each ovary producing a 3-6-seeded fleshy globose to subglobose berry 5-6mm in diameter orange to red when ripe.

summary.text:
Pseudowintera axillaris, the lowland horopito, is a shrub like tree, endemic to New Zealand.
It is known that New Zealand forests are quite unique, where the actions of tectonism, volcanism, stratification, erosion, flooding and other naturally occurring processes all contribute to the production of soil development. We have harsh, however adaptable environments where soil is enriched with nutrients and provides a stable habitat for over 80% of New Zealand's native vascular plants. These native species are also usually endemic to New Zealand as it provides such a specified location where adaptations occur to fit these environments and nowhere else.
Photosynthesis can occur at low rates with the help of nutrient dense soil, water and shade tolerance. The most important macronutrients needed for plant growth is Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P) and Potassium (K). Nitrogen or protein rich soils are often found where manures, food scraps, decay and green leaves are present. This is why the Humus layer within Lower montane forests provides such a strong nutrient enriched base for shade loving plants.
Predators, parasites, and diseases
Pseudowintera species are not a threatened or endangered species as herbivore animals and insects do not appreciate the pungent, peppery taste given off the plant when eating. Both P. colorata and P. axillaris have this aromatic effect. There are however the common animal species that do provide hazards and disadvantages for New Zealand's native plant species. Possums for example are a huge pest to New Zealand as they eat and damage the forest at every point, taking mainly leaves, buds and fruits, as well as scratching tree bark and breaking small branchlets.
A common invasive species found in New Zealand's lowland forests are the large shrub Epiphytes. An epiphyte is a plant that grows off another plant. Griselinia lucida is the most common of the large shrub epiphytes and is distributed throughout both the North and South Island. Although these epiphytes usually intend to exploit larger trees, their biggest threat to the lowland horopito is their large roots that overcome the water supply and soil nutrients. They exploit the habitat around them.
A common parasite found in lowland to montane forests throughout the North Island is Dactylanthus taylorii (Pua Reinga – Flower of the Underworld). This species takes a liking toward smaller tree species, like the lowland horopito, and therefore poses a threat to Pseudowintera species, only in the North. The embryo root of a Dactylanthus seed exploits the slender root of its suitable host, by penetrating it, then gradually expands into a tube-like structure, eventually surrounding the host root.
Due to P. axillaris preferring cold, damp locations, it is often in competition with species of fungi. As a result, the Winteraceae family has managed to adapt with an efficient built-in defence mechanism of a compound called Sesquiterpene Dialdehyde polygodial which has many biological purposes including anti-fungal properties.
There are also many types of insects that use Pseudowintera as a host plant. Plant-SyNZ gives a reliability score: 0-10. 10 indicating a strong association to the Pseudowintera axillaris. The below species all received a 10

identification.text: It is a small, bushy tree reaching 8–12 m in height with a trunk diameter of 20–50 cm. The branches are closely set, with slender branchlets. Adult leaves are somewhat glossy and hairless; they are dark green or yellow-green above and often mottled with maroon or purple and a pale wine-red underneath. The fruit is a non-poisonous juicy berry, containing two small seeds, usually oblong and 6–8 mm in length. The flowers have insignificant petals and are wind pollinated, with long anthers and stigmas. The thin, mottled leaves have a small pit where the veins join. Young plants have small spoon-shaped leaves like those of Coprosma spathulata; run a finger along a young branchlet: in māmāngi it feels smooth, while in C. spathulata it is finely wrinkled and feels like a cat's tongue.

habitat.text:
Mānuka is one of the few New Zealand native species which are adapted to fire, able to respond to fire by opening seed pods and dispersing in recently disturbed ground.

Mānuka can quickly colonise areas of disturbed land, and can create environments where other native species can establish more successfully.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Mānuka' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Mānuka is a prolific shrub-type tree and is often one of the first species to regenerate on cleared land. It is typically a shrub growing to 2–5 m tall, but can grow into a moderately sized tree, up to 15 m or so in height. It is evergreen, with dense branching and small leaves 7–20 mm long and 2–6 mm broad, with a short spine tip. The flowers are white, occasionally pink, 8–15 mm – rarely up to 25 mm – in diameter, with five petals. The wood is tough and hard.
Mānuka is often confused with the related species kānuka (Kunzea ericoides) – the easiest way to tell the difference between the two species in the field is to feel their foliage – mānuka leaves are prickly, while kānuka leaves are soft. Alternatively, the seed capsules of mānuka are large (5–7 mm in diameter) and often remain on the plant year round, whereas the seed capsules of kānuka are much smaller (2.2–4.6 mm in diameter) and are not present for much of the year.

summary.text:
Mānuka (Māori pronunciation: [ˈmaːnʉka]; Leptospermum scoparium) is a species of flowering plant in the myrtle family Myrtaceae, native to New Zealand (including the Chatham Islands) and south-east Australia.
Because of this, mānuka is often utilised by conservation projects in New Zealand.
Pests and diseases
The adult mānuka beetle (Pyronota festiva) and its larvae feed on Leptospermum scoparium in New Zealand. The scale insect, Eriococcus orariensis, is a sap-sucking insect that feeds on L. scoparium.

Pollinators
Pollinators that visit Leptospermum scoparium include Melangyna novaezelandiae, Hylaeus, and honeybees.

Continued evolution
Leptospermum scoparium is in the process of evolutionary differentiation as a result of its isolation from fellow members of the Leptospermum genus. New studies demonstrate a loss of lignotubers among populations of Leptospermum scoparium located in relatively fire-free zones of New Zealand's South Island, while Australian and Tasmanian populations retain their lignotubers along with stronger manifestations of serotiny. Australian populations of Leptospermum scoparium are shown to be chemically distinct from their New Zealand counterparts, with significantly higher levels of cinteole and monoterpines. Chemotypical variations also exist between different populations within New Zealand, leading some to suggest that L. scoparium be divided into three subspecies: those with high pinenes, high triketones, and high sesquiterpenes. Recently, however, new research suggests that plant-to-plant variation far outstrips the variation seen between geographically isolated manuka sites, at least with regard to nectar chemistry.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Mespilus germanica' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
habitat.text: The species requires temperate and sub-mediterranean climate conditions with warm summers and mild winters. Air temperatures of 18 to 20 °C are mentioned as favourable for growth, cold of as low as −20 °C is tolerated and late frosts hardly cause any damage. The wild form was observed in dry areas with annual precipitation of 700 mm and at altitudes from 0 to 1,100 m. The species grows in a wide range of soil types and prefers fresh, well-drained loamy soils with a pH that is between 6 and 8.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Mespilus germanica' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Under ideal circumstances, the deciduous plant grows up to 8 metres tall. Generally, it is shorter and more shrub-like than tree-like. With a lifespan of 30–60 years, the tree is rather short-lived. Its bark is greyish brown with deep vertical cracks forming rectangular plates that tend to lift off.
The wild form of M. germanica is mostly a thorny, more shrub-like than tree-like plant, which is between 1.5 and 4 m high. In the cultivated forms, the thorns are usually reduced or even completely absent. In general, the medlar is a small, deciduous tree with an overhanging, almost round crown. The trunk is irregularly shaped. The tree has a height between 1 and 6 m, but can become significantly larger in culture. The diameter at breast height is usually between 20 and 25 cm, but in exceptional cases it can be up to 50 cm. The roots are heavily branched and far-ranging, with a somewhat fibrous root system.
The wood has a fine texture, but is very hard. It has a white, slightly pink-tinted sapwood. The core is brownish. The annual rings are clearly visible.
The winter buds are pointed, ovoid and up to 5 millimetres long. The leaves are dark green and elliptic, 8–15 centimetres long and 3–5 cm wide. The leaves are densely hairy (pubescent) below, and turn red in autumn before falling.
Medlar flowers are 2–5 cm in diameter, have a short stalk and are terminal and single on short side shoots. They have five elongated, narrow sepals and five free, white or pale pink petals. Compared to other fruit trees in the European latitudes, the medlar flowers very late (May or June).  The flowers are hermaphrodite and pollinated by bees. Normally, self-pollination occurs in this plant. The flower then develops flattened, reddish-brown, hairy fruits with juicy flesh. The reddish-brown fruit is a pome, 2–3 cm diameter, with wide-spreading persistent sepals around a central pit, giving a 'hollow' appearance to the fruit. In cultivated forms the diameter is even between 3 and 8 cm.
Sexual reproduction is the norm in wild forms of the medlar. The resulting seeds have a germination capacity lasting from 18 to 20 months. The seeds are distributed by various animals such as birds, squirrels and deer. Some varieties are sterile and can therefore only be propagated vegetatively.
The number of chromosomes is given as 2n = 32 or 2n = 34.

summary.text:
Mespilus germanica, known as the medlar or common medlar, is a large shrub or small tree in the rose family Rosaceae.
From an extensive study of literature and plant specimens, Kazimierz Browicz concluded that the true homeland of M. germanica is only in the southeastern part of the Balkan peninsula, in Asia Minor, on the Caucasus, Crimea, northern Iran, and possibly also in Turkmenistan. It is also found in southeastern Europe, especially the Black Sea coasts of Bulgaria and Turkey. Fossil remains, however, have been reported from a wider area, including from Oriolo, Italy (c. 800 kya thousand years ago) and Burgtonna, Germany (130-115 thousand years ago), dating from the Pleistocene.
It is found across southern Europe where it is generally rare. It is reported to be naturalised in some woods in southeast England, but is found in few gardens.

identification.text:
Shrub up to 3–(6) m. tall, sts depressed or prostrate. Branches divaricate; branchlets ± pubescent, ± interlacing, becoming glab. Lvs opp. or in opp. fascicles on slender pubescent petioles 1–2 mm. long. Stipules subacute to obtuse, pubescent, sheath short, cilia absent or very few, denticle solitary. Lamina linear- to broad-oblong, obtuse to subacute, coriac., dark green above, paler below; (7)–10–14–(16) × 2–3–(5) mm. Reticulations of veins evident, at least below. ♂ 1–4 axillary clusters on very short arrested branchlets; calyx minutely toothed; corolla narrow-funnelform, lobes ovate-oblong, acute, < tube. ♀ solitary, terminal on short branchlets; calyx-teeth short, obtuse; corolla-tube short, lobes long, acute. Drupe pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, globose, c. 7 mm. long.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Mingimingi's are more or less hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Both are twiggy shrubs with wide-angled, interlacing branches and more or less hairy young twigs, so neither the branching nor the twig hairs separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Swamp coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. The Flora's key separates them by the leaf veins: mingimingi shows the midrib and the net of veins, sand coprosma the midrib alone. Sand coprosma's leaves are yellowish green, mingimingi's dark green. Both have pale blue fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Sand coprosma

habitat.text:
On Guadalupe Island, located 280 km (150 nmi) off the mainland coast, the pines are found on the steep northern end of the island, at elevations of around 500 to 1,200 m, where they follow the ridgetops and steep slopes.
 They are found at lower elevations than on Guadalupe, at around 285 to 690 m, on the windward ridges and canyons of the north and central parts of the island. In both cases, the pines seem to be heavily dependent on locations with a high frequency of fog.
