identification.text:
Pinus radiata is a coniferous evergreen tree growing to 15–30 m tall in the wild, but up to 60 m in cultivation in optimum conditions, with upward pointing branches and a rounded top. The leaves ("needles") are bright green, in clusters of three (two in var. binata), slender, 8–15 cm long and with a blunt tip. The ovulate cones are 7–17 cm long, brown, ovoid (egg-shaped), and usually set asymmetrically on a branch, attached at an oblique angle. The bark is fissured and dark gray to brown. When not cut short by disease or harvesting, it has a lifespan of 80 to 90 years.
The specific epithet radiata refers to the cracks which radiate from the umbo of the cone scales.
It is closely related to bishop pine and knobcone pine, hybridizing readily with both species; it is distinguished from the former by needles in threes (not pairs), and from both by the cones not having a sharp spine on the scales.
The modern plantation tree is vastly different from the native tree of Monterey. In plantations the tree is commonly planted at 4 square meter spacing on a wide variety of landscapes from flat to moderately steep hills. Because of selective breeding and more recently the extensive use of growth factor seedlings, forests planted since the 1990s have very straight tall trunks without the problem of twin leaders. The trees are pruned in three lifts so that the lower two-thirds of a mature tree is free of branches and hence of knots.

summary.text:
Pinus radiata (syn. Pinus insignis), the Monterey pine, insignis pine or radiata pine, is a species of pine native to the Central Coast of California, and the Guadalupe and Cedros islands of Mexico.
In the United States, it is native to three very limited areas located in Santa Cruz, Monterey, and San Luis Obispo Counties of California.
In Mexico, it is found on two islands in the Pacific Ocean, Guadalupe Island and Cedros Island.
Edward Palmer and Francescho Franceschi were the first to discover the pines on Guadalupe Island. When Franceschi visited in 1892, he noted that they extended all over the northern and northwestern part of the island, comprising a very thick forest, with some of the finest trees growing with the Guadalupe palm.
On Cedros Island, the pines are more abundant, being found in far greater numbers partly due to the lack of feral goats. (Goats were exterminated on Guadalupe island by 2007.)
In Australia, New Zealand, and Spain it is the leading introduced tree and in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Kenya, and South Africa it is a major plantation species. It is also an introduced tree on the world's most remote inhabited island, Tristan da Cunha.

identification.text:
C. indivisa is very distinctive. The species can be distinguished from all other Cordyline species by its very broad blue-grey leaves, and its smaller, tightly compacted inflorescence which is produced from beneath the foliage. It forms a stout tree up to 8 metres tall, with a trunk from 40–80 centimetres in diameter. The stem is usually unbranched, or has very few branches. The foliage, which droops with age, is blue-green and shaped like a broad sword, with a broad and conspicuous midrib which is often tinged red, orange red or golden. The inflorescence is a panicle that arises from the base of the growing points underneath the leaves.
Plant to c. 8 m high; stems massive, rather sparingly branched. Leaves to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly ensiform, narrowed above base to short petiole; midrib and several nerves conspicuous, reddish. Panicle tightly compact, 60–160 cm long. Flowers long-pedicelled, ± fleshy; segments 7–8 mm long. Berry bluish.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cabbage tree grows into a tree up to 12–(20) m tall, its trunk massive on large old trees and many-branched above; its leaves are 30–100 × 3–6 cm, light green and much the same on both sides, only slightly narrowed above the base, with an indistinct midrib and fine, equal nerves; its panicle is large and lax, 60–150 cm long, with sweet-scented white flowers, and its berries are whitish, about 4 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree (Cordyline indivisa) grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key puts mountain cabbage tree apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Garden plants sold as 'Cordyline indivisa' or 'Dracaena indivisa' are often young cabbage trees, according to Wikipedia, so a nursery label does not settle it.
lookalikes.name: Cabbage tree

lookalikes.howToTell: Forest cabbage tree grows to 4 m, usually as a number of roughly equal stems from near the ground, sparingly branched; its leaves are 1–2 m × 4–8 cm, broad at the middle and drooping from there, narrowed above the base into a channelled stalk that often takes up a quarter to a fifth of the leaf's length, paler underneath, with the midrib prominent underneath and several stronger nerves; its panicle is 1–2 m long and openly branched, with very fragrant white flowers, and its berries are white or bluish, 4–5 mm across. Mountain cabbage tree (Cordyline indivisa) grows to about 8 m with massive, rather sparingly branched stems; its leaves are up to 1–2 m × 10–15 cm, broadly sword-shaped, drooping only with age, glaucous underneath, narrowed above the base to a short stalk, with a broad, conspicuous midrib that is often reddish, the stronger nerves often reddish too; its panicle is tightly compact, 60–160 cm long, its crowded, rather fleshy flowers on longer stalks than in the other species, and its berries are bluish, about 6 mm across. Flora of New Zealand's key puts mountain cabbage tree apart from all the others on its leaves: up to 10–15 cm wide, glaucous underneath, with a strong, often reddish midrib and main nerves, and a tightly compact flower cluster. The other species' leaves are rarely over 10 cm wide, often much less, not or scarcely glaucous underneath, and their flower clusters are lax and open. Kirk (1874) listed 'dubious forms' among New Zealand cabbage trees, some intermediate between these two.

summary.text:
Cordyline indivisa is a monocot tree endemic to New Zealand.
In the North Island, Cordyline indivisa occurs from south of Kohukohunui in the Hunua Ranges and Te Moehau (Coromandel Peninsula) but becomes common only south of Raukūmara Ranges and the central Volcanic Plateau. In the South Island it is widespread and common along the north and western portions of the island, but occurs more locally in the drier eastern regions.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Phormium colensoi' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
The leaves are under 2 metres in length while those of P. tenax range from 1 to 3 metres in length. The scape is much shorter than that of P. tenax, rising up to 2 metres in height while that of P. tenax is around 5 metres in height. The colour of the inner tepals is green while the outer tepals are yellow to red. In contrast the tepals of P. tenax are a dull red, with the tips of the inner tepals being less strongly recurved. The capsules of P. colensoi, unlike those of P. tenax are twisted and pendulous, and may be twice as long (up to 20 cm in length). The numerous seeds in each pod are glossy black, flat and elongated with a frilled margin 
Phormium colensoi has two distinct geographic forms, one occurring in lowland parts of the North Island, and the other in the southern and mountainous areas of the South Island as well as ranges in the North Island. The lowland form has green or yellow tepals and the mountain form has red tepals. In the Cook Strait area, both forms and intermediates can be found.

identification.text:
Berberis oiwakensis is a shrub or tree up to 7 m tall. Leaves are up to 45 cm long, compound with 12-20 pairs of leaflets plus a larger terminal one, dark green above, yellow-green below. The inflorescence is a fascicled raceme up to 25 cm long. The berries are egg-shaped, dark blue, sometimes almost black, up to 8 mm long.
In recent times another Chinese sp., M. lomariifolia Takeda, has become very popular for N.Z. gardens. It is easily distinguished from M. japonica by the lvs which have 14–20 pairs of broad-lanceolate leaflets.
In gardens it grows upright, on mostly unbranched, cane-like stems, and its lightly scented yellow flowers come in dense clusters at the stem tips (San Marcos Growers, restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves, up to 45 cm long, carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets; Oregon grape's carry 3–7 pairs of ovate ones, 2.5–5 cm wide. Mountain grape grows to 7 m; Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed shrub, usually about 1 m. Mountain grape's flower clusters reach 25 cm; Oregon grape's 6–7 cm. Mountain grape's berries are egg-shaped, up to 8 mm long; Oregon grape's round, about 10 mm across. Dark blue bloomed berries and spiny-edged leaflets do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Oregon grape

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets (14–20 pairs of broad-lanceolate leaflets is the Flora of New Zealand's test between the two); Japanese mahonia's carry 5–9 pairs of ovate ones. Mountain grape's flower clusters are dense and upright (Auckland Council); Japanese mahonia's lax and spreading. Blue-black bloomed berries do not separate them, and neither test settles the garden hybrid B. × hortensis ('Charity', 'Winter Sun'), whose parents are these two species.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain grape's leaves carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets, 1–2.5 cm wide; leatherleaf mahonia's carry 4–10 pairs of broad ones, roundish to ovate and 2–6 cm wide (Flora of China). Mountain grape's berries are up to 8 mm long; leatherleaf mahonia's up to 15 mm. Upright flower clusters, a tall habit and dark blue bloomed berries do not separate them, and the garden hybrid 'Arthur Menzies' has both as parents.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

summary.text:
Berberis oiwakensis is a species of plant in the barberry family, Berberidaceae. It is native to Taiwan, China (Guizhou, Hong Kong, Sichuan, Xizang (Tibet) and Yunnan) and Myanmar, where it occurs at elevations of 600 to 3800 m. It has recently been found naturalized in South Africa.
Berberis oiwakensis is one parent of the important garden hybrid Berberis × hortensis, which includes popular cultivars such as 'Charity', 'Winter Sun' and 'Lionel Fortescue' (the other parent is Berberis japonica).
Other names: Mahonia lomariifolia; Flora of New Zealand Online files it as Berberis lomariifolia; Auckland Council calls it Chinese holly grape.
Biota of New Zealand lists it as exotic and casual, not naturalised, from eight databased collections, all in Canterbury; its English names there include mountain grape and Chinese holly grape. In the wild it is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (Wikipedia). It has been grown in the West since 1931, from seed collected near Tengchong, Yunnan, and raised in England (San Francisco Botanical Garden); birds favour its berries (San Marcos Growers).
Environment Canterbury reported it showing invasive tendencies in Christchurch in 2006; mahonia seed is spread by birds.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Stolons slender, with numerous long simple eglandular hairs and dense stellate hairs.  Rosette lvs dull glaucescent green above, white-hairy beneath, oblanceolate, sessile or shortly petiolate, entire or very obscurely dentate, (1.5)–2.5–5–(7) × 0.6–1.5–(1.8) cm, subacute and often apiculate, cuneate at base;  upper surface with scattered coarse simple hairs 4–6 mm long;  lower surface with fine eglandular hairs 1–2 mm long and very dense stellate hairs. Stem lf 0–(1), scale-like.  Flowering stems erect, (2)–5–10–(15) cm tall, with 0-few simple eglandular hairs, numerous short glandular hairs and dense stellate hairs.  Capitula solitary;  involucre 8–13 mm long;  bracts with dense stellate hairs and varying proportions of simple eglandular and glandular hairs. Florets yellow, often with red stripe on outer face,  c. 2× length of involucre. Achenes dark,  c. 2 × 0.5 mm.  Pappus 5–6 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Hieracium pilosella L.]

summary.text:
Pilosella officinarum (synonym Hieracium pilosella), known as mouse-ear hawkweed, is a yellow-flowered species of flowering plant in the daisy family Compositae (= Asteraceae), native to Europe and northern Asia.
It is a known allelopathic plant, whose roots secrete several substances inhibiting root growth, including its own. It can be controlled through rotation with clover and grasses where possible.
Recent research claims that Pilosella officinarum exhibits an atavism by the reemergence of sexual reproduction.
The plant has been found as an invasive species in Sphagnum peatlands disturbed by peat extraction in southern Patagonia.

habitat.text: Lawns, playing fields, verges and grazed pasture, especially where the grass has been fertilised. One of the commonest mushrooms of mown grass, often appearing in numbers a day or two after rain.

identification.text:
Cap 1–4 cm across, conical at first then opening out to convex — it does not hold the sharp point a liberty cap keeps, and it has no nipple. Hygrophanous like a liberty cap: brown when moist, drying tan from the centre outwards, which often leaves a two-tone cap. There is no peelable gelatinous skin.
Gills are broad and attached, brown with paler edges, going distinctly mottled or blotchy as the spores ripen rather than an even colour. Stipe 3–8 cm by 1–3 mm, fragile and hollow, beige to light brown, with no ring. Spore print is deep brown, sometimes with a purplish cast.
It does not bruise blue anywhere.

lookalikes.howToTell: A liberty cap is sharply conical to bell-shaped, often tipped with a small nipple, and keeps that shape as it ages. A mower's mushroom is conical or bell-shaped when young but opens out to broadly convex and lacks the liberty cap's point. A liberty cap stains bluish where it is handled or bruised, and its stem is sometimes blue towards the base; the mower's mushroom's flesh does not change colour when cut. Bend back a piece of a damp liberty cap and a thin gelatinous skin peels away (not once the cap has dried out); the mower's mushroom is not described as having this skin. A liberty cap's gills are narrow and moderately crowded, darkening to dark grey or purple-brown. The mower's mushroom's are broad and often go mottled as the spores ripen. Both can have paler gill edges. Do not try to separate them on spore print or on where they grow. A liberty cap prints very dark purple-brown and a mower's mushroom dark brown, sometimes purplish to nearly black, and both come up in grass.

edibleParts.text: The leaves and flowers can be added to salads. The seeds are also edible. Leaves - raw or cooked. The leaves are mucilaginous and fairly bland. Flowers - raw. A very decorative addition to the salad bowl, they have a very mild flavour. Seed - raw. Best used before it is fully mature, the seed has a pleasant nutty taste but it is rather small and fiddly to harvest.

identification.text:
Erect perennial herb. Stems moderately hairy with only simple hairs. Lvs sparsely to moderately hairy with simple hairs and rarely a few stellate hairs below, ± glabrous above; lower lvs reniform, shallowly 3–5-palmately lobed and crenate, 5–8 cm diam.; upper stem lvs deeply divided ± to base with usually 5, 2-pinnatifid lobes; ultimate segments ± linear; petiole 1–20 cm long; stipules linear to lanceolate, 5–8 mm long. Fls solitary in lower axils and racemose at apex; fruiting pedicels (8)–10–50 mm long; epicalyx segments linear or narrow-ovate, < calyx; calyx teeth ovate, acute to acuminate, moderately hairy with simple and stellate hairs, enlarged at fruiting; petals usually pink, sometimes white, 2–4× as long as calyx, (15)–20–30 mm long. Mericarps c. 15–20 per fr., densely hairy, smooth on back; edges rounded.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
The rounded mericarps of M. moschata are densely covered in long hairs.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the upper stem leaves (cut almost to the base in musk mallow, shallowly lobed in common mallow) and the fruit (densely hairy and smooth-backed against usually hairless and net-veined). Petal lengths overlap ((15–)20–30 mm against 12–30 mm), so the flower does not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.

summary.text:
Malva moschata, the musk mallow or musk-mallow, is a species of flowering plant in the family Malvaceae. It is native to Eurasia and has been introduced elsewhere, being cultivated as an ornamental plant.
In New Zealand it is known from scattered places in South Auckland, Taranaki and Wellington, and in the South Island from Tākaka and the Taieri Plain, with one collection from Southland. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1904.

warnings: When grown on nitrogen rich soils (and particularly when these are used inorganically), the plant tends to concentrate high levels of nitrates in its leaves.

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked. Delicious in salads, they start off being sweet and then develop a fairly strong garlic-like flavour, they are liked by most people who try them. Bulb - raw or cooked. Rather small but a very nice mild garlic flavour. Flowers - raw or cooked. Excellent in salads, making them look attractive as well as adding a strong onion flavour.

habitat.text:
In New Zealand: Garden escape.
In its native Mediterranean range: Dry grassy places and fields. Macchie, phrygana, rocky places, weedy banks, rivulets, ruins, often in shade; at elevations from sea level to 1,035 metres.

identification.text: Bulb globose, 1–2 cm diam., with non-stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves 2–3, c. 25 × 1–2 cm, flat, margins finely toothed or ciliate. Scape 20–60 cm high, sheathed at base only, subtriquetrous with 2 angles acute, almost winged, the third more obtuse. Umbels 5–8 cm diam., many-flowered, ± flat-topped; pedicels ± 3 times length of flowers, rigid; spathe-valve 1, persistent. Flowers white, 8–10 mm long, ± 10 mm diam., campanulate; segments ovate-elliptic, obtuse. Stamens c. ½ length of perianth; filaments simple without appendages. Capsule c. 7 mm long, ± globose, papery, few-seeded. Seeds black, angled, 2–3 mm long.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's flowers are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment; Naples garlic's are pure white. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Onion weed carries 3–15 flowers on drooping stalks; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across on stiff stalks. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; Naples garlic's are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins. The onion-garlic smell, a 20–60 cm flower stalk, white flowers and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's flowers are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves; Naples garlic's are pure white. Rosy garlic carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers. Rosy garlic's flower stalk is round in section; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one. Flat leaves, the garlic smell, an umbel 5–8 cm across and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; Naples garlic's are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils; Naples garlic carries a many-flowered umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long. Wild garlic's flower stalk is slender and rush-like; Naples garlic's has two sharp, almost winged angles. The garlic smell does not separate them.

preparation.text:
Of the bulbs: Sliced up, they make a delicious addition to salads and can also be used as a vegetable or as a flavouring in cooked foods. The bulbs, harvested once the plant dies down, will store for 6 months or more.
In Cyprus it is eaten fresh with olives, onions and bread (Della et al. 2006).
In Jódar, in Spain's Sierra Mágina, people out in the fields commonly ate it raw, mostly the stems (Mesa 1996).
The leaves keep well chopped and frozen, and the bulbs store like other garlic. The flowers are only good while in bloom, before the seed capsule in the middle starts to swell (Amici dell'orto due, Rome).
Dried bulbs can stand in for cultivated garlic, with a less pungent flavour (Flora d'Abruzzo).

recipes.method: Written for Naples garlic by a Chilean forager, who says it suits onion weed too. Cook a cauliflower (or broccoli, or another vegetable in season) in very little water until soft. Meanwhile chop the stems, leaves and bulbs of the Naples garlic small and fry them gently. Drain the cauliflower, chop it small and mix it in a bowl with 3 eggs, the fried Naples garlic, and salt and pepper to taste. Pour into a dish and bake at 180 °C for about 30 minutes, until the top is golden; grated cheese on top is optional. Cut into pieces and serve with a salad or a grain. The source gives no amounts for the cauliflower or the Naples garlic.
recipes.title: Naples garlic and cauliflower bake

recipes.method: Recorded in Jódar, in Spain's Sierra Mágina, where it was prepared the same way as wild leek. Cut up the bulbs, the white bases of the leaves, or both, as you prefer. Boil them first with a little salt. Then fry them and eat them as they are, or scramble them with egg, or make them into an omelette. Or let the boiled pieces cool to room temperature and dress them with a little vinegar.
recipes.title: Boiled and fried Naples garlic, Jódar style

recipes.method: From a Roman garden club's note on Naples garlic: make a frittata with the leaves, the tender stems and the flower clusters. The source gives no amounts or method beyond that.
recipes.title: Naples garlic frittata

recipes.method: From the same Roman note. Mix ricotta with a good handful of Naples garlic flowers, salt and olive oil, and toss it through cooked pasta. The source gives no other amounts.
recipes.title: Pasta with ricotta and Naples garlic flowers

recipes.method: From the same Roman note. Boil Naples garlic leaves together with chicory, which tones down their flavour. Or fry cooked chicory in a pan with the leaves, in place of a garlic clove.
recipes.title: Chicory with Naples garlic leaves

summary.text:
Allium neapolitanum is a bulbous herbaceous perennial plant in the onion subfamily within the Amaryllis family.
Its native range extends across the Mediterranean Region from Portugal to the Levant. The species is cultivated as an ornamental and has become naturalized in many areas, including Pakistan, Australia, New Zealand, and in southern and western parts of the United States. It is classed as an invasive species in parts of the U.S., and is found primarily in the states of California, Texas, Louisiana, and Florida.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N. Auckland City; Gisborne - Opotiki; Hawkes Bay - Napier, abundantly naturalised; Wellington - Palmerston North. S. Canterbury - Rangiora.
Other names (Flora of New Zealand Online, NZPCN): daffodil garlic, flowering onion, Naples onion.

warnings: Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

NC State Extension rates every part of this plant as poisonous to eat, at low severity: it may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, from its sulfides. The same source calls the leaves and bulbs edible and gives garlic and wild garlic low-severity ratings too, so this reads as a caution for the genus.

Perennial stoloniferous herb.  Stems trailing, glabrous, up to 1 m long.  Lvs glabrous, all similar but becoming smaller near infl., pinnate, petiolate, 2–10–(25) × 1–5 cm;  basal auricles very small;  leaflets rounded, ovate;  margins entire or sinuate.  Pedicels glabrous, slender, erecto-patent, spreading to deflexed at fruiting, (8)–12–20–(30) mm long.  Sepals 2.5–3.5 × 1 mm.  Petals white, (4)–5–6 × 1.5–2.5 mm. Seeds in ± 1 row per locule, brown, c. 1 mm long, reticulate with 100–150 polygonal depressions per face.

summary.text:
Disphyma australe is a species of flowering plant in the family Aizoaceae and is endemic to New Zealand.
Disphyma australe is endemic to New Zealand, that is, it occurs naturally only in New Zealand. It now also grows on a few Australian islands, such as Tasmania, Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island.
The two subspecies of Disphyma australe, D. australe australe and D. australe stricticaule, are common in different parts of New Zealand.
D. australe stricticaule is only found on Kermadec Islands, whereas D. australe australe is found on both the North and South Island throughout the coast. It also occurs on some smaller New Zealand islands, like Stewart Island, Chatham Islands and Solander Islands. Additionally, it coexists with D. australe stricticaule on the Kermadec Islands.

identification.text: Hormosira is a perennial species of seaweed (brown algae, Fucales). It is abundant on low-energy rocky reefs within the intertidal zone, where it outcompetes other algal species due to its high tolerance to desiccation. Plants vary significantly in morphology. The thallus (or frond) of the species is made up of strings of olive-brown, spherical, gas-filled pneumatocysts (or beads), which taper towards a small holdfast. While the holdfast attaches strongly to a substrate, it can be easily dislodged by human trampling. The spheres are buoyant and rise to the surface of the water during high tide, allowing plants to move with the flow of the current and obtain more sunlight. Hormosira also produces a slime layer to reduce desiccation, and plants often grows in high densities, which reduces their surface area exposed to the sun and further reduce dehydration. Due to the buoyant thallus, Hormosira plants can drift out to sea over considerable distances, and floating plants can remain fertile for several weeks.

summary.text:
Hormosira is a genus of seaweed in the family Hormosiraceae.
Hormosira is native to southeastern Australia (including Tasmania, Lord Howe Island and Norfolk Island) and New Zealand. Despite substantial morphological variation across its range, the species represents a single species and the genus Hormosira is monotypic. Genetic analyses of mitochondrial COI and microsatellite DNA sequence data have indicated that there is low genetic variation across the range of the species in Australia.

lookalikes.howToTell: Ongaonga (tree nettle) is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m tall; common nettles are herbs — Urtica urens an annual to 60 cm, Urtica dioica a perennial to 1.5 m — so height alone will not separate a tall Urtica dioica from a small ongaonga. Ongaonga's leaves are pale green, triangular to ovate-triangular and coarsely toothed, and it carries white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long on the leaf teeth, young stalks and leaf veins; the Flora of New Zealand describes ongaonga's stinging hairs as long-stalked and common nettles' as short-stalked. Ongaonga has 2 stipules at each node, common nettles 4. Its sting has killed: in 1961 a young man died of paralysis and breathing problems several hours after walking through tree nettles, and stung dogs and horses have developed convulsions and breathing distress within minutes, often dying within hours. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so do not touch a stinging plant unless you are sure it is not woody.

harvestEthics.text: Leave it where it stands. This is an endemic beech associate listed At Risk – Naturally Uncommon, known from three sub-populations, and the forest it was first described from has already been cleared for pasture. Photograph it, note where it was, and submit the record to iNaturalist NZ — the gap between 1971 and 2015 was a gap in observations as much as in the fungus. Picking is prohibited in reserves and on conservation land, and there is no reason to take one.

identification.text:
Cap 5.5–13 cm across, convex when young and flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry and finely powdered to velvety under a lens; dark brown to almost black, sometimes with salmon patches, and without concentric zones. Gills light orange to salmon with dark brown edges, thick, moderately crowded, up to 9 mm deep, attached to slightly running down the stem. Stem 4.5–8 cm long and 1.3–2.8 cm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap. The milk is viscid, white, unchanging in the air, and dries pale cream. The flesh is granular and white at first, then runs through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where it is cut or broken — that colour change, against unchanging white milk, is the species. Gills taste mild and the flesh turns slowly faintly acid; no distinctive smell. Spore print ochraceous. Solitary or in groups under beech.

Lactarius novae-zelandiae McNabb, described from New Zealand, is a similar large and dark brown to brownish black species from this subgenus. The species differs by the lamellae that are moderately crowded and have dark brown edges, a character that was not observed in L. megaplinthogalus. The latex in this New Zealand species is unchanging and not staining the lamellae pinkish to blackish. The context does change to pink, salmon, and orange-red to finally vinaceous on exposure to air. The pseudocystidia are sparse and scattered. The spores are larger (9–12 × 8.2–10.5 µm).

The macroscopic appearance of this taxon is striking, and the fact that there was a 44-year gap between the initial records (1968–1971) and subsequent records (2015–2018) suggests it is uncommon.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream. Its flesh does change, slowly, from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red where cut - so judge the milk, not the cut flesh. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre, where saffron milk cap's is orange, often with darker rings. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

The endemic it is most easily confused with, and that confusion has no page here. McNabb's own note separates this species from Lactarius sepiaceus, another New Zealand endemic under beech: both are dark greyish brown to brownish black, dry and finely bloomed, azonate and wrinkled, with white unchanging latex and dark brown gill edges. The differences are that L. sepiaceus has pale creamy-white to cream gills rather than light orange to salmon ones, flesh that stays white apart from very faint salmon tints rather than running through pink and orange-red to wine red, a white spore print rather than an ochraceous one, and prominently apiculate reticulate spores. L. sepiaceus has no iNaturalist NZ records and so no entry in this catalogue. Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius sepiaceus', description attributed to McNabb (1971), restated not quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5189

How many Lactarius New Zealand actually has, which is more than the iNaturalist list shows. The Virtual Mycota carries twelve described species for the region — the ten with entries here, plus two further endemics with full McNabb (1971) descriptions and no iNaturalist NZ observations at all: Lactarius sepiaceus (pk 5189) and Lactarius maruiaensis (pk 5183, solitary under beech, recognisable by its pale yellow cap and stem and reticulate spores). Three more names are indexed with no biostatus recorded (L. helvus, L. oculatus, L. pusillus). Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5183

summary.text:
This striking milkcap is endemic of New Zealand, where it is apparently ectomycorrhizal with Fuscospora truncata, growing in relatively mature forests.

There has been extensive surveying of the Russulaceae by Ross McNabb in the 1960/70s and by Jerry Cooper and Pat Leonard from 2005 onwards, and there are three known and extant sub-populations of this species. The single original locality from which the species was described (Karamea) has been lost due to the conversion of forest habitat to pasture.

Since 2017, two additional locations in Nelson and Buller have been identified and confirmed from sequence data. These locations significantly change the value of the area of occupancy (AOO of known sites), making the 2017 IUCN assessment of Endangered no longer appropriate. The distribution of records suggests some degree of regional restriction, but as an associate of beech, the potential distribution of this species remains considerable, and there is no reason to suspect population decline. For that reason, the panel re-assessed this species as Naturally Uncommon.

habitat.text:
Its natural habitat is sandy shorelines and bluffs, often in disturbed areas. It is a halophyte and grows well in saline ground.
In New Zealand: the coastal strand — beaches among driftwood and seaweed, sand dunes, boulder and cobble beaches, cliff faces and rock ledges. It also turns up in landfills and as a casual weed in towns, and some coastal plants may have started from garden waste (NZPCN, restated).

identification.text:
The plant has a trailing habit, and will form a thick carpet on the ground or climb through other vegetation and hang downwards. It can have erect growth when young. The leaves of the plant are 3–15 cm long, triangular in shape, and bright green. The leaves are thick, and covered with tiny papillae that look like waterdrops on the top and bottom of the leaves. The flowers of the plant are yellow, and the fruit are small, hard capsules each with 4–10 seeds.
Sphaeraphides are found in at least the leaves, calyx and ovary.

lookalikes.howToTell: Beach spinach is most reliably told apart when fruiting: its fruit is a round, succulent berry 5–8 mm long, pink to dark red, with no horns and 1–3 seeds, where this plant's is typically top-shaped and angled, 8–10(–15) mm long, with 2–4 hardened horns and 4–10 seeds. Out of fruit, look at the flower stalks: beach spinach's flowers sit on slender stalks, about 5 mm long in Allan (1961) and 5–30 mm in NZPCN, against the stalkless or nearly stalkless flowers here. Do not go by leaf shape, the papillae on the thick leaves or the yellow flowers; the two share all of these.

recipes.method: Blanch the greens in a large pot of boiling water for 1–3 minutes, refresh under cold running water, squeeze dry and roughly chop 1 cup. Heat the grill. Whisk 8 eggs with ½ cup milk, then stir in ½ cup sliced spring onions, the greens and 200 g Persian feta, chopped, and season. Brush a cast-iron pan with 2–3 tbsp oil, pour in the mixture and cook on medium-high until the bottom sets while the top is still liquid, then finish under the grill.

summary.text:
Tetragonia tetragonioides, commonly called New Zealand spinach, warrigal greens or by its Māori name of Kōkihi, is a flowering plant in the fig-marigold family (Aizoaceae). It is often cultivated as a leafy vegetable.
It is a widespread species, native to eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. It has been introduced and is an invasive species in many parts of Africa, Europe, North America, and South America.

warnings: Like spinach, it contains oxalates; its medium to low levels of oxalates need to be removed by blanching the leaves in hot water for one minute, then rinsing in cold water before cooking.

identification.text:
Annual herb.  Stems erect, branched above, finely ribbed, with fine crisped eglandular hairs especially below, 15–100–(150) cm tall.  Lvs glabrous or sparsely to densely hairy;  margins ciliate.  Rosette and lower stem lvs petiolate, lyrate-pinnatifid;  terminal lobe large, broadly ovate to deltoid to orbicular, bluntly dentate, (1.5)–3–8 × (1.5)–3–8 cm;  lateral lobes in (0)–1–3 pairs, the distal pair = or < width of terminal lobe, the proximal pairs successively smaller, all dentate.  Upper lvs undivided, becoming sessile, linear-lanceolate to ovate, sharply dentate to serrate, smaller than lower lvs.  Capitula in diffuse corymbose panicles;  peduncles > 2× length of involucre.  Involucre 5–8 mm long;  bracts glabrous except for ciliate apex, strongly veined or keeled, erecto-patent;  outer bracts 1–1.5 mm long.  Florets few,  c. 1.5× length of involucre;  corolla yellow;  tube < ligule.  Achenes fusiform, glabrous, pale,  c. 20-ribbed, 3–5 mm long;  pappus 0. 
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

habitat.text: Lactarius quietus is found growing exclusively at the base of oak trees, solitarily or in scattered groups, in soil. It is ectomycorrhizal, feeding symbiotically exclusively with oak, though studies have suggested it is also able to feed saprotrophically, growing from organic soil matter.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lactarius quietus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Lactarius quietus typically has a convex cap of 5 to 8 centimetres across, which later flattens or develops a small depression in the centre. In colour, the cap is a dull reddish brown with a tint of cinnamon, sometimes with darker concentric bands or spots. This zoning is one of the most distinctive features of the species. The cap is dry and matt, and not sticky when moist. It features a thick layer of firm, whitish-buff flesh. The stem measures from 4 to 9 centimetres in height, and is typically 10 to 15 millimetres thick. It is cylindrical in shape, but is sometimes furrowed lengthways, and it lacks a ring. It is concolorous with the cap, or a little darker, and is sometimes hollow. The brownish-white gills are slightly decurrent, and change colour with age to a pale reddish brown with mauve hints. The milk is white or cream in colour. The mushroom has a distinctive, strong oily smell, which has also been likened to bedbugs and wet laundry. The spores are oval, with plentiful warts joined by numerous ridges, forming a well-developed network. The spores typically measure 7.5 to 9 by 6.5 to 7.5 μm, and leave a cream print.


var. incanus
Lactarius quietus var. incanus is typically slightly larger than the nominate variety, and younger specimens feature a whitish bloom, after which the variant is named. It has a sweet smell reminiscent of maple syrup, and can be commonly found under oak trees. It can be confused with L. aquifluus and L. mutabilis, but both of these species are found in coniferous woodland.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. Its cap is dull, matt reddish brown with a cinnamon tint and stays dry, not sticky, when moist, and it has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. Oakbug milkcap grows with oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Both can show concentric zones on the cap, so zoning is not the difference.
lookalikes.name: Saffron milk cap / Pine mushroom

summary.text:
Lactarius quietus (commonly known as the oak milkcap, oakbug milkcap or southern milkcap) is a mushroom of the genus Lactarius.

It can be found very commonly throughout autumn months. In the United Kingdom, it is one of the one hundred most commonly encountered mushroom species. L. quietus var. incanus is found commonly in eastern North America.

edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. Used as a cereal, it is probably best known as the breakfast cereal porridge but it can also be used in many other ways. The seed can be sprouted and used in salads, the grain can also be ground into a flour and used in making biscuits, sourdough etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute.

identification.text:
Erect, green to glaucous tufts, 50–150 cm. Leaf-sheath glabrous or slightly hairy. Ligule (2)–3–5 mm, ± rounded, finely denticulate, abaxially finely scabrid. Leaf-blade 15–40 cm × (2.5)–7–15 mm, ± finely scabrid on ribs; margins finely scabrid, sometimes with a few scattered hairs. Culm erect or decumbent and rooting at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle 14–32 cm, very variable in shape, loose or contracted, equilateral to secund; branches horizontal to ± erect, slender, finely scabrid. Spikelets (15)–20–30–(40) mm, 2–(3)-flowered, pendulous on fine unequal pedicels; falling intact at maturity. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma 10–18 mm, ovate-lanceolate, glabrous, or with a few hairs towards base, apex obtuse or shallowly notched, red-brown, grey, yellow, white or blackish, usually awnless, but lowest or sometimes all florets in certain cultivars bearing a weak, straight or curved awn, not geniculate and scarcely twisted at base. Palea keels with 1 row of cilia, interkeel scabrid or glabrous. Anthers 2–4.2 mm. Caryopsis 4–9 × 1.5–3 mm.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are edible; this is about which you have. When ripe, the cultivated oat's spikelet falls as a whole, where slender oat's breaks apart below each floret. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff reddish hairs below the awn, and each of its two tip-lobes is drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; the cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, with a blunt or shallowly notched tip. Slender oat's lemmas carry an awn 30–36 mm long, bent at a knee and twisted, with a very dark brown lower part; the cultivated oat's are usually awnless, and any awn is weak, straight or curved, and not bent. Slender oat is often a very slender plant with very fine panicle branches, but the cultivated oat's pedicels are fine too, so build is only a clue.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the awn: winter wild oat's lowest one or two florets each carry an awn bent at a knee and twisted in its lower part, 25–50 mm long in subsp. ludoviciana and 60–70 mm in subsp. sterilis; the cultivated oat is usually awnless, and where an awn is present it is weak, straight or curved, not kneed and scarcely twisted. Winter wild oat's lemmas are hairy below the awn; the cultivated oat's are hairless or have a few hairs near the base. Size helps but overlaps: cultivated oat spikelets are (15)–20–30–(40) mm with 2–(3) florets, winter wild oat's 3.5–6 cm with 2–3 florets (subsp. ludoviciana) or 6–8 cm with 3–5 (subsp. sterilis).
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild oat's spikelets break up at maturity, separating below each floret; the cultivated oat's spikelets fall intact. Wild oat's lemma is stiffly hairy below where the awn joins, though sometimes hairless, and carries a stout awn 30–40 mm long, bent at a knee, with a twisted dark-brown lower column. The cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, and is usually awnless; any awn is weak, straight or curved, not bent at a knee and scarcely twisted. Spikelet length does not separate them cleanly: wild oat's are 35–50 mm, the cultivated oat's usually 20–30 mm but 15–40 mm at the extremes. None of these tests holds for fatuoids, or false wild oats — a mutant form that turns up in oat crops: their florets look like wild oat's, with a bent, twisted awn and a horseshoe-shaped callus bordered by hairs, and the spikelet breaks below every floret.

preparation.text: Oats are harvested when grain is in the hard dough stage and straw is slightly green (when the moisture content of the grain is 14% or less). If too ripe, shattering causes seed loss. Seeds are threshed and cleaned by winnowing, and artificially dried to below 14% moisture for storage. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

recipes.method: Made from the green straw — stems and leaves cut before the grain hardens, then dried. Put about 60 ml of dried oatstraw in a 1 litre jar, fill with boiling water and cover. Leave it to steep several hours or overnight, then strain. Drink through the day; it keeps about three days in the fridge.
recipes.title: Oatstraw infusion

recipes.method: Built on the infusion above. Warm about 350 ml of milk — dairy, almond or soy — with 2 tbsp honey and 1/2 tsp cinnamon, stirring until smooth. Pour into a jar with 175 ml of strained oatstraw infusion, cover and shake before serving.

summary.text:
The oat (Avena sativa), sometimes called the common oat, is a species of cereal grass (Avena) grown for fodder and for its seed, which is known by the same name (usually in the plural).

Oats tolerate cold winters less well than cereals such as wheat, barley, and rye, but need less summer heat and more rain, making them important in areas such as Northwest Europe that have cool, wet summers. They can tolerate low-nutrient and acid soils. Oats grow thickly and vigorously, allowing them to outcompete many weeds, and compared to other cereals are relatively free from diseases.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.; S.; Foveaux Strait on Pig Id; St.; C. Naturalised from Eurasia.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

Oat products are frequently contaminated by other gluten-containing grains, mainly wheat and barley, requiring caution in the use of oats if people are sensitive to the gluten in those grains. Use of pure oats in a gluten-free diet offers improved nutritional value, but remains controversial because a small proportion of people with coeliac disease react to pure oats.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Dense bushy shrub or small tree to  c. 7 m high;  bark becoming rough. Shoots angular, lepidote when young.  Lvs shortly petiolate.  Lamina 5–11 × 0.8–2 cm (juvenile lvs smaller), lanceolate or narrow-elliptic, sparsely to densely lepidote beneath and appearing pale green or slightly silvery, dark green and lepidote or elepidote above;  base attenuate;  apex mucronate. Panicles axillary.  Calyx 1–1.5 mm long;  lobes broad-triangular, glabrous or somewhat lepidote.  Corolla lobes 3–4 mm long, whitish, ± oblong, almost fleshy, patent at first, ultimately reflexed.  Stamens slightly < corolla. Drupe 5–8 mm diam., globose to broad-ovoid, glossy, becoming red and ultimately black.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

habitat.text: Forest margins, regenerating bush, stream banks and coastal scrub, often in dense stands. Common along tramping tracks in the North Island and the top of the South Island.

harvestEthics.text: Do not harvest. This entry exists so you can recognise it.

identification.text: A shrub 2–3 m tall with woody stems — you look up at it, not down. Leaves are pale green, triangular and coarsely toothed, and both the leaves and stems carry stiff white spines up to 6 mm long that are clearly visible from a metre away. Common nettle is soft, herbaceous, knee-high and has fine hairs you have to look for.

lookalikes.howToTell: Common nettles are herbs: Urtica urens is an annual to 60 cm and Urtica dioica a perennial to 1.5 m, so not always below waist height. Both have short-stalked stinging hairs and 4 stipules at each node. Ongaonga is a woody shrub, about 2 m and up to 3 m, with long-stalked white stinging hairs up to 6 mm long and 2 stipules at each node. Young ongaonga can be confused with other native nettles, so size is not reliable on a young plant. If it is woody, walk away. Young common nettle leaves are eaten cooked.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urtica_ferox Corrects the death count on this page from one to two, and locates both: 'two recorded human deaths from contact with U. ferox. One death occurred in 1961, when a young hunter died five hours after walking through a patch of U. ferox bushes in the Ruahine Range. In 2002, another young man's death in the Ruahine Range was retrospectively attributed to U. ferox by a pathologist.' Endemic to New Zealand, a woody shrub or small tree to 3 m, covered in trichomes carrying the toxins; stings can also cause ataxia, blurred vision, confusion, polyneuropathy, respiratory distress and hypersalivation, lasting days to weeks, and are strong enough to kill cattle, dogs and horses. Not closely related to the other New Zealand native nettles — its sister species is the South African U. lobulata — and its ferocity has been hypothesised as a response to browsing by moa.

summary.text: Tree nettle. A woody native shrub with visible stinging spines that has killed a person and regularly kills dogs and horses. Not the nettle you make soup from.

warnings: The sting causes intense pain, then numbness and weakness that can last days; heavy exposure has caused death. Dogs and horses die from it every year.
Do not push through it on a track. Do not touch it to test the sting.
Seek medical help for widespread stings or any weakness, blurred vision or breathing difficulty.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, flowers, flower stalks and the small bulbs.

habitat.text: Damp shady ground: roadsides, stream banks, under hedges and trees, neglected gardens. Forms dense carpets in winter and spring.

identification.text: Strap-like leaves and a flower stalk with three distinct edges — roll it between your fingers and you feel the triangle. Nodding white bell flowers, each petal with a fine green stripe down the middle, in late winter and spring. Crush any part: a strong onion smell. No smell, not onion weed.

lookalikes.howToTell: Snowflake has none of onion weed's strong garlic-onion smell. Its flower stalk is hollow and somewhat flattened, with winged edges; onion weed's is three-angled. Snowflake's white bells have green-tipped segments; onion weed's have a green stripe down the centre. Strap-shaped leaves, nodding white bells and damp ground do not separate them, and they can flower at the same time (snowflake July–October, onion weed October–November). If a plant does not smell of onion when crushed, leave it.
lookalikes.name: Snowflake and daffodil leaves

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's flowers are pure white; onion weed's have a green stripe down the centre of each segment. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; onion weed's is sharply three-angled. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered, roughly flat-topped umbel 5–8 cm across on stiff stalks; onion weed carries 3–15 flowers on drooping stalks. Naples garlic's flat leaves have finely toothed or hairy-edged margins; onion weed's are strongly channelled. The onion-garlic smell, a 20–60 cm flower stalk, white flowers and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's flowers are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves; onion weed's are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment. Rosy garlic's flower stalk is round in section; onion weed's is sharply three-angled. Rosy garlic carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers; onion weed's umbel has no bulbils. Rosy garlic's leaves are flat; onion weed's are strongly channelled. The onion-garlic smell, a flower stalk of similar height (30–60 cm against 20–60 cm) and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; onion weed's are solid and strongly channelled. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long, green to white and often purplish; onion weed carries 3–15 white flowers 10–15 mm long (up to 20) and no bulbils. Wild garlic's slender, rush-like stalk is sheathed by the leaves for a third to a half of its length; onion weed's is three-angled and sheathed only at the base. The garlic smell and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Wild garlic

preparation.text: Use like spring onion or chives, raw or cooked. Flowers scatter well over salads. Milder than it smells.

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Serves 4. Heat the grill. Beat 6 eggs with 3 tbsp milk or cream, season well, and stir in most of 50 g grated hard cheese (Parmesan, Gruyère or aged Cheddar). Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a 24 cm ovenproof frying pan over medium heat; if you like, soften a thinly sliced courgette in it for 3–4 minutes. Add 80 g roughly chopped onion weed leaves and stems and stir for 1 minute, until just wilted. Pour in the eggs and cook undisturbed on medium-low for 5–6 minutes, until the edges set. Scatter the rest of the cheese over and grill 3–4 minutes, until set and lightly golden. Scatter a small handful of raw onion weed flowers over the top and serve in wedges, warm or at room temperature.
recipes.title: Onion weed frittata

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Serves 4. Soften a diced white onion in 2 tbsp olive oil or butter for 8 minutes. Add 2 sliced garlic cloves and a peeled, diced potato (or a small cauliflower) and cook 2 minutes. Add 1 litre of vegetable or light chicken stock and simmer 12–15 minutes, until the potato is tender. Stir in 300 g onion weed leaves and stems and cook exactly 3 minutes, to keep the colour. Off the heat, add 3 tbsp crème fraîche (or coconut cream) and the juice of half a lemon, and blend smooth straight away. Season with salt and white pepper and serve at once, with more crème fraîche and a few flowers; it loses colour if it sits.
recipes.title: Onion weed soup

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Cut onion weed into pieces about 4 cm long, enough to fill 2 cups (about 500 ml). Toss them in a bowl with a quarter of a cucumber, thinly sliced, 1 tsp each of red pepper flakes, sugar, sesame seeds and salt, and 1 tbsp each of sesame oil and white vinegar. Serve straight away while crunchy, or leave a few minutes to marinate. Good with fishcakes, grilled meat or rice.
recipes.title: Korean-style onion weed salad

recipes.method: Written for three-cornered leek (onion weed). Pick the flower stalks with their buds before the buds open. Melt some butter in a pan, add a large bunch of the stalks, cover to keep the moisture in, and stir; they cook very quickly. Finish with sea salt and lemon juice.
recipes.title: Buttered onion weed flower stalks

recipes.method: From an Italian wild-herb cookbook, written for aglio triangolo (Allium triquetrum). Stew the bulbs and leaves of a generous bunch of onion weed in extra-virgin olive oil with a little water, keeping the flowers aside. Toss tagliatelle cooked al dente through it and add the flowers. The authors prefer it plain to taste the garlic best; or toss the tagliatelle for 10 minutes with 500 g cherry tomatoes before adding the flowers.
recipes.title: Tagliatelle with onion weed

recipes.method: Written for lágrimas de la Virgen (Allium triquetrum). Cut the tenderest part of a bunch of wild asparagus into pieces, and leave a dozen onion weed flower heads whole. Beat 2 eggs with salt and black pepper, mix in the asparagus and flowers, and pour into a frying pan with a little olive oil. When set underneath, turn it over with a plate and cook a few minutes more. The flowers give a very mild garlic flavour.
recipes.title: Onion weed and wild asparagus omelette

summary.text: Three-cornered leek. A weedy wild onion with a triangular stem and drooping white bell flowers that smells unmistakably of onion — the smell is the whole identification.

warnings: The onion smell is the test. Every leaf you pick should smell of onion when crushed — bulb lookalikes cause vomiting.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial with hairy, usually branched, purplish stems  c. 60 cm tall.  Lvs shortly petiolate, 1.2–3 × 0.6–1.8 cm, ovate, or rhombic to suborbicular, entire or obscurely serrulate, ciliate, hairy and dotted with glands below, often becoming glabrous above.  Infls dense, corymbose or paniculate, terminal and axillary;  bracts 3–5 mm long, ovate, glabrous, often purple.  Calyx  c. 2.5 mm long, often purple, hairy outside, and with a prominent, long, white, pilose tuft in throat;  teeth 0.5–1 mm long, almost regular, triangular.  Corolla 4–7 mm long, pink or purplish, hairy outside; tube > calyx;  limb 4–6 mm diam.;  upper lip emarginate.  Stamens exserted, lacking in the occasional ♀ plants.  Nutlets 8–9 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

edibleParts.text:
Fruit - raw or cooked. The fruit is almost as large as a blackcurrant and is produced in large bunches so it is easy to harvest. It has an acid flavour, but it is rather nice raw and is especially good when added to a porridge or muesli. Unfortunately, there is relatively little flesh and a lot of seeds, though some plants have larger and juicier fruits. The cooked fruit tastes somewhat like blackcurrants. The fruit can also be dried and stored for later use.
Flowers - raw. They can also be used to make a lemonade-like drink.
The small purplish-black fruits, which are quite tart and contain large seeds, are edible raw after the season's first frosts.

habitat.text:
Roadsides, semi-shade by plantation margins or beneath deciduous trees.
In New Zealand the wild mahonias grow in native and exotic forest, forest margins and shrubland, most often near gardens or historic sites (Environment Canterbury, restated, for the four species together).
In its native range in the Pacific Northwest: rocky woods and open coniferous forest, on dry to moist rocky sites and forested slopes at 400–2,100 m (Missouri Botanical Garden; NatureServe, restated).

identification.text:
Shrub 0.5–1–(2) m high, many-stemmed and stoloniferous. Lvs to c. 25 cm long, composed of 3–7 pairs of sessile (excluding the terminal) leaflets, without basal pair of stipule-like leaflets; petiole (0)–1–4 cm long, dark red. Most leaflets 5–9.5 × 2.5–5 cm, ovate or elliptic-ovate, glossy above, prominently reticulate; margins undulate and spinose-dentate; apex spiny. Scales at base of fascicled racemes 5–10 mm long, membranous, brown. Racemes eventually to 6 or 7 cm long. Bracts broadly ovate, much < pedicels at anthesis. Perianth segments to 7 mm long, ovate to obovate, imbricate; segments of innermost whorl shorter and emarginate. Stamens included; filaments with 2 teeth. Stigma sessile. Berry c. 10 mm diam., globose, blue-black, pruinose.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4, as Mahonia aquifolium (Pursh) Nutt.]
Environment Canterbury describes the New Zealand plant as up to 2 m tall with few branches but often many upright stems, its leaves usually of 3–4 pairs of shiny, dark green, holly-like leaflets (restated).

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves are compound, up to about 25 cm long, of 3–7 pairs of holly-like leaflets 5–9.5 cm long plus one at the tip, and its stems carry no spines; Darwin's barberry has simple leaves 1–3 (rarely 3.5) cm long in clusters, with five-parted spines on the stems. Oregon grape's berries are about 10 mm across; Darwin's barberry's 5–7 mm, with a conspicuous style 1.5–3 mm long at the tip. Glossy, spiny-edged foliage, dark berries with a bloom and yellow to orange flowers do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Darwin's barberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves have no pair of small, stipule-like leaflets at the base, and usually sit on a dark red stalk up to 4 cm long; Japanese mahonia's leaves are stalkless and their lowest pair of leaflets is small and stipule-like (the Flora of New Zealand's key). Oregon grape is a many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m and rarely 2 m; Japanese mahonia has few stems to about 3 m, each topped by a crown of leaves. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; Japanese mahonia's are lax, spreading and up to about 20 cm. Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; Japanese mahonia's broadly egg-shaped, 8–10 mm long. Leaflet counts overlap (3–7 pairs against 5–9), and blue-black bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. Most plants grown as Oregon grape are casual hybrids with other mahonias (Useful Temperate Plants), so expect in-between plants.
lookalikes.name: Japanese mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves are up to about 25 cm long with 3–7 pairs of leaflets; leatherleaf mahonia's are up to about 50 cm with 4–10 pairs and a much larger terminal leaflet. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; leatherleaf mahonia's stand upright, 7–26 cm long (Flora of China). Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; leatherleaf mahonia's are egg-shaped and up to 15 mm long. Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed, suckering shrub, usually about 1 m; leatherleaf mahonia has stiff upright stems and can reach 8 m. Leaflet counts overlap at 4–7 pairs, and dark bloomed berries and spiny leaflets do not separate them. NC State Extension, though, describes leatherleaf mahonia's berries as globose, so shape alone does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Leatherleaf mahonia

lookalikes.howToTell: Oregon grape's leaves carry 3–7 pairs of ovate leaflets, 2.5–5 cm wide; mountain grape's, up to 45 cm long, carry 12–20 pairs of lance-shaped ones. Oregon grape is a low, many-stemmed shrub, usually about 1 m; mountain grape grows to 7 m. Oregon grape's flower clusters reach 6–7 cm; mountain grape's up to 25 cm. Oregon grape's berries are round, about 10 mm across; mountain grape's egg-shaped, up to 8 mm long. Dark blue berries with a bloom and spiny-edged leaflets do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Mountain grape

preparation.text:
They were included in small quantities in the traditional diets of Pacific Northwest tribes, mixed with salal or another sweeter fruit. Today, they are sometimes used to make jelly, alone or mixed with salal.
The berries are rather sour straight off the plant but make excellent jellies (Missouri Botanical Garden, restated).

recipes.method: Written for Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium, or its low relative M. nervosa) by a preserving author in Oregon. Pick about 1.6 kg berries once they are evenly dark; sliding your fingers down a bunch drops them into the basket. Simmer the berries, covered, with half their volume of water for 15 minutes, mashing them after the first 10. Let the juice drip through a jelly bag for several hours, then boil it for 10 minutes to reduce it a little. Combine about 720 ml (3 cups) juice with about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar in a wide, heavy, non-reactive pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves. Raise the heat and boil, skimming now and then, until it begins to jell, which takes only a few minutes: drops falling from a tipped metal spoon thicken and run together. Skim, pour into three sterilised half-pint (about 240 ml) jars and process in a boiling-water bath for 5 minutes. It should be firm by the next day. The author advises against doubling the batch. Metric amounts are converted from the source's pounds and cups.
recipes.title: Oregon grape jelly

recipes.method: Written for Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium) by a native-plant nursery propagator, reprinted by the Washington Native Plant Society. Crush about 1.4–2.3 kg (3–5 lb, about 2 quarts) washed, stemmed berries and add about 720 ml (3 cups) water; if you use a hand blender, keep it on low, because over-mixing can make it frothy. Boil for 10 minutes, mashing a little. Drain through a cheesecloth-lined colander for a few hours, until you have about 950 ml (4 cups) juice. Bring the juice and about 1 kg (5 cups) sugar to a rapid boil, add one packet of liquid pectin and return to a full boil for 1 minute. Pour into warm sterilised jars (the recipe makes six half-pints, about 240 ml each), lid them and process in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes; leave to set overnight. The source does not give the size of the pectin packet. Metric amounts are converted from the source's pounds and cups.
recipes.title: Oregon grape jelly with pectin

summary.text:
Berberis aquifolium, the Oregon grape, holly-leaved barberry, or Mahonia, is a North American species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae. It is an evergreen shrub growing up to 3 metres tall and 1.5 m wide. It has pinnate leaves consisting of spiny leaflets, exhibiting dense clusters of yellow flowers followed by dark bluish-black berries.
Berberis aquifolium is invasive in parts of Western Europe, having escaped cultivation in parks.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: occasional, particularly in the Wellington area; S.: fairly common but scattered throughout, particularly Canterbury and Otago.
Oregon grape was introduced to N.Z. in the early days of European settlement and is often found around old gardens and churchyards, where it may persist long after the area has been abandoned.
Most plants grown under this name are casual hybrids with Mahonia repens. This species is easily confused with Mahonia pinnata, with which it also hybridizes.
It spreads by stolons into colonies, and a lone plant with no other nearby to pollinate it fruits poorly, if at all (Missouri Botanical Garden, restated).

warnings: All parts of the plant contain the alkaloid berberine - this is most concentrated in the roots, stems and inner bark, and least concentrated in the fruits. In small quantities berberine has a range of effective medicinal applications but, in excess, can cause vomiting, lowered blood pressure, reduced heart rate, lethargy, and other ill-effects.

habitat.text: It is a typical grassland perennial wildflower, growing in a variety of plant communities including meadows and fields, under scrub and open-canopy forests, and in disturbed areas.  It grows in temperate regions where average annual rainfall exceeds 750 mm, and often where soils are heavy and damp. It is often a weed of degraded pastures and roadsides.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Scarcely scented, perennial herb.  Stems erect, up to  c. 1 m tall, usually sparsely to densely villous below and glabrous above, rarely hairy or glabrous above and below, striate, simple or branched at base or sometimes above, rooting toward base.  Basal and lower cauline lvs long-petiolate, elliptic, obovate or spathulate, obtuse at apex, cuneate, coarsely 1–2-serrate, crenate, or shallowly 1–(2)-pinnatifid, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy on petiole and midrib, very rarely moderately hairy, up to 12–(18) × 2–(4) cm; cauline lvs similar to basal but above becoming smaller, apetiolate, narrow-oblong, amplexicaul, with few distant teeth or sometimes entire, and often auriculate at base.  Involucral bracts 3–8 mm long, glabrous;  margins and apex brown, membranous;  inner bracts with extended, broad, apical flap. Capitula solitary or few in corymbs, (25)–30–60–(65) mm diam.;  ray florets (9)–18–33;  ligules white;  disc florets numerous, yellow.  Achenes  c. 2.5 mm long, dark brown with pale ribs;  achenes of disc florets mostly ± terete, with 10 ± equal ribs, and corona 0;  achenes of ray florets similar to those of disc florets, but sometimes flattened with lateral ribs somewhat extended, 3 ribs on outer surface and 5 ribs on inner surface, rarely achene 3-angled, sometimes with irregular corona  c. 0.3 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
