summary.text:
Leucanthemum vulgare, commonly known as the ox-eye daisy, oxeye daisy, dog daisy, marguerite (French: Marguerite commune, "common marguerite") and other common names, is a widespread flowering plant native to Europe and the temperate regions of Asia, and an introduced plant to North America, Australia and New Zealand.
The species is native to Europe, and to Turkey and Georgia in Western Asia.
The species is widely naturalised in many parts of the world, including North America, and is considered to be an invasive species in more than forty countries.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, flowers and stems.

habitat.text: Bush, gardens, roadsides, disturbed sites, also along the seaside. Tolerates shade well.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Perennial, almost glabrous herb with thick fleshy contractile root;  main bulb  c. 2 cm long, subterranean;  tunic brown, with scale nerves inconspicuous; secondary aerial bulbs or bulbils small, common in branch axils.  Stems spreading to sub-erect, glabrous, with many flexuous, slender branches.  Lvs 3-foliolate, glabrous.  Petiole 2–7–(12) cm long;  stipules forming a narrow to broad wing. Lamina of leaflets subequal, subsessile, 4–16 × 5–22 mm, mostly broadly obcordate, with ± divergent lobes, finely reticulate beneath, with a submarginal irregular row of orange calli;  base ± narrow-cuneate, often slightly hairy.  Fls solitary;  peduncles 2.5–12 cm long, filiform.  Bracts  c. 1/2 way along pedicel, 2–2.8 mm long, linear-subulate;  calli prominent.  Sepals 4.5–5.5 mm long, ovate-oblong, often slightly hairy;  calli 2, apical, prominent, orange.  Petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes becoming almost white, glabrous;  limb broad-obovate.  Stamens in 2 whorls; filaments hairy, dilated towards base, < 4 mm long.  Styles much > longer whorl of stamens, hairy except near apex.  Capsule not seen.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Its stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: white clover's leaflets are c. 5–25 mm long, can be notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings, so leaflet size, shape and markings overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Its leaf stalks and leaflet undersides are usually moderately hairy, and its leaflets, c. 15–40 mm long, usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Red clover's leaflets are mostly larger, but the ranges meet at 15–16 mm, so use size only as a guide. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 5–10 mm long, usually pink. Its stems are erect or ascending and do not root at the nodes, and its leaflets are c. 10–35 mm long. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Leaflet size overlaps between 10 and 16 mm, so it does not separate them. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Shamrock wood sorrel: a hairy, clump-forming plant with all its leaves in basal rosettes on stalks (3)–7–30 cm long, and no leafy stem. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to c. 35 cm tall; petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are usually 8–35 mm long, up to 55 mm. Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Flora of New Zealand gives it longer petals, but Australian floras give its petals from 10–12 mm long, so petal size alone does not separate them, and both can be pale or white. Several flowers on one stalk point to shamrock wood sorrel, but a single flower does not rule it out: an Australian flora gives it clusters of 1 to at least 30. Look for a leafy, branched stem, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Shamrock wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. Use it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: About 950 ml (1 US quart) water, 125 ml (½ cup) wood sorrel leaves, stems, flowers and seed pods, 15 ml (1 tbsp) agave nectar or honey, and a dash of salt. Mix everything in a blender. If you can, leave it in the fridge overnight before drinking.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel cooler

recipes.method: Fresh wood sorrel leaves and boiling water, one part leaves to three parts water. Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

Origin checked 15/10/2026 (owner: "revise their bio status"), retrieved 15/10/2026: NZPCN 'Oxalis incarnata' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-incarnata/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1944. Origin 'introduced' stands. Kept introduced, not pest: none of NZPCN's DOC-weed, Pest Plant Accord or unwanted-organism listings appear on its page, and no regional pest management plan naming it was found (web search 15/10/2026).

Habitat as first written: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (Lucid), 'Oxalis incarnata', Where found, author Betty Wood, CC BY 4.0, https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/oxalis_incarnata.htm, retrieved 16/10/2026 — first two sentences verbatim; its Australian distribution ('Coast and Blue Mountains. Occasionally elsewhere.') omitted. This is an Australian habitat statement, not a New Zealand one. Habitat tags forest (bushland), urban (gardens) and disturbed (roadsides, disturbed sites). New Zealand fact, not quoted (all rights reserved): Johanna Knox, Wild Picnic blog (cited below) — grows around borders and against rises and mounds. The owner has since replaced that text with their own ('Bush, gardens, road site, disturbed sites also along the sea side. Tolerates shade well.', in the editor, by 16/10/2026), so the field's source is now this guide; spelling regularised 16/10/2026 ('road site' → 'roadsides', 'sea side' → 'seaside'). 'Along the seaside' is the owner's; no source read for this entry says it. Lucid says 'Tolerates deep shade'. The tag grassland is not supported by either text.

Summary sentences two and three: Wikipedia, 'Oxalis incarnata' (revision 1306452215; CC BY-SA 4.0), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxalis_incarnata, retrieved 16/10/2026, verbatim. Flora of New Zealand Online and Biota of New Zealand (https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/b7628927-693d-4389-8488-03820477ba6f, retrieved 16/10/2026) give the New Zealand vernacular names 'Lilac oxalis' and 'Pale oxalis', and Biota of New Zealand Biostatus Exotic, Wild; Flora of New Zealand gives 'Flowering: Jan.–Dec.'.

Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

OWED (16/10/2026), preparation and warnings (edible parts since written by the owner, 'Leafs, flowers and stems.', spelling regularised 16/10/2026) — no openly licensed source found that records this species as edible (Useful Temperate Plants has no record; Plants For A Future returned no entry; Wikipedia and Flora of New Zealand say nothing of use). The only species-specific source is Johanna Knox's Wild Picnic post above (all rights reserved, so not quoted), which records: raw leaves and stalks have a bright, sour taste and suit sweet and savoury dishes; leaves and flowers in a green salad, flowers as a garnish; it goes with root vegetables, fish, chicken and cream; used in place of lemon. Its caution: high oxalic acid levels, so not too much, and avoid it if you have gout, kidney trouble or rheumatoid arthritis and are avoiding high-oxalic-acid foods. Knox's A Forager's Treasury and Langlands' Foraging New Zealand (both owned, cited above) are the book routes. Not copied from creeping-wood-sorrel, whose text is about Oxalis corniculata. Web search 16/10/2026 (owner: "do a web search and find what you can") found no openly licensed text either; details in the next line.

Web search for edibility and safety, 16/10/2026, pages saved and read in full. Species-specific, all rights reserved, facts only: (1) Heartland Folk, 'Pale Wood Sorrel ~ Oxalis incarnata', Wild Food Wednesday issue 10 (Substack, 2026, Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia), https://heartlandfolk.substack.com/p/pale-wood-sorrel-oxalis-incarnata — all aerial parts edible, leaves and flowers; young leaves sour, eaten fresh in salads, chopped as a garnish or in green pestos in small amounts; best used fresh in small amounts because of its oxalic acid; pick young tender leaves, flowers by day when open; harvest only from unsprayed sites away from roadsides; clovers named as close lookalikes; the plant goes dormant in heat and drought. Its leaflet size (1.5–3 cm long) is larger than Flora of New Zealand's 4–16 mm and is not used. (2) PictureThis, 'Pale pink-sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)' (plant-identification app wiki, author not named), https://www.picturethisai.com/wiki/Oxalis_incarnata.html — leaves edible but not in large amounts because of oxalic acid; not used further, no named author. (3) EdiblePlantDB, 'Oxalidaceae' family page, https://edibleplantdb.org/families/Oxalidaceae — lists O. incarnata with edible parts leaves and stems; an aggregated list with no author or primary source given. Genus-level, not used for this species: Wild Food UK, 'Pink-Sorrel' (Oxalis articulata page), https://www.wildfooduk.com/wild-plants/pink-sorrel/ — names pale pink-sorrel among pink-flowered Oxalis it calls 'all too similar and unnecessary to distinguish as all green leaved Oxalis are edible'. Conflict, recorded: Calflora, 'Oxalis incarnata' (https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=6012), Toxicity: 'Possible skin irritation from touching any part of this plant. Do not eat any part of this plant.' — Calflora shows the same two sentences on every Oxalis checked (O. albicans, O. corniculata, O. hirta, O. latifolia, O. oregana); its field notes say the toxicity value follows the California Poison Control System, whose 'Oxalates' class covers plants whose sap contains oxalate crystals. It is a genus-wide flag, not a finding about this species, but it is the only source found that says not to eat it. Seasonal, for the owner's months decision: Pacific Bulb Society wiki, 'South African Oxalis Five' (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US; Copyright Pacific Bulb Society, www.pacificbulbsociety.org), https://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/SouthAfricanOxalisFive — 'It can stay evergreen with moisture'; Massey (below) 'more active in winter'; Knox (above) cooking with it in July and pairing it with "two other herbs that you can forage for at the moment". Not found: any traditional South African food use of this species, or any source on eating its bulbs.

Lookalike fact, not carded (no entry for the other species): Massey University, New Zealand Weeds Database, 'Pink shamrock' (Oxalis vallicola), all rights reserved, https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/colleges-schools-and-institutes/college-of-sciences/our-research/themes-and-research-strengths/plant-science-research/new-zealand-weeds-database/pink-shamrock/, retrieved 16/10/2026 — names lilac oxalis (O. incarnata) as another pinkish-flowered oxalis, which 'has branched stems unlike pink shamrock and is more active in winter'. The page's case of cattle killed by oxalates is about pink shamrock, not this species, and is not used here.

Petal lengths for O. incarnata outside New Zealand: Flora of Tasmania Online, Oxalidaceae (12–20 mm), https://flora.tmag.tas.gov.au/vascular-families/oxalidaceae/, and Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (10–22 mm, CC BY 4.0, cited above), retrieved 16/10/2026; the Tasmanian key also separates O. incarnata ('Stems well developed and leafy') from species with 'Stems absent or very short, never leafy'. Every test: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 16/10/2026: 'Oxalis incarnata', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-incarnata.html; 'Oxalis articulata', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-articulata.html. 'Almost hairless' is Flora's 'almost glabrous'. Ranges overlap: both are Exotic in New Zealand (Flora) and shamrock wood sorrel's habitat text (Plants of South Eastern NSW) names gardens, roadsides and other disturbed areas; Flora of Tasmania (cited above) gives O. articulata 'along roadsides, in waste places and some cultivated areas', and pale-pink wood sorrel's habitat text names roadsides and disturbed sites (the owner's own text since 16/10/2026; it was Plants of South Eastern NSW's when the card was written). Risk edible on cards opening pale-pink wood sorrel: its edibility is recorded only in all-rights-reserved, species-specific sources (Knox, Wild Picnic; Heartland Folk — see the OWED and web-search lines on that entry); Calflora's 'Do not eat' is a genus-wide flag. Owner to confirm. The owner has since written that page's edible parts in their own words ('Leaves, flowers and stems.'), which the risk matches; its preparation and warnings are still owed. Risk edible on the card opening shamrock wood sorrel: when the card was written its own page had no edible parts and the basis was Wild Food UK's O. articulata page (cited above), 'The leaves, stem and flowers are edible' — all rights reserved, species-specific. Since 16/10/2026 its page lists edible parts from Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis articulata' (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, species-specific), which supports the risk.

The seven recipes from 'Wood sorrel sauce' onward were copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner, 16/10/2026: "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"); none is written for this species. Their provenance, as recorded there: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026).

summary.text: Oxalis incarnata is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common names pale pink-sorrel and crimson woodsorrel. It is native to southern Africa, but it can be found on other continents where it is an introduced species, often the descendant of garden escapees. It is grown and kept as an ornamental plant.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

habitat.text: This styphelia grows in forest, shrubland and heath, often in poorly-drained or sandy soils or among rocks, and usually occurs at an altitude of above about 500 m. It is found on the tablelands of northern and southern New South Wales, in eastern Victoria, on the Central Plateau of Tasmania, and in New Zealand.

identification.text:
Prostrate to low-growing shrub up to c. 15 cm. tall or more, forming extensive dense patches; branches decumbent to ascending; branchlets close-set, minutely puberulous when young, densely clad in erect imbricate lvs. Lamina sessile or subsessile, coriac., glab., us. brownish green above, paler below, finely nerved, ± 4–9 × 1–2 mm., obovate-oblong; margins scarious to cartilaginous, finely ciliolate; abruptly narrowed to pungent tip ± 2 mm. long. Infl. of axillary solitary sessile fls; bracts minute, apiculate. Fls small; calyx-lobes acute. Corolla-tube cylindric. > twice length calyx; lobes short, acute, densely hairy on upper surfaces. Fr. orange to yellow, broad-oblong in outline, 8–9 mm. long.
[From:  Allan  (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1 as Cyathodes fraseri (A.Cunn.) Allan]

summary.text: Styphelia nesophila, commonly known as sharp beard-heath, is a species of flowering plant in the heath family Ericaceae and is native to south-eastern Australia and New Zealand, where it is known as pātōtara, or dwarf mingimingi.

identification.text: Hericium novae-zealandiae has a relatively large (10 cm + diameter), white fruiting body, initially described (as Hydnum nova zealandia) as looking somewhat like a cauliflower nearing flowering. Lacking a pileus or defined stipe, basidiomata are highly and irregularly branched. Growing from a short, corkish stem, culminating in numerous, densely arranged, fine tips. The hymenium (spore bearing surface) is located on the surface of the fine tips, there is no delineation between the stipe and the hymenium until spore maturity when tips become reddish.

Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Pelargonium tomentosum'
identification.text:
Subshrub to c. 75 cm tall, smelling strongly of peppermint. Stems, lvs and infl. with ± velvety white tomentum, and glandular scales beneath hairs. Petiole to c. 30 cm long. Stipules ovate-acuminate, brown and membranous. Lamina to 12 × 15 cm, broadly obovate, rather shallowly 3-lobed with each lobe usually lobulate, serrate-dentate and extending 1/4–1/2 way to midrib; base usually shallowly cordate, sometimes deeply so. Infl. of several umbels, each with 5–8 fls; hairs dense, mostly long and simple but some short and glandular; peduncles often = petioles; pedicels 2–3.5 cm long, generally radiating widely in umbels of 6–8 fls. Sepals 5.5–6.5 mm long, ± triangular-ovate, green, with copious long white hairs; calyx spur c. 2 mm long. Corolla white or pinkish; upper 2 petals 7–8.5 mm long, ± oblong, usually with asymmetric base, crimson-purple-marked in lower 1/2; lower 3 petals 8–10.5 mm long, linear or ligulate. Style crimson or purplish, c. 4 mm long; stigmas crimson or purplish. Mericarps not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
It is easily recognised by its rather large, velvety hairy lvs, strongly smelling of peppermint.

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium by its leaves (lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; a quarter to half way in peppermint geranium), and the two descriptions also differ in the flower stalks (1–6 mm against 2–3.5 cm). Peppermint geranium's flowers are white or pinkish, rose geranium's pink, so a pink flower does not separate them. A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; Flora of New Zealand calls rose geranium only "strongly aromatic". The leaf test works without flowers.
lookalikes.name: Rose geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the umbels (dense, with almost stalkless flowers, in rose-scented geranium; diffuse, with long flower stalks, in peppermint geranium) and the calyx spur (4–5 mm against about 2 mm). Leaf lobing meets at about half way, so it does not settle a plant on its own. Both plants are hairy, and flower colour does not separate them (Wikipedia gives rose-scented geranium white through pink to purple flowers). A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Most of these tests need flowers.

preparation.text: A peppermint-flavoured tea is infused from the fresh leaves. PlantZAfrica (South African National Biodiversity Institute) passes on Barbara Hey's (1994) suggestion to line the tin with the leaves before baking a chocolate cake, and says the leaves can flavour puddings, jellies and hot or cold drinks.

recipes.method: Written for rose geranium leaves; the author suggests mint-scented geranium as a substitute. Makes about 300 ml. 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and about five sprigs of peppermint geranium 10–13 cm long. Put the water, sugar and sprigs in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup. Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The original uses it in a chocolate dessert.
recipes.title: Peppermint geranium syrup

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — the species descriptions and notes and the Pelargonium key (couplet 4: P. ×asperum "Lamina lobed to > 3/4 way to midrib"; couplet 6: P. tomentosum "Umbels diffuse; fls on long pedicels; calyx spur c. 2 mm long" against "Umbels dense; fls subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; couplet 7: P. capitatum "Habit sprawling; lvs strongly undulate, with ± oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina"), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b8f32527-4c30-4f9b-bab4-9155d157a597, retrieved 21/10/2026; plus Wikipedia 'Pelargonium capitatum' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1195218505) for that species' scent and flower-colour range. Webb gives P. capitatum no full description, only a note and its key couplets, so its side of every card rests on those. Webb's key is inconsistent for P. capitatum (couplet 4 sends it down "Lf blade not lobed or lobed to < 1/2 way to midrib", couplet 7 says its lobes extend "at least 1/2 way") — the cards say lobing does not settle rose geranium against rose-scented geranium for that reason. Card risks: `edible` into all three — peppermint geranium from the start; rose geranium and rose-scented geranium since 21/10/2026, when their pages gained edible parts (a card is not more certain than its page). Not carded, no entry: P. vitifolium (Webb: "very closely-related" to P. capitatum and "often confused"; 0 wild iNaturalist NZ records 21/10/2026), the native kopata P. inodorum, P. ×fragrans. These cards clear `warnings` on all three pages with no warning text added. Corrected 21/10/2026 (owner: "check and double check all Pelargoniums"): the peppermint geranium ↔ rose geranium cards said the key separates them by leaves and flower stalks; couplet 4 uses the leaves only, so the stalk lengths are now credited to the species descriptions.

summary.text:
Pelargonium tomentosum, the peppermint-scented geranium, is a pelargonium species native to South Africa.
In New Zealand, Flora of New Zealand (1988) recorded it wild at Eastbourne and Paekākāriki, near Wellington; it was first recorded growing wild here in 1944. Peppermint geranium is fairly commonly cultivated and can be expected to occur wild at other suitable coastal localities.

edibleParts.text: This mushroom contains toxins and is usually considered inedible. It has been used as a condiment in many countries, with the Italian chef Antonio Carluccio recommending it be used only to add its peppery flavour to other mushrooms.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Chalciporus piperatus' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Fruit bodies of Chalciporus piperatus occur singly, scattered, or in groups on the ground. The fungus occurs naturally in or near coniferous or beech and oak woodlands, often on sandy soils. Fruit bodies appear in Europe in late summer and autumn from August to November. The fungus is widespread across North America, fruiting from July to October in the eastern states and from September to January on the Pacific Coast. It is found in Mexico and Central America. In Asia, it has been collected from Pakistan, West Bengal (India), and Guangdong Province (China). In South Africa, it is known from the southwestern Cape Province and the eastern Transvaal Province.
Chalciporus piperatus grows in conifer plantations associated with the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) and the chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius). It has been recorded under introduced loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) plantations in Santa Catarina and Paraná states in southern Brazil, and under introduced trees in the Los Lagos Region of Chile. It has also spread into native forest in northeastern Tasmania and Victoria, having been found growing with the native myrtle beech (Nothofagus cunninghamii). The rare variety hypochryseus occurs only in Europe, including Austria, Czechia, Greece, Italy, and Spain. Also rare, variety amarellus is widespread in European coniferous forests, where it usually found near pines, spruce, and sometimes fir.
Fruit bodies can be parasitised by the mould Sepedonium chalcipori, a highly specialised mycoparasite that is only known to infect this bolete. Infections result in necrotic mushroom tissue and the production of copious yellow conidia.
Initially thought to be ectomycorrhizal (symbiotic with plants, like most Boletaceae), C. piperatus has not been confirmed as such in multiple synthesis studies or in isotope fractionation studies. There is some speculation that C. piperatus is a mycoparasite on the mycorrhiza of A. muscaria. In New Zealand, A. muscaria is thought to have been introduced with Pinus radiata, and has made a host jump to the native Nothofagus trees; C. piperatus has since been observed fruiting near Nothofagus trees with A. muscaria associations.  Buchwaldoboletus lignicola is in the same clade as C. piperatus and is thought to be a parasite as well, strengthening the evidence that C. piperatus and its relatives may be mycoparasites.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Chalciporus piperatus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
One of the smaller boletes, Chalciporus piperatus  has an orange-fawn 1.6–9 cm cap that is initially convex before flattening out in age. The cap surface can be furrowed; shiny when dry, it can be a little sticky when wet, and may crack with age. The colour of the pore surface ranges from yellowish to dark reddish brown in maturity. When bruised, the pore surface stains brown. Individual pores are angular, measuring about 0.5–2 mm wide, while the tubes are 3–10 mm deep. Slender for a bolete, the stipe measures 4–9.5 cm long by 0.6–1.2 cm thick, and is either roughly the same width throughout its length, or slightly thicker near the base. The colour of the stem is similar to the cap, or lighter, and there is yellow mycelium at the base. The flesh is yellow, sometimes with reddish tones, maturing to purplish brown. It has no odour. The spore print is brown to cinnamon. Variety hypochryseus is essentially identical to the main form except for its bright yellow tubes and pores. Variety amarellus has pinker pores and a taste that is bitter rather than peppery.

The spores are smooth, narrowly fusiform (fuse-shaped), and measure 7–12 by 3–5 μm. The basidia (spore-bearing cells) measure 20–28 by 6–8 μm and are hyaline (translucent), four-spored, and narrowly club-shaped, with many internal oil droplets. The cystidia are fusiform, sometimes with a rounded tip, and have dimensions of 30–50 by 9–12 μm. Some are more or less hyaline, while others are encrusted with a golden pigment. The cap cuticle is a trichodermium, an arrangement in which the outermost hyphae emerge roughly parallel, like hairs, perpendicular to the cap surface. These hyphae are 10–17 μm wide and have elliptical to cylindrical cells at their ends that are not gelatinous. Clamp connections are absent from the hyphae.


Similar species
The fruit body of the North American species Chalciporus piperatoides are similar, but can be distinguished by its flesh and pores staining blue after cutting or bruising. It has a less peppery taste. Another mild-tasting relative, C. rubinellus, has brighter colours than C. piperatus, including completely red tubes. One European species, C. rubinus, has a shape similar to C. piperatus, but has red pores and a stem covered in red dots.

lookalikes.howToTell: Do not decide on the tree. The endemic grows under native beech, but this introduced peppery bolete, usually found with fly agaric under pines and introduced broadleaved trees, also turns up in beech forest where fly agaric has become naturalised. Cap colour helps but the ranges meet at orange. The endemic's cap is golden yellow, apricot or occasionally reddish orange, dry and finely felted. This one's is fawn to light brown, brownish orange or cinnamon brown, and slightly slimy when wet. Look at the stem. This one's stem is golden yellow at the base, with yellow flesh. The endemic's matches the cap or is reddish, pale yellow at the very top, with pale reddish-brown flesh. A crumb of this one, chewed and spat out, is acrid and peppery; the endemic's taste is not distinctive.

summary.text:
Sonchus arvensis, the field milk thistle, field sowthistle, perennial sow-thistle, corn sow thistle, dindle, gutweed, swine thistle, or tree sow thistle, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Sonchus arvensis is native to Eurasia, where it is widespread across most of the continent. It has also become naturalized in many other regions, and is considered an invasive noxious weed in some places, such as North America (including Prince Edward Island), Russia, New Zealand, and Australia.
A study conducted in 2003 has shown that with future global atmospheric carbon levels, S. arvensis shows increased growth with increased atmospheric carbon which could potentially expand its range and outcompete native species.

identification.text:
Perennial wall-rocket is a glabrous herb with an erect or sprawling habit, that grows up to 1.3 m tall, with a solid, almost woody terete stem and spreading branches.
The deeply pinnate leaves are up to 12 cm long and often rather fleshy, with a peppery taste and a musty smell.

In the British Isles, it flowers from May to September (or through October in a warm year). In Spain, it can be seen flowering between April and December. The inflorescence is a branched raceme up to 30 cm long with up to 30 flowers, each of which has 4 free bright yellow petals up to 15 mm long, and 4 free yellow/brown sepals up to 7.5 mm long. Each flower has 6 stamens and a single style.

The fruit is a straight, flat silique (pod) up to five centimeters long. The pedicels are shorter than the fruits and ascend at an acute angle to the stem. Above the receptacle is a short (2 mm) stalk (or stipe) below the pod (a useful feature for separating this species from annual wall-rocket). The seeds are arranged in 2 rows, or staggered in a zigzag pattern, towards the centre of the pod, which in turn consists of 2 valves, so a cross-section of the fruit shows 4 seeds in total. This is a distinguishing feature of the genus Diplotaxis, although it is not always easy to see, as plants are not self-pollinating, so ripe seeds do not always develop.

summary.text:
Diplotaxis tenuifolia is a species of flowering plant in the mustard family known by the common name perennial wall-rocket.
It is native to parts of Europe, reaching in the east to Turkey and Syria. It is extinct from Morocco and Algeria, but has been introduced in a number of regions: Cyprus, the Caucasus, the Levant, Yemen, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, New Caledonia, Canada (Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia), the United States, Costa Rica, Argentina and Uruguay.

Within Europe, its native range covers much of France, the Low Countries, Italy, the Pannonian Basin and the western Balkans up to Macedonia, with generally more thinly scattered populations in northern Greece, Bulgaria, Romania, Crimea, Sicilly, Malta, Sardinia, Corsica and parts of Spain. It has extensively been introduced further north from its native range. In the British Isles the plant is an archaeophyte, with industrial regions and ports still at the centre of the distribution. It is established especially in parts of England and Wales (some believing the plant could even be native to the south-east). Its range has been expanding to the west since the 19th century, but it is still very rare in Scotland and Ireland. It has also been introduced into much of Central Europe: throughout Switzerland, Austria, Germany and Poland, with more scattered instances on the southern shores of Norway and Sweden (where it is found in fewer areas that in the recent past), the Baltic States, Belarus and a few locations further east in Ukraine and European Russia. It has also been introduced on Menorca and near Lisbon in Portugal.

habitat.text: Garden beds, pots, paths, cultivated ground — exactly where chickweed grows, and usually mixed through it.

identification.text: A soft, upright weed 10–30 cm tall with smooth oval leaves and odd, cup-like green flowers with no petals at the top of the stem. The test is the sap: snap any stem and it bleeds white milky latex immediately. Chickweed does not.

lookalikes.howToTell: Chickweed's stem is round and weak, with a single line of hairs down one side (very occasionally two), and its leaves are in opposite pairs; its flowers have white petals split almost to the base. Petty spurge has a hairless stem, alternate leaves, small green flower heads with no petals, and white milky sap; no milky sap is recorded for chickweed. Missing petals alone does not prove spurge, because chickweeds rarely lack them too — check the leaves, the hairs and the sap together. Snap a stem from every clump before picking.

warnings: The latex is a severe irritant: it blisters skin and can damage the cornea. Wash hands before touching your face.
Eating it causes burning of the mouth and vomiting.

edibleParts.text: The unfurled young frond tips only.

habitat.text: Damp shaded native forest floor and gullies, often under tree ferns.

harvestEthics.text: Take no more than one or two fronds per plant and move on. Pikopiko is culturally significant and slow-growing; commercial demand has already stripped accessible stands. Seek permission from mana whenua and the landowner.

identification.text: Finely divided lacy fronds, with tiny bulbils (plantlets) growing on the upper surface of mature fronds — the 'chickens' that give it its name. Harvest only the tightly curled, still-unfurling koru at the tip.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bracken has long-creeping underground rhizomes and forms extensive stands, mostly in the open — rough pasture, road cuttings and banks, forest margins and clearings — though it also grows under forest and in scrub. Its fronds carry hairs and no scales, and its stalks become woody and chestnut brown at the base. Pikopiko grows from a short upright rhizome in wetter, shaded forest-floor places; its stalks and fronds carry scales, its fronds lack hairs, and they usually bear bulbils. Do not eat bracken shoots: IARC classes bracken fern (assessed as the northern-hemisphere Pteridium aquilinum) as possibly carcinogenic to humans, with sufficient evidence of cancer in animals, and its constituent ptaquiloside caused tumours in rats. Bracken rhizome was a major traditional Māori food and the young shoots were occasionally eaten, but the young fronds have been found to be highly carcinogenic.

identification.text:
Aromatic herb.  Stems erect or ascending, 5–20–(40) cm tall, striate, glabrous or with a few hairs below capitula, usually much-branched from base. Basal and lower cauline lvs appearing shortly petiolate but usually with very reduced leaflets along sheath, narrow-obovate to elliptic, usually glabrous, sometimes sparsely hairy when young, 2–3-pinnatisect, 2–8 × 0.5–2 cm; ultimate segments narrow-linear or subulate, ± all in one plane;  cauline lvs similar to basal but above becoming smaller, with fewer segments, ovate, and apetiolate.  Corymb diffuse, of 1-many capitula.  Involucral bracts glabrous, 3–5 mm long;  margins pale, membranous.  Capitula 4–10 mm diam.;  ray florets 0;  disc florets numerous, dull yellow to greenish yellow, 4-toothed.  Achenes c. 1.5 mm long, very pale brown, narrow-obovoid;  inner surface with usually 4 narrow ribs, the outer 2 with glandular groove for > 1/2 length;  outer surface smooth;  corona < 0.1 mm long or 0.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Matricaria discoidea, commonly known as pineappleweed, wild chamomile, disc mayweed, and rayless mayweed, is an annual plant native to North America, northern Asia, and Europe where it grows as a common herb of fields, gardens, and roadsides.
It occurs across Canada and the United States, especially as a common weed in Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories.  However, there is disagreement over whether it originated in North America or in Siberia.  This species has been introduced to Europe, Asia, Iceland, South America, and New Zealand and is now widespread and naturalized in Britain, where it has become one of the fastest-spreading plants of the 20th century.

identification.text:
Vigorous vine;  young shoots angular, downy.  Lvs 3-lobed;  petioles 1–3 cm long, white-lanate, with (2)–4–8 glands almost hidden in indumentum; stipules pinnate with dark filiform segments almost to the base of the very narrow-linear rachis;  lamina lobes 5–9 cm long, extending ?-3/4 distance in from margin;  middle lobe largest, 3–8 × 1.5–3 cm, lanceolate to elliptic-ovate, dentate, grey- or white-tomentose below, glabrate above except when young, dark shining green, ± rugose, acute or mucronate.  Fls ☿, solitary.  Pedicels much > petioles, hairy.  Bracts free, 1.5–2.3 cm long, ovate, hairy or glabrate outside, serrate with teeth setose.  Hypanthium (4)–4.5–5 cm long, tomentulose.  Sepals 3–4.8 cm long, elliptic, green outside, with tomentulose band, white or very pale pink inside, with short horn near apex;  petals similar to sepals but all pink;  corona threads violet-blue,  c. 1/2 perianth.  Filaments 1.3–1.7 cm long, much > anthers;  anthers 6–9 mm long.  Ovary white-villous.  Fr. 4–7 cm diam., globose or depressed globose, yellow, tomentulose;  pulp sweet and edible, orange.  Seeds 5–6 mm long, ellipsoid-ovoid, dark brown or dark red, alveolate.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tripartita) has densely hairy shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, the lobes usually 5–14 cm long, usually more or less felted underneath and hairy or nearly hairless above; its stipules are 5–10 mm wide, kidney-shaped and gland-toothed, and they stay on the stem; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube 8–9.5 cm long, with sepals only 2–3.8 cm long; its fruit is (6)–7–12 × 2–3 cm, more or less ellipsoid, yellow or orange-yellow and finely downy, with dark red to black seeds. Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Flora of New Zealand's key: pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal (Flora of New Zealand's key; NZPCN). Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Banana passionfruit

lookalikes.howToTell: Kōhia is hairless apart from slightly hairy young stems; its leaves are undivided and untoothed, (4)–5–12–(14) cm long, leathery and dark glossy green above; its flowers are small and yellowish green, (1)–3–4 together, with segments 5–6 mm long and no floral tube, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants; its fruit is (2)–2.5–3 cm across, round or broadly ellipsoid and orange, with sparse reddish pulp. Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Flora of New Zealand's key first splits the genus on the flower: the banana passionfruits and pink-flowered passionfruit have a cylindrical, much elongated floral tube, while black passionfruit and kōhia have none, or only an inconspicuous saucer-shaped one. Without flowers the leaves settle it: Flora of New Zealand's key gives kōhia undivided, leathery leaves and flowers under 2 cm across, against lobed leaves and flowers over 4 cm across in the passionfruits it keys out beside, and pink-flowered passionfruit's leaves are 3-lobed. Only female kōhia plants bear fruit (Wikipedia: the plant is dioecious), so a fruitless kōhia is common; use the leaves. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Kōhia

lookalikes.howToTell: Banana passionfruit (Passiflora tarminiana) has hairy stems; its leaves are 3-lobed and usually hairless above (the sources disagree about the underside); its stipules are small, 4–7 × 2–3 mm, and soon fall, so a mature stem usually has none; its pink flowers hang from a floral tube given as up to 6 cm (NZPCN), 6–7 cm (Flora of New Zealand's weed profile) or 6–8 cm (Wikipedia), with sepals and petals 3–6 cm long that spread flat or bend back; its fruit tapers at both ends and ripens yellow or light orange, and is given as up to 9 cm long (NZPCN) or 10–14 cm (Wikipedia). Pink-flowered passionfruit has downy young shoots; its leaves are 3-lobed, grey- or white-felted underneath and dark shining green above; its stipules are pinnate, with dark thread-like segments almost to the base of a very narrow central strip; its flowers have a floral tube (4)–4.5–5 cm long, pink petals and violet-blue corona threads; its fruit is 4–7 cm across, round or slightly flattened, yellow and finely downy. Flora of New Zealand's key: pink-flowered passionfruit's stipules are pinnate, with thread-like segments, and its fruit is more or less round; a banana passionfruit's stipules are simple — either ovate and toothed or awl-shaped and untoothed — and its fruit is ellipsoid. Both have pink flowers and edible orange pulp, so flower colour does not separate them. P. tarminiana's stipules soon fall, so look for them on young growth. A hybrid, Passiflora × rosea, which has no entry here, looks very like pink-flowered passionfruit, but the central strip of its stipules is lanceolate and its stamens are usually abnormal (Flora of New Zealand's key; NZPCN). Both are edible.

identification.text:
When supported, the plant can grow up to 6 metres in height. The compound leaves with 5 to 9 leaflets are dark green on the upper surface and a lighter green beneath, with glabrous, terete or angular branches. The terminal leaflet is noticeably larger than the other leaflets.


Inflorescence
The species is heterostylous, meaning that a few distinct flower morphs (forms) are available, though each plant bears only one morph. In late winter and early spring it produces an abundance of reddish-pink flower buds, followed by fragrant five-petalled starry white flowers which are about 2 cm in diameter. The bracts are subulate (tapering to a point), 1-6  mm. Each flower is carried by a pedicel (single stalk) of 0.5 - 2.5cm The calyx forms a 1-2 mm tube terminating in 5 triangular or subulate-linear lobes, only 2 mm long, and a corolla, white, with a red underside and red buttons. The fruit is a black, globular berry.

habitat.text:
It also occurs naturally on the shores of lakes in the Rotorua area and in Abel Tasman National Park at the top of South Island.
The tree is renowned as a cliff-dweller, able to maintain a hold in precarious, near-vertical situations. Like its Hawaiian relative the ʻōhiʻa lehua (M. polymorpha), the pōhutukawa has been shown to be efficient in the colonisation of lava plains – notably on Rangitoto, a volcanic island in the Hauraki Gulf.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Pōhutukawa' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Pōhutukawa grow up to 25 metres high, with a spreading, dome-like form. They usually grow as a multi-trunked spreading tree. Their trunks and branches are sometimes festooned with matted, fibrous aerial roots. The oblong, leathery leaves are covered in dense white hairs underneath.
The tree flowers from November to January with a peak in early summer (mid to late December), with brilliant crimson flowers covering the tree, hence the nickname New Zealand Christmas tree. The first published reference to pōhutakawa as a Christmas tree was in 1857, in a newspaper report of a feast held by Eruera Patuone. There is variation between individual trees in the timing of flowering, and in the shade and brightness of the flowers. In isolated populations genetic drift has resulted in local variation: many of the trees growing around the Rotorua lakes produce pink-shaded flowers, and the yellow-flowered cultivar 'Aurea' descends from a pair discovered in 1940 on Mōtītī Island in the Bay of Plenty.

summary.text:
Pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa), also known as the New Zealand Christmas tree, or iron tree, is a coastal evergreen tree in the myrtle family, Myrtaceae, that produces a brilliant display of red (or occasionally orange, yellow or white) flowers, each consisting of a mass of stamens.
The pōhutukawa's natural range is the coastal regions of the North Island of New Zealand, north of a line stretching from New Plymouth (39° S) to Gisborne (38° S), where it once formed a continuous coastal fringe. By the 1990s, pastoral farming and introduced pests had reduced pōhutukawa forests by over 90%.

edibleParts.text: Cap and stem. Trim any maggot-riddled stem base.

habitat.text: Mycorrhizal with introduced trees: oak, birch, pine and sweet chestnut. Look along the drip line of mature street and park trees and in old shelter belts, especially in Canterbury. It does not grow with native bush trees, so a bolete under beech or kānuka is something else.

identification.text:
Cap 8–30 cm, tan to chestnut brown, smooth and slightly tacky when wet, often with a fine pale line at the rim. Underneath is a sponge of tiny pores, never gills: white and firm when young, ageing to yellow then olive. The stem is thick and club-shaped, pale brown, with a fine white net (reticulation) at least over the top third — look closely, it is subtle. Flesh is white and stays white when cut or bruised; any blueing, pinking or reddening rules porcini out. Taste a crumb of raw cap and spit it out: it should be mild and nutty, never bitter.

Turn the mushroom over. Porcini's pore surface is white, yellow or olive. If it is red, orange or any warm colour, stop. Cut the cap in half and watch for a minute: if the flesh blues, stop. Some of these are edible after long cooking in other countries; none is worth the gamble in a field guide.

preparation.text: Cook before eating. Brush clean rather than wash, slice, and check the stem for maggots. Sauté in butter, or slice thinly and dry for stock — the flavour concentrates.

recipes.method: Brush the caps clean — do not wash them, they drink water. Slice thickly, about the width of a finger. Melt a good knob of butter in a wide pan until it foams, add the slices in one layer and leave them alone until the undersides are deep brown, then turn. Salt only at the end, or they weep. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and a little chopped parsley, pile onto thick toast rubbed with garlic, and eat immediately. Two medium caps feed one person who has had a good day.
recipes.title: Porcini on toast

recipes.method: The way to keep a glut. Slice caps and stems 5 mm thick and lay them on a rack or a tea towel in a warm, airy spot — a dehydrator at 45 °C, or an oven on its lowest setting with the door ajar, takes six to eight hours. They are done when they snap rather than bend. Store in a jar with a tight lid; the smell will be stronger than the fresh mushroom ever was. To use, soak a handful in warm water for twenty minutes, lift the pieces out, and pour the soaking liquid through a paper filter to catch the grit — that liquid is the best part, and goes into risotto, soup or gravy.

summary.text: A stout brown-capped bolete with a sponge of pores instead of gills, white flesh that stays white when cut, and a pale net over the top of the stem. In Aotearoa it fruits under introduced oak, birch and pine in autumn.

warnings: Cut every cap and stem lengthwise before it goes in the basket: white flesh that stays white, and a white pore surface. Colour change of any kind means put it down.
Check the pore surface of every specimen, not just the first — mixed patches under the same tree are common.

lookalikes.howToTell: Black nightshade is a herb to about 75 cm, usually hairy, where poroporo is a hairless, soft-wooded shrub to about 3 m. Its flowers are 10–13 mm across, usually white, sometimes pale mauve, in clusters that are usually few-flowered; poroporo's are usually 4–5 cm and violet, though the other poroporo, Solanum aviculare, can have white flowers from 10 mm. Its berries are 7–10 mm across and round, usually dull black but sometimes green, yellowish green or pale yellow; poroporo's are 23–30 mm long, egg-shaped, usually yellow or pale orange. The unripe green berries hold the most toxin, but eating mature leaves raw may also cause poisoning, so no part is safe to assume.

identification.text:
Angelica pachycarpa is a short-lived, stout fleshy plant. It grows about one meter tall, with very glossy dark green foliage. It has creamy-white to greenish-white flowers in flat umbels that are ten to twenty centimeters wide. The foliage and hollow stems have a faint aniseed odor.  The stems are grooved.  The base foliage is two to three pinnate and noticeable petiolate; the stem leaves are one to three pinnate with very short petioles.  The fruit are up to twelve millimeters long, brown with lighter colored wings, and have a pepper-like scent.
Angelica pachycarpa is found growing in the Crithmo-Armerion maritimae (Géhu 1968) community of plants in Spain and Portugal which includes these species also: Armeria berlengensis, Armeria euscadiensis, Armeria maritima subsp. miscella, Armeria pubigera subsp. depilata, Armeria pubigera subsp. pubigera, Centaurea borjae, Daucus gingidium subsp. atlanticum, Leucanthemum ircutianum subsp. crassifolium, Leucanthemum merinoi, Leucanthemum pluriflorum, Rumex acetosa subsp. biformis, Rumex rupestris, Sesamoides suffruticosa subsp. latifolia, Silene uniflora, Spergularia rupicola subsp. rupicola, Trifolium occidentale.

identification.text:
Lactuca serriola has a spineless reddish stem, containing a milky latex, growing up to 2 metres.
The leaves get progressively smaller as they reach its top. They are oblong or lanceolate, often pinnately lobed and (especially for the lower leaves), waxy grey green. Fine spines are present along the veins and leaf edges. The undersides have whitish veins. They emit latex when cut.
The flower heads are 1–1.5 cm wide, pale yellow, often tinged purple, with 12–20 ray flowers but no disc flowers. The bracts are also often tinged purple. It flowers from July until September in the northern hemisphere. The achenes are grey, tipped with bristles. The pappus is white with equal length hairs.
Lactuca serriola is known as the compass plant because in the sun the upper leaves twist round to hold their margins upright, pointing roughly south or north from the stem.
Similar to Mycelis muralis but showing more than 5 florets.

Erect or spreading shrub up to c. 5 m. tall; bark black, branchlets divergent. Lvs coriac., patent or reflexed, sessile to very shortly petioled, glaucous below, 6–15–(20) × 0·5–1 mm.; margins ± recurved, ciliolate; apex with fine pungent tip c. 1 mm. long; veins 3–7, branched above. sources: Wikipedia, 'Opuntia ficus-indica' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
O. ficus-indica is polyploid, hermaphroditic, and autogamous. As Opuntia species grow in semiarid environments, the main limiting factor in their environment is water. They have developed several adaptations to dry conditions, notably succulence.
A perennial shrub, O. ficus-indica can grow up to 5 m in height, with thick, succulent, and oblong to spatulate stems called cladodes. It has a water-repellent and sun-reflecting waxy epidermis. Cladodes 1–2 years old produce flowers, with the fruit's colours ranging from pale green to deep red.
The plants flower in three distinct colours: white, yellow, and red. The flowers first appear in early May through the early summer in the Northern Hemisphere, and the fruits ripen from August through October. The fruits are typically eaten, minus the thick outer skin, after chilling in a refrigerator for a few hours. They have a taste similar to sweet watermelon. The bright red/purple or white/yellowish flesh contains many tiny hard seeds that are usually swallowed but should be avoided by those who have problems digesting seeds.

identification.text:
Rosa gallica is a deciduous shrub forming large patches. The slender, straight prickles are various in size and frequency in this species. The leaves are pinnately-compound, with three to seven bluish-green leaflets. The flowers are clustered one to four together, on glandular pedicels. Each flower has five or more petals, sometimes producing double corollas. The flowers are fragrant and deep pink. The hips are globose to ovoid, 10–13 mm diameter, and orange to brownish.
In the field of Food science, rose petal extract from Rosa gallica has been shown to have properties that reduce inflammation and wrinkling in human skin.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe aucklandiae' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
The cap is 15–55 mm diam., broadly conic, expanding to broadly umbonate to more or less flattened, with edges becoming slightly upturned and often splitting; dry; lacking veil remnants; dark brown to yellow-brown, striate (radially lined) to edge, hygrophanous, drying to pale yellow-brown to straw-coloured; staining greenish-blue with damage or age; flesh white. The gills are adnate (broadly attached to the stem), close, greyish yellow-brown, maturing dark violaceous, with a conspicuous pale narrow margin. The stipe is 35-100 x 1.5–5 mm, cylindric, finely pruinose in the upper part and silky-fibrillose near the base, white, yellow or pinkish purple brown, with brownish flesh. Veil cortinoid and poorly developed, disappearing as caps mature. All parts staining deep greenish-blue or blackish-blue with damage. Spore print violet brown.
Spores measure (6.5-)7-9.5 x 4–5.5 x 3.5-4.5 μm, 8.1 x 4.9 x 4.3 μm average, ovate in face view, elliptic-ovate in side view; brown-walled and smooth, 0.5 μm thick with apical pore; Basidia 20-28 x 4.5-6 μm, cylindric, with 4 spores, clamped; Cheilocystidia 15-32 x 4-8 μm, ventricose-rostrate (swollen and uneven with a beak), with long, tapering, flexuous and sometimes bifurcate neck (forked in two), transparent, thin-walled, up to 12 μm long; Pleurocystidia 13-19 x 4.5-6 μm, scattered, similar to cheilocystidia but with shorter neck, up to 4.5 μm.


Similar species
Psilocybe zapotecorum in Mexico and South America, as noted by Guzman et al. (1991), "P. aucklandii is very similar to P. zapotecorum R. Heim emend. Guzman, which is common in Mexico and known from South America. The two species are barely distinguishable microscopically, although comparison with published descriptions (Guzman 1983) show that P. aucklandii may have slightly narrower pleurocystidia and slightly wider spores. Published illustrations of P. zapotecorum (Guzman 1983) appear to show that P. aucklandii is a less robust species."

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe makarorae' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: Like all Psilocybe species, it is saprobic, and feeds on decomposing organic matter. Fruit bodies grow scattered or in groups on the fallen, rotting wood of southern beeches (genus Nothofagus), and are often encountered near lakes and picnic grounds.

harvestEthics.text: Mostly found on conservation land, where collecting needs a DOC permit — and there is nothing here to permit, because this is a Class A drug and picking it is against the law. It fruits on fallen beech wood, which is habitat in its own right, so leave the log as you found it.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe makarorae' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
The cap is initially conical to bell shaped, but as the mushroom grows, it expands to become convex with a prominent umbo, and attains a diameter of 15–55 mm (0.6–2.2 in). The cap surface is dry to slightly tacky. Its colour is yellow-brown to orange-brown, often paler towards the margin, which has fine striations corresponding to the gills on the underside. The flesh is white. Gills have an adnexed attachment to the stem, and are pale greyish brown. The whitish stipe is 30–60 millimetres (1.2–2.4 in) long by 2–4 mm wide. It is cylindrical, with a surface of pressed silky fibrils. The base of the stem is often brownish, with white rhizoids present. The veil of young fruit bodies is cortinate—resembling the cobweb-like partial veil found in Cortinarius species. As the mushroom grows, its remnants often remain visible on the stem, but it never forms a complete ring. Both the cap and the stem stain greenish-blue when damaged.
The spore print is dark purplish brown. Spores typically measure 7.5–9.5 by 5.5–6.5 by 4.5–5.5 μm, averaging 8.7 by 6.0 by 5.3 μm. Its shape in face view is ovate (egg-shaped) to roughly rhomboid, while viewed from the side it appears elliptical. The spore wall is brown, smooth, about 0.8–1 μm thick, and has a germ pore. The basidia (spore-bearing cells) are four-spored and somewhat club-shaped, tapering slightly to the base; they are clamped, and measure 25–31 by 7–8.5 μm.
The cheilocystidia (cystidia on the gill edge) have dimensions of 18–26 by 6–9 μm, and a shape ranging from ventricose-rostrate (broad in the middle and tapering to a beaklike neck) to mucronate (ending abruptly in a short sharp point). They are hyaline (translucent), thin-walled, and clamped, with necks that are 3–5 μm long. The pleurocystidia (cystidia on the gill face) are similar in shape to cheilocystidia, but narrower (4–8 μm wide), and usually have a shorter neck measuring 2.5–4 μm.  The cap cuticle is a cutis (characterised by hyphae that run parallel to the cap surface) of long-celled, 2–3 μm diameter, gelatinised hyphae. The hypodermium (the tissue layer under the cap cuticle) is filamentous, comprising 4–6 μm diameter cells with pale brown walls. Clamps are common. The subhymenium (the tissue layer under the hymenium) is poorly developed, containing 2–4 μm diameter cells with pale brown walls. The tissue comprising the hymenophore is made of short cylindric, 3–6 μm diameter hyaline cells.
P. makarorae contains the psychedelic compounds psilocybin and psilocin. Although the potency is not known definitely, Paul Stamets suggests that, based on the degree of the bluing reaction, they are "probably moderately potent".


Similar species
Psilocybe makarorae is related to Psilocybe weraroa and Psilocybe subaeruginosa, though not as closely as they are to each other.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small brown mushrooms with a bump in the centre of the cap, often more or less pointed, and both grow on fallen, rotting wood - P. makarorae on southern beech, and wood nipple fungus mainly on beech wood too - so shape and habitat do not separate them. Cap colour overlaps too: P. makarorae is yellow-brown to orange-brown, and wood nipple fungus ochre-yellow to bay or honey-coloured. Damage the cap or stem: P. makarorae stains greenish-blue, and no blue staining is recorded for wood nipple fungus. Look at the stem: wood nipple fungus has a well-developed ring, though in its close relative the ring often disappears with age. P. makarorae has only cobwebby veil remnants and never a complete ring. A spore print may help: wood nipple fungus drops cinnamon-brown, and Psilocybe prints generally run lilac-brown to dark purple-brown, though rusty-brown prints are known in at least one species. Wood nipple fungus has not been tested for toxins, but it sits in the group that includes the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same amatoxins.

habitat.text:
Psilocybe subaeruginosa grows solitary to gregarious from wood debris in Australian native forests, pine plantations and is occasionally observed growing on dung. The species is also known from Australian native and Eucalyptus forests, and famously in New Zealand on wood chip.
In New Zealand: most often in gardens mulched with wood chip, and now and then on rotted wood in native bush (psilverlinings.nz, restated).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe subaeruginosa' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
The cap averages 12–50 mm in diameter. It is conical to conic-convex with slightly inrolled edges when young, and becomes convex, often slightly upturned, sub-gibbous, or sometimes with a small acute umbo. It is slightly tacky. There may be veil remnants at the margin when young. Coloured yellow-brown to orange-brown, paler towards the margin, which is a little striate, hygrophanous, fading in drying to pallid biscuit brown or pale orange-yellow. The cap stains greenish blue with age or handling and the flesh inside is whitish. The gills are moderately close, pale smoky brown when young, violet-brown or brownish fuscous in age, with narrow pale edges, slightly ventricose, in three series, the middle reaching halfway to the stipe, with an adnate or broadly adnexed attachment and lines sometimes running down the stipe. The stipe is 25–70 × 2–3.5(-5) mm, tall and slender, equal or slightly wider towards the cap, finely vertically lined, mealy at the top with fine fibrils below, the base somewhat swollen or becoming a mass of mycelium, hollow inside, cartilaginous, pale whitish streaked with dark greyish brown, staining greenish blue, flesh brownish. A white cortinate partial veil soon disappears, leaving traces as a raised area around the upper stipe.
Taste and odour are farinaceous and the spore print is purple brown.
The cheilocystidia are 17–29 x 5.5–11 μm, hyaline, fusoid-ventricose, subpyriform or mucronate, often with an elongated neck at the apex which is 2–4.5 μm.  The pleurocystidia measure 22–47 x 6–16 μm and is shaped like the cheilocystidia and also hyaline. The spores are smooth, subellipsoid, with an apical germ pore, measuring (10) 13.2–14.3 (15.4) x 6.6–7.7 x 6–7.5 μm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Never separate these on one character. The Galerina is deadly-suspect and both grow on rotting wood. Look for a ring. Landcare describes the common NZ Galerina as having a well-developed ring on the stem, though in the related Galerina marginata the ring may disappear. P. subaeruginosa has only a short-lived cobweb-like veil that leaves at most a raised zone on the upper stem. Check the gills: cinnamon to rusty brown in the Galerina, pale smoky brown ageing to violet-brown in P. subaeruginosa. P. subaeruginosa's cap and stem stain greenish blue with age or handling. The related Galerina marginata is described as not bruising and unchanging when cut. Cap shape and colour do not separate them. Both have yellowish to orange-brown caps, and P. subaeruginosa can also have a small pointed centre. A spore print confirms it: P. subaeruginosa purple-brown, Galerina cinnamon-brown. The Galerina's toxicity is unknown, but it sits in the group containing the deadly Galerina marginata and is thought likely to contain amatoxins.

summary.text:
Psilocybe subaeruginosa is a species of agaric fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae described in 1927 and known from Australia and New Zealand.

It is common in southern parts of Australia from April to August. It is recorded as present in New Zealand, but DNA sequencing of collections so far indicates P. allenii and P. cyanescens there as well as P. subaeruginosa. Its tendency to live on wood chips, as well as on plants and in soil, contribute to the likelihood that these were the materials it was transplanted to the Northern Hemisphere on, and the transplantation led to a decrease in genetic diversity. This concept also led to the idea that they exist in disturbed areas, rather than natural.

warnings: Psilocybine and psilocine are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and New Zealand Police list magic mushrooms as Class A. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

Maximum penalties are six months' imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine for possession, and life imprisonment for supplying or manufacturing. This entry is here so you can recognise the species, not so you can collect it.

identification.text: Rosette of deeply lobed leaves with soft prickly margins, clasping the stem. Stems and leaves exude a white milky sap when broken. Small yellow dandelion-like flowers on a branched stem. The native S. kirkii is fleshier and coastal.

lookalikes.howToTell: Prickly sow thistle's leaves are firm and somewhat shiny, with prickly-spined teeth on wavy margins, and its upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded lobes. Common pūhā (Sonchus oleraceus) has soft leaves with small spine-tipped teeth, and its clasping leaf bases have pointed lobes. Rounded clasping lobes do not separate prickly sow thistle from native pūhā (Sonchus kirkii), whose upper leaves also clasp the stem with more or less rounded lobes; S. kirkii's leaves are thick, dull and blue-grey, with toothed margins that the Flora of New Zealand does not describe as prickly. In seed, prickly sow thistle's achenes are winged with smooth spaces between the ribs; S. oleraceus's are not winged and are finely wrinkled crosswise; S. kirkii's are winged, so the seed does not separate it from S. kirkii. Prickly sow thistle is edible: it is recorded as a popular Māori food (pūhā tiotio), and its young leaves are described as mild-flavoured; bruise the stems and wash out the bitter milky juice.
