identification.text:
Apparently acaulous perennial, but with underground stem above bulb;  bulb narrow-ovoid;  outer scales dark brown or blackish, ± shining, viscid, with inconspicuous nerves.  Lvs radical, 3-foliolate.  Petiole (1)–2–10–(20) cm long, hairy;  stipules 3–7 mm long, appearing as a broad wing, sometimes ciliate.  Lamina of leaflets sessile, somewhat unequal, the terminal larger and 10–35–(45) × 1–37–(45) mm, broadly obovate, sometimes broader than long, glabrous above, hairy beneath and densely marked with short, black, glandular dashes when dry; margins long-ciliate;  base cuneate;  apex rounded;  lateral leaflets somewhat asymmetric at base.  Fls solitary, erect;  peduncles 1–11 cm long, hairy.  Bracts 2–3 mm long, linear-subulate, usually in lower 1/2 of pedicel;  calli 0.  Sepals 6–7.5 mm long, elliptic, with longitudinal black streaks when dried, with dense long, white cilia, otherwise glabrous;  calli 0. Corolla forming a deep cup 2.5–4 × 2.5–3 cm, with a lower, tubular part; petals 2–4 cm long, ± suborbicular, glabrous except for ciliate margins; lower part yellowish;  limb usually rose or purplish, sometimes white flushed pink outside.  Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous;  filaments with broad membranous wing, often almost to apex in shorter stamens.  Styles < or > longer stamen whorl, hairy.  Capsule not seen.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. It has leafy stems, erect or lying along the ground, and its leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Purple wood sorrel: no stem shows above ground and the leaves all rise from the base. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size (red clover's c. 15–40 mm long, purple wood sorrel's 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm), leaflet tips (both can be rounded or blunt) or hairs (both usually have hairy leaf stalks and leaflet undersides).

summary.text: Oxalis purpurea is a species of flowering plant in the woodsorrel family known by the common name purple woodsorrel. It is native to southern Africa, including South Africa, but it is known on most continents as an introduced species. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant.

warnings: Do not eat. Sources describe this species as toxic because of the oxalic acid it contains, and no reliable source records it as food.

habitat.text: Purslane has an extensive distribution, assumed to be mostly anthropogenic (or hemerochoric), extending from North Africa and Southern Europe through the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent to Malesia and Australasia. The species status in the Americas is uncertain. In general, it is often considered an exotic weed, but there is evidence that the species was in Crawford Lake deposits (Ontario) in 1350–1539, suggesting that it reached North America in the pre-Columbian era. Scientists suggested that the plant was already eaten by Native Americans, who spread its seeds. How it reached the Americas is currently unknown.

Glabrous taprooted annual herb.  Stems reddish, prostrate to ascending, (5)–10–30–(45) cm long.  Lvs alternate to subopposite, fleshy, shiny, often red-tinged, obovate to oblong, cuneately narrowed to a short petiole, obtuse to almost retuse, (5)–10–15–(30) × (2)–3–8–(10) mm;  axillary hair-tufts short.  Fls < 1 cm diam., (1)–3–(7) in sessile terminal clusters soon overtopped by subapical branches, subtended by membranous, ovate-acuminate, pinkish bracts.  Sepals green, hooded, overlapping, fleshy, falling at fruiting, 5 mm long.  Petals yellow, soon falling.  Stamens 6–15;  anthers yellow.  Style branches 3–6. identification.text:
Radishes are annual or biennial brassicaceous crops grown for their swollen tap roots which can be globular, tapering, or cylindrical. The root skin colour ranges from white through pink, red, purple, yellow, and green to black, but the flesh is usually white. The roots obtain their color from anthocyanins. Red varieties use the anthocyanin pelargonidin as a pigment, and purple cultivars obtain their color from cyanidin. Smaller types have a few leaves about 13 centimetres long with round roots up to 2.5 cm in diameter or more slender, long roots up to 7 cm long. Both of these are normally eaten raw in salads. A longer root form, including oriental radishes, daikon or mooli, and winter radishes, grows up to 60 cm long with foliage about 60 cm high with a spread of 45 cm.
Radishes harvested at the proper time are crisp and mild  but become bitter and tough if  left in the ground too long. Leaves are arranged in a rosette. They have a lyrate shape, meaning they are divided pinnately with an enlarged terminal lobe and smaller lateral lobes. The white flowers are borne on a racemose inflorescence. The fruits are small pods which can be eaten when young.
The radish is a diploid species, and has 18 chromosomes (2n=18). It is estimated that the radish genome contains between 526 and 574 Mb.

identification.text:
Plants 1–3 m. tall, us. growing in large colonies, summer-green. Rhizome to 3–4 cm. diam., fleshy, with ∞ membr. scale lvs. Lf-sheath often > 30 cm. long; lamina 1–3 cm. wide, ± plano-convex at base, mesophyll spongy. Peduncle us. < lvs, c. 1 cm. diam. Infl. us. 30 cm. or more long, the female part ultimately c. 2.5 cm. diam., the male part narrower and either continuous with or separated ± widely from the female. Bracteoles in male part more ∞ than stamens, c. = anthers, narrow-linear proximally, broader at tip and there variously shortly laciniate, arising directly on axis and remaining ± curled up after fls fall. Male fl. almost sessile; filaments at first shorter than anther-width, elongating later; anthers 1–3, tipped with blunt extension of connective; pollen clear yellow, grains single. Bracteoles in female part very few, absent from many fls, c. = gynophore hairs, filiform except for a few-celled expansion at tip. Female fls very much smaller than male, several grouped on proximal part of a short compound pedicel. Ovary at fl. almost sessile, narrow-elliptic; style long, slender; stigma broader, spathulate, ± concave; gynophore hairs very ∞, barely reaching base of stigma, stiff, filiform, very narrowly clavate at tip. Gynophore elongating at fr. to 1–2 times style-length, hairs then confined to proximal third of gynophore and in groups or ± whorled; persistent stigmas brown. Carpodia oblong-obovate, tips just projecting between the hairs. Seed c. 1.2 mm. long, cuneate at base, truncate at tip, yellow. n = 30.
[From:  Moore and Edgar (1970) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 2.]

identification.text:
Perennial;  stems sparsely hairy below, moderately or densely hairy in upper parts, erect or decumbent, not rooting at nodes.  Lvs usually moderately hairy on petioles and undersurface of leaflets, ± glabrous or sparsely hairy on uppersurface;  petioles up to c. 200 mm long;  leaflets ovate, elliptic or obovate, usually obtuse, sometimes acute or slightly emarginate, rarely shortly mucronate, cuneate to obtuse at base, usually ± entire, usually with a crescentic spot toward base, c. 15–40 mm long; lateral veins thin and ± straight or somewhat recurved and thickened toward leaflet margin;  petiolules 1–2 mm long, ± equal;  stipules ovate-oblong, acuminate.  Infls terminal, spicate, globose to ovoid, usually sessile, ± = or > subtending lvs;  fls numerous, sessile; bracts 0, but an involucre present at base of infl. only and stipules of subtending lvs partly enfolding young infl.  Calyx moderately hairy, 10-veined, not inflated at fruiting;  throat open, with a ring of hairs; calyx teeth unequal, much < corolla, triangular with linear apex, spreading at fruiting;  upper teeth ± = tube;  lowest tooth up to 1.5–2× as long as other 4, much > tube; sinuses narrowly obtuse.  Corolla pink, purple-pink or rarely cream, persistent, 10–16 mm long.  Pod glabrous, straight, < calyx, thickened at apex, 2–3 mm long, 1-seeded;  seeds  c. 2 mm diam., with a blunt projection on one side.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Alsike's flower heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks longer than the leaves; red clover's head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, whose stipules partly wrap the young head. The Flora of New Zealand describes alsike's stems and leaves as hairless (one overseas source says its upper stem can be hairy); red clover's stems are sparsely hairy low down and moderately to densely hairy higher up, and its leaf stalks usually moderately hairy. Alsike's leaflets are described as unmarked, where red clover's usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base. Alsike's corolla is 5–10 mm long, red clover's 10–16 mm. Colour is not a safe test: alsike is usually pink, red clover pink to purple-pink and rarely cream. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: White clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes, and its flower heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks longer than the leaves; red clover's stems are erect or lie along the ground at the base but do not root at the nodes, they are hairy (sparsely low down, more densely higher up), and its flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it. White clover is more or less hairless. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base and white clover's often carry light or dark markings, so the mark will not separate these two — use the stems and the flower stalk. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: White clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Least yellow sorrel's thread-like stems creep and root at the nodes, often forming mats; red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, red clover's 15–40 mm long. Out of flower, leaflet size is a guide, as the published ranges do not meet. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually stalkless on the leaves beneath it, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Creeping wood sorrel's stems lie along the ground or rise a little and often root at the nodes; red clover's hairy stems stand erect or lie along the ground at the base and do not root at the nodes. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), red clover's 15–40 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. Its leaf stalks and leaflet undersides are usually moderately hairy, and its leaflets, c. 15–40 mm long, usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Red clover's leaflets are mostly larger, but the ranges meet at 15–16 mm, so use size only as a guide. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Purple wood sorrel: no stem shows above ground and the leaves all rise from the base. Each flower stalk, 1–11 cm long, carries a single flower forming a deep cup, its petals 2–4 cm long, usually rose or purplish, sometimes white, yellowish at the base. Red clover: its flowers come many together in a round to egg-shaped head, usually without a stalk, sitting among the top leaves, each a pea-type floret 10–16 mm long, pink, purple-pink or rarely cream. It has leafy stems, erect or lying along the ground, and its leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped mark towards the base. Out of flower, do not rely on leaflet size (red clover's c. 15–40 mm long, purple wood sorrel's 10–35 mm, up to 45 mm), leaflet tips (both can be rounded or blunt) or hairs (both usually have hairy leaf stalks and leaflet undersides). Whether purple wood sorrel is safe to eat is not settled; see its page.
lookalikes.name: Purple wood sorrel

preparation.text: Young leaves are harvested before the plant comes into flower and used in salads and soups, or cooked like spinach. They can also be dried, powdered and sprinkled over food. A delicate sweet herb tea is made from the fresh or dried flowers. The dried flowers and seed pods can be ground into a powder and used as flour.

recipes.method: A handful of young red clover leaves and 3 flower heads, 4 tbsp couscous, a quarter of a red pepper, half an onion, 2 cloves of garlic, the juice of half a lemon, 1 tbsp olive oil and salt. Make the couscous up and let it cool. Whisk the lemon juice, oil and salt into a dressing. Chop the leaves, pepper, onion and garlic finely, pull the flower heads apart, and fold everything through the couscous. Leave it to sit for 15 minutes before serving so the dressing soaks in.
recipes.title: Red clover tabbouleh

recipes.method: About 700 ml of flower heads, 1 litre of water, 250 ml lemon juice and 200 g sugar. Bring the flower heads and water to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Add the lemon juice and sugar and simmer another 5 minutes, stirring until the sugar has gone. Let it cool, strain the flowers out, and chill.
recipes.title: Red clover lemonade

recipes.method: About 500 ml of flower heads packed down, with no stems or leaves, 600 ml boiling water, 60 ml lemon juice, 800 g sugar and a sachet of pectin. Pour the boiling water over the flower heads and leave them to infuse overnight, then strain and press the liquid out. Bring the infusion, lemon juice, sugar and pectin to a rolling boil for about 20 minutes, testing on a cold saucer until it sets, then jar it hot.
recipes.title: Red clover jam

recipes.method: 500 ml brown or wild rice, 500 ml red clover florets pulled out of the flower heads, 125 ml butter and 1 tsp salt. Cook the rice in 1.5 litres of water until done. While it is still hot, mix in the florets, butter and salt, and serve hot. For a sweet version, add 125 ml honey and some chopped nuts; quinoa or another grain can stand in for the rice.
recipes.title: Red clover rice

recipes.method: 500 ml rice, 45 ml olive oil, 90 ml lemon juice, 1½ tsp salt, 6 spring onions minced, 250 ml walnuts or other nuts, 250 ml chopped dried fruit (raisins, cranberries, dates or apricots) and 500 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads. Cook the rice in 1.5 litres of water until done, without stirring it while it cooks or cools, and let it cool completely so it does not go sticky. Mix everything together thoroughly and serve chilled or at room temperature. Wild rice, alone or half and half with brown or white rice, makes it special; boil the wild rice separately, since it cooks in a different time, and mix the two once cooked.
recipes.title: Red clover rice salad

recipes.method: About 1 litre of red clover blossoms, 1 litre water, 4 cups (about 800 g) sugar and, if you like, half a lemon or orange chopped up, peel and all; leave the citrus out for the pure clover flavour. Put the blossoms and water in a pot and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, then turn off the heat, cover and leave overnight. Next day, strain and press the liquid out of the spent flowers. Add the sugar and citrus and heat slowly, stirring now and then, for several hours, until it has reduced to a thick, honey-like syrup, then bottle it in jars. It comes out brownish, like a light maple syrup; a tablespoon of beetroot or berry juice colours it. Makes a little over 500 ml.
recipes.title: Red clover blossom syrup

recipes.method: 250 ml wholemeal flour, 250 ml white flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder, 2 eggs, 60 ml oil, 125 ml honey or red clover blossom syrup, 500 ml milk and 250 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads. Mix the dry ingredients first, then add all the wet ingredients before mixing them in thoroughly, which keeps the batter from going lumpy. Add a little milk or flour until the batter pours but is not runny. Cook on an oiled griddle and serve with butter and red clover blossom syrup.
recipes.title: Red clover pancakes

recipes.method: 500 ml wholemeal flour, 3 tsp baking powder, 60 ml butter, 125 ml almonds, 125 ml buttermilk, 2 eggs, ¼ tsp almond extract and 375 ml red clover flowers pulled out of the flower heads. Whizz the flour, baking powder and almonds in a food processor until the almonds are chopped fine, add the butter and whizz again to a crumbly mixture, then add the eggs, buttermilk, almond extract and clover and whizz just until the dough forms a lump. Shape into biscuits and bake on an ungreased tray at 230 °C for 10–15 minutes, until golden brown. They are sweet, dessert-like biscuits; serve hot with butter and jam.
recipes.title: Red clover almond biscuits

recipes.method: Put a bunch of red clover blossoms and leaves in a large jar and cover them with water just brought to the boil. After about 15 minutes, strain out the flowers.
recipes.title: Red clover tea

recipes.method: Put red clover flowers in a jar with some mint, a few slices of lemon and lime, and anything else good to hand, fill it with water and stand it in the sun for a while.
recipes.title: Red clover sun tea

summary.text:
Trifolium pratense (from Latin prātum, meaning meadow), red clover, is a herbaceous species of flowering plant in the bean family, Fabaceae.
The red clover is native to Europe, Western Asia, and northwest Africa, but it has been naturalised in other continents, like North and South America. Specifically, the red clover was brought to Argentina and Chile over 100 years ago, although it is not clear how exactly it was introduced. Additionally, it has been introduced to New Zealand.

warnings: Due to its coumarin and flavonoid derivatives, T. pratense should be used with caution in individuals having coagulation disorders or prescribed with anticoagulation therapy.
Red clover contains isoflavones, also called phytoestrogens, which have structural similarity to estrogens.
Diseased clover, even if no symptoms of disease are visible, can contain toxic alkaloids.

edibleParts.text: Fruit - raw or cooked. The fruit can vary in colour - usually red in colour, it can range from white through to amber and is 5 - 20mm in diameter. Root - cooked. Young shoots - peeled and eaten raw or cooked like asparagus. They are harvested as they emerge through the ground and whilst they are still tender. A herb tea is made from the dried leaves.

identification.text:
Plants of Rubus idaeus are generally perennials, which bear biennial stems ("canes") from a perennial root system. In its second year (as a "floricane"), a stem does not grow taller, but produces several side shoots, which bear smaller leaves with three or five leaflets. In raspberries (various species of Rubus subgenus Idaeobatus), the drupelets separate from the core when picked, leaving a hollow fruit, whereas in blackberries and most other species of Rubus, the drupelets stay attached to the core.
Suckering, erect shrub, up to 1.5–(3) m high; stems erect when young, sometimes almost decumbent when older, terete, sparsely to densely hairy when young, soon becoming glabrous, somewhat pruinose, suckering by adventitious buds; armature of weak, ± terete, erect prickles, these often very numerous (rarely almost 0) on young stems and sometimes sparse on older stems. Lvs usually imparipinnate with 2–(3) pairs of leaflets, rarely pinnately 3-foliolate, rugose, glabrescent, sometimes with whitish bloom on upper surface, densely white-tomentose on lower surface, 1–2-serrate; terminal leaflet ovate to ovate-oblong, sometimes slightly lobed, up to 115 × 85 mm, acuminate, truncate to cordate at base, petiolulate; stipules linear. Infl. a few-flowered leafy raceme; axis and branches pilose and prickly. Fls 20–25 mm diam. Sepals long-triangular, acuminate, tomentose, paler on margins, deflexed at fruiting. Petals narrow, flat, white. Stamen filaments white. Fr. of waxy, red or orange drupelets, cylindric, up to 15 mm long.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk, where blackberry's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point; raspberry's are densely white-felted underneath. A ripe raspberry comes away from its core when picked and is hollow; a blackberry keeps its core.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Raspberry's leaves are pinnate, with side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; bush lawyer's are palmate, all leaflets spreading from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; bush lawyer is a climbing liane with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. Both can be white-felted underneath, so the felt does not separate them: count the leaflets and see how they are attached. Raspberry's are pinnate, side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; white-leaved lawyer's are palmate, usually three from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; white-leaved lawyer is a liane or a tangled mound with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: White-leaved lawyer

preparation.text: Aromatic and delicious when eaten out of hand, the fruit is also used in pies, preserves etc. The root, which should be neither too young nor too old, requires a lot of boiling.

recipes.method: Written for wild raspberries. Fills 2 jam jars. About 570 ml (1 UK pint) wild raspberries, pressed down, and about 285 ml (½ pint) sugar — half the volume of the berries. Put a small saucer in the freezer. Put the berries and sugar in a heavy-based pan, mash them gently with a potato masher and leave somewhere warm for half an hour so the sugar starts to dissolve in the juice; the author says this cold step keeps more of the flavour. Stir well, then heat on low to medium, stirring until the last of the sugar has dissolved. Bring to a gentle boil; once bubbles cover the surface, skim off the froth and boil for 12 minutes (longer for a bigger batch). Take off the heat and drop a blob on the cold saucer: as it cools it should set to jam. If not, boil 2 minutes more and test again. Pour into sterilised jars and seal with sterilised lids. It is ready once cool and keeps six months unopened in a cupboard. It uses about half the sugar of many jams.
recipes.title: Wild raspberry jam

recipes.method: Written for raspberries; the page names no species. Serves 6. 800 g raspberries, 55 g icing sugar plus extra for dusting, 2 teaspoons rosewater, 2 drops vanilla essence, the finely grated zest of ¼ lemon and 450 ml cream (35% fat). Put 300 g of the raspberries into 6 glasses. Blend 350 g more with the icing sugar to a thick purée, then stir in the rosewater, vanilla and lemon zest. Set aside 170 g of the purée and drizzle a generous tablespoon of the rest over the berries in each glass. Whip the cream to soft peaks and fold the reserved 170 g of purée through it. Share this between the glasses, spoon over the last of the purée, top with the remaining raspberries and dust with icing sugar. The original serves it with home-made sponge fingers (6 eggs, 180 g caster sugar, 180 g plain flour, piped and baked at 220 °C for 7–9 minutes); bought ones will do.

summary.text:
Rubus idaeus (raspberry, also called red raspberry or occasionally European red raspberry to distinguish it from other raspberry species) is a red-fruited species of Rubus native to Eurasia and commonly cultivated in other temperate regions.
In New Zealand it was first recorded wild in 1870. Flora of New Zealand (1988) lists it in the North Island at Hunua, Wellington City and the Hutt Valley, and in the South Island scattered through Canterbury's plains and foothills, Banks Peninsula and Mt Cook, at Gabriels Gully, Beaumont and Skippers in Otago, and in Southland's Eglinton Valley.

identification.text:
The yellow and green podetia form cushiony clumps up to15 cm tall. The branches may be isotomous (of equal length) or sometimes anisotomous (unequal). The trichotomous branches have perforate axils. The apothecia are terminal, brown, and convex. The surface is arachnoid, cobwebby, or cottony. The primary thallus is evanescent.
This species is known to contain usnic, perlatolic, and sometimes ursolic acids.

summary.text:
Cladonia confusa is a species of lichen, native to and found in New Zealand, Australia, Africa and South America.
In New Zealand, it is known from across both the North and South Island. It is also found on the Three Kings Islands. It is one of the most common lichens in the neotropics. It is found in Tasmania and South Australia, as well as on Lord Howe Island and Norfolk Island. It has also been found on the island of Réunion.

identification.text: The leaves are 30–60 cm long and 3–10 cm wide. The flower stalk often reaches one metre, and bears many white six-petalled flowers, in groups of two or three, each about 2 cm across. The stamens are tricoloured - purple and white, with yellow at the curled end. The roots are 2–3 cm wide.

identification.text: Rhizomes erect, up to 70 mm long (in herbarium material), bearing scales. Rhizome scales linear to narrowly ovate, 5–12 mm long, 0.4–0.7 mm wide, dark brown, concolorous. Fronds strongly dimorphic; sterile fronds 120–700 mm long, forming a prostrate to suberect rosette; fertile fronds on same plant usually a little shorter, 85–620 mm long, positioned centrally, held erect. Sterile fronds. Stipes 10–140 mm long, red-brown, bearing a few scales proximally. Rachises yellow-brown, grooved adaxially, glabrous. Laminae 80–600 mm long, 15–115 mm wide, or very rarely to 125 mm wide, deeply pinnatifid to pinnatisect, narrowly elliptic to narrowly obovate, with a short apical segment, similar colour on both surfaces, red-tinged when young, herbaceous to coriaceous, glabrous. Pinnae in 7–54 pairs, closely spaced, narrowly oblong or narrowly triangular or triangular, straight or falcate, gradually reducing to short, rounded flanges at the lamina base; the longest pinnae at or above the middle, 14–60 mm long, or very rarely only 8 mm long or up to 68 mm long, 6–15 mm wide, or rarely only 4 mm wide, apices usually acute or rarely obtuse, margins shallowly crenate, bases adnate; the basal pinnae sub-opposite or alternate. Veins free. Fertile fronds. Stipes 20–250 mm long. Laminae 40–530 mm long, 10–70 mm wide. Pinnae in 15–52 pairs, linear, straight or falcate, 5–40 mm long, 1–3 mm wide, reducing to tiny sterile flanges at the lamina base. Sori and indusia in one row either side of costa, continuous along the length of the pinna.

identification.text:
Dacrydium cupressinum (rimu) is a species of dioecious (either male or female) evergreen conifer in the family Podocarpaceae, and usually reaches 35 metres in height, but may reach up to 60 m tall, and can have a stout trunk up to 1.5–2 m in diameter. The trunk is usually cylindrical and smooth. D. cupressinum grows in an erect (occasionally forked), and usually a monopodial manner, meaning it grows from the main stem. When reaching its maximum height, it is typically unbranched for 20 m of its height. The tree exhibits a pyramid-like shape in the early growth stages, and the crown of mature trees evolves into a domed shape, with the main branches spreading outwards or ascending.
Its bark is grey to dark-brown in colour, shedding in large, elongated, thick flakes. When the outer layers of bark flake off, a distinctive wavy pattern of parallel raised ridges is visible on the new bark beneath. These lines of ridges have been described as resembling the contour lines on a topographic map. Areas of bark between the ridges have small pointed projections with porous tissue that allow air to penetrate the bark, providing oxygen to the cells of the tree beneath the bark. The wood is typically a dark-red colour, gradually becoming a yellow-brown colour after exposure to sunlight. D. cupressinum has an estimated lifespan of 600–800 years, but can reach 1000 years old, although some specimens examined at the foothills of Mount Ruapehu suggest it may live as long as 1200 years.
Dacrydium cupressinum is characterised by its drooping and hanging foliage. Juvenile branches are slender, with hanging branchlets. In adult specimens, there are fewer branches, which are spreading, and also have slender and hanging branchlets. The tree's leaves vary in colour from dark-green to bronze-green, red-green, or in some cases orange. They are typically a yellowish-green colour and about 4 mm long, and arranged in an overlapping pattern (imbricated). Juvenile leaves measure 4–7–(10) millimetres in length and 0.5–1 mm in width. They are acute, long and narrow, slightly curved, and vaguely sickle-shaped (subfalcate) in character. Subadult leaves are ascending and are 4–6 mm long. Adult leaves are similar, but they are flattened down (appressed), rigid, and are triangular in shape.
Like all conifers, D. cupressinum does not have flowers, but instead has cones (strobili); with male and female examples first seen on subadult specimens. In male specimens, cones are solitary or paired, terminal, measuring 5–10 mm, and are oblong in shape, producing yellow pollen. The tree's ovules (female reproductive structures) are solitary and at the tip of up-curved branchlets. Its receptacles (fleshy fruit-holding structures) form a cup that is red or deep-orange in colour and measures about 1–2 mm in length. The pollen cones are found at the tips of branches and are oval to oblong in shape, measuring 7–10 mm long and 4 mm wide. Each pollen-bearing leaf (microsporophyll) has a pointed tip, is green in colour, and is 2–2.5 mm long. At its base, it holds two yellow pollen sacs.
Fruiting takes over a year to mature and often coincides with the presence of young female cones. The fruits are most commonly seen between February and May. D. cupressinum is a morphologically distinctive species, although it is sometimes misidentified with the seedlings of Manoao colensoi, which instead have glossier, coarser leaves. The tree's seed cones grow at the ends of short, curved branchlets or on the sides, measuring about 6–10 mm long. The bracts (specialised leaves) attached are short and barely visible when the cones mature into a swollen, orange to red colour. The tree's seeds are ovoid in shape, dark brown to black in colour, slightly flattened, are tiny at about 4–5 mm long, and they ripen to a black colour. D. cupressinum has a genetic diploid chromosome count of 20.


Phytochemistry
In terms of chemical composition, the foliage of D. cupressinum contains various sesquiterpenes, with their levels showing significant variation between specimens, which is similar to the differences observed in diterpene levels. There are twelve known sesquiterpenes in the tree that have been identified by a 1985 study, but none of which show any structural similarity to lauren-1-ene. The distinctive diterpene lauren-1-ene was first discovered in the foliage of the tree, however, the concentration of this compound, along with other diterpenes, also shows significant variation between D. cupressinum specimens.
Dacrydium cupressinum contains high levels of the unique sesquiterpene terpene compounds of 9-epi-β-caryophyllene. The tree also has a distinctive flavonoid glycoside profile; the tree possesses flavonol-3-O-rhamnoglucosides and also, to a lesser extent, 3-0-methyl-myricetin glycoside compounds.

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Rimu' entry.

summary.text:
Dacrydium cupressinum, commonly known as rimu, is a species of conifer in the family Podocarpaceae, native to New Zealand.
Dacrydium cupressinum is known for exhibiting mast seeding, which is the synchronised periodicity of seed production. In the Pureora Forest and the Wanganui Forest, in the North Island and the South Island, respectively, seedfall data show clear yearly fluctuations in seed production in studied specimens. A 1988 study proposes that a combination of low seed production and cool temperatures two years before, followed by warm temperatures during seedfall are necessary, but not solely responsible for triggering a mast year in the tree. The relationship between seed production in one year and conditions from two years earlier also plays an important role. Canham et al. 2014 analysed D. cupressinum specimens growing in less fertile marine terrace sites had a higher seed production rate in comparison to specimens that grew on more fertile alluvial soils. Researchers suggested that the tree has adapted to seed production in less fertile soils rather than being displaced by other species.

habitat.text: It can be found in wet woodland — pond edges, boggy ground and stream banks — growing by poplars, silver birch, willows, alders or oaks. The New Zealand collections so far are under poplar, silver birch and goat willow.

identification.text: The cap is up to 6 cm, bright blood-red to carmine fading to apricot or ochre with age, and it is often cracked. The pores are pale yellow with an olive tint. The stipe is yellow, with fine red granules towards the base. The flesh is a pale yellow, red at the base of the stipe, and stains blue when injured.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bluefoot bolete's cap is usually ochre to brown, grey-brown or blackish brown, though it can have a reddish tint or be entirely red; riverine bolete's is bright red, carmine, dark red or reddish brown, often fading with age to apricot or ochre with a reddish tint. Cap cracking and blueing do not separate them: both caps often crack, both stain blue, and colour and cracking tend to intergrade between species in this group. Habitat may help: about half of bluefoot's New Zealand collections are under oak, and others under cedar, lime, beech, pine and silver birch; riverine bolete grows in wet woodland, and its New Zealand collections are under poplar, goat willow and silver birch.

summary.text: This is a mushroom that was introduced from Europe. It is one of four red-cracked boletes that have long been confused with each other.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Chamaemelum nobile' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Chamaemelum nobile has daisy-like white flowers and procumbent stems; the leaves are alternate, bipinnate, finely dissected, and downy to glabrous. The solitary, terminal flowerheads, rising 20–30 cm above the ground, consist of prominent yellow disk flowers and silver-white ray flowers. The flowering time in the Northern Hemisphere is June and July, and its fragrance is sweet, crisp, fruity and herbaceous.
Although the plant is often confused with German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), its morphology, properties and chemical composition are markedly different.

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

summary.text:
Chamaemelum nobile, commonly known as chamomile (also spelled camomile), is a low perennial plant found in dry fields and around gardens and cultivated grounds in Europe, North America, and South America.
Roman chamomile is native to Western Europe and the northwestern Maghreb, but has been introduced to a variety of areas outside its native range, where it has become naturalised. Its native range includes the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Algeria and the Azores. In Great Britain, it grows wild in Southern England and portions of Wales – primarily in Cornwall, Dartmoor, the New Forest and the Welsh coastline – with populations found north of Derbyshire considered to be naturalised.

edibleParts.text: Flowers - raw. Added to salads. The leaves are rose-scented and are used as a flavouring in desserts, jellies, vinegars etc. As a flavoring, the flowers and leaves are used in cakes, jams, jellies, ice creams, sorbets, salads, sugars, and teas.

identification.text:
Soft-wooded subshrub up to c. 75 cm tall, strongly aromatic, densely hairy. Stems with hairs deflexed. Stipules c. 1 cm long, ovate, acuminate. Petioles of lower lvs to > 8 cm long. Lamina to c. 7 × 10 cm on flowering plants, ± triangular, deeply divided into 3 lobes; lobes toothed and sinuate, rough above; 2 side lobes to c. 2 cm across, each with a secondary lobe near base; terminal lobe to c. 2.5 cm across, with a pair of secondary lobes. Umbels c. 10-flowered, densely covered in glandular hairs; peduncles 2–6 cm long; pedicels 1–6 mm long. Sepals 8–12 mm long, elliptic-lanceolate, green, densely hairy; calyx spur c. 3 mm long. Corolla pink; upper 2 petals 1–1.6 × 0.5–0.8 cm, with ± prominent purple markings and white central patch, and claw well developed; lower 3 petals 0.9–1.4 × 0.25–0.5 cm, with purple median line in lower 1/2, and claw not well differentiated. Style and stigmas becoming rose. Mericarps not seen.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Its parents are P. graveolens Aiton, which has a soft lf indumentum and broader lf lobes, and P. radens H. Moore (often known as P. radula) which has finely dissected lvs with linear lobes.

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium by its leaves (lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; a quarter to half way in peppermint geranium), and the two descriptions also differ in the flower stalks (1–6 mm against 2–3.5 cm). Peppermint geranium's flowers are white or pinkish, rose geranium's pink, so a pink flower does not separate them. A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; Flora of New Zealand calls rose geranium only "strongly aromatic". The leaf test works without flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.

preparation.text: The fresh leaves are brewed into a tea. The Herb Society of America guide says the leaves are mostly used to scent food and then taken out: a leaf added to apple jelly as it boils, or a green sprig dropped into a syrup, custard or jelly and lifted out as soon as it thickens, before the leaves break up; leaves can also be layered in sugar or flour to flavour baking. Finely chopped leaves can be flecked through cakes, biscuits and puddings — 15–30 ml (1–2 tablespoons) of chopped leaves is enough for most dishes that serve six. The guide advises using them sparingly so they do not overwhelm a dish.

recipes.method: Put 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and 10–12 rose geranium leaves in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup. Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The original uses it in a chocolate dessert.
recipes.title: Rose geranium syrup

recipes.method: Firmly pack about 125 ml of fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems. Bring them to the boil with part of 750 ml apple juice, take off the heat and steep for at least 15–20 minutes. Strain, add the rest of the juice and top up to 750 ml if needed. Put the juice in a heavy, large saucepan over high heat, add one packet of powdered fruit pectin and bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Add 1.2 kg sugar, keep stirring and bring back to a full rolling boil; boil hard for 1 minute, stirring all the time. Take off the heat, skim off the foam quickly and pour at once into sterilised jars — a whole leaf can be pressed into each jar. Seal and process for 5 minutes in a hot water bath, following the jar maker's instructions. Makes about eight 250 ml jars. The ingredient list also has 30 ml lemon juice, but the method does not say when it goes in. Use it to fill or glaze cakes, as a sauce for fresh fruit, or with poultry.
recipes.title: Apple and rose geranium jelly

recipes.method: Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Roughly chop 6–8 rose geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Serves 6. Put 250 ml cream (heavy cream in the original), 2 tablespoons finely chopped rose geranium leaves and about 50 g sugar in a metal bowl over a pot of simmering water. Stir until the sugar dissolves and the cream is hot but not boiling, about 5 minutes. Take off the heat, cool a little, then chill until cold, about 45 minutes. Strain and discard the leaves. Beat about 115 g softened cream cheese with the cream using an electric mixer until thickened but not holding peaks, about 2 minutes. Divide about 370 g blackberries and 225 g blueberries between six bowls or glasses and spoon the cream over. The cream can be beaten up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge.
recipes.title: Berries in rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Makes 8 wedges. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

sources: SPLIT 21/10/2026 from the catch-all draft `scented-geraniums` (Pelargonium spp.; Langlands, Peter. Identification, habitat, summary (verbatim unless marked): Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, 'Pelargonium ×asperum' factsheet, CC BY 3.0 NZ, retrieved 21/10/2026, https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Pelargonium-xasperum.html; Webb, C.J.; Sykes, W.R.; Garnock-Jones, P.J. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Pelargonium ×asperum', https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/54414bb3-a4f0-405b-84d3-2de4eebebabe, retrieved 21/10/2026 (Webb's stray space in "P. radula )" closed); Wikipedia contributors, 'Pelargonium graveolens', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169, retrieved 21/10/2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelargonium_graveolens.

Name: "Rose geranium" — NZ Flora Online and NZPCN give no vernacular ("Pelargonium hybrid"); Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens': "Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium", and its cultivated rose-scented P. 'Graveolens' is "possibly a hybrid between P. graveolens and P. radens or P. capitatum" — Webb's parents for P. ×asperum are P. graveolens × P. radens. That the cultivated rose geranium and Webb's P. ×asperum are the same plant is my reading, not a source's. iNaturalist calls it "Rose Storksbill". Close to "Rose-scented geranium" (P. capitatum), whose summary already says several species are called rose geranium.

Omitted on purpose: Webb's "It apparently spreads vegetatively - ripe mericarps have not been observed." — Colin Ogle's 2022 iNaturalist note on obs 231378051 (Whanganui) says "Commonly self-establishing from seed - becoming a weed in this garden!", and its photos show seedlings; a 1988 negative left out rather than contradicted.

Edibility, DECIDED 21/10/2026 (owner: "there are no edible parts and recipies") — option (1) of the earlier lead taken. Bridge: the Herb Society of America guide (2006) puts "P. graveolens and members of the P. 'Graveolens' cultivar group" among the culinary rose-scenteds, and says of that group "Members of this group were once classified as P. xasperum" — so the guide itself ties the culinary rose geranium to this name. Edible parts: Useful Temperate Plants 'Pelargonium graveolens' (Ken Fern, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Pelargonium+graveolens, retrieved 21/10/2026; cites Facciola, Cornucopia, and Bown; Known Hazards "None known") verbatim, citation markers dropped; Wikipedia 'Pelargonium graveolens' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1361378169) Uses sentence verbatim. Both are written for P. graveolens / cultivated rose geranium, not for P. ×asperum by name. Preparation: UTP tea sentence verbatim; the rest restated from the HSA guide's Culinary Uses section (Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay's kitchen tips, Susan Belsinger's "sparingly so that they don't overwhelm"), https://www.herbsociety.org/file_download/inline/2b2f9fc8-e827-446c-99da-1c1e8b6559d0. Not used: the guide's note that rose geranium oil is GRAS (oil, not leaves) and that "Most individual species, hybrids and cultivars do not have GRAS status". No warning added: no trusted source records a hazard for the leaves or flowers.

Recipes (all from the HSA guide above, © the named authors / HSA, all rights reserved — methods paraphrased, not quoted; written for "rose geranium" / "rose-scented geranium" leaves, which the guide does not tie to one species — that they suit this plant rests on the bridge above): 'Rose geranium syrup' — Susan Belsinger, the syrup in "Chocolate rose-scented soufflé", excerpted from Not Just Desserts (2005); 'Apple and rose geranium jelly' — Madalene Hill and Gwen Barclay, "Apple rose geranium jelly", The Flavour Connection (frozen apple juice "diluted according to directions" or bottled juice; the source lists 2 tablespoons lemon juice but never uses it in the method — said so on the page); 'Pineapple and rose geranium ice' — Ann Wilson, "Pineapple rose freeze". Conversions: 1 cup = 250 ml, 1 cup sugar ≈ 200 g, ½ pint jar ≈ 250 ml, 2 tbsp = 30 ml. Not used: the guide's other recipes (liqueur and wine: alcohol; couscous, lime curd and cooler: rose geranium is one herb among many).
Months: empty = year-round. The leaves and flowers are the parts used; Webb 1988 gives flowering Jan–Dec (FL Jan–Dec), so both are there through the year.

Origin checked 21/10/2026: NZ Organisms Register 'Pelargonium ×asperum' (https://data.nzor.org.nz/names/search?query=Pelargonium%20asperum): no biostatus record returned; NZPCN 'Pelargonium x asperum' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/pelargonium-xasperum/): Biostatus Exotic, year naturalised 1869; NZ Flora Online: Exotic. Origin 'introduced'. Kept introduced, not pest: not on DOC's List of environmental weeds in New Zealand 2024 (McAlpine & Howell, Science for Conservation 340, https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf; no Pelargonium in the text), and not in Wildland Consultants' table of weed taxa in every regional pest management plan (2021, Contract Report 5396 for the PCE, Appendix 2 p. 75, read by eye: Passiflora apetala is followed by Persicaria chinensis; https://pce.parliament.nz/media/fx4pjock/hutchison-et-al-review-of-weed-management-programmes-pdf-6mb.pdf).

Lookalike cards (rose-scented geranium, peppermint geranium and rose geranium, all three pairs both ways; written by the assistant on the owner's instruction, owner, 21/10/2026: "find what you can and fill in according to the rules for Pelargonium"): every test restates Webb, C.J.; Sykes, W.R.; Garnock-Jones, P.J. 1988, Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — the species descriptions and notes and the Pelargonium key (couplet 4: P. ×asperum "Lamina lobed to > 3/4 way to midrib"; couplet 6: P. tomentosum "Umbels diffuse; fls on long pedicels; calyx spur c. 2 mm long" against "Umbels dense; fls subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; couplet 7: P. capitatum "Habit sprawling; lvs strongly undulate, with ± oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina"), https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/b8f32527-4c30-4f9b-bab4-9155d157a597, retrieved 21/10/2026; plus Wikipedia 'Pelargonium capitatum' (CC BY-SA 4.0, revision 1195218505) for that species' scent and flower-colour range. Webb gives P. capitatum no full description, only a note and its key couplets, so its side of every card rests on those. Webb's key is inconsistent for P. capitatum (couplet 4 sends it down "Lf blade not lobed or lobed to < 1/2 way to midrib", couplet 7 says its lobes extend "at least 1/2 way") — the cards say lobing does not settle rose geranium against rose-scented geranium for that reason. Card risks: `edible` into all three — peppermint geranium from the start; rose geranium and rose-scented geranium since 21/10/2026, when their pages gained edible parts (a card is not more certain than its page). Not carded, no entry: P. vitifolium (Webb: "very closely-related" to P. capitatum and "often confused"; 0 wild iNaturalist NZ records 21/10/2026), the native kopata P. inodorum, P. ×fragrans. These cards clear `warnings` on all three pages with no warning text added. Corrected 21/10/2026 (owner: "check and double check all Pelargoniums"): the peppermint geranium ↔ rose geranium cards said the key separates them by leaves and flower stalks; couplet 4 uses the leaves only, so the stalk lengths are now credited to the species descriptions.

Owner's links, 21/10/2026, read and not used for page text: NZPCN 'Pelargonium xasperum' ("Pelargonium hybrid", Exotic, naturalised 1869, origin South Africa; its similar-taxa line "lamina lobed to > 3/4 way to midrib" is Webb's key couplet, already on the cards); NZ Flora Online 'Pelargonium ×asperum' (Webb's description, already used); PlantSnap 'Pelargonium asperum' (care-app page, no sources; its "small and white with pink markings" flowers contradict Webb's "Corolla pink" — not trusted); Jade Shutes, 'Pelargonium graveolens or Pelargonium x asperum', School of Aromatic Studies (ARR) — about commercial geranium oil, no food use; it quotes Kew and PROTA treating "Pelargonium asperum Ehrh. ex Willd." as a synonym of P. graveolens. Checked 21/10/2026: Catalogue of Life lists "Pelargonium asperum Ehrh. ex Spreng." as a synonym of P. graveolens, while GBIF's backbone accepts "Pelargonium × asperum Willd." (Webb's name) as its own taxon — two names sharing an epithet, so this does not show that Webb's hybrid is P. graveolens and does not settle the edibility LEAD above.

summary.text:
This hybrid is very commonly cultivated and is the commonest of the scented-leaved geraniums to occur wild. In New Zealand it grows wild in coastal areas and on offshore islands of the North Island, and in the South Island at Nelson City, Gore Bay (North Canterbury) and Banks Peninsula; it was first recorded growing wild here in 1869. Most plants grown in N.Z. as P. graveolens are hybrids or represent other spp.
Many plants are cultivated under the species name "Pelargonium graveolens" but differ from wild specimens as they are of hybrid origin (probably a cross between P. graveolens, P. capitatum and/or P. radens). Both the true species and the cultivated plant may be called rose geranium – pelargoniums are often called geraniums, as they fall within the plant family Geraniaceae, and were previously classified in the same genus.

edibleParts.text: Leaves, as a flavouring. SANBI (South African National Biodiversity Institute) names this plant among the rose-scented pelargoniums and says pelargonium leaves can be used to flavour puddings, jams, soft drinks and alcoholic drinks. Kew also records it as used for food. Neither source says more than that for this species on its own.

habitat.text: Its habitat is usually beach sand or other well-drained sandy soils. Its preferred habitat is on sand dunes, but it is a fast grower on any reasonable base, including hard clayey soil, so it readily colonises disturbed habitat.

identification.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is a low shrub up to about 100 cm in height and 1.5 m across. The stems are soft and coated in green, glandular hairs. Brushing against a bush releases a copious scent of the essential oil from damaged hairs. The scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. The flowers range from white through various shades of pink to purple.
P. capitatum differs from P. vitifolium in its sprawling habit, more undulate and velvety lvs, generally lobed more than 1/2 way to the midrib, and the typically more compact infl. The fls are very similar to those of P. vitifolium with the corolla irregular and the petals oblanceolate and pink with the larger upper pair marked purple.
Flora of New Zealand key: "Umbels dense; fls subsessile; calyx spur 4-5 mm long"; "Habit sprawling; lvs strongly undulate, with ± oblong lobes extending at least 1/2 way to the centre of the lamina".
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Peppermint geranium is a subshrub to about 75 cm that smells strongly of peppermint, with more or less velvety white hairs and broad leaves up to 12 × 15 cm, rather shallowly three-lobed, the lobes reaching a quarter to half way to the midrib; its flowers are white or pinkish, 5–8 to an umbel, on stalks 2–3.5 cm long that generally radiate widely, with a calyx spur about 2 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them by the umbels (diffuse, with long flower stalks, in peppermint geranium; dense, with almost stalkless flowers, in rose-scented geranium) and the calyx spur (about 2 mm against 4–5 mm). Leaf lobing meets at about half way, so it does not settle a plant on its own. Both plants are hairy, and flower colour does not separate them (Wikipedia gives rose-scented geranium white through pink to purple flowers). A crushed leaf of peppermint geranium smells strongly of peppermint; rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Most of these tests need flowers.
lookalikes.name: Peppermint geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Rose geranium (P. ×asperum) is a strongly aromatic, densely hairy subshrub to about 75 cm, with more or less triangular leaves up to about 7 × 10 cm that are deeply divided into 3 toothed lobes, lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib and rough above; its pink flowers, the upper 2 petals with more or less prominent purple markings and a white central patch, sit about 10 to an umbel on stalks 1–6 mm long, with a calyx spur about 3 mm long. Rose-scented geranium is a sprawling plant whose leaves are strongly undulate and velvety, generally lobed more than half way to the midrib, with more or less oblong lobes; its pink flowers, the larger upper pair of petals marked purple, sit in dense heads on almost no stalks, with a calyx spur 4–5 mm long. Flora of New Zealand's key separates rose geranium first, by leaves lobed more than three-quarters of the way to the midrib; rose-scented geranium's lobes reach at least half way, and the key's other branch says "lobed to < 1/2 way", so a leaf cut between half and three-quarters is not decided by lobing alone. The calyx spur is a little longer in rose-scented geranium (4–5 mm against about 3 mm). Both have short-stalked heads of pink flowers with purple-marked upper petals, so the flowers do not separate them; rose geranium's leaves are described as rough above, rose-scented geranium's as velvety. Smell does not separate them: rose geranium is strongly aromatic and rose-scented geranium's scent varies from faint sweetness to a strong rosy scent. Flora of New Zealand notes that P. ×asperum is a hybrid of P. graveolens and P. radens; Wikipedia says P. capitatum hybridises readily, so in-between plants are possible and this card may not decide them.
lookalikes.name: Rose geranium

preparation.text: No source gives a method written for this species. The Herb Society of America guide's general advice for rose-scented pelargoniums is to steep the leaves in the syrup, jelly, custard or drink and lift them out before the leaves break up, and to use them sparingly so they do not overwhelm the dish.

recipes.method: Written for "rose-scented geranium" leaves without naming a species. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose-scented geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up). Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.
recipes.title: Pineapple and rose geranium ice

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose-scented geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil. Take off the heat and cool. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.
recipes.title: Rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Roughly chop 6–8 rose-scented geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it. Strain the juice over it. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose-scented geranium leaves and caster sugar. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.
recipes.title: Rose geranium sugar

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose-scented geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour). Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.
recipes.title: Rose geranium lemonade

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Serves 6. Put 250 ml cream (heavy cream in the original), 2 tablespoons finely chopped rose-scented geranium leaves and about 50 g sugar in a metal bowl over a pot of simmering water. Stir until the sugar dissolves and the cream is hot but not boiling, about 5 minutes. Take off the heat, cool a little, then chill until cold, about 45 minutes. Strain and discard the leaves. Beat about 115 g softened cream cheese with the cream using an electric mixer until thickened but not holding peaks, about 2 minutes. Divide about 370 g blackberries and 225 g blueberries between six bowls or glasses and spoon the cream over. The cream can be beaten up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge.
recipes.title: Berries in rose geranium cream

recipes.method: Written for rose-scented geraniums without naming a species. Makes 8 wedges. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours. Let it soften a little. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose-scented geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose-scented geranium leaves.
recipes.title: Rose geranium shortbread

recipes.method: Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named. Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.
recipes.title: Scented geranium and lemon icing

summary.text:
Pelargonium capitatum is one of several species (including Pelargonium graveolens) known as rose geranium or rose-scented pelargonium in English.
It is found in fynbos along the coast of South Africa, from Lamberts Bay in the Western Cape east to Kwazulu-Natal.
It is a popular and convenient ornamental plant and it also is one of the species of Pelargonium cultivated as a source of essential oils.
Pelargonium capitatum is one of a number of related plants that have become a major problem in coastal regions of southwest Western Australia, where it invades banksia woodland and coastal heathland.
P. capitatum, rose-scented geranium, is occasionally wild in the Hokianga area of N. Auckland, as well as there being unconfirmed reports from Nuhaka, Poverty Bay and Napier. It seems to be less common in cultivation than the very closely-related P. vitifolium and the 2 spp. are often confused. P. capitatum is the main sp. used for the production of oil of geranium.

edibleParts.text: The flesh of the ripe hip only.

habitat.text: Dry hill country, riverbeds and farmland, especially Marlborough, Canterbury and Central Otago.

harvestEthics.text: A declared pest in several South Island regions. Harvest freely.

identification.text: Thorny arching shrub with compound leaves that smell of green apple when crushed. Pink single flowers, followed by bright orange-red oval hips.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_hip Corroborates both warnings almost word for word: hips 'can be eaten raw, like berries, if care is taken to avoid the hairs inside the fruit. These urticating hairs are used as itching powder' — so the itching-powder line on this page is literal, not a figure of speech — and 'It is often recommended to harvest rose hips after a first frost has softened the fruits for a sweeter flavor.' Hips are used in bread and pies, jam, jelly, marmalade, syrup, soup, tea and wine.

identification.text: Bulb 2 × 1.5 cm, tunic scarious, outermost layer with prominent round pits, whitish-grey with stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves 2–4, c. 35 × 1 cm, flat < scape, light green to ± glaucous; sheaths reddish-purple. Scape 30–60 cm high, cylindrical, sheathed by leaves at base. Umbels 5–8 cm diam., ± lax, with flowers and bulbils; pedicels 4–6 times length of flowers, or longer; spathe-valve 1, persistent. Flowers 10–12 mm long, ± 12 mm diam., pale pink, with deeper pink central nerves; segments ± oblong, obtuse, margins slightly dentate. Stamens c. ⅔ length of perianth; filaments entire, without appendages. Bulbils c. 5 mm long, becoming reddish, shining. Capsule not seen.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's flowers are white with a green stripe down the centre of each segment; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves. Onion weed's flower stalk is sharply three-angled; rosy garlic's is round in section. Onion weed's umbel has no bulbils; rosy garlic carries bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among its flowers. Onion weed's leaves are strongly channelled; rosy garlic's are flat. The onion-garlic smell, a flower stalk of similar height (20–60 cm against 30–60 cm) and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's flowers are pure white; rosy garlic's are pale pink with deeper pink central nerves, with bulbils about 5 mm long, becoming reddish, among them. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles and a third more rounded one; rosy garlic's is round in section. Flat leaves, the garlic smell, an umbel 5–8 cm across and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Wild garlic's leaves are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical; rosy garlic's are flat. Wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long; rosy garlic carries a loose umbel 5–8 cm across of pale pink flowers 10–12 mm long. Both carry bulbils in the flower head and both smell of garlic, so bulbils and smell do not separate them.

summary.text:
Allium roseum, commonly called rosy garlic, is an edible, Old World species of wild garlic.
It is native to the Mediterranean region and nearby areas, with a natural range extending from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey and the Palestine region. It is cultivated widely, and has become naturalised in scattered locations in other regions outside its natural range.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand) the plant recorded is subsp. bulbiferum, which carries bulbils among its flowers: N. Auckland City; Gisborne - Tahunga. S Canterbury - Christchurch. Of the other subspecies (Useful Temperate Plants): The sub-species Allium roseum roseum does not produce bulbils.

warnings: Although no individual reports regarding this species have been seen, there have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of certain members of this genus. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

identification.text:
Slender tufts. Corm c. 1 cm diam., globose, rounded at base where smooth brown tunic splits into acuminate teeth bent to one side. Leaves 10–30 cm × 1–2 mm, rush-like, compressed-cylindrical, narrowly grooved, dark shining green. Scapes hidden by sheathing leaf-bases, 2–4–(10) from each corm, 5–15 cm long, stouter than leaves, semiterete, arched over after flowering; spathe-valves 2, long-persistent, outer longer, greenish with fine brown veins, inner with membranous reddish-brown flecked margins. Flowers lilac-pink, rosy-cerise or magenta, with yellow centre and violet-blue band at throat, 1.5–2 cm long, to 3 cm diam.; tube very short; outer lobes greener on back than inner. Capsules c. 1cm long, short-cylindrical, scapes straightening when capsules mature. Seeds 2 mm long, reddish-brown, globose-triangular.
[From:  Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

Plant to c. 80 cm tall, very scabrid.  Roots becoming very thick.  Basal lvs with lamina very large, ovate to oblong; upper side especially densely covered with rigid, bulbous-based hairs; base cuneate to subcordate; cauline lvs similar but smaller, with the narrowly winged petiole not decurrent on stem; uppermost lvs subsessile or with short petiole. Corolla 12 - 17 mm long, light purple or purplish blue at first, becoming blue, especially when dried; lobes c. 1 mm long, rounded; scales narrowtriangular.  Filament width usually < anther width except at base; anthers = or shortly projecting beyond scales.  Nutlets 3–5 mm long, finely rugose or granular.

habitat.text:
It is widespread from plains to mountains up to the tree line where it grows as the only deciduous tree species among krummholz. In the Alps it grows at elevations of up to 2,000 m. S. aucuparia appears north of the boreal forest at the arctic tree line; in Norway, it is found up to the 71st parallel north.
S. aucuparia is an undemanding species and can withstand shade. It is frost hardy and can tolerate winter dryness and a brief growing season. The plant is also resistant to air pollution, wind, and snow pressure. It mostly grows on soil that is moderately dry to moderately damp, acidic, low on nutrients, sandy, and loose. It often grows in stony soil or clay soil, but also sandy soil or wet peat. The plant grows best on fresh, loose, and fertile soil, prefers average humidity, and does not tolerate saline soil or waterlogging. It can be found in light woodland of all kinds and as a pioneer species over fallen dead trees or in clearcuttings, and at the edge of forests or at the sides of roads. The seeds germinate easily, so the plant may appear on inaccessible rock, ruins, branch forks, or on hollow trees.
