identification.text:
Tree up to 8–(12) m high, usually with an erect trunk and spreading branches;  young shoots pilose, sometimes densely so, but soon becoming glabrate.  Buds large;  outer scales glabrous, purplish, inner scales densely covered with white hairs towards apex.  Lvs imparipinnate with up to 8 pairs of leaflets;  petiole 20–35–(45) mm long, green or brown to purplish, pilose, but hairs deciduous, sometimes with stalked glands; leaflets (excluding smaller ones near base) narrowly oblong or  oblong-elliptic, sometimes lanceolate-elliptic, (20)–30–50–(60) × 8–20–(25) mm, obtuse to acute, ± sessile, deep green and glabrous or finely hairy above, paler and finely to densely pilose below, serrate along whole length or sometimes in upper ⅔ only; leaflets of juvenile plants and suckering shoots narrowly elliptic to elliptic-ovate, deeply and jaggedly toothed; stipules ± deciduous, small, acuminate.  Infl.  drooping, up to  c. 120 mm across; pedicels and branchlets white-villous, becoming glabrate by fruiting.  Sepal lobes broadly triangular, 0.6–1.3 mm long, obtuse, white-villous, at least at base, sometimes glabrous in upper part;  margin with several short glandular teeth.  Petals 3–4.5 mm diam., ± orbicular with abbreviated claw, white.  Fr.  depressed-globose, sometimes  ± oblong-obovoid, 5–10 mm diam., deep orange to scarlet, sometimes crimson, glossy.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Sorbus aucuparia, commonly called rowan (, also UK: ) and mountain-ash, is a species of deciduous tree or shrub in the rose family.
Sorbus aucuparia is found in five subspecies:

Sorbus aucuparia subsp. aucuparia: found in most of the species' range, less in the South
Sorbus aucuparia subsp. fenenkiana (Georgiev & Stoj.): has thin, sparsely hairy leaflets and depressed-globose fruit, restricted to Bulgaria
Sorbus aucuparia subsp. glabrata (Wimm. & Grab.): less hairy, found in Northern Europe and Central European mountains
Sorbus aucuparia subsp. praemorsa (Guss.): has hairy leaflets and ovoid fruit, found in Southern Italy, Sicily, and Corsica
Sorbus aucuparia subsp. sibirica (Hedl.): nearly hairless, found in North Eastern Russia
It can be found in almost all of Europe and the Caucasus up to Northern Russia and Siberia, but it is not native to Southern Spain, Southern Greece, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands, the Azores, and the Faroe Islands. The species was introduced as an ornamental species in North America.
It has naturalised in America from Washington to Alaska and eastward in Canada and the northeast of the US very successfully.
The tallest S. aucuparia in the United Kingdom stands in the Chiltern Hills in South East England. This exceptional specimen is 28 m tall and has a trunk diameter of 56 cm. The stoutest is in the Scottish Highlands near Kingussie, with a girth of 4.31 m (approximately 1.37 m diameter); another near Stapleton in Herefordshire is almost as stout at 4.29 m girth. In Germany, an unusually large specimen is located near Wendisch Waren, a village in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. This tree stands at more than 15 m tall, is around 100 years old, and has a diameter of 70 cm. The tallest known specimen in Ireland is an 18 m tall specimen at Glenstal Abbey, County Limerick.

habitat.text: It is most commonly found with pine trees, but can also appear with birch, conifer, or spruce.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lactarius rufus' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text: The cap is up to 10 centimetres in diameter. It is dark brick, bay, or red-brown.  At first it is convex, and often has a small central boss (umbo), but later flattens, eventually acquiring a shallow central depression. The surface is dry and matt. The concolorous, but paler  stem  often becomes hollow with age. The gills are slightly decurrent, cream, becoming coloured as the cap later, only paler. The spore print is creamy white, with a slight salmon tinge. The flesh is white, as is the (abundant) milk, which tastes mild initially, gradually becoming very hot, and acrid after a minute or so.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.

Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-rufus.php Cap 4–10 cm, dark reddish brown, dry and finely matt and slightly sticky when wet, convex then funnel-shaped, often with a small central umbo; gills pale reddish cream, weakly decurrent, crowded, going blotchy with age; stem 4–9 cm by 5–20 mm, no ring; latex watery white; spores 6.5–9 × 5.5–6.5 µm; spore print pale cream with a slight salmon-pink tinge; no distinctive smell; taste mild at first, then extremely hot and acrid. Coniferous woodland on acid soil, typically under pines and occasionally under birch. Inedible in most western sources; dried and powdered after thorough cooking as a seasoning in Scandinavia and Russia. Lactarius subdulcis is similar but smaller and grows under beech.

Why this one shares saffron milk cap's ground, and the test that still separates them. First Nature puts it in coniferous woodland 'typically under pines' on acid soil — the same plantation floor saffron milk cap is gathered from, so place cannot be used to rule it out the way it can for the beech and oak milk caps. The latex does: watery white and unchanging, then extremely hot, against saffron milk cap's carrot-orange bleed. Checked 06/10/2026.

summary.text:
Lactarius rufus is a common, medium-sized member of the mushroom genus Lactarius, whose many members are commonly known as milkcaps.

It is frequent in the northern temperate zones in Europe and North America. It is common in northern California, and the Pacific Northwest from late summer to early winter.

warnings: Not recommended for eating: it carries toxins that may cause gastric upset and may be poisonous raw. It is eaten in Scandinavia after canning and was one of Finland's most harvested wild mushrooms, but no amount of that makes it a beginner's mushroom here.

edibleParts.text: Firm young caps.

habitat.text: Exclusively under pine, in plantation forest and shelter belts. Never in native bush.

harvestEthics.text: Cut rather than pull, and leave the smallest and the largest.

identification.text: Orange cap with darker concentric rings, often depressed in the centre. Orange gills that bruise dull green. The confirming test: cut the flesh and it bleeds bright carrot-orange latex, and the cut surface slowly stains green. Brittle, not fibrous, flesh. Test every cap for latex rather than reading the cap: other milk caps are zoned the same way, so the cap alone tells you nothing, and a spore print will not separate them either — the prints run white to ochre across the genus, this one's cream included.

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. Coconut milk cap's milk is white, rather watery and unchanging, its cap is greyish lilac, pale greyish brown or brownish grey with leaden tints rather than orange, and it smells of coconut - faintly, in the New Zealand description. It grows under silver birch; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.
lookalikes.name: Coconut milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Downy milk cap's milk is white and does not change colour or stain the flesh. Downy milk cap's cap margin is rolled in and bearded with coarse white hairs when young, and the cap is white to cream, reddening at the centre with age. Saffron milk cap's cap is orange to salmon, with an incurved margin. In New Zealand and Australia, downy milk cap grows with birch, saffron milk cap only with pine. Downy milk cap's milk and flesh taste acrid, and some authors consider it toxic.
lookalikes.name: Downy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, does not change, and dries pale cream, though its cut flesh slowly runs from white through pink, salmon and orange-red to wine red. Its cap is dark brown to almost black and unzoned, often with dull salmon patches near the centre. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: New Zealand milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Oakbug milkcap's milk is white or cream. Its cap is dull, matt reddish brown with a cinnamon tint and stays dry, not sticky, when moist, and it has a strong oily smell likened to bedbugs or wet laundry. In Europe it grows only with oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Both can show concentric zones on the cap, so zoning is not the difference.
lookalikes.name: Oakbug milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and abundant. Its cap is dark brick, bay or red-brown, dry and matt, often with a small central boss, which can sit in a shallow depression on older caps. Both grow under pine, so habitat does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rufous milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Slimy milkcap's milk is white and plentiful and dries grey, and its cut gills turn grey-buff. Its cap is drab greenish-grey or olive-grey with rings of darker blotches, and slimy in wet weather. In Europe it grows with beech, very occasionally oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine. Its taste is bitter and hot.
lookalikes.name: Slimy milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, sticky and unchanging, drying cream. Both species have zoned caps, so zoning does not separate them. Tawai's cap is a dull orange-brown or drab ochre with purplish-grey to reddish-brown bands. It is endemic, and recorded under beech.
lookalikes.name: Tawai milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine. Its milk tastes acrid, and it is reported to contain carcinogenic compounds.
lookalikes.name: Ugly milkcap

lookalikes.howToTell: Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and unchanging, drying cream. Its cap is small, 1-3.5 cm across, where saffron milk cap's is 3-20 cm, so a small saffron cap can overlap. It is a dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned. It is an endemic of beech forest.
lookalikes.name: Umere milkcap

preparation.text: Dry-fry or roast hard — they release a lot of water and go slimy if cooked gently. Do not eat raw.

recipes.method: 12 medium caps, 15 ml olive oil, salt and pepper. Brush the caps clean — rinse only if they are really dirty — and pat them dry. Cut them to size, or leave the small ones whole. Get the oil hot in a skillet over medium-high, add the mushrooms, season, and stir now and then for about 5 minutes until they have shrunk down and cooked through. Serve hot alongside something else.
recipes.title: Sautéed saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 250 g caps, cleaned and sliced, 200 ml sherry or red wine vinegar, 200 ml water, 100 g sugar, 50 ml olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 5 black peppercorns, 3 cloves garlic, 3 juniper berries, 2 bay leaves, a sprig each of rosemary and thyme. To clean them first, soak them in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Bring everything but the mushrooms to the boil, add them, and simmer one minute. Off the heat, let it cool, then pack into a sterilised jar with the liquid above the mushrooms. Keeps up to 6 months in the fridge as long as they stay covered.
recipes.title: Pickled saffron milk caps

recipes.method: 400 g caps sliced, 4 cloves garlic chopped, oil, 80 ml white wine, 125 g cream cheese, 3 tbsp sour cream, 2 sage leaves, 2 sprigs thyme, salt and pepper, 1 sheet butter puff pastry, 1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tsp water. Fry the garlic a minute in oil over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook 5 minutes, adding oil as they take it. Stir in the wine, cream cheese, sour cream, sage and thyme and cook until creamy and tender, then season and cool completely — this can be done a day ahead. Heap the filling down the centre of the pastry sheet, seal the edges with the egg wash, press the ends with a fork, and bake at 220 °C for 30 minutes until golden.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap, sage and thyme strudel

recipes.method: An onion and 2 cloves garlic, finely diced, oil, 50 g butter, 3 tbsp flour, 200 g sliced caps, 3 tsp paprika, 600–700 ml chicken stock, 60 ml sour cream, parsley. Fry the onion and garlic in oil a few minutes until translucent, melt the butter into them, then stir in the flour. Add the mushrooms, paprika and stock and simmer about 10 minutes until the mushrooms are done. Serve with a spoonful of sour cream and parsley.
recipes.title: Hungarian mushroom soup

recipes.method: 125 ml olive oil, 2 tbsp butter, 300 g caps with the stems off and thinly sliced, 3 sprigs thyme, an onion, 105 g arborio rice, 1 litre chicken stock, a pinch of saffron, 165 ml dry white wine, 125 ml cream, 25 g blue cheese. Sauté the mushrooms in half the oil with the butter over medium-high until coated, season, and set aside. Soften the diced onion in the rest of the oil over medium heat for 5–8 minutes without browning, while the stock warms with the saffron in another pan. Stir the rice through the onion, then add the hot stock a ladle at a time, letting each one absorb, for 15–20 minutes until the rice is cooked. Stir in the wine, blue cheese and cream, fold through half the mushrooms, and season. Plate it with the remaining mushrooms on top and chopped chives or parsley.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap risotto

recipes.method: Pastry: 480 g plain flour, 150 g cold cubed butter, 240 ml finely grated parmesan, 2.5 ml fine salt, 1 egg, 120–160 ml ice water. Filling: 5 caps, 4 cloves garlic sliced, olive oil, 150 g ash brie sliced, 3 eggs, 240 ml cream, 240 ml parmesan, 2 sprigs thyme. Clean the mushrooms in 1.4 litres of water with 120 ml white vinegar. Pulse the flour, butter, cheese and salt in a food processor, add the egg and 120 ml water and run it until it starts to come together, then knead on a floured bench with more water if it needs it and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature. Line an oiled 31 × 21 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, trim, and chill 45 minutes or freeze 15. Meanwhile fry the garlic then the mushrooms — whole if small, sliced if not — in oil over medium heat only until they keep their bright orange, then season and cool a little. Blind bake at 200 °C under oiled foil and weights for 20 minutes, then 10–15 minutes uncovered. Drop the oven to 150 °C, whisk the eggs, cream and parmesan, pour it into the case, arrange the mushrooms and brie on top with the thyme, and bake 30–35 minutes until just set. Serve warm.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and ash brie tart

recipes.method: 500 g desiree potatoes, 125 g Italian 00 flour plus extra for the bench, 40 g chestnut flour (or just more 00), 2 tbsp oil, an onion sliced, 2 cloves garlic sliced thinly, 250 g caps with the stalks off and sliced, 150 g bacon or prosciutto (optional), 100 g roasted and peeled chestnuts, 100 g butter, salt and pepper. Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender, rice them, and cool completely before working the flours in. Roll the dough into logs, cut it into pieces, and shape each one against a fork. Boil them and lift them out as they float. Fry the onion and garlic until fragrant, add the mushrooms until the edges crisp, then the bacon, chestnuts and butter. Add the drained gnocchi and fry until golden all over, then season.
recipes.title: Saffron milk cap and chestnut gnocchi

Season. Plant & Food Research gives a January-to-May season for Lactarius deliciosus under Pinus radiata here; iNaturalist NZ holds only 11 research-grade records and they run March to July, peaking in May. March to June is where the two overlap, and is what this entry lists. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/155197

Which other New Zealand milk caps have zoned caps: Lactarius quietus ('darker concentric bands or spots'), L. blennius ('blotches of darker colouration in concentric bands') and the endemic L. tawai ('distinctly or indistinctly concentrically zonate'). The first two from Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; the third from McNabb (1971) via the Virtual Mycota, restated. Checked 06/10/2026.

The eleven Lactarius taxa on record in New Zealand: Lactarius rufus, L. pubescens, L. turpis, L. glyciosmus, L. tawai, L. novae-zelandiae, L. umerensis, L. deliciosus, L. blennius, L. quietus, and the undescribed Lactarius sp. 'Hauroko' (6 records, no published name). All ten named species have entries here. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/observations?taxon_id=54597&place_id=6803&view=species

Downy milk cap belongs on the list of zoned caps too, which is why that count went from three to four. First Nature describes Lactarius pubescens with 'faint pinkish concentric bands and pinkish-brown centre zone' — fainter than this species' banding, but present, and it is a do-not-eat entry. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-pubescens.php

summary.text: The best beginner's mushroom in NZ — it bleeds bright orange, and nothing dangerous does.

warnings: Eleven Lactarius species are on record in New Zealand and this is one of them; others are undescribed or unnamed, and related milk-bleeding genera grow here too. Any milk cap bleeding white, cream or watery latex is a different species — the acrid ones announce themselves on the tongue, but several cause vomiting and diarrhoea, and ugly milk cap contains a mutagen that boiling does not remove.
Only harvest from pine. A mushroom that looks similar in native forest is not this species.
Many plantation forests are private land or actively logged — get permission and check for harvesting operations.
Some plantations are aerially sprayed. Check with the forest manager.

identification.text:
Herb with branching rhizomes;  stems ± erect, up to 35–(70) cm tall at flowering, glabrous to sparingly pilose, sparingly branched, greenish yellow to purplish, grooved.  Lower lvs in basal rosettes;  petiole short; blade oblong to narrowly oblanceolate, up to 150–(300) × 45 mm, imparipinnate;  leaflets in (5)–7–10–(12) pairs, shortly petiolulate or subsessile, narrowly obovate to elliptic or orbicular, 5–12–(30) mm long, glabrous above, sparsely finely puberulent and often with a few longer hairs on veins beneath, deeply serrate, sometimes purplish especially towards margins or pale to ± glaucous below.  Cauline lvs few, similar to basal lvs but with fewer and narrower leaflets.  Infl. a dense globose head, elongating somewhat at fruiting.  Sepals ovate-oblong, (2)–3–4 mm long, free, ± emarginate with a small cusp, green;  margins whitish or pink to purple.  Stamens numerous.  Hypanthium usually broadly ellipsoid, rarely ellipsoid at fruiting, glabrous, almost glabrous or pubescent, (2)–4–5 mm long, usually sharply angled and winged, rarely obscurely winged;  faces usually reticulate and the ridges with small projections, rarely faintly reticulate.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Tragopogon porrifolius is a species of plant commonly known as purple or common salsify, oyster plant, vegetable oyster, Jerusalem star, Jack go to bed, goatsbeard, or simply salsify.
Tragopogon porrifolius is a common biennial wildflower, native to southeast Europe, Mediterranean Turkey, and north Africa, but introduced elsewhere, for example, into the British Isles (mainly in central and southern England), other parts of northern Europe, North America and southern Africa, and in Australia. In the United States, it is now found growing wild in almost every state, including Hawaii, except in the extreme south-east.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Salicornia quinqueflora' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
In New Zealand it is found mostly on the shoreline in regions throughout the North Island.
In New Zealand, the species is found in mainly coastal areas.
The preferred habitat of Salicornia quinqueflora is anywhere where salty water tends to be – so along coastlines, salt marshes, sandy beaches and rocky areas. It grows below and above the high tide mark along the coasts.
The species is a halophyte, so it prefers soils with high salinities. This is the main factor determining its success. It is typically found in areas with high moisture levels because of the high salinity of the soils near coastlines; however, glassworts are tolerable to a wide range of soil moistures. They can handle areas with completely dry soil and soils that are completely water logged.
Like other halophytes, Salicornia quinqueflora can handle a wide range of temperatures and are evolved to handle sudden environmental changes. The preferred climate type is warm-temperate and subtropical regions, where they can easily reproduce through seeds to keep populations genetically stable.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Salicornia quinqueflora' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Beaded glasswort, Salicornia quinqueflora, is a species of succulent, salt tolerant plant. It grows as a small shrub, with a lifecycle of several years – which is also known as a perennial lifecycle. They are normally found near salt water bodies (along the coast or estuaries) and grow in a mat form along the ground. The stems are jointed and fleshy when young, but they dry out and appear woody when ageing. The young, fleshy stems are grey or green with sometimes red colouring along the tips. The leaves grow opposite to each other and are connected at the base. They grow on small bumpy petioles – which is the part of a stalk that attaches the leaf to the stem. The leaves then extend down the stem – which in turn, forms the noticeable joints. The leaves look like tiny blades, wrapped around the stem. This formation of the leaves gives the stems a ‘beaded’ look. Growing at the end of the stem, the inflorescences (another name for clusters of flowers) are spikey, and made up of small segments with large cymes. Cymes are a group of flowers with a central stem that matures before the others. Each cyme usually has three flowers entirely immersed in the fleshy part of the joint. The unisex or bisexual flowers are nearly always identical in size and grow in an outwardly symmetrical style along the stems. The flowers have three to four fleshy exterior parts that connect to the apex (highest part of the stem), one or two stamens (the pollen-producing reproductive organ) and an ovary with two or three parts that hold the pollen (the stigma). There is a lot of fruit found in the outer part of the flower, and the fruit wall has a membrane. The seeds are vertical and spherical in shape, light brown, hairy and also have a membrane on the exterior. The hairs take on many forms – they can be angular, slight, curved, conic or straight. There is no feeding tissue (also known as the perisperm) within the seed.


Reproduction and life cycle

Glassworts are perennials, meaning that they go through many reproductive cycles and they do not necessarily need to produce genetically unique seeds all the time. For this reason, they often use ramets to propagate clonally. They make genetically identical copies of the healthiest organisms to spread quickly and asexually. When growth is strong and the environment is right, glassworts will produce genets, a genetically unique individual through seeds in order to keep the population diverse and evolving. Ranets often remain connected to the parent plant in order to survive in harsh conditions until they are fully developed and do not have enough nutrients and water to survive on their own. Seeds generally germinate during the early spring when temperatures begin to warm.


Flowers
Salicornia quinqueflora is characterized as gynodioecious, meaning that there are populations containing only hermaphrodite plants as well as populations containing both female and hermaphrodite plants. Most populations are entirely hermaphrodite except for the coasts of Nelson & Foxton, Tasman Bays, and the central regions of Otago in New Zealand. For the hermaphrodite flowers, they are protogynous. This means that the female stigma matures before the male anther to prevent self-fertilization. For these hermaphrodites, the stigma protrudes 1–2 days before the anther, and the stigma are then visible for 4–6 days. Anthers are revealed individually, one at a time. Anthers open up in the early morning to release pollen. This pollen is then distributed by wind. The flowers produce no nectar and are generally not pollinated by insects. Although, introduced honeybee, Apis mellifera, has been recorded visiting the flowers of the plant and collecting pollen on parts of its body, so this species is thought to possibly help spread pollen. For the female flowers, the stigma protrudes at the same time as the anthers of the hermaphrodite plants. This allows the pollen from the hermaphrodite plants to fertilize the female plants, and the life cycle can begin.

summary.text:
Salicornia quinqueflora, synonym Sarcocornia quinqueflora, commonly known as beaded samphire, bead weed, beaded glasswort or glasswort, is a species of succulent halophytic coastal shrub.
Salicornia quinqueflora is not endemic to New Zealand.
In Australia it occurs on the south west and south east areas, and also in parts of the Nullarbor Plain, and part of the east coast of Cape York Peninsula.
In the South Island S. quinqueflora is widespread on the east coast, but isn't found on the west coast. It can be found on all islands of New Zealand – including Stewart and the Chatham Islands. Glasswort grows on both coasts of the North Island and down the east coast of the South Island. Interestingly, it is also found in Central Otago, in two locations, roughly 70 km inland. Salicornia quinqueflora has a healthy population in Otago, where it is extremely dry and arid. It also has a large population on the extremely wet coastlines of Nelson. Producing offspring through clonal reproduction allows them to survive in conditions that are less than ideal.

identification.text: Low-growing, with slender flexible, sprawling to prostrate, interlacing branches and branchlets, forming a ± cushionlike mass up to c. 2 m. diam., occ. up to 2m. tall. Branchlets ∞ with yellowish brown bark, pubescent when young. Lvs in opp. Pairs or fascicles, on yellowish petioles. Stipules rounded-obtuse to broadly triangular, ± pubescent, ciliolate. Fls solitary, terminal on short branchlets. ♂ with calyx 0 or vestigial; corolla funnelform, lobes ovate-oblong, subacute, ± = tube. ♀ with acute, narrow-triangular calyx-teeth; corolla funnelform, lobes narrow-oblong, obtuse. lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; sand coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. The Flora's key separates them by the leaf veins: mingimingi shows the midrib and the net of veins, sand coprosma the midrib alone. Sand coprosma's leaves are yellowish green, mingimingi's dark green. Both have pale blue fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

habitat.text: Gardens, paths, waste ground, dry banks and dunes.

identification.text: Sprawling stems that are square in cross-section, with paired oval leaves — similar in size and shape to chickweed's. The flowers give it away: five salmon-orange (occasionally blue) petals, open in sunshine and closed in dull weather. Chickweed's flowers are white and its stem is round.

lookalikes.howToTell: Roll the stem: chickweed's is round with a single line of hairs, pimpernel's is four-angled and hairless. Any orange, orange-red or blue flower means pimpernel — chickweed's petals are white, divided almost to the base, and rarely absent. Pimpernel carries its flowers singly in the leaf axils, chickweed in usually loose clusters at the stem tips. Pimpernel's leaves are stalkless and often indistinctly black-dotted underneath; chickweed's lower leaves are stalked. Leaf size and the sprawling habit do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Chickweed

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysimachia_arvensis Corroborates the saponins and the contact dermatitis, and gives the dose picture the entry's warning summarises: the herb and its seed contain saponins, and fresh material is strongly haemolytic; the root also yields cyclamin, a highly toxic triterpenoid glycoside. Experimental doses taken by mouth caused twenty-four hours of intense nausea, headache and bodily pain, and some people get dermatitis from handling the leaf. Experimental feeding to horses and dogs caused gastroenteritis and sufficiently high doses were fatal; it is also reported toxic to poultry and rabbits, and the seed to birds. Grazing stock avoid it — the plant is acrid and bitter — except under overgrazing.

habitat.text: It is found in sunny sites, usually on dry, sandy soils at low altitudes, tolerating very acidic soil conditions.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Cytisus scoparius' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Plants of C. scoparius typically grow to 1–3 metres tall, rarely to 4 m, with main stems up to 5 centimetres thick, rarely 10 cm. Stems are ridged and green. The shrubs have green shoots with small deciduous trifoliate leaves 5–15 millimetres long, and in spring and summer are covered in profuse golden yellow flowers 20–30 mm from top to bottom and 15–20 mm wide. Flowering occurs after 50–80 growing degree-days. The seed pods have long hairs only along their seams. In late summer, its legumes (seed pods) mature black, 2–3 cm long, 8 mm broad and 2–3 mm thick; they burst open, often with an audible crack, forcibly throwing seed from the parent plant. This species is adapted to Mediterranean and coastal climates, and its range is limited by cold winter temperatures. It also adapts to windy oceanic climates. The seeds, seedlings, and young shoots are sensitive to frost; adult plants are hardier, and branches affected by freezing temperatures regenerate quickly. C. scoparius contains toxic alkaloids that depress the heart and nervous system.
As a legume, this shrub can fix nitrogen in the soil through a symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium bacteria.


Phytochemicals

One of the main alkaloids of this plant is cytisine. The characteristic constituents are biogenic amines (mostly tyramine in the young shoots), flavonoids (spiraeoside and scoparoside), isoflavones and their glycosides (genistin), as well as allelopathic quinolizidine alkaloids (mostly sparteine, lupanine, scoparin and hydroxy-derivatives), which defend the plant against insect infestation and herbivores (with the exception of the resistant aphid species Aphis cytisorum).

Cytisus scoparius (syn. Sarothamnus scoparius), the common broom or Scotch broom, is a deciduous leguminous shrub native to western and central Europe.

habitat.text:
Fuchsia perscandens is usually found in forests (especially in clearings or at forest edges), coastal shrub and shrubland. Sometimes, the species is found among rocks in the open, and the altitude at which it grows ranges from sea level to 750 m.
Fuchsia perscandens's preferred habitats are river terraces and remnants of white pine swamp forest, but the species has also been found in limestone, for example in the Wairarapa or in Marlborough.

harvestEthics.text: Be mindful when foraging. Take only what you need.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Fuchsia perscandens' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Fuchsia perscandens is a semi-trailing, climbing shrub, also defined as a scrambling liane. According to Godley and Berry and Wilson, the plant’s appearance depends on the support it gets. The primary shoot starts growing up without support, then climbs bushes or crawls on the ground to find some support. Fuchsia perscandens can form a shrub in exposed situations or adopt a lianoid form.
The plant has thick main stems, with a diameter of up to 5 cm and a length of about 5 m. Fuchsia perscandens is sparingly branched, and its bark is pale brown, or pale orange-fawn on older stems. The bark tends to peel off in papery-thin flakes and strips, and the small branches are hairy at first.


Leaves
The leaves are suborbicular, measure about 3 cm long and 2 cm wide, and are carried on slender petioles, 10–20 mm long. They are thin, green or dark green on the upper side, and glaucescent underneath (paler silvery bluish grey). They are toothed and glabrous, except on veins and margins. The base of the leaf blade is subcordate to truncate, and the apex is subacute.
Webb et al. describe the leaves as deciduous, but according to Godley and Berry, even if exposed plants lose their leaves at the beginning of winter, they might only lose their foliage for a few weeks if located in the shade, and specimens have been observed in full leaf in July on the North Island.


Flowers
Fuchsia perscandens is a gynodioecious species, which means that some plants bear female flowers and others hermaphrodite flowers (with both male and female parts). In this case, female flowers are smaller than hermaphrodites.
The flowers are pendant, or drooping, and measure 1–3 cm long. They are often produced singly, but there can sometimes be a set of two or three flowers. They are supported by very slender pedicels. They can appear directly from the trunk, but also from the short stems holding the leaves.
The floral tube is 7–15 mm long, 2–4 mm wide, and green shading into a reddish brown. The sepals are 6–10 mm long, in a narrow-ovate form. They are reddish brown as well, but shade out to green at the center and the tips, with red streaks. They can be patent to reflexed.
The petals on the corolla are 1–6 mm long and narrow-oblong. They are initially green and dark purple, and red appears when the flowers age.
These flowers are very similar to those of Fuchsia excorticata, also called tree fuchsia, in a smaller version.
Hermaphroditic flowers are the only ones bearing stamens. Stamens are prominent, with filaments 10–15 mm long and a purple color. According to Godley and Berry, female flowers still have shorter filaments, but their anthers are aborted. The flowers present a capitate stigma, meaning that its head is rounded. The stigma is yellow or green, 1–2 mm thick, held by a 20–30 mm long style which is pale cream to purple.


Berries
Fuchsia perscandens produces small berries. They are subcylindrical (imperfectly cylindrical) and measure 5–10 mm. They are red to purple and ripen to a very dark purple. These berries are not as prolific as those of Fuchsia excorticata.
The seeds are oblong-triangular, 0.8–0.9 mm long, and 0.4–0.6 mm wide.

sources: Knox, Johanna. A Forager's Treasury: A New Zealand guide to finding and using wild plants (Allen & Unwin, 2013).

summary.text:
Silene uniflora is a species of flowering plant in the carnation family known by the common name sea campion.
Silene uniflora is a maritime species growing in many European countries, but almost entirely along the coasts bordering the Atlantic Ocean and Baltic Sea. In northern Europe, it is native to the coasts of Scandinavia including Finland, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Russia as far east as the Kola Peninsula. It is also listed as native to Poland by POWO. It is not found in, or native to, the Baltic States or Russia on the Baltic Sea. In western Europe, it is native to the west coast of France, the northern coast of Spain, and a limited area in northern Portugal. It grows all around the shores of Ireland and the United Kingdom, and is also found in some mountainous areas near fresh water, though only rarely. Further out in the Atlantic Ocean, it is native to the Azores, the Canary Islands, Madeira, and Iceland.
It has been introduced to Germany, Argentina, and New Zealand.

lookalikes.howToTell: NZPCN describes hemlock as one of the most poisonous plants in New Zealand; all parts are poisonous if eaten. Look under the umbels: hemlock has about 4–8 narrow, pointed, down-turned bracts beneath each umbel and 3–6 bracteoles on the outer side of each small umbel; sea celery usually has none, occasionally a single bract that falls early. Hemlock is erect, up to 2–(3) m, with hollow stems usually spotted or blotched purple; sea celery is prostrate to ascending, its sprawling stems 0.3–1.2 m long. Hemlock's leaves are 2–4 times divided and sea celery's three-parted to 1–2 times divided with lobed, toothed segments that are narrow in some plants, so leaf shape alone does not separate them. Hemlock smells foetid or musty when crushed and sea celery has a celery-like aroma, but no source here treats smell as a reliable test on its own. Sea celery is mostly coastal but also grows beside lakes and streams inland, and hemlock grows in damp waste ground and riverbeds, so place does not rule hemlock out. Flora of New Zealand gives both white flowers in compound umbels; NZPCN gives sea celery's flower colour as cream or yellow.

identification.text: A plant of C. racemosa consists of a number of branches linked to stolons which are anchored to the sandy substrate by rhizoids. The branches are a few centimetres apart and can grow to a height of 30 centimetres. Many spherical or ovate side-shoots branch off these and give the seaweed its name of sea grapes. Like other members of the order Bryopsidales, each C. racemosa plant consists of a single enormous cell with a large number of nuclei. The chloroplasts containing chlorophyll are free to migrate from any part of the organism to another and there is a network of fibrous proteins that helps movement of organelles.

summary.text:
Caulerpa racemosa is a species of edible green alga, a seaweed in the family Caulerpaceae.
In 1926 a new form of the alga was reported off Tunisia, possibly an immigrant from the Red Sea, and this later spread to much of the eastern Mediterranean Sea. In 1990, a new, larger form with two vertical rows of branches on opposite sides of the stem was found off Libya. It spread widely, invading much of the Mediterranean Sea and becoming more widespread than the invasive species, Caulerpa taxifolia. It is known as var. cylindracea and may have originated from Australian waters. In America C. racemosa is found in shallow water in the Caribbean Sea, around Bermuda and along the eastern seaboard of America from Florida to Brazil.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_lettuce Puts the specifics behind both of this entry's warnings. On the heavy metals: 'Contamination with toxic heavy metals at certain sites where it can be collected makes it dangerous for human consumption.' On the rotting windrows — the deaths this page alludes to are the Brittany blooms of August 2009, where decomposing sea lettuce produced large quantities of hydrogen sulfide: near Saint-Michel-en-Grève a horse rider lost consciousness and his horse died from the fumes, and a lorry driver carrying a load of the decomposing weed passed out, crashed and died. Thirty-one wild boars found dead on the beaches in July 2011 were attributed to the same fumes. The gas inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, as hydrogen cyanide does, so it kills by stopping cellular respiration. Environmentalists attributed the blooms to nitrogen from pig and poultry slurry and fertiliser washing out to sea — the same nutrient-runoff mechanism this entry's habitat warning describes. Eaten elsewhere in Scandinavia, Britain, Ireland, China and Japan, where it is called aosa.

Perennial herb.  Rhizome short;  aerial stems long and decumbent, becoming erect and then often purplish.  Petiole often = lamina in lower lvs, becoming short in lvs below infl.  Lamina 1.7–6 × 0.7–2.3 cm, ovate or ovate-oblong, hairy, especially on veins below, usually entire or shallowly toothed, or rarely upper lvs with narrow lobes (hybrids);  base cuneate to rounded.  Bracts 2–10 cm long, broad-ovate to broad-reniform, acuminate, the uppermost often acute, with prominent white cilia and often purple-tinged.  Calyx 7–9 mm long, purplish;  upper lip shallowly 3-toothed and mucronate;  lower lobe of 2 lanceolate, acuminate teeth.  Corolla 10–15 mm long, usually violet, rarely pink or white. summary.text:
Prunella vulgaris, the common self-heal, heal-all, woundwort, heart-of-the-earth, carpenter's herb, brownwort or blue curls, is an herbaceous flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).
Prunella vulgaris is a perennial herb native in Europe, Asia, Africa, and North America, and is common in most temperate climates.
Prunella vulgaris can spread aggressively through creeping stolons and roots, forming dense mats that can displace other plants. Because of its ability to outcompete other desirable vegetation, it can become weedy in lawns and damp shady locations. Prunella vulgaris is listed in Weeds of the Northeast and Weeds of the Great Plains. It was introduced to many countries in the 1800s and has become invasive in the Pacific Islands, including Australia, New Zealand, and Hawaii. In Ireland, it is generally abundant. It also grows in Kashmir where it is known as kalyuth and used as a decoction to wash and bathe in order to relieve muscle pain.
The conspicuous flowers are a favorite of bumblebees and butterflies.  Prunella vulgaris is a host species for the larvae of the  Clouded sulphur butterfly, Colias philodice.

identification.text:
The shaggy ink cap is easily recognizable from its almost cylindrical cap which initially covers most of its stem. The cap ranges from 4–8 cm in width and 6–20 cm in height. It is mostly white with shaggy scales, which are more pale brown at the apex. 
The free gills change rapidly from white to pink, then deliquesces (melts) into a black liquid filled with spores (hence the "ink cap" name). It is deliquescent. The white and fairly thick stipe measures 6–40 cm high by 1–2.5 cm in diameter and has a loose ring near the bottom. Microscopically, the mushroom lacks pleurocystidia. The spore print is black-brown and the spores measure 10–13 by 6.5–8 μm. The flesh is white and the taste mild.


Similar species
The mushroom can be confused with the poisonous Coprinopsis picacea (magpie fungus). In America, the 'vomiter' mushroom Chlorophyllum molybdites is responsible for most cases of mushroom poisoning due to its similarity with shaggy mane and other edible mushrooms. Coprinopsis atramentaria (the common ink cap) is similar, and contains coprine which can induce coprine poisoning, particularly when consumed with alcohol. Podaxis pistillaris is also similar.

sources: Langlands, Peter. Foraging New Zealand (Penguin Random House NZ, 2024), 'Shaggy inkcap' entry.

identification.text:
The shaggy parasol is a large and conspicuous agaric, with thick brown scales and protuberances on its fleshy white cap. The gills and spore print are both white in colour. Its stipe is slender, but bulbous at the base, is coloured uniformly and bears no patterns. It is fleshy, and a reddish, or maroon discoloration occurs and a pungent odour is evolved when it is cut. The egg-shaped caps become wider and flatter as they mature.
In all three species, the cap reaches about 6 to 20 centimetres in width and the stipe grows to 5 to 20 cm tall with a diameter up to 2 to 3 cm.


Similar species
The shaggy parasol is similar in appearance to the similarly edible parasol mushroom, Macrolepiota procera. The latter grows considerably larger however, and is more likely to be found in the open than C. rhacodes, which prefers more shade and dislikes open pastures and fields. Another distinguishing feature is that C. rhacodes lacks the brown bands that are on the stem of M. procera.

identification.text:
Clump-forming, hairy perennial; rhizomes short, thick, fleshy, sometimes with short offsets, rough from numerous lf base scars. Lvs 3-foliolate, in basal rosettes. Petiole (3)–7–30 cm long, hairy or nearly glabrous; stipular wing inconspicuous, membranous, hairy. Lamina of leaflets often unequal, sessile, usually 8–35–(55) × 15–(60) mm, broadly obcordate with narrow sinus to ⅓ lamina, with appressed hairs above and below, with basal tuft of hairs; calli orange and forming marginal band; lobes 2, rounded. Infl. to c. 35 cm tall, glabrate, a terminal cyme or panicle of (4)–7–35 fls; pedicels ± deflexed at first, later erect, very variable in length, with antrorse hairs. Bracts at base of pedicels 2–2.5 mm long, lanceolate to ovate, with 2 elongated orange calli. Sepals 3–5 mm long, ovate-elliptic or elliptic, with appressed hairs; calli 2, orange, terminal. Petals 9–16 mm long, oblique-obovate to oblong, usually rose above with darker veins and paler pink with band of appressed hairs outside, rarely white. Stamens in 2 whorls; filaments hairy, dilated and sometimes toothed in lower part, those of longest whorl 2–3 mm long. Styles usually much > longer stamen whorl at anthesis (if petals white, then much < longer stamen whorl), densely hairy. Capsule not seen.  
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. Shamrock wood sorrel: a hairy, clump-forming plant with all its leaves in basal rosettes on stalks (3)–7–30 cm long, and no leafy stem. Its flowers come (4)–7–35 together in a branched cluster on a stalk up to c. 35 cm tall; petals 9–16 mm long, usually rose with darker veins, rarely white. Its leaflets are usually 8–35 mm long, up to 55 mm. Pale-pink wood sorrel is almost hairless. Flora of New Zealand gives it longer petals, but Australian floras give its petals from 10–12 mm long, so petal size alone does not separate them, and both can be pale or white. Several flowers on one stalk point to shamrock wood sorrel, but a single flower does not rule it out: an Australian flora gives it clusters of 1 to at least 30. Look for a leafy, branched stem, which only pale-pink wood sorrel has. Both are eaten.

preparation.text: Use them to flavour salads, in moderation.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. Use it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: About 950 ml (1 US quart) water, 125 ml (½ cup) wood sorrel leaves, stems, flowers and seed pods, 15 ml (1 tbsp) agave nectar or honey, and a dash of salt. Mix everything in a blender. If you can, leave it in the fridge overnight before drinking.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel cooler

recipes.method: Fresh wood sorrel leaves and boiling water, one part leaves to three parts water. Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis articulata: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. summary.text: Oxalis articulata, known as pink-sorrel, pink wood sorrel, windowbox wood-sorrel, sourgrass, is a perennial species of flowering plant in the genus Oxalis native to Northern Argentina, Southern Brazil and Uruguay.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Rumex acetosella', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumex_acetosella Corroborates the oxalic acid and the dose caution: the plant contains oxalic acid and its derivatives, and is 'toxic in large amounts because of oxalates'. The Italian agronomist Nicola Onorati (1764–1822) first noticed that it damages the teeth of animals that graze it, for the same reason. On eating it: the leaves can be taken raw or cooked, with the water changed to reduce the strong taste, and are used as a garnish, a tart flavouring, a salad green and a curdling agent for milk in cheese-making — a lemony, tangy, rhubarb-like flavour. Note also that the similarly named Rumex acerosella likewise contains oxalic acid and should not be eaten in excess.

habitat.text: C. bursa-pastoris is the second-most prolific wild plant in the world and is common on cultivated ground and waysides and meadows.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Capsella bursa-pastoris' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Capsella bursa-pastoris is a ruderal and an annual or biennial plant. It grows from a rosette of lobed leaves at the base. From the base emerges a stem most often 10–50 cm tall, but occasionally as much as 70 cm or as little as 2 cm, which bears a few pointed leaves partly grasping the stem, each up to 6.5 cm long.
The flowers, which appear in any month of the year in the British Isles, are white and small, 2.5 mm in diameter, with four petals and six stamens. They are borne in loose racemes, and produce flattened, two-chambered seed pods known as silicles, which are about 6 mm long and triangular to heart-shaped, each containing several seeds.


Research
Like a number of other plants in several plant families, its seeds contain a substance known as mucilage, a condition known as myxospermy. Recently, this has been demonstrated experimentally to perform the function of trapping nematodes, as a form of 'protocarnivory'.
Capsella bursa-pastoris is closely related to the model organism Arabidopsis thaliana and is also used as a model organism, because the variety of genes expressed throughout its life cycle can be compared to genes that have been well studied in A. thaliana. Unlike most flowering plants, it flowers almost all year round. Like other annual ruderals exploiting disturbed ground, C. bursa-pastoris reproduces entirely from seed, has a long soil seed bank and short generation time; it is capable of producing several generations each year.
Fumaric acid has been isolated from the plant.

summary.text:
Capsella bursa-pastoris, commonly known as shepherd's purse or lady's purse, is a small flowering plant in the mustard family.
It is native to eastern Europe and Asia minor, but is naturalized and considered a common weed in many parts of the world, especially in colder climates, including the British Isles (where it is regarded as an archaeophyte), North America, and China, but also in the Mediterranean and North Africa.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 3–(6) m. tall; branches and branchlets stout, glab.; bark reddish brown. Lvs opp. on stout glab. petioles 10–30 mm. long; wing narrow, decurrent. Stipules short, triangular-truncate, ± ciliolate; denticles 1–3, prominent. Lamina thick, coriac., glab., glossy dark green above, paler below, obovate to narrow-obovate to broad-elliptic, abruptly narrowed to produced midrib, cuneately narrowed to petiole; ± (8) - 12–17 × 3–4 cm.; margins sts waved or distantly crenulate. Veins with close reticulations, evident below and often above. ♂ in dense clusters on simple or branched peduncles 10–15 mm. long, often with Iflike bracts at angles; calyx cupular, teeth 4–5, obtuse; corolla funnelform, lobes 5–6, acute, ± = tube. ♀ 3–4 per cluster, on trichotomously branched peduncles, main peduncle c. 3 cm. long; calyx cupular, teeth 5–6, short, triangular; corolla funnelform, tube ± 2 mm., lobes 5–6, acute. Drupe orange-red, oblong 8–12 mm. long.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. The Flora's key separates them by leaf thickness: shining karamū's are thick, kanono's rather thin. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. The Flora's key separates them by leaf shape and stipule: shining karamū's leaves are widest above the middle and its stipules acute; karamū's are elliptic to ovate with tapering, long-pointed (acuminate) stipules. Shining karamū's leaf is glossy, karamū's rather dull. Wikipedia adds that shining karamū's roots and inner bark are yellow, karamū's dull brown, and that shining karamū lacks karamū's foul smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

lookalikes.howToTell: Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Taupata's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Taupata

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Māmāngi's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Māmāngi

lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Hūpiro

lookalikes.howToTell: Mingimingi has small, narrow, leathery, dark green leaves, usually 10–14 × 2–3 mm (7–16 × 2–5 mm), with the net of veins visible at least underneath, on wide-angled branches with interlacing twigs; its fruit is pale blue, translucent, or flecked pale and darker blue, round, about 7 mm long. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Mingimingi's young twigs are more or less hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Mingimingi

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. Swamp coprosma's young twigs are hairy; shining karamū's are hairless. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

Shining karamū has thick, leathery, glossy dark green leaves, widest above the middle (obovate), about 12–17 × 3–4 cm (from 8 cm long), on stalks 10–30 mm long; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 8–12 mm long. summary.text:
Coprosma lucida, commonly known as shining karamū, karamū, kāramuramu, shiny karamū, or kakaramu, is a shrub or tree endemic to New Zealand.
C. lucida is endemic to New Zealand.
C. lucida is found throughout both mainland islands of New Zealand and some smaller surrounding islands, extending as far south as Big South Cape Island. The latitudinal range of C. lucida in New Zealand is between 34.42°S and 46.75°S. However, C. lucida is rare on Stewart Island, where deer populations have drastically reduced the population.
C. lucida is a plant that lives in warm, temperate regions.

identification.text: Terrestrial, rupestral, or epiphytic ferns. Rhizomes stout, erect, or short-creeping, sometimes forming a woody mass above ground, bearing scales. Rhizome scales ovate or narrowly ovate with filiform apices, 15–35 mm long, 1.5–8 mm wide, pale brown, shining, clathrate. Fronds 70–1400 mm long. Stipes 25–780 mm long, dark brown to pale brown or rarely green, densely covered in acicular or subulate scales with very long filiform apices. Rachises brown abaxially, green adaxially, or green on both surfaces, scaly. Laminae 1-pinnate, ovate or elliptic, narrowed to a long undivided or rarely lobed terminal segment with serrate margins similar to the primary pinnae; laminae 45–800 mm long, 25–450 mm wide, dark green on both surfaces, glossy on adaxial surface, herbaceous, bearing scattered scales on abaxial surface, lacking hairs (although scales becoming hair-like); laminae very rarely undivided, ovate or oblong, 60–70 mm long, 15–20 mm wide, apices acute or acuminate, margins serrate, borne on stipes 30–55 mm long. Primary pinnae in 0–22 pairs below an entire or lobed stalked apical segment, not overlapping, ovate or narrowly ovate or narrowly oblong, the longest at or below the middle, 10–260 mm long, 10–55 mm wide; pinna apices acuminate to acute or rarely obtuse or rounded in small fronds, margins serrate to almost entire, bases cuneate and stalked. Sori away from margins; indusia 4–35 mm long, straight or curved away from costae on largest fronds; free margins of indusia entire. Mean spore size 33–38 μm long, 20–24 μm wide; perispores reticulate.

edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. Rather small. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. The seed can be cooked whole, though it is more commonly ground into a flour and used as a cereal in all the ways that oats are used, especially as a porridge but also to make biscuits, sourdough bread etc. The seed can also be sprouted and eaten raw or cooked in salads, stews etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute. The seed is sometimes harvested from the wild for local use as a food - though usually only in times of shortage or mixed as a weed with other grain crops.

identification.text:
Tufts green to dark green, often very slender, 65–100–(170) cm, erect or drooping above in taller plants. Leaf-sheath smooth, or slightly scabrid above, occasionally red-tinged. Ligule 2.7–5–(9) mm, obtuse, denticulate, abaxially finely scabrid. Leaf-blade 12.5–30 cm × 2–8 mm, finely scabrid on ribs and margins. Culm internodes glabrous. Panicle (12)–18–40 cm, very lax, equilateral; rachis smooth, branches and pedicels very filiform, finely scabrid. Spikelets 40–50 mm, 2–(3)-flowered; disarticulation below each floret at maturity. Glumes 7–9-nerved. Lemma 12–18 mm, narrow-lanceolate, light brown, with long stiff reddish hairs below level of awn insertion, green and scabrid above, each lobe-tip produced to a fine bristle (2–3 mm); lemmas awned, awns 30–36 mm, geniculate, column very dark brown, twisted. Palea keels with 1–2 rows of cilia, interkeel glabrous, flanks sometimes sparsely scabrid. Callus long hairy, with horse-shoe shaped scar. Rachilla long hairy. Anthers 2–3 mm. Caryopsis 5–7 × 0.8–1.3 mm, light brown, silky hairy.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are edible; this is about which you have. When ripe, the cultivated oat's spikelet falls as a whole, where slender oat's breaks apart below each floret. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff reddish hairs below the awn, and each of its two tip-lobes is drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; the cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base, with a blunt or shallowly notched tip. Slender oat's lemmas carry an awn 30–36 mm long, bent at a knee and twisted, with a very dark brown lower part; the cultivated oat's are usually awnless, and any awn is weak, straight or curved, and not bent. Slender oat is often a very slender plant with very fine panicle branches, but the cultivated oat's pedicels are fine too, so build is only a clue.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Size does not reliably separate them. Winter wild oat is a strong, rather stiff plant with heavy panicles, and slender oat is often very slender, but their measurements can overlap: slender oat's spikelets are 40–50 mm with awns 30–36 mm; winter wild oat's are 3.5–6 cm with awns 25–50 mm in subspecies ludoviciana (overlapping slender oat), and 6–8 cm with awns 60–70 mm in subspecies sterilis. Leaf width overlaps too (2–8 mm against 3–15 mm), and reddish hairs on the lemma occur in slender oat and in subspecies sterilis. Check how a ripe spikelet breaks up: slender oat's breaks apart below each floret, while winter wild oat's florets stay joined and fall together from above the glumes. Slender oat's lemma tip-lobes are each drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; winter wild oat's lemma narrows to a papery, two-toothed tip, and only its lower one or two lemmas carry an awn. Both have edible seeds.
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both shed below each floret and both have a bent, twisted awn — 30–36 mm in slender oat, 30–40 mm in wild oat — so the awn will not separate them. Look at the lemma tip: slender oat draws each lobe out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long, while Flora of New Zealand describes wild oat's as narrowed to a two-toothed papery tip, with no bristles mentioned. Slender oat's lemma carries long, stiff, reddish hairs below the awn; wild oat's is stiffly hairy there or sometimes hairless, and Flora gives no hair colour for it. Slender oat's grain is narrower, 0.8–1.3 mm wide against 1.8–2.2 mm, and light brown and silky where wild oat's is light grey and densely hairy.
lookalikes.name: Wild oat

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant one at a time, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena barbata is a species of wild oat known by the common name slender wild oat.
A. barbata is native to central Asia (as far east as Pakistan) and the Mediterranean Basin. As an introduced species it also occurs in other Mediterranean-like habitats of New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, Argentina, Chile, Brazil, and Uruguay. In Europe it has been reported in Finland, France, Germany, Norway, Bulgaria, and Austria. In North America it is an introduced species and noxious weed, where it is especially widespread in California. In California it has displaced native species of grass.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: North Auckland, South Auckland, Bay of Plenty (Opotoki), Hawke's Bay (near Napier), Wellington (Wanganui, Paekakariki and Wellington City). Naturalised from Mediterranean.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.
