habitat.text: Lactarius blennius is very common and is found in broad-leaved woodland, favouring beech; it is most associated with Fagus sylvatica, the European beech, though it has also been observed growing in association with species of oak. It forms an ectomycorrhizal association with trees, and can grow on a wide variety of subsoil types, but is more typical of acidic soil.

identification.text: Lactarius blennius has a flattened convex cap that is 4–10 cm across that later becomes depressed in the centre. In colour, it is pale olive to a greenish grey, sometimes a dull green or pale grey-sepia, and has blotches of darker colouration in concentric bands, though the colour can vary greatly. Heavily spotted specimens are also known, and a very brown specimen similar to Lactarius circellatus was recorded in Scotland. The cap is very slimy when moist and has a margin that is curved inwards. The stem is a paler colour than the cap, but also very slimy, and measures from 4–5 cm tall by 1–1.7 cm thick, tapering a little towards the bottom. The flesh is whitish, similar in colour to the gills, which later become a creamy or pale buff colour. The gills turn a brownish-grey colour when wounded, and are crowded. In shape, they are slightly decurrent or adnate, meaning that they run a small way down the stem in attachment, or that they are attached to the stem by the whole depth of the gills. The milk is white and dries grey, and is very plentiful. L. blennius spores leave a creamy print, and are elliptic with low warts joined by ridges with a small number of cross-connections, measuring from 6–9 by 5.5–7 μm.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Slimy milkcap's milk is white and plentiful and dries grey, and its cut gills turn grey-buff. Its cap is drab greenish-grey or olive-grey with rings of darker blotches, and slimy in wet weather. In Europe it grows with beech, very occasionally oak; in New Zealand and Australia, saffron milk cap grows only with pine.

summary.text:
Lactarius blennius (commonly known as the slimy milkcap or beech milkcap) is a medium-sized mushroom of the genus Lactarius found commonly in beech forests in Europe, where it is mycorrhizal, favouring the European beech (though associations with other trees are known).

It is native to Europe. The distribution of the mushroom coincides with the distribution of beech. In the British Isles, the species is one of the one hundred most common mushrooms. Other areas in which it has been recorded include Sweden, France, Italy, and Poland.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suillus_luteus Corroborates the peeling rule and adds the field characters this entry was short of. Edible, 'but the slime/pileipellis must be removed', and 'the slime coating … may cause indigestion if not removed before eating' — which is this page's warning, independently. The cap is 4–10 cm and rarely to 20, conical then flattening, slimy, smooth and glossy even when dry, with a cuticle that peels off easily; the pores are initially yellow, turning olive to dark yellow. The three good field characters are the slimy brown cap, glandular dots on the upper stipe, and a prominent purplish ring. The frequent lookalike is S. granulatus — also common and also edible, yellow-fleshed and exuding latex droplets when young, but with neither a partial veil nor a ring. Regarded as low quality by some authors and a delicacy in Slavic cultures (maslyata, maslyuky), and often sold dried. Ectomycorrhizal with pine.

identification.text:
Taprooted annual, to over 30 cm tall, but often much less, densely clothed in short hairs. Stems decumbent to spreading, often branched from the base. Lvs with long eglandular, and short glandular hairs. Lower lvs long-petiolate. Lamina palmately lobed, 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, reniform to almost orbicular; lobes 5–9, extending 3/4 way to petiole, 2–3-lobed; secondary lobes oblong to obovate. Upper lvs smaller and simpler with shorter petioles. Fls numerous, often paired; peduncles short; pedicels usually longer than peduncles, curving upwards after flowering, densely clothed in glandular hairs. Sepals 2–3 mm long (to c. 4 mm at fruiting), ± ovate, densely clothed in long, white, pilose and short glandular hairs, mucronate. Petals 2.5–3.5 mm long, obovate, emarginate, pale mauve; claw short. Stamens 10, 4–5 reduced to staminodes (lacking anthers); filaments whitish; anthers mauvish brown. Mericarps 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in appressed hairs on outer face. Seed smooth. 
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Dove's-foot cranesbill is an annual densely covered in short or long hairs; its leaves are 1.5–5 × 1.5–6 cm, kidney-shaped to round, cut about 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes, usually with 3 rounded secondary lobes towards the tip; its sepals are 2–3.5 mm long and end in a short point; its petals are rosy pink or pink, (3)–4–6 mm long and deeply notched, its anthers mauve, and its fruit segments (mericarps) about 1.5 mm long, hairless, with prominent pale cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Flora of New Zealand says the two are similar in habit but can always be told apart by the fruit: small-flowered cranesbill's fruit segments (mericarps) are hairy but otherwise smooth, dove's-foot cranesbill's hairless with cross-ridges. Small-flowered cranesbill also has only 5–6 fertile anthers where dove's-foot cranesbill's 10 stamens all carry one (NatureGate), is usually less hairy, and generally has smaller petals (2.5–3.5 mm against (3)–4–6 mm). Both are hairy annuals with round leaves cut about 3/4 of the way into 5–9 lobes, so the leaves do not separate them. Dove's-foot cranesbill's fruits are recorded as eaten by young people in Spain as a nibble (CONECT-e).
lookalikes.name: Dove's-foot cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Small-flowered cranesbill is a taprooted annual densely clothed in short hairs; its leaves are 1–3.5 × 1.5–4.5 cm, kidney-shaped to almost round, cut 3/4 of the way to the leaf stalk into 5–9 lobes that are themselves 2–3-lobed; its sepals are 2–3 mm long (to about 4 mm in fruit) and end in a short point; its petals are pale mauve, 2.5–3.5 mm long and notched; only 5–6 of its 10 stamens carry anthers (mauvish brown); and its fruit segments (mericarps) are 1.5–2 mm long, densely clothed in hairs pressed flat on the outer face. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the leaves and stamens: cut-leaved cranesbill's lower leaves are divided nearly to the base into linear segments, its sepals end in an awn and all 10 stamens are fertile; small-flowered cranesbill's are divided to about 3/4 of the way into oblong to ovate segments, its sepals end in a point under 0.5 mm, and 4–5 of its 10 stamens lack anthers. Both have hairy fruit segments (mericarps), so the fruit alone does not separate them, though cut-leaved cranesbill's hairs spread and small-flowered cranesbill's are pressed flat. Its petals are pink or rose and 3.5–5 mm long against small-flowered cranesbill's pale mauve 2.5–3.5 mm, and its anthers blue against mauvish brown. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Useful Temperate Plants).

summary.text:
Geranium pusillum, commonly known as small-flowered crane's-bill or (in North America) small geranium, is a herbaceous annual plant of the genus Geranium.
Small geranium is native to Europe but is introduced in almost every region of the USA and Canada, where it is associated with ecologically disturbed sites.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Wellington area; S.: mainly in Canterbury and Otago, also collected in Southland.
This sp. is similar in habit to G. molle, but can always be distinguished by its hairy but otherwise smooth mericarps. Also, G. pusillum has only 5-6 fertile anthers, is usually less hairy than G. molle and generally has smaller petals.

identification.text:
Annual, rarely perennial.  Stems ascending to erect, sparingly branched or not branched, glabrous, 4–45–(60) cm tall.  Lvs usually all basal, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, simple and shallowly to deeply dentate, or pinnatifid, (0.6)–2.5–10–(15) × (0.1)–0.5–2–(3) cm, glabrous or sometimes with sparse short strigose hairs.  Stem bracts few, minute;  rarely whorls of rosette lvs formed on stems.  Capitula narrowly cylindric.  Involucral bracts narrow-oblong with subacute apex, glabrous, green,  c. 8 mm long at flowering; inner bracts with broad scarious margin, up to 20 mm long at fruiting.  Florets yellow,  c. = involucre.  Achenes dark brown, scabrid;  outer achenes obconic, not beaked, 4–5 mm long;  inner achenes fusiform, beaked, up to 8 mm long. Pappus in 2 rows, the outer hairs short, slender, scabrid, the inner up to 15 mm long, stout, plumose.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Annual or biennial.  Stems erect, branching, ribbed or grooved, (5)–15–45–(100) cm tall;  hairs white, slender, crinkly;  stouter pale crinkly hairs usually present also, at least below.  Rosette and lower stem lvs thin, petiolate, oblanceolate to linear-oblanceolate, dentate to runcinate-pinnatifid, (2)–5–20–(30) × (0.3)–1–3–(6) cm, often glabrous or with pale hairs  c.  0.5 mm long confined to middle of lf beneath or rarely distributed on both lf surfaces.  Upper stem lvs similar, becoming sessile and not lobed, narrowly triangular to linear, usually with narrowly triangular teeth especially at subauriculate base.  Capitula campanulate;  buds erect.  Involucral bracts with sparse to dense short white tangled hairs and usually sparse dark glandular hairs on outer surface, glabrous on inner surface;  outer bracts 6–10, linear, ?-1/2length of inner bracts;  inner bracts linear, not keeled, 5–8 mm long, with pale to scarious ± glabrous margins.  Receptacle areoles with flat or depressed, glabrous margins.  Corolla yellow, often with pink or red stripe on outer face of ligule.  Achenes brown, 10-ribbed, fusiform, smooth or ± scabrid, not beaked, 2–2.5 mm long.  Pappus bristles in 2 rows, fine, white.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: The seed separates them: beaked hawksbeard's achenes are all long-beaked and 6–9 mm long; smooth hawksbeard's are not beaked and are 2–2.5 mm. Before seed, look at the rosette and lower stem leaves: beaked hawksbeard's are thick, with pale hairs 0.2–0.5 mm long on both surfaces and the margins, where smooth hawksbeard's are thin and often hairless, or hairy only along the middle beneath, rarely on both surfaces. Beaked hawksbeard's stems carry stout, straight, spreading red-based hairs as well as slender crinkly white ones; smooth hawksbeard's stem hairs are white and crinkly. Beaked hawksbeard's inner involucral bracts are usually longer, (6)–9–12 mm against 5–8 mm, but the ranges overlap at 6–8 mm, so bract length alone does not settle it. Both have yellow flowers that may carry a red or pink stripe on the outer face of the ligule — sometimes in beaked hawksbeard, often in smooth hawksbeard — and branching stems with erect buds, so none of those separates them. Beaked hawksbeard's leaves are eaten raw and taste bitter.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Podocarpus nivalis' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Podocarpus nivalis grows as a shrub of 20–40 cm. with spreading branches. It can also be semi-erect and up to 2 or 3m tall. Branches that contact the soil often root. It forms mats of a few square metres.
Leaves are thick, rigid and close together. They are arranged spirally and are a brownish green colour when they age. The leaves are 3–10 mm long and 2–2.5 mm wide and boat-shaped (naviculate) to ovate-linear. They may be curved outwards or down. The leaves are obtuse or mucronate at the apex. The cones are edible bright-red arils that grow to about 1 cm in length.

identification.text:
Erect or rather spreading shrub, usually 0.5–2 m high;  branchlets densely to rather sparsely setose, often puberulent also.  Lvs alternate; petioles slender, to  c. 2 mm long.  Lamina (5)–7–10–(20) × (3)–6–10–(20) mm, broadly elliptic-oblong or elliptic to orbicular, coriaceous, glabrous or nearly so;  margins ± undulate, crenulate-denticulate to serrate;  base cuneate to rounded;  apex rounded, mucronulate, sometimes ± acute.  Fls solitary, axillary, but uppermost lvs sometimes so reduced that fls appear racemosely arranged;  pedicels glabrate to densely hairy; bracteoles 0.7–1.5 mm long, broadly ovate.  Calyx lobes 1.5–2.5 mm long, ovate-triangular, subacute to acute.  Corolla ± urceolate;  tube 1.5–2.5 mm long;  lobes triangular.  Fr. 4–6 mm diam.;  calyx ± fleshy, white to red or purplish.

identification.text:
Perennial, sometimes mat-forming.  Stems to  c. 15 cm long, thin, creeping, glabrous, rooting at nodes.  Lvs 3-foliolate, the rosettes in tufts at intervals, glabrous or hairy.  Petiole (0.5)–1.5–5–(9) cm long, often dark reddish;  stipules 3–5 mm long, broad and scarious.  Lamina of leaflets equal, subsessile or nearly so, 2.5–9 × 2.5–9 mm, broadly obcordate, often dark reddish or deep purple below;  sinus broad or narrow, rather shallow.  Fls solitary;  peduncles slender, 1–6–(11) cm long, hairy.  Bracts 2.5–4 mm long, linear-lanceolate, glabrate;  calli 0.  Sepals 3–5–(6) mm long, ± elliptic, with ± appressed hairs;  calli 0.  Petals 8–15–(20) mm long, broad-obovate, white, usually glabrous, sometimes ciliate.  Stamens at 2 levels, glabrous; filaments not dilated at base.  Styles slightly to obviously > longer stamens, glabrous.  Capsule 4–5 mm diam., globose.  Seed 5–7 mm long, ± ellipsoid-ovoid, with prominent raised reticulations.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

preparation.text: The flowers make a pleasant and decorative addition to salads. Use the leaves in moderation.

recipes.method: 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, 30 ml (2 tbsp) butter, 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) lemon juice and 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) maple syrup or honey. Melt the butter in a saucepan, add the sorrel and stir for 1–2 minutes, until it wilts. Put it in a blender or food processor with the lemon juice and the syrup or honey and blend until well combined. Serve it straight away, or refrigerate it and warm it before use; the author finds it even better the next day. The author serves it on fish, or as a dipping sauce for grilled prawns.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel sauce

recipes.method: About 500 ml (2 cups) wood sorrel leaves, stems or flowers, or a mix, about 250 ml (1 cup) water, and maple syrup or another sweetener to taste. The amounts are rough: use as much sorrel as you like and enough water to cover it. Blend the sorrel and water until well combined, strain through a fine sieve and sweeten to taste.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel 'lemonade'

recipes.method: Equal parts wood sorrel, sugar and water; the author usually uses 250 ml (1 cup) of each. Put everything in a saucepan and bring it to a simmer, stirring. Simmer for 15–30 minutes, strain through muslin (cheesecloth) and pour into sterilised bottles. Use it in tea, topped up with soda water, over ice cream or fresh strawberries, or in vinaigrettes and marinades.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel syrup

recipes.method: About 950 ml (1 US quart) water, 125 ml (½ cup) wood sorrel leaves, stems, flowers and seed pods, 15 ml (1 tbsp) agave nectar or honey, and a dash of salt. Mix everything in a blender. If you can, leave it in the fridge overnight before drinking.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel cooler

recipes.method: Fresh wood sorrel leaves and boiling water, one part leaves to three parts water. Put the leaves in a container, pour the boiling water over them and leave to steep for 5–15 minutes. Strain out the leaves and sweeten to taste if you like. Drink it hot, or pour it over ice for an iced tea.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel tea

recipes.method: 2 cloves garlic, minced; olive oil for cooking; 2 spring onions, chopped; 500 ml (2 cups) vegetable stock; 500 ml (2 cups) lightly packed wood sorrel leaves, with the flowers kept back for garnish; 3 medium mint leaves; 250 ml (1 cup) full-fat coconut milk; salt and pepper. Rinse the sorrel well and let it dry, then strip the leaves and flowers from the stems and throw away the bare stalks. Heat a little olive oil in a small saucepan and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the spring onions. Cover with the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for about 5 minutes, then add the sorrel for about 30 seconds. Take it off the heat, add the mint and blend smooth with a stick blender (or an ordinary blender). Stir in the coconut milk and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until well chilled, a couple of hours, and serve garnished with the sorrel flowers.
recipes.title: Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup

recipes.method: About 450 g (1 lb) Italian or breakfast sausage; 1 medium spaghetti squash; several cups of wood sorrel, washed and drained, stems removed (the recipe gives no closer amount); olive oil; 1 red onion, halved and sliced; 1 egg; 125 ml (½ cup) coconut milk or any milk; 1 garlic clove, minced; 15 ml (1 tbsp) garlic powder; 5 ml (1 tsp) tarragon; 5 ml (1 tsp) salt; 2.5 ml (½ tsp) black pepper; 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) ground sage. Heat the oven to 200 °C. Halve the squash, spoon out the seeds and stringy threads, set the halves cut side up on a baking tray, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and pepper and bake for 20–25 minutes, until the flesh gives a little when pressed. Meanwhile cook the sausage and onion in a large pot over medium-high heat. When the sausage is cooked through, add the garlic and sauté for 2 minutes, then add the sorrel, milk and spices, cover and simmer until the sorrel wilts. Take the squash out of the oven and scrape out the flesh with a fork (careful, it will be hot). Combine the mixture with the egg, stirring thoroughly, spread it evenly in a baking dish (or the same pot, if it is ovenproof) and bake for 15–20 minutes, until the top is lightly browned.
recipes.title: Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel

recipes.method: Two handfuls of wood sorrel, chopped; potato and kūmara, boiled first and sliced; cream. Layer the sorrel with the sliced potato and kūmara in a baking dish, pour cream over the top and bake at 180 °C until it starts to brown.
recipes.title: Wood sorrel, kūmara and potato gratin

recipes.method: Chop a big handful of wood sorrel leaves, stalks and flowers and mix them through a potato salad dressed with a cream dressing.
recipes.title: Potato salad with wood sorrel

Summary text: Wikipedia contributors. 'Oxalis magellanica', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 15/09/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxalis_magellanica

Origin checked 15/10/2026 (owner: "revise their bio status"), retrieved 15/10/2026: NZPCN 'Oxalis magellanica' (https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-magellanica/): Biostatus Native; Distribution 'Indigenous. New Zealand (North, South, Stewart, and Chatham Islands), Australia and South America'; Endemic taxon No. Origin 'native' stands.

Recipes copied 16/10/2026 from creeping-wood-sorrel (owner: "yeah copy the recepies to the sorrels", after "the recipies are interchangeble betwwen sorrel species"). None is written for Oxalis magellanica: seven are written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally, and the gratin and potato salad for Oxalis incarnata. When they were copied this page recorded no edible parts of its own (it now has them, from Useful Temperate Plants, 'Oxalis magellanica'); the recipes rest on the owner's word that wood sorrel recipes are interchangeable. Provenance as recorded on creeping-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (cups at 250 ml, 1 tbsp = 15 ml, 1 tsp = 5 ml; every page all rights reserved; retrieved 15/10/2026; supplied by the owner). None is written for this species: each is written for wood sorrels (Oxalis) generally. The sauce, 'lemonade' and syrup from Kate MacQuarrie, 'Wood Sorrel Recipes', PEI Untamed, 09/07/2023 (https://www.pei-untamed.com/post/wood-sorrel-recipes) — written for 'the Wood Sorrels' of Prince Edward Island, no species named; 'grilled shrimp' given as prawns; the lemonade's 'leaves, stems, and/or flowers' and its note that the author does not measure are kept. 'Wood sorrel cooler' is Sunny Savage's 'Oxalis Cooler' as given in Green Deane, 'Oxalis: How To Drown Your Sorrels', Eat The Weeds (dated 16/01/2018 on the page, with reader comments from 2012; https://www.eattheweeds.com/oxalis-how-to-drown-your-sorrels/; the owner's second link, https://www.eattheweeds.com/tag/oxalis-deppei/, is a tag page showing the same article) — written for Oxalis generally, the article naming the Florida species including O. corniculata; 1 US quart is about 946 ml; the recipe does not strain the drink and neither does this. 'Wood sorrel tea' from Jesse, 'Wood Sorrel: Identification, Uses, and Precautions', Feral Foraging, 11/07/2024 (https://feralforaging.com/wood-sorrel/) — written mainly for O. stricta and O. violacea; the page gives the ratio only as '1:3' after 'Gather wood sorrel leaves' and 'Pour over boiling water', without saying by volume or by weight, so 'one part leaves to three parts water' is this guide's reading. 'Chilled lemony wood sorrel soup' from Valerie Zemba, 'Chilled Lemony Wood Sorrel Soup', Very Vegan Val, 03/07/2019 (https://veryveganval.com/chilled-lemony-wood-sorrel-soup/) — written for 'Oxalis stricta and others'; scallions given as spring onions, vegetable broth as stock; the rinsing and stripping step is from the page's prose above the recipe card. 'Spaghetti squash casserole with wood sorrel' from Chosen Weeds Farm, 'Cooking With Wood Sorrel', 15/03/2017 (https://thechosenweeds.com/cooking-with-wood-sorrel/) — written for the purple-leaf wood sorrel that grows in the author's south-east Texas garden; 400 °F given as 200 °C, 1 lb as about 450 g; 'Several cups' of sorrel kept because the page gives no closer amount; the page says only 'Combine mixture with the egg' after forking out the squash, and the method keeps that wording rather than saying where the squash goes. Not used from the recipe pages (15/10/2026): the casserole page's 'If you are short on time you can skip the oven step', because skipping the final bake would leave the stirred-in egg uncooked; Feral Foraging's statements that all species of wood sorrel are edible and can be used in similar ways (genus-level claims), its estimate that about 30 g a day, several times a week, is safe and its view that oxalate warnings are overblown (it contradicts every other page read here and is not a trusted source for a safety amount), and its cold-infusion and dried-leaf variants; Green Deane's statements that cooking reportedly renders oxalic acid harmless, particularly with calcium, that eating a lot raw can leach calcium from the bones, and that the juice curdles milk for cheese, and that all parts including the root bulb are edible (said of the Florida species as a group); the casserole page's medicinal and vitamin claims; the reader comment on Eat The Weeds suggesting more sorrel for a sharper cooler. Two of the owner's links have no recipe: Rachel Lambert, 'Wild Food: Wood Sorrel family', Wild Walks Southwest, 07/05/2021 (https://wildwalks-southwest.co.uk/wild-food-wood-sorrel-family/), and Diego Bonetto, 'How to identify and eat wood Sorrel', 10/08/2021 (https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/wood-sorrel-id-forage-edible-weed) — both name O. corniculata among the species they describe. Lambert says all of them have a lemony, tart flavour and uses them in salads, in soups and as an edible decoration; Bonetto says the stalks, flowers and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, in salads and as a garnish; recorded here for edibleParts and preparation, which were empty on creeping-wood-sorrel when this was written (15/10/2026). Gratin and potato salad, as recorded on pale-pink-wood-sorrel: Recipes, restated in this guide's own words, metric (all rights reserved; retrieved 16/10/2026; supplied by the owner): Johanna Knox, 'Wood sorrel (Oxalis incarnata)', Wild Picnic, 16/07/2009, https://wildpicnic.blogspot.com/2009/07/wood-sorrel-oxalis-acetosella.html — the gratin and the potato salad. The post was first written as O. acetosella; a commenter (AJB, 26/11/2009) identified the plant pictured as 'the South African Ox. incarnata', which the author accepted, and the title now names O. incarnata. The blog covers Wellington and the Wairarapa; the post does not say where the plant grew. Not used as recipes: adding it to apple, peach or pear pie and a jelly (suggestions, not made by the author); its use to curdle milk for cheese (the author had not got it to work).

Edible parts, preparation and warning: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis magellanica', https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Oxalis+magellanica, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 16/10/2026 — Edible Uses 'Leaves - raw or cooked' (cited there to Crowe, Native Edible Plants of New Zealand, 1990, and Kunkel, Plants for Human Consumption, 1984), 'A pleasant acid flavour, but the leaves are rather small and they are also a bit chewy' and 'Use in moderation', 'Flowers - raw', 'A pleasant and decorative addition to the salad bowl' (the tasting notes are Ken Fern's own); General Information 'The plant is harvested from the wild for local use as a food.' Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses) is word for word the text on Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis corniculata' (compared 16/10/2026), so the warning is the same sentence as on creeping-wood-sorrel and shamrock-wood-sorrel: oxalic acid, all right in small quantities but not in large amounts since it can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. Not used: its habitat 'Walls and stony places' (cited to the RHS Dictionary of Plants, a garden source, and not what NZPCN describes); the Chilean use of Oxalis juice to remove fruit stains (said of 'various species'); propagation. PFAF (https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Oxalis+magellanica, all rights reserved) is the same database. With edible parts now sourced for this species, the nine wood sorrel recipes copied here on the owner's word stay.

Habitat, paraphrased 16/10/2026 from the owner's link: NZPCN, 'Oxalis magellanica' factsheet (P.J. de Lange 2005; all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/oxalis-magellanica/, retrieved 16/10/2026 — 'Coastal to montane where it is mainly confined to indigenous forested habitats, though sometimes extending into the alpine zone. A species of riparian habitats, usually found within the flood zone of streams and rivers, and around the plunge pools of waterfalls. Provided its habitat is permanently moist it may be found growing in full sun but it is more usually seen in semi-shaded situations.' and, under propagation, 'It does not cope with drying out.' Nelson Natives (owner's link, https://www.nelsonnatives.co.nz/oxalis-magellanica-white-oxalis) gives the same habitat text word for word, so it is not a second source. Tags [forest, wetland]: 'riparian' and 'flood zone' are the wetland definition's streamsides, 'indigenous forested habitats' is forest; coastal left out ('Coastal to montane' is an altitude range) and alpine left out ('sometimes'), the same rule as least-yellow-sorrel. NZPCN's wetland indicator rating is FAC (facultative).

Māori names: Biota of New Zealand (Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research), 'Oxalis magellanica G.Forst.', owner's link, https://biotanz.landcareresearch.co.nz/scientific-names/30135eb8-6c4f-46a3-8bac-e6fbe28b025f, retrieved 16/10/2026 — vernacular names, Māori: Retireti, Tūtae kāhu, Tūtae kākā; English: White oxalis. Biota of NZ also gives Biostatus 'Indigenous, non-endemic'.

Months left empty (year-round) 16/10/2026: the leaves are the main part eaten. Flora of New Zealand gives 'Flowering: Jul.–Apr.'; NZPCN gives flowering 'September - March (sometimes year round)'; iNaturalist NZ (597 research-grade records, retrieved 16/10/2026) has flowering annotations Oct–Feb, peak Nov–Dec, none Mar–Sep; observations exist in every month (Jul 5, Aug 2). No source dates the leaves; this guide looked at three NZ research-grade photos from June–August (iNaturalist 379854858, Ōwhiro Bay, 07/07/2026; 369210339, Upper Waitati, 07/06/2026; 392865364, Mahoenui, 20/08/2026) and all three show green leaves — a reading of photos, not a source. Xera Plants (owner's link) says the cultivar 'Nelson' is 'Deciduous in most winters' in Oregon; not used (a garden cultivar, northern hemisphere).

A seed longer than its capsule suggests a misprint in the seed size; the identification text is verbatim and is left as published.

summary.text: Oxalis magellanica or snowdrop wood-sorrel is an Oxalis species found in Chile, Argentina, New Zealand, and Tasmania.

warnings: The leaves contain oxalic acid. Eat them only in small amounts: eaten in large quantities over time, they can stop the body taking up calcium. Cooking reduces the oxalic acid. Take particular care if you have rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity.

habitat.text: Damp ground: stream banks, drains, old gardens and the shade under trees, often with onion weed nearby.

identification.text: Clumps of strap-shaped leaves and a round, hollow flower stalk with several nodding white bells, each petal tipped with a green spot. Crush a leaf: no onion smell at all. Onion weed has a triangular stalk, a green stripe down the whole petal, and smells strongly of onion.

lookalikes.howToTell: Smell first: crushed onion weed smells strongly of garlic or onion; snowflake does not. Onion weed's flower stalk is three-angled; snowflake's is hollow and somewhat flattened with winged edges. Onion weed's white bells have a green stripe down the centre of each segment; snowflake's segments are green-tipped. Strap-shaped leaves, nodding white bells, damp ground and season do not separate them.

summary.text: A garden bulb that has gone wild along streams, with strap leaves and white bells much like onion weed's — but no onion smell, and a poisonous bulb.

warnings: The bulbs and leaves contain lycorine: vomiting and diarrhoea. The bulbs are the usual mistake, dug up with onion weed's.

habitat.text:
Open lowland places, mostly near the coast in natural and partially modified grasslands, very occasionally in waste places.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the montane zone (sea level to 600 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

harvestEthics.text: This species is at risk. If you harvest it, take only a little, and never in a way that kills it or stops it from reproducing and spreading.

Flora of New Zealand vol. IV (Webb et al. 1988), Flora of New Zealand Series (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform or cylindric taproot to c. 2.5 cm diam.; caulorrhiza short and thick, bearing long weakly ascending flowering stems. Hairs variable; longer hairs straight to slightly curved; glandular hairs short and inconspicuous. Basal lvs: petiole to 30 cm long, with fine, straight or curved long hairs and shorter straight and crisped retrorse hairs; lamina to c. 7 cm diam., reniform to orbicular, lobed to 3/4-⅞ way to midrib, glabrous or densely hairy above; lobes (5)–7, obovate; larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; median and larger lateral teeth ± oblong, usually obtuse. Cauline lvs similar to basal but smaller, usually 3–5-lobed; teeth usually 3–5 per lobe. Peduncle and pedicels with hairs as on petioles; bracteoles lanceolate or narrow-triangular; fls usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals ovate or elliptic-ovate; outer sepals c. 5.5 × 3.5 mm excluding mucro; inner sepals slightly narrower; hairs straight or slightly curved, antrorse and ascending. Petals to c. 7.5 × 4.5 mm, obovate, rose-pink. Mericarp hairy; beak to c. 15 mm long. Seed c. 2 × 1.6 mm diam., subglobular to oblong, dark reddish brown or almost black; dorsal alveolae deep, usually 4–6-sided, isodiametric or longer than wide.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
'Large petals' form (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV): Taproot napiform; lamina of lf glabrous above except for margin and base; hairs of petioles and pedicels straight, to c. 1.5 mm long, perpendicular to surface; petals usually > 7 × 4 mm; alveolae of seed mostly 5-6-sided, isodiametric.

lookalikes.howToTell: Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. NZPCN gives the same test. The key adds the leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. NZPCN also gives the root, often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Flora of New Zealand allows Solander's geranium a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and NZPCN's measurements give both petals up to 8–9 mm. No source read records turnip-rooted geranium as food, and it is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (NZTCS 2023). The names do not separate them: Biota of New Zealand gives Solander's geranium the names turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku, and Flora of New Zealand Online gives the same three to turnip-rooted geranium, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Turnip-rooted geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates Australasian cranesbill from Solander's geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in Solander's geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga).
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from Solander's geranium on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in Solander's geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in Solander's geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of Solander's geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut-leaved cranesbill is a hairy annual with a large basal rosette; its leaves are 3.5–8 × 3.5–9 cm, cut almost to the leaf stalk into 5–7 lobes that are lobed again, ending in linear or narrow-oblong pointed segments; its flower stalks carry plain hairs and often pink-tipped glandular hairs; its sepals end in an awn (1)–2–3 mm long; its petals are pink or rose, 3.5–5 mm long and notched, its anthers blue, and its fruit segments (mericarps) carry white spreading hairs. Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them at its first step: cut-leaved cranesbill is an annual, usually with a thin fibrous taproot and glandular hairs prominent in the flower clusters, while Solander's geranium is a perennial with a rather stout to tuberous rootstock and no, very few, or short and inconspicuous glandular hairs on the flower clusters. Cut-leaved cranesbill's leaves are cut almost to the leaf stalk into linear segments; Solander's geranium's are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into broader lobes. Both have pink petals. Older floras placed Solander's geranium under Geranium dissectum (NZPCN lists Geranium dissectum var. pilosum Hook.f. and var. australe Benth. among its synonyms), so older records may use that name. Cut-leaved cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Useful Temperate Plants).

preparation.text: Every method in the sources read is Australian: the slender, carrot-like taproot was boiled and eaten (Cribb & Cribb 1987) or roasted (Flood 1980), and tough roots were pounded and eaten after cooking, though some contain tannin, which makes them unpalatable (Zola & Gott 1992). Digging the root kills the plant.

Name: 'Solander's geranium' is NZPCN's first common name and iNaturalist's; maoriName 'Matua-kūmara' from Te Aka Māori Dictionary ('matua-kūmara … Geranium solanderi'), retrieved 23/10/2026, https://maoridictionary.co.nz/search?keywords=matua-kumara. Identification text: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research. 'Geranium solanderi' factsheet (description from Webb et al. 1988). CC BY 3.0 NZ. Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Geranium-solanderi.html — quoted verbatim. Flora of New Zealand vol. IV treats G. solanderi in a broad sense, as the two forms of Gardner (1984): 'Large petals' and 'Coarse hairs'. NZPCN says the 'coarse hairs' form is now Geranium gardneri (naturalised, probably from Australia). The NZ Flora Online description still covers both forms, so it is quoted as published. Second line: Webb's paragraph for the 'Large petals' form (Flora of New Zealand vol. IV, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, URL as in the Summary line), quoted verbatim, its lead '(1) "Large petals" of Gardner (1984, loc. cit.).' replaced by the label. Why that form: Biota of New Zealand (owner's link, 23/10/2026) lists Geranium solanderi f. "large petals" among the synonyms of Geranium solanderi, and Gardner (1984, quoted there) says that form 'matches exactly the type'; NZPCN's Geranium gardneri page says gardneri 'Has been treated in New Zealand as Geranium solanderi “coarse hairs”'. NZPCN still describes the root as parsnip- or carrot-like where Webb gives the 'Large petals' form a napiform root; the cards keep both.

Summary (first and second lines): Wikipedia contributors. 'Geranium solanderi', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, revision 1380155408. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geranium_solanderi — quoted verbatim. Cut: the naming history, the Description section (its 'stemas', 'stald' and leaf sizes are not used), and the Noongar diarrhoea remedy (medicine, not food).

Summary (third line) and habitat: Webb, C.J.; Sykes, W.R.; Garnock-Jones, P.J. 1988: Flora of New Zealand vol. IV, Naturalised Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, Dicotyledons (Flora of New Zealand Series, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 'Geranium solanderi'. Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/bc022784-0cdc-42be-8a34-43f1919b5a90 — quoted verbatim. Webb gives two habitat lines, one after each form; the first is used ('Open lowland places…'); the second reads 'Dry, open, lowland places, mostly near the coast in natural or modified grassland, sometimes in waste places.' NZPCN (all rights reserved) adds: coastal to montane (0–600 m), formerly widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields, clay pans and rocky coastal headlands. Habitat tags coastal, grassland, disturbed from 'near the coast', 'grasslands', 'waste places'.

Edible parts: Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Geranium solanderi'. CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Geranium+solanderi — quoted verbatim, reference numbers removed. UTP cites Cribb & Cribb, Wild Food in Australia (1976) and Crowe, Native Edible Plants of New Zealand (1990) for it. Cut: 'There is a form with turnip-shaped roots that might be better' — turnip-shaped roots are what NZPCN gives to Geranium retrorsum, which is Threatened, so the sentence would steer a reader to the wrong plant. Known Hazards: 'None known'. OPEN LEAD: Crowe's own entry (owner may own the book).

Preparation and months: Australian National Botanic Gardens, 'Native Geranium — Geranium solanderi' (Aboriginal Plant Use, all rights reserved — restated, not quoted). Retrieved 23/10/2026. https://www.anbg.gov.au/apu/plants/gerasola.html — it quotes Cribb & Cribb 1987 p. 169 ('boiled and eaten the slender, carroty taproot was well packed with starch but not particularly palatable with a slight bitter flavour'), Flood 1980 p. 95 ('Large fleshy roots were roasted'; 'Available summer-autumn') and Zola & Gott 1992 p. 47 ('Plants with tough roots - need to be pounded; contain nutritious starch and can be eaten after cooking; some contain tannin - unpalatable'). 'Digging the root kills the plant' is my sentence (the root is the plant's perennial stock — Flora of New Zealand: 'Perennial herb with napiform or cylindric taproot'). Months December–May = Flood's 'summer-autumn' (an Australian, species-specific season word) read as the New Zealand summer and autumn; no New Zealand source dates the root.

Origin and harvest ethics: NZPCN gives biostatus Native and the 2023 assessment 'At Risk – Declining (qualifiers DPR, DPS, DPT, SO)' (de Lange et al. 2024, Conservation status of vascular plants in Aotearoa New Zealand, 2023, NZTCS 43; NZTCS data CC BY 4.0). https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/geranium-solanderi/ — Flora of New Zealand Online: Indigenous (Non-endemic). harvestEthics is the owner's sentence for At Risk species with a food use (owner, 19/10/2026). NZPCN: it has declined from large parts of its former range due to rabbit browsing and the spread of taller weeds.
Warnings: none found (UTP Known Hazards 'None known'); the lookalike cards satisfy the field.

IV key to Geranium (Webb et al. 1988, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/20ca5ec6-fafe-4592-9d67-3d7491229fcc) and the Flora of New Zealand descriptions of both species in each pair; NZPCN's 'Similar taxa' notes (all rights reserved, facts restated) on the Solander's / turnip-rooted pair. summary.text:
Geranium solanderi (common names - native geranium, Australian cranesbill, Austral cranesbill, Cut-leaf cranesbill, native carrot, and hairy geranium) is a species of plant in the family Geraniaceae. It is native to Australia (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, and Tasmania), and to New Zealand.
In New Zealand, in both 2004 and 2009 it was declared "Not threatened", but in 2012, under the New Zealand Threat Classification System it was declared "At Risk - Declining", with the qualifiers SO (safe overseas) and DP (data poor), and this status was reaffirmed in 2017.
Gardner, R. O., New Zealand J. Bot. 22: 131-134 (1984), stated that most N.Z. material of G. solanderi belongs to 1 or other of 2 forms. He did not give them taxonomic recognition because their distinctness is lost in Australia.
Its 2023 national assessment is At Risk – Declining. Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Regionally Threatened – Regionally Endangered in Wellington (2025) and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025), and Regionally Data Deficient in Otago (2025). Rabbit browsing and the spread of taller, faster-growing weeds have caused it to decline across large parts of its former range (NZPCN, restated).

identification.text:
Urtica australis (southern nettle) is a stout, dense, bushy, shrub that reaches 1 by 1 metre in diameter. The base can be somewhat woody. The plant can also be semideciduous. The petioles are up to 50 mm long.
Leaves are dark green, 100–150 mm long and 80–140 mm wide, with a heart-shaped base. The margins are usually coarsely toothed, sometimes nearly smooth, and rarely completely smooth. The stinging hairs or trichomes are mainly found along the leaf edges and veins on the underside, and may be sparse or absent. Flowering occurs from December to January. The achenes are 1.5–2 mm long, and pale brown.

identification.text: Spartium junceum is a vigorous, deciduous shrub growing to 2–4 metres tall, rarely 5 m, with main stems up to 5 centimetres thick, rarely 10 cm. It has thick, somewhat succulent grey-green rush-like shoots with very sparse small deciduous leaves 1 to 3 cm long and up to 4 millimetres broad. The leaves are of little importance to the plant, with much of the photosynthesis occurring in the green shoots (a water-conserving strategy in its dry climate). The leaves fall away early. In late spring and summer shoots are covered in profuse fragrant yellow pea-like flowers 1 to 2 cm across. In late summer, the legumes (seed pods) mature black and reach 8–10 cm long. They burst open, often with an audible crack, spreading seed from the parent plant.

identification.text:
A pouch fungus around 20 by 60 mm that never opens out into gills. The cap is smooth and powder blue, purplish-blue or greenish. The stem is stout and solid, yellowish to bright yellow, widening where it meets the pouch.
Cut lengthways, the gleba inside is reddish-brown or orange, held in regular cell-like chambers behind a purple-brown sack-like wall. It does not bruise blue.

lookalikes.howToTell: Colour and shape do not separate them reliably. Spindle pouch is powder blue, purplish blue or greenish, usually elongated and tapering towards the tip. Weraroa is light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey (sometimes pale green), and can be roundish, egg-shaped or elongated. The stem is the better field check. Spindle pouch's is stout, solid, smooth and slippery, off-white to yellow and yellower towards the base, and widens towards the pouch. Weraroa's is slender, the same width throughout, fibrous and hollow, whitish to french-grey with a yellowish-brown base. Weraroa slowly bruises blue or greenish where injured, on both pouch and stem. Spindle pouch is naturally blue but does not blue when damaged. Cut one lengthways. Spindle pouch's gleba is brown to reddish-brown, rarely orange, in regular cell-like chambers inside a purple-brown sack-like layer. Weraroa's is sepia to chocolate-brown in contorted, gill-like chambers, with no sack.

The test that separates it from weraroa, which is the whole reason this page exists. Clavogaster virescens is *naturally* blue to greenish blue and has **no bluing reaction**, and contains no psilocybin; Psilocybe weraroa is a bluing Psilocybe containing psilocin and psilocybine. Because a secotioid cap never opens to show gills, the identification needs a cut through the fruitbody: in C. virescens the gleba is a reddish brown or orange chambered mass inside a sack-like structure within the peridium, and the stem is stout, smooth and slippery rather than fibrous, off-white to yellow, swollen at the top where it runs smoothly into the pouch and tapering to a yellower base. The taxonomy is why the two are tangled: the genus Weraroa was erected in 1958 for W. novae-zelandiae and this species was moved into it, and only in 2015 did it become Clavogaster virescens (Massee) J.A. Cooper again while W. novae-zelandiae became Psilocybe weraroa. Clavogaster holds two endemic species — this one and Clavogaster sp. identification.text:
Strong, rather stiff, erect green tufts to 150 cm, with heavy panicles. Leaf-sheath glabrous, or rarely with scattered soft hairs. Ligule 3–8 mm, truncate, or more tapered centrally, shortly denticulate, finely ciliate. Leaf-blade 15–45 cm × 3–15 mm, very finely scabrid on ribs, adaxially sometimes smooth, rarely with scattered hairs; margins minutely scabrid. Culm internodes glabrous. Panicle 20–40 cm, equilateral, lax; rachis smooth, branches few, widely spreading, filiform, scabrid. Spikelets often drooping; disarticulation above glumes; rachilla tough and continuous between florets. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma elliptic-lanceolate, tough and hairy below level of awn insertion, greenish above and scabrid on nerves, narrowed to scarious bidentate apex; lower 1–2 lemmas awned; awn geniculate, column red-brown, twisted. Palea keels with 1–3 rows of cilia, interkeel usually minutely hairy above. Callus bordered by dense short hairs.

subsp. ludoviciana (winter wild oat): Spikelets 3.5–6 cm, 2–3-flowered, spreading. Lemma 18–20 mm, light brown or greyish, with ± dense light brown or whitish hairs below awn insertion; awn ± slender, 25–50 mm. Anthers 2–5 mm.

subsp. sterilis: Spikelets 6–8 cm, 3–5-flowered, often drooping. Lemma 25–30 mm, light reddish brown, with dense stiff reddish brown hairs below awn insertion; awn very stout, 60–70 mm. Anthers 3–4 mm.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: Both edible; this is about which you have. Look at the awns: winter wild oat's lowest one or two florets each carry an awn bent at a knee and twisted in its lower part, 25–50 mm long in subsp. ludoviciana and 60–70 mm in subsp. sterilis, where the cultivated oat is usually awnless or has a weak, straight or curved awn that is not kneed and scarcely twisted. Winter wild oat's lemmas are hairy below the awn; the cultivated oat's are hairless or have a few hairs near the base. Winter wild oat's spikelets are usually larger — 3.5–6 cm or 6–8 cm against the cultivated oat's (15)–20–30–(40) mm — but the ranges meet, and floret number (2–5 against 2–3) overlaps.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Size does not reliably separate them. Winter wild oat is a strong, rather stiff plant with heavy panicles, and slender oat is often very slender, but their measurements can overlap: slender oat's spikelets are 40–50 mm with awns 30–36 mm; winter wild oat's are 3.5–6 cm with awns 25–50 mm in subspecies ludoviciana (overlapping slender oat), and 6–8 cm with awns 60–70 mm in subspecies sterilis. Leaf width overlaps too (2–8 mm against 3–15 mm), and reddish hairs on the lemma occur in slender oat and in subspecies sterilis. Check how a ripe spikelet breaks up: slender oat's breaks apart below each floret, while winter wild oat's florets stay joined and fall together from above the glumes. Slender oat's lemma tip-lobes are each drawn out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long; winter wild oat's lemma narrows to a papery, two-toothed tip, and only its lower one or two lemmas carry an awn. Both have edible seeds.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both have long, bent, twisted awns and both drop their seed, but differently. Wild oat's spikelet breaks up below each floret, so the florets fall one by one; winter wild oat's breaks above the glumes with the florets held together, so they fall as one unit. At the base of each floret, wild oat has a horseshoe-shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs; winter wild oat's is bordered by dense short hairs. Wild oat's awn column is dark brown, winter wild oat's red-brown. Size does not reliably separate them: wild oat's spikelets are 35–50 mm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 30–40 mm; in New Zealand, winter wild oat subsp. ludoviciana has spikelets 35–60 mm with 2–3 florets and awns 25–50 mm, and subsp. sterilis spikelets 60–80 mm with 3–5 florets and awns 60–70 mm.

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant together, as one unit, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena sterilis (animated oat, sterile oat, wild oat, wild red oat, winter wild oat; syn. Avena ludoviciana Durieu; Avena macrocarpa Moench; Avena sterilis ssp. sterilis; Avena sterilis ssp. ludoviciana) is a species of grass weed whose seeds are edible.
A. sterilis is native to the Mediterranean Basin and West, Central and South Asia, but is widely naturalized elsewhere. The species grows on all continents except Antarctica.

In North America, it grows as an introduced species in the U.S. states of California, Oregon, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

Because it thrives in the same conditions as many agricultural crops and has similar lifecycles, the grass directly competes with and reduces yield in arable crops.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): subsp. ludoviciana: N.: Feilding, Wellington City; S.: Nelson City, Blenheim, more common in Canterbury, North Otago (near Oamaru). Naturalised from Eurasia. subsp. sterilis: N.: North Auckland (near Whangarei), Auckland City, Waikato (Waerenga); Cook Strait (Stephens Id); S.: Dunedin. Naturalised from Mediterranean.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

identification.text:
This is an annual herb growing from a slender taproot. It produces a branched stem up to 45 centimeters tall, with abundant glandular and non-glandular hairs. The leaves are opposite, hairy, up to 2 cm long, and the basal ones typically die back before flowering. The bracts are green, hairy and generally similar to the leaves.
The inflorescence bears as few as 3 or as many as 50 small, dioecious flowers arranged in a cyme and borne on very short pedicels. Each flower has 5 hairy green sepals which are occasionally red-tipped, and 5 white bifid petals which are a few millimeters long and generally about the same length as the sepals. The fruit is a capsule less than a centimeter long which is tipped with ten tiny teeth.

identification.text:
The "stinking chamomile" Anthemis cotula is so-named for its resemblance to the true chamomile plant, Anthemis nobilis; both have branching upright stems each topped by a single large flower head, although the "stinking chamomile" is distinguished by lacking the membraneous scales underneath the flowers of the true chamomile, as well as by its characteristic strong odor. The leaves of Anthemis cotula have a similar appearance to those of the fennel plant (Foeniculum vulgare), from which the name "Dog's Fennel" is derived.
Anthemis cotula is an annual glandular plant with a harsh taste and an acrid smell. Its height varies from 30–60 cm.

Leaves
The leaves of the plant sometimes have very fine and soft hairs on the upper surface, although the plant is mostly hairless. There is no leaf stalk; leaves grow immediately from the stems. The leaves are pinnate in shape, with many extremely thin lobes, and can be around 25–50 mm long.
Flowers
Each stem is topped by a single flower head which is usually around 25 mm in diameter. The flower head is encompassed by between 10 and 18 white ray florets, each with a three-toothed shape; the florets tend to curve downwards around the edges and may occasionally have pistils, although these do not produce fruit. Beneath the flower proper, oval bracts of the plant form an involucre, with soft hairs on each; further bracts are bristled and sit at right angles to the flowers.
Fruits
The fruits are achenes (with no pappus). They are wrinkled, ribbed with ten ridges, and have small glandular bumps across the surface.

identification.text: A grey-brown mushroom that emerges from a sac (volva) at the base, with white then pink-brown gills and no ring on the stem. The death cap shares the sac, but has gills that are white at first (turning cream, sometimes with a slight pinkish tinge, with age), a skirt-like ring high on the stem that typically persists but is sometimes lost, and a white spore print.

lookalikes.howToTell: Death cap has a skirt-like ring on the stem that usually persists but is sometimes lost, a white volva, gills that are white at first (turning cream, sometimes with a slight pinkish tinge, with age) and a white spore print. Straw mushroom has no ring, a volva that is brownish grey to nearly black above and whitish below, gills that start white and turn pink, and a pink to brownish-pink spore print. The buttons of the two look alike, and young straw mushroom gills are white too, so the gill and spore tests do not work on the buttons people usually pick. In New Zealand death cap was apparently introduced with exotic trees such as oak or spruce. GBIF lists only a few New Zealand records of straw mushroom (an urban park in Christchurch, Kaikoura, and compost in Auckland). Treat any mushroom with a sac at its base as a possible death cap.

identification.text:
Shrub or small tree with fissured bark (to  c. 10 m high in cultivation).  Young shoots glandular-hairy.  Lvs glabrous, with very short petioles.  Lamina 4.5–9 × 2–3.5 cm, a little larger on vegetative shoots, elliptic to obovate, crenate-serrate to serrate, sometimes almost entire on flowering shoots;  base cuneate;  apex usually obtuse.  Panicle usually 4–6 cm long;  peduncles and pedicels glabrous or puberulent.  Bracts ovate to lanceolate, conspicuous and often tinged reddish, < or > pedicels.  Calyx 2–3 mm long, often reddish;  lobes broad, ciliate, obtuse.  Corolla tube 7–8 mm long, white or pinkish, hairy towards apex; lobes broad,  c. 1 mm long.  Filaments villous;  anther awns aristate, curved.  Style shortly exserted.  Fr. 1.5–2 cm diam., globose, orange-red or scarlet, with conic papillae giving a warty appearance.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Arbutus unedo, commonly known as strawberry tree, also called madrone, is an evergreen shrub or small tree in the family Ericaceae, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe.
Arbutus unedo is widespread in the Mediterranean region: in Portugal, Spain, and southeastern France; southward in Algeria, Morocco, Libya, and Tunisia, and eastward in Italy, Malta, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Greece, Turkey, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. It is also found in western France, Albania, Bulgaria, and southwestern Ireland.
A. unedo has been noted for its disjunct distribution, with isolated relict populations in southern and western Ireland in addition to its Mediterranean range. It is commonly cited as an example of the Lusitanian flora, a small assemblage of plants native to Iberia and South-Western Ireland, but generally absent from Britain. Recent genetic studies have suggested that A. unedo may not be truly native in Ireland, but a Chalcolithic introduction.
The red-flowered variant, named A. unedo rubra by William Aiton in 1785, was discovered growing wild in Ireland in 1835.

identification.text:
Shrub up to c. 3 m. tall; branches slender, subdivaricate, us. ± interlacing; branchlets slender, pubescent. Lvs on ± winged slender pubescent petioles 3–5 mm. long. Stipules small, triangular, subacute, ± pubescent, ciliate, terminal tuft consipicuous. Lamina subcorica., glab., orbicular-ovate, spathulate, obtuse, minutely apiculate, ± 8–13 × 8–10 mm. Reticulations of veins evident on both surfaces. ♂ in fascicles of 3–6; calyx 0; corolla funnelform, lobes ± = tube, ovate, acute. ♀ solitary or in axillary clusters of 2–4 along short branchlets; calyx-teeth minute; corolla funnelform, lobes ovate, acute, = or > tube. Drupe black, globose, 3–4 mm. diam.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]
In the field: the leaves have darker margins and a paler blotch in the middle of the upper surface; there is a small tuft of longer hairs (sometimes with a small dark tooth) on the hairy stem between each pair of leaf bases; the ripe fruit has dark reddish-black to black skin and dark purple flesh.

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; swamp coprosma's are hairy. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text:
Coprosma tenuicaulis, commonly called swamp coprosma is a native shrub of New Zealand. It grows in the North and South Islands, from Kaitaia south to about Okarito.
The shrub flowers in early spring and produces black/red fruit that ripen between February and June.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Lobularia maritima' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
Lobularia maritima is an annual plant (rarely a short-lived perennial plant) growing to 5–30 cm tall by 20–30 cm broad. The stem is very branched, with dense clusters of small flowers. The leaves are 1–4 cm long and 3–5 mm, broad, alternate, sessile, quite hairy, oval to lanceolate, with an entire margin. 
The flowers are about 5 millimetres in diameter, sweet-smelling, with an aroma similar to that of honey, with four white rounded petals (or pink, rose-red, violet. yellow and lilac) and four sepals. The six stamens have yellow anthers. The flowers are produced throughout the growing season, or year-round in areas free of frost. They are pollinated by insects (entomophily) as its sweet honey-like fragrance is attractive to bees, flower flies, stingless wasps and butterflies. The fruits are numerous elongated seedpods rather hairy, oval to rounded, each containing two seeds. The dispersal of seed is affected by the wind (anemochory).

summary.text:
Lobularia maritima (syn. Alyssum maritimum) is a species of low-growing flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
This plant is native to the Mediterranean Basin and the Macaronesia region: (Canary Islands, Madeira, Cape Verde). It is widely naturalized elsewhere in the temperate world, including the United States. There is an endemic subspecies in the local flora of the Columbretes Islands of the western Mediterranean.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Genista stenopetala' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
It is an evergreen shrub growing to 3 metres tall. The leaves are trifoliate, the leaflets 1–3 centimetres long, narrow elliptic, coated with fine silky, silvery hairs. The strongly scented flowers are yellow, 1–2 centimetres long, produced in racemes 5–11 centimetres long. The flowers appear in late winter or early spring. The fruit is a pod 2–3 centimetres long.
Under the name Genista × spachiana, it has won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It is not a hardy plant, and does not tolerate temperatures below 5 °C, so in temperate climates it is usually grown under glass. However, it may be placed outside during the summer months, in a sheltered, sunny spot.

identification.text: Long narrow leaves with sharply toothed edges. Nuts sit inside a dense casing covered in fine, sharp, needle-like spines — like a sea urchin — usually two or three flattened glossy brown nuts per case, each with a pointed tip and a tassel.

lookalikes.howToTell: Horse chestnut has hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk; sweet chestnut's leaves are single, long and boldly toothed. Horse chestnut's case is spiky, reportedly with short spikes rather than sweet chestnut's many fine spines, and usually holds one round, glossy, dark brown seed — a conker — with a large pale scar, sometimes two; sweet chestnut's usually holds two or more nuts with a tufted tip. Do not rely on nut count alone, because some sweet chestnut varieties bear a single nut. Raw horse chestnut seeds are toxic, with several toxic compounds including aesculin, and cause sickness when eaten.

warnings: Count the spines: dense and needle-sharp means sweet chestnut, sparse and blunt means horse chestnut.

identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial;  aerial stems 0.  Lvs all rosulate, with fine hairs above and beneath, (2)–4–8 × (2)–3–7 cm, broadly ovate-cordate, obtuse to subacute, with > 15 crenations each side;  stipules linear to lanceolate, dentate, 1–2 cm long;  petiole (3)–5–10–(20) cm long, with deflexed hairs.  Peduncles erect, glabrous or hairy;  bracts linear-acuminate, dentate, 5–10 mm long.  Fls 1.5–2.5 mm diam.  Sepals narrowly oblong, subacute to obtuse, 4–6 mm long;  appendages 1–2 mm long.  Petals violet or white or pink, exceeding sepals, the lateral bearded;  spur 3–5 mm long, > sepal appendages.  Style not geniculate at base, 2.5 mm long;  stigma beaked.  Capsule globose, hairy, c. 1 cm long.  Seeds obovoid, pale brown, 2.5 mm long.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

Viola odorata is a species of flowering plant in the family Violaceae.
Viola odorata is native to Europe south of Scandinavia, northwest Africa (Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia), Macaronesia, the Caucasus, Western Asia, and Kazakhstan. It has been introduced to the Americas, Scandinavia, southern and eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

identification.text:
Sweet William grows in the mountains of southern Europe from the Pyrenees east to the Carpathians and the Balkans, with a variety disjunct in northeastern China, Korea, and southeasternmost Russia. It grows to 13–92 cm tall (depending on the variety), with green to glaucous blue-green tapered leaves 4–10 cm long and 1–2 cm broad. The flowers are produced in a dense cluster of up to 30 at the top of the stems (known as an umbel) and have a spicy, clove-like scent; Each flower is 2–3 cm in diameter, with five petals with serrated edges.
There are two varieties:

Dianthus barbatus var. barbatus. Southern Europe. Leaves broader, up to 2 cm broad.
Dianthus barbatus var. asiaticus Nakai. Northeastern Asia. Leaves slenderer, not over 1 cm broad.

summary.text:
Acacia longifolia is a species of Acacia native to southeastern Australia, from the extreme southeast of Queensland, eastern New South Wales, eastern and southern Victoria, southeastern South Australia, and Tasmania.
The species is endemic to coastal area of south eastern Queensland close to the border with New South Wales extending southward down the coast of New South Wales.
The range then extends south and east through Victoria and into South Australia, where it is found on the Eyre Peninsula, Yorke Peninsula, Kangaroo Island, southern Mount Lofty Ranges, and throughout the south-eastern region, where it is mostly restricted to sand dunes.
It has become naturalised in the south west of Western Australia in coastal areas extending from around Perth in the north down to around Albany in the south. It is thought to have been introduced by escaping from gardens or being used in revegetation plantings. Control methods include hand pulling seedlings, ringbarking, or cutting the plant down and painting the stump with glyphosate.

Deciduous, small, spreading tree, 3–8 m high when mature (narrow in outline with ± erect branches when young), not armed;  trunk short. Lf petiole 12–20 mm long, glabrous;  blade thin, obovate to broadly elliptic, (50)–60–130–(170) × 20–60–(90) mm, cuspidate, rounded or occasionally obtuse at base, with both surfaces glabrous with major veins obvious, serrulate with teeth acute;  stipules short, triangular, laciniate, deciduous.  Fls in umbel-like clusters of (1)–2–3–(5), on very short shoots which elongate after anthesis, not fragrant, pendent; pedicels (8)–12–25 mm long, glabrous.  Hypanthium narrowly campanulate; sepals triangular, 3–6 mm long, acute, magenta to dark deep red, glabrous, shining, at first erect but becoming spreading or reflexed.  Petals 5, (5)–6–12 mm diam., the lower parts remaining semi-erect and corolla  appearing ± campanulate;  upper portion eventually spreading,  ± broadly elliptic-ovate to orbicular, narrowly emarginate, deep pink to rose-magenta.  Stamens slightly < to just > corolla; filaments flushed magenta to crimson.  Fr. up to 12 × 10 mm, ovoid, ellipsoid or ovoid-oblong, glabrous, glossy scarlet;  stone smooth.

lookalikes.howToTell: Japanese cherry's petals more or less spread open and are white or pink-flushed to rose, its sepals greenish to magenta; Taiwan cherry's flowers are more or less bell-shaped, the lower part of each petal staying semi-erect while the upper part eventually spreads, deep pink to rose-magenta, with magenta to dark deep red sepals. Weedbusters names the bell-shaped flower as what sets Taiwan cherry apart from Japanese hill cherry. Fruit: Japanese cherry's fruit is round, black-purple and bitter, under 15 mm across; Taiwan cherry's glossy scarlet and egg-shaped to ellipsoid, up to 12 × 10 mm. Auckland Council describes Japanese cherry fruit as red or black, so a red cherry is not proof of Taiwan cherry. Leaf teeth: Japanese cherry's end in a bristle and are often gland-tipped; Taiwan cherry's are pointed. Flowering overlaps (Taiwan cherry July to September, Japanese cherry August to October), as do leaf size and leaf-stalk and flower-stalk lengths; neither has spines.

summary.text:
Prunus campanulata is a species of cherry native to Japan, Taiwan, southern and eastern China (Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan, Hunan, Fujian, and Zhejiang), and Vietnam.
The tree is an invasive plant species in some areas of New Zealand. In the Northland Region of New Zealand it is illegal to distribute, sell or propagate the plant or to distribute soil, gravel, etc., that contain the seeds or other parts of the plant.

warnings: The plant (especially the seed and young shoots) contains cyanogenic glycosides, especially amygdalin and prunasin. When injested, these compounds break down in the digestive tract to release cyanide.

identification.text:
Shrub or tree up to 8 m. tall, depressed to prostrate when very stongly insolated; branches stout, bark light brown; branchlets pubescent when young. Lvs on stout glab. petioles 8–16 mm. long. Stipules broad-triangular, subacute to subtruncate, glab.; denticles several, conspicuous, central one prominent. Lamina thick, subfleshy, very glossy, dark green above, paler below; broad-oblong to broadly ovate-oblong, rounded to truncate to retuse or emarginate, sts apiculate; ± 6–8 × 4–5 cm. (shade lvs); 2–3 × 1·5–2 cm. (sun lvs); margins recurved, sts inrolled. Reticulations evident above and below. Fls in compound clusters on branched peduncles. ♂ many per cluster; calyx-teeth minute; corolla funnelform, lobes 4–5, acute, ± = tube. ♀ us. 3 per cluster; calyx-teeth short, obtuse; corolla subfunnelform, c. 5 mm. long, lobes acute or obtuse, < tube; stigmas stout. Drupe orange-red, depressed-obovoid, ± 10 × 8 mm.
[From:  Allan (1961) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 1.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Kanono has very large, thin to slightly leathery, slightly glossy leaves, usually 15–20 × 7–10 cm (as small as 10 × 5 cm), on stalks about 2–5 cm long; its fruit is reddish orange, oblong, 7–9 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Kanono's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Kanono

lookalikes.howToTell: Karamū has leathery, rather dull dark green, elliptic to broadly ovate leaves about 7–12 × 3–4 cm (up to 5 cm wide), on stalks about 10–20 mm long; its fruit is dark orange to yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 8–9 × 4–5 mm. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Karamū's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Karamū

Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Shining karamū's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Large-seeded coprosma has slightly leathery, broad- to elliptic-ovate leaves about 9–13 × 4–8 cm, on stout stalks about 12–25 mm long, with the stipules joined into a broad thin sheath tipped by one long sharp tooth; its fruit is orange-red, oblong, 10–25 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Large-seeded coprosma's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
lookalikes.name: Large-seeded coprosma

lookalikes.howToTell: Māmāngi has rather thin, hairless leaves about 50–60 × 35–40 mm (15–25 × 10–17 mm on young plants), with a rounded or notched tip and a stalk winged in its upper half; its fruit is white, broadly oblong, about 7 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Both can have a rounded or notched leaf tip, so the tip does not separate them; taupata's leaf is very glossy, māmāngi's not or only slightly glossy. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.
