lookalikes.howToTell: Hūpiro has thin to slightly leathery leaves that smell foul when bruised, usually 30–50 × 14–20 mm (as small as 20 × 10 mm); its fruit is pale to full orange, oblong, 7–10 mm long. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hūpiro's leaves smell foul when bruised, but smell is a weak test: Wikipedia says karamū and some other coprosmas smell foul too, and the genus is named for its dung smell. Hūpiro's young twigs are hairless; Taupata's are hairy. Both have orange (from yellow-orange to orange-red) fruit, so fruit colour does not separate them. Their leaf sizes overlap, so size alone does not separate them. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp coprosma has small, rounded to spoon-shaped leaves about 8–13 × 8–10 mm, on slender, more or less interlacing, somewhat wide-angled branches; its fruit is black, round, 3–4 mm across. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sand coprosma has yellowish green, needle-narrow leaves 7–12 × 1–1.5 mm (up to 2 mm wide) with only the midrib visible, on a low, sprawling, cushion-like plant with yellowish brown bark; its fruit is translucent, very pale to pale blue, often with darker flecks, round, about 7 mm across. Taupata has thick, slightly fleshy, very glossy leaves with a rounded, squared-off or notched tip and edges rolled under, about 6–8 × 4–5 cm in shade but 2–3 × 1.5–2 cm in sun; its fruit is orange-red, about 10 × 8 mm. Hybrids between taupata and sand coprosma are common (Coprosma ×kirkii), so plants in between exist; if a plant fits neither description, do not use this card. Most coprosmas are male or female plants and males bear no fruit, so on a fruitless plant use the leaves.

summary.text:
Coprosma repens is a species of flowering shrub or small tree of the genus Coprosma, in the family Rubiaceae, native to New Zealand.
The species is native to the North Island, South Island, Kermadec Islands and Three Kings Islands in New Zealand.
In Australia, it has become naturalised in coastal areas of Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania, and it is now classified as an environmental weed.

habitat.text: Found on the ground under beech (Nothofagus), in beech forest, singly or in groups. Beech forest is the whole of its recorded habitat, and it grows nowhere outside New Zealand.

harvestEthics.text: There is no reason to pick this mushroom. You can observe and photograph it without disturbing it.

identification.text: Cap 4–7.5 cm across, convex at first and sinking in the centre as it matures, and markedly sticky to slimy. Its ground colour is a muted orange-brown, sometimes closer to a drab ochre, and it is banded in concentric zones of purplish grey or reddish brown. Gills thin and crowded, running a little way down the stem, pale ochre with a pink tint. Stem 2–4 cm long and 1–1.8 cm thick, even or tapering towards the base, pale orange-cream to yellowish cream, now and then with a violet tint. Flesh brownish white, firm, and unchanging where cut. The milk is white and viscid, it does not change colour in the air, and it dries cream — this is the character that separates it from saffron milk cap, whose latex is carrot-orange. The gills taste slightly acrid, the flesh is mild, and there is no distinctive smell. The spore print is creamy-white.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white, sticky and unchanging, drying cream. Both species carry concentric bands on the cap, so zoning does not separate them. Saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine, this one under beech.

habitat.text: The species is found mostly in New Zealand and Australia, from November to June. It grows on native and introduced trees where it can cause heart rot, and does not seem to be associated with conifers.

identification.text:
The cap is centrally attached, buff coloured, and darker at center. The stem is pale with white flesh. The partial veil presses against the pink-to-dark gills and turns into a prominent ring, often striated with dark brown spore deposit upon the stem expansion. The spores are cylindrical and thick walled with a prominent germ pore.


Similar species
It resembles the more orange-coloured Gymnopilus junonius.

edibleParts.text: Leaves and flowering stems - used as a flavouring in couscous and various other traditional dishes in N. Africa. The aerial parts, as a drink: a 2022 survey of the wild edible plants of the Messiwa people of Morocco lists it under the local name 'Khzama'.

identification.text:
Small, densely branched shrub, with stellate tomentum, strongly aromatic. Lvs 0.8–3 cm long, sessile, revolute, grey, linear-lanceolate or linear, (linear lvs commonly forming axillary fascicles subtended by a larger linear-lanceolate lf). Peduncle c. = spike. Spike 1.5–3 cm long (excluding plume of sterile apical bracts), composed of very densely packed verticels of fls. Fertile bracts 5–6 mm long, rhombic-cordate, green or brownish; sterile bracts 1–2 cm long, obovate or spathulate, mauve. Calyx 4–7 mm long, tubular, tomentose outside; teeth acute; appendage broad and ± reniform. Corolla 5–8 mm long; tube > calyx; upper tube and lobes dark purple; lobes 1–1.5 mm long, broader than long, subequal. Nutlets c. 2 mm long, broad-oblong, mucilaginous when wet.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]
Lvs entire; corolla dark purple.

lookalikes.howToTell: Topped lavender's leaves are entire; French lavender's are toothed or cut along the edges (pinnate-dentate), much less commonly only scalloped. Topped lavender's flowers are dark purple; French lavender's are mauve. Topped lavender's flower stalk is about as long as its spike; French lavender's, up to 30 cm, is much longer than its spike. The sterile bracts crowning the spike are 1–2 cm long in topped lavender, 7–10 mm in French lavender. Wetted, topped lavender's nutlets turn mucilaginous; French lavender's do not. Leaves that are often grey with star-shaped hairs, a strong aromatic smell and a crown of sterile bracts on the spike do not separate them: both belong to the same section of the genus.
lookalikes.name: French lavender

lookalikes.howToTell: Topped lavender's flower spike is crowned by a plume of mauve sterile bracts 1–2 cm long, and has no bracteoles; common lavender's spike has no enlarged bracts at its tip, and has bracteoles. Topped lavender's flower stalk is only about as long as its spike; common lavender's spikes, 2–8 cm long, sit on slender leafless stalks 10–30 cm long. Narrow leaves, a strong aromatic smell and purple flowers do not separate them. Lavandins (L. × intermedia), common lavender's hybrids with spike lavender, are very common in gardens in many colder parts of New Zealand and, like common lavender, lack enlarged terminal bracts.
lookalikes.name: Common lavender

preparation.text:
In Loja, in southern Spain, some people dress table olives with its leaves together with other herbs, and it has at times seasoned stews and other dishes such as roast meat (Benítez Cruz 2009). In the Alt Empordà, Catalonia, it is recorded as a culinary seasoning (Parada 2008).
In Elche, in south-east Spain, the flowers are picked at full bloom, washed and dried, and kept in a bag or tin; to make a tea, boil water, add the flowers, then strain and let it cool (Gonzálvez 2008).

summary.text:
Lavandula stoechas, the Spanish lavender or topped lavender (U.S.) or French lavender (U.K.), is a species of lavender native to the Mediterranean Basin.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): S.: Kaiteriteri (Nelson), Birdlings Flat (Canterbury), Lake Wanaka (C. Otago). Allan (1940) recorded L. stoechas as "a somewhat persistent escape"; it seeds prolifically and germinates freely. It is a fairly common ornamental plant, particularly in E. and C. areas of the South Id, where its greater tolerance of frost makes it generally a more suitable plant to grow than L. dentata. The wild, and most cultivated plants in N.Z., belong to subsp. stoechas from Spain eastwards to Greece.
Since its introduction into Australia, it has become an invasive species, widely distributed within the continent. It has been declared a noxious weed in Victoria since 1920.
Other names: bush lavender, French lavender, Spanish lavender (Flora of New Zealand Online); French lavender is the Flora of New Zealand's and NZPCN's name for it.

warnings: The Hawaiʻi–Pacific Weed Risk Assessment lists it as potentially toxic to dogs and cats.

Podocarpus totara is found in both the North Island and the South Island, growing in both lowland, montane and lower subalpine habitats, at elevations of up to 600 metres It is rarely found on Stewart Island / Rakiura. Tōtara is commonly found in lowland areas where the soil is fertile and well drained.
Tōtara is often found regenerating on farmland, as it is not eaten by livestock.

identification.text:
The tōtara is a medium to large tree, which grows slowly to around 20 to 25 metres exceptionally to 35 m; it is noted for its longevity and the great girth of its trunk. The bark peels off in papery flakes, with a purplish to golden brown hue. The sharp, dull-green, needle-like leaves are stiff and leathery, 2 cm long. This plant produces highly modified cones with two to four fused, fleshy, berry-like, juicy scales, bright red when mature. The cone contains one or two rounded seeds at the apex of the scales.
The largest known living tōtara, the Pouakani Tree, near Pureora in the central North Island, is over 35 m tall and nearly 4 m in trunk diameter at breast height. Bushmen discovered it in 1950. Other large trees are known in this area, while Whirinaki Forest, to the east, but also on deep recent volcanic soils, has groves of very tall tōtara (over 40 m in height).

summary.text:
Fuchsia excorticata, commonly known as the kōtukutuku and tree fuchsia, is a species of tree in the family Onagraceae that is endemic to New Zealand.
Fuchsia excorticata's fruits are dispersed by fruit-eating animals (frugivores). F. excorticata's fruits are an important food source for numerous New Zealand native birds, and they are an especially important food source for the kererū (Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae). Other birds, such as the tūī (Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae) and the New Zealand bellbird (Anthornis melanura) consume the fruits frequently. Beveridge (1964) estimated that a single dropping from an introduced blackbird (Turdus merula) produced 178 seedlings, thus proving the efficiency of blackbirds as seed distributors. The fruits of F. excorticata can also be part of the diet of the flightless kākāpō (Strigops habroptilus). German-born New Zealand explorer Julius von Haast said that he saw a kākāpō "sitting on a Fuchsia-tree, 3 m from the ground, and eating berries". Fuchsia excorticata has a gynodioecious breeding strategy, meaning individual trees are either hermaphroditic or female. According to Robertson et al. (2008), hermaphroditic individuals occur at a higher frequency than females. F. excorticata can be pollinated by birds, primarily by bellbirds and tūī. Other birds, such as stitchbirds (Pogonornis cincta) and silvereyes (Zosterops lateralis), as well as bumblebees (Bombus spp.) have been reported as visitors on F. excorticata flowers. Evidence presented by a 2012 study shows that the upland moa (Megalapteryx didinus) fed on the nectar. Green flowers stand out compared to the orange bark and produce more nectar, thus making them more attractive and rewarding to bird pollinators than red flowers. New Zealand botanist Eric Godley suggested that F. excorticata is capable of self-pollination "in the absence of pollinator visitors". The introduction of the common brushtail possum to New Zealand has led to a decline in this species. F. excorticata appears to be one of the possum's preferred food sources, and they will browse individual trees to the point of defoliation after which the trees can die. F. excorticata plays host to the endemic insect, the lemon tree borer (Oemona hirta). Wyman et al. (2011) investigated interactions between tree wētā (Hemideina spp.) and F. excorticata, finding that tree wētā consumes its seeds. F. excorticata has very low flammability rates. A 2025 study in the American Journal of Botany found that F. excorticata had a moderate ignition percentage, burn time, and burned amount of biomass.

Stout biennial up to 2–(3) m high, usually with a single main stem.  Stems moderately to densely clothed in stellate hairs when young, becoming ± glabrous and woody at base when older.  Lvs densely clothed in stellate hairs, velvety to touch, suborbicular, cordate at base, shortly 5–7-palmately lobed and crenulate, up to 20 cm diam., rarely variegated;  petioles 3–30 cm long; stipules narrow- to ovate-triangular, 4–8 mm long.  Fls in axillary and terminal clusters of 2–7–(10) or rarely in irregular racemes;  fruiting pedicels 5–20–(30) mm long;  epicalyx segments broadly ovate to suborbicular, united for lower ?-1/2, > calyx, distinctly enlarged and spreading at fruiting; calyx shallowly campanulate;  calyx teeth ± = tube, triangular, acute to acuminate, densely clothed in stellate hairs, usually ± connivent at fruiting; petals lilac or deep pink with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long. Mericarps 6–8–(9) per fr., usually glabrous, sometimes densely clothed in fine hairs, finely transversely ribbed on back;  edges sharply angled.  
[From:  Webb et al.  (1985) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4 as Lavatera arborea L.]
This robust sp. is most easily distinguished by the fused, enlarged, spreading fruiting calyx.

lookalikes.howToTell: Annual mallow is an annual up to 1.5 m tall with single flowers in the leaf joints and pink or mauve petals 20–35 mm long (white-flowered garden forms are common and have been recorded escaping); its lower leaves are not lobed; its epicalyx segments are joined for almost their whole length, half to three-quarters the length of the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; its fruit segments, about 12, are hidden under a disc-like expansion of the central axis. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have an epicalyx that grows larger and spreads in fruit, so that alone does not separate them. Flora of New Zealand says the disc hiding annual mallow's fruit segments readily distinguishes it from the other New Zealand species it then called Lavatera (tree, island and Cretan mallow); annual mallow's flowers are single, tree mallow's in clusters. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Annual mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cheeseweed mallow has tiny white, pale mauve or pink-tipped petals 3–5 mm long, about as long as the calyx or only slightly longer; its calyx grows much larger and spreads as the fruit forms; the fruit splits into (9–)10(–11) segments that are strongly net-veined on the back, with slightly winged, sometimes toothed edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the flowers and fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cheeseweed mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Common mallow has deep pink to reddish or bluish purple petals with darker markings, 12–30 mm long and 2–5 times as long as the calyx, though flower size and colour vary a lot, from pale pink to deep bluish purple; the base of its calyx tube is moderately to densely hairy and the calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–12(–15) segments, usually hairless, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. The flowers overlap: both are pink to purple with darker veins or markings, and tree mallow's 15–20 mm petals sit inside common mallow's 12–30 mm range. Use the epicalyx, which is longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow but shorter than the calyx in common mallow (whose epicalyx segments may be somewhat joined at the base, so joining alone is not a test), and the fruit, ribbed crosswise against net-veined. Both have lobed leaves that can reach 20 cm across. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Common mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Cretan mallow is a stout annual to biennial up to 2 m tall but often smaller, often branched from the base, with lilac or pink petals with darker veins, (8–)10–18 mm long; its epicalyx segments are broad (ovate to broadly ovate), joined for their lower quarter, about two-thirds to four-fifths the length of the calyx, and unchanged in fruit; its calyx teeth taper to a long point; the fruit splits into 8–10 hairless segments, more or less smooth or faintly ribbed on the back with a single low lengthwise rib, usually with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Cretan mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Dwarf mallow has white to lilac petals, often with lilac to pink veins, (7–)8–15 mm long and usually at least twice as long as the calyx; its calyx does not enlarge in fruit; the fruit splits into 12–15 segments that are hairy (rarely only sparsely), smooth or faintly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Both have round, palmately 5–7-lobed, round-toothed leaves, so the leaves do not separate them; use the petal length, the epicalyx and the fruit. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Dwarf mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: French mallow has pale lilac or pink petals with darker veins and tips, 6–10 mm long and about twice as long as the calyx; the base of its calyx tube is more or less hairless, and the calyx is slightly enlarged in fruit; the fruit splits into 8–9(–10) segments, often hairy when young but usually hairless later, strongly net-veined on the back, with sharply angled edges that are not winged. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: French mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Island mallow is a woody shrub up to 2(–4) m tall, much-branched from the base, with magenta petals with darker veins 30–40 mm long and a long, tube-shaped calyx; its epicalyx segments are about half as long as the calyx and barely change in fruit; the fruit splits into 7–9 segments that are smooth on the back apart from a single low lengthwise rib, which is usually present. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Flora of New Zealand separates them by the epicalyx (longer than the calyx and enlarged in fruit in tree mallow, shorter and barely changed in island mallow), the fruit segments, the calyx (shallowly bell-shaped in tree mallow, long and tube-shaped in island mallow) and the petals (15–20 mm against 30–40 mm). Both are tall, both grow at coastal sites, and both have lobed leaves up to 20 cm across and pink to purple flowers with darker veins, so the leaves and flower colour do not separate them. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Island mallow

lookalikes.howToTell: Musk mallow is an upright perennial whose upper stem leaves are cut almost to the base into usually 5 lobes that are themselves deeply divided into narrow segments (its lower leaves are only shallowly lobed); its petals are usually pink, sometimes white, (15–)20–30 mm long and 2–4 times as long as the calyx; the fruit splits into about 15–20 segments that are densely hairy and smooth on the back, with rounded edges. Tree mallow is a stout biennial up to 2(–3) m tall, usually with a single main stem, with velvety leaves up to 20 cm across and lilac or deep pink petals with purple or red veins and base, 15–20 mm long; the segments of its epicalyx (the ring of lobes just outside the calyx) are broad, joined in their lower part, longer than the calyx, and grow larger and spread in fruit; the fruit splits into 6–8(–9) segments that are finely ribbed crosswise on the back. Compare the petals, the calyx and epicalyx, and the fruit segments described above. Most of these tests need flowers or fruit.
lookalikes.name: Musk mallow

preparation.text: Young leaves raw or cooked, cut very thinly or as part of a chopped mixed salad. In Andratx, Mallorca, it has been used to make omelettes and mallow salads dressed with oil and vinegar. One British grower found that its leaves needed steaming for longer than the 15–20 minutes a common-mallow recipe gives, or they stayed furry, and would have been better chopped more finely, and that they are not very slimy compared with other mallows. The young, green seed heads can be eaten fresh or fried for a few minutes; one forager found them a bit like raw peanuts fresh and like fried sweetcorn cooked.

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Lavatera arborea), on an Irish foraging blog. Pick young, green seed heads (their texture is better). Fry them for a few minutes, then season with salt and ground cayenne pepper. The three leaf-like parts around each head can be taken off before cooking or while eating. The author also toasts them in a popcorn maker.
recipes.title: Fried tree mallow seed heads

recipes.method: Written for tree mallow (Malva arborea), improvised by the author on molokhia, the Egyptian soup of jute mallow sometimes made with common mallow; the page gives no quantities. Purée finely chopped raw tree mallow leaves in a blender with some water. Fry chopped onion in oil until soft. Crush garlic cloves, coriander seeds, salt and pepper in a mortar and add them with some vegetable stock and lemon juice, then add the puréed leaves. Simmer gently for a while, and purée again if it is not smooth enough. The lemon is meant to offset the mucilage, though the author found tree mallow not very slimy; one of the two tasters found it too lemony.
recipes.title: Tree mallow and lemon soup (molokhia style)

summary.text:
Malva arborea (previously known as Lavatera arborea, or, more recently as Malva eriocalyx), the tree mallow, is a species of mallow native to the coasts of western Europe and the Mediterranean region, from Ireland and Britain south to Algeria and Libya, and east to Greece.
Malva arborea tolerates sea water to varying degrees, at up to 100% sea water in its natural habitat, excreting salt through glands on its leaves. This salt tolerance can be a competitive advantage over inland plant species in coastal areas. Its level of salinity tolerance is thought to be improved by soil with higher phosphate content, making guano enrichment particularly beneficial.
In New Zealand it has established on several seabird-dominated islands where it is considered to be a serious ecological weed and for which there are active eradication programmes, such as on North Brother Island in Cook Strait.
In New Zealand it is local throughout the North Island (not recorded from Taranaki) and throughout the South Island, and on Ruapuke Island and the Chatham Islands. It was first recorded growing wild here in 1870.

habitat.text:
T. versicolor commonly grows in tiled layers in groups or rows on logs and stumps of deciduous trees. It is a white rot fungus which degrades lignin from lignocellulosic materials, such as wood.
The species may be eaten by caterpillars of the fungus moth Nemaxera betulinella, maggots of the fly Polyporivora picta, and the fungus gnat Mycetophila luctuosa.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Trametes versicolor' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The fruiting body is somewhat tongue-shaped, with no discernable stalk, and the tough flesh is 1–3 millimetres thick. The cap is flat, up to 10 centimetres across. It is often triangular or round, with zones of fine hairs coloured rust-brown or darker brown, sometimes with black zones. Underneath a layer of tomentum is a black layer, topping the whitish flesh. Older specimens can have zones with green algae growing on them.
The bottom surface of the cap shows typical concentric zones of different colors, with the margin always the lightest. There are 3–5 pores per mm. They are whitish to light brown, with pores round and with age twisted and labyrinthine.


Similar species
One similar-looking mushroom is Stereum ostrea (false turkey tail).
Other similar species include Trametes betulina, T. hirsuta, T. ochracea, T. suaveolens, Bjerkandera adusta, Cerrena unicolor, Lenzites betulina, and Stereum hirsutum. Other species of Stereum are similar, typically with a smooth undersurface, as well as some species of Trichaptum.

Widely distributed in open habitats, especially in lowland grassland and scrub, on cliffs, often in modified communities of herbs.
In New Zealand: from the coast up into the lower montane zone (sea level to 400 m); it was once widespread in short tussock grassland, on lava fields and clay pans, and on rocky headlands by the sea (NZPCN, restated).

identification.text:
Perennial herb with napiform taproot c. 3 cm diam.; caulorrhiza short, bearing a number of flowering stems. Hairs variable, the longer mostly curved or bent near base. Basal lvs with petioles to c. 25 cm long with retrorse hairs. Lamina to 5 cm diam., suborbicular to orbicular, lobed to c. ⅞ way to midrib; lobes 5–7, linear, inconspicuously but uniformly hairy on both sides; larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; median and larger lateral teeth usually oblong, occasionally obovate to clavate, obtuse, subacute or mucronate. Cauline lvs smaller, with fewer lobes. Flowering stems with dense retrorse hairs or occasionally glabrescent; bracteoles linear to narrowly triangular; fls usually in pairs, occasionally solitary. Sepals c. 5 × 3 mm excluding awn, ovate or elliptic-ovate; awn to 1 mm long; hairs mostly short, appressed, longer on margins. Petals c. 6 × 4 mm, obovate, white to pink. Mericarps hairy; beak to 14 mm long. Seed c. 2 × 1.4 mm, oblong, dark; dorsal alveolae usually deep, 4–6-sided, ± isodiametric.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Solander's geranium is a perennial with a taproot to about 2.5 cm across (Flora of New Zealand: turnip-shaped or cylindrical; NZPCN: more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot); its leaves are up to about 7 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into (5)–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes with (3)–5–(9) teeth; its long hairs are straight to slightly curved; its flowers are usually paired, with rose-pink petals up to about 7.5 × 4.5 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the hairs of the leaf and flower stalks: in turnip-rooted geranium they are sharply bent near the base, point backward and lie pressed flat; in Solander's geranium they are straight to curved, stand out or point backward, but never lie flat. NZPCN gives the same test. The key adds the leaf lobes (usually linear-obovate in turnip-rooted geranium, obovate in Solander's geranium) and the seed: pits about 0.1 mm across against usually more than 0.1 mm. NZPCN also gives the root, often turnip-shaped in turnip-rooted geranium and more like a long tapering parsnip or carrot in Solander's geranium, but Flora of New Zealand allows Solander's geranium a turnip-shaped root too, so the root alone does not settle it. Flower colour does not separate them: both can have pink petals, and NZPCN's measurements give both petals up to 8–9 mm. Solander's geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants). The names do not separate them: Biota of New Zealand gives Solander's geranium the names turnip-rooted geranium, Matua-kūmara and pukupuku, and Flora of New Zealand Online gives the same three to turnip-rooted geranium, so a record under any of them may mean either plant.
lookalikes.name: Solander's geranium

lookalikes.howToTell: Australasian cranesbill is a perennial with a cylindrical taproot up to about 2 cm across, often divided; its leaves are up to about 9 cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way to the midrib into usually 5–7 obovate lobes, the larger lobes usually with (5)–9 teeth; its flowering stems become almost hairless, the hairs mostly pressed flat or pointing upward; its flowers are paired, with pale pink petals about 4.5 × 3 mm. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates Australasian cranesbill from turnip-rooted geranium on three characters: the middle teeth of its leaf lobes are about as long as broad (mostly longer than broad in turnip-rooted geranium); the pale, see-through border of its inner sepals is mostly more than 0.3 mm wide near the tip (mostly less than 0.3 mm); and its seeds are red-brown with rather shallow rectangular pits (red-brown to dark brown, with rather deep rectangular to polygonal pits). Its sepals are mostly elliptic to obovate, against ovate. The lobing does not separate them (both are cut 3/4–7/8 of the way), and both have paired flowers. Australasian cranesbill's root is recorded as a famine food (Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga).
lookalikes.name: Australasian cranesbill

lookalikes.howToTell: Cinquefoil geranium is a perennial with slender stems that lie flat or spread, usually with many branches; its basal leaves rarely last through the growing season; its leaves are usually up to 3–(4) cm across, cut 3/4–7/8 of the way into (3)–5 lobes, the larger lobes usually with 2 secondary lobes; its flowers are single or sometimes two, on thread-like stalks usually 1–3–(4) cm long, with pink petals 4–5 mm long. Turnip-rooted geranium is a perennial with a turnip-shaped taproot about 3 cm across; its leaves are up to 5 cm across, cut about 7/8 of the way to the midrib into 5–7 linear lobes, the larger lobes usually with 7 or 9 teeth; its flowering stems usually carry dense backward-pointing hairs; its flowers are usually paired, with white to pink petals about 6 × 4 mm. Flora of New Zealand's key separates cinquefoil geranium from turnip-rooted geranium on the basal leaves, nearly always less than 3 cm across in cinquefoil geranium and mostly more than 3 cm in turnip-rooted geranium, and on the flowers, generally single in cinquefoil geranium and usually in pairs in turnip-rooted geranium. Cinquefoil geranium's leaves can reach 4 cm and its flowers are sometimes paired, so a small plant of turnip-rooted geranium overlaps on both counts; its slender, flat or spreading, much branched stems are the other sign. Petal colour does not separate them. Cinquefoil geranium's root is recorded as food (Useful Temperate Plants).
lookalikes.name: Cinquefoil geranium

summary.text:
Geranium retrorsum is a species of Geranium known by the common name New Zealand geranium in the United States and common cranesbill in Australia. It is native to Australia and New Zealand but can be found on other continents as an introduced species which is often a noxious weed as well.
In New Zealand this species has been classified by the Department of Conservation as Threatened - Nationally Vulnerable.
Plants treated here as G. retrorsum were treated by Allan (1961) within his concept of G. pilosum.
Its 2023 national assessment is Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable (it was Not Threatened in 2004). Regional assessments rate it Regionally Threatened – Regionally Critical in Northland (2026), Wellington (2025) and Otago (2025), and Regionally Threatened – Regionally Vulnerable in Auckland (2025). It has become very uncommon over most of its North Island range, where it now grows mainly on northern offshore islands, but is still common in parts of the eastern South Island. Rabbits threaten it by digging the plants up for their roots, and taller exotic weeds now dominate the open places it favours. Besides the typical form, two other races grow in New Zealand: one on weedy sites around Canterbury, and one so far known only around Oakley Creek, Auckland, perhaps also at Tawa, Wellington; both are treated as indigenous for now (NZPCN, restated).
In Victoria (VicFlora): Most Victorian plants differ from the type form of Geranium retrorsum from New Zealand as circumscribed by Gardner (1984). Further assessment of this species may result in Victorian (?and Australian) material being reclassified at an infraspecific level.

identification.text: Shrub or small tree with arching stems and glossy, strongly veined opposite leaves. Long drooping strings of small flowers followed by shiny purple-black fruit, each holding several small seeds. The fleshy purple 'petals' surround the seeds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Tutu is highly poisonous, and eating its fruit has been linked with deaths of children in New Zealand. Both have opposite leaves (tutu occasionally in whorls of three), so arrangement does not separate them. Elder's leaves are compound, of (3)-5-7 leaflets toothed except near the base, and its tiny white flowers are in large flat-topped clusters mostly 10-20 cm across, followed by berries 4-8.5 mm across, usually shining black. Tutu's leaves are simple, with flat or slightly wavy edges, and its flowers hang in slender drooping strings 10-30 cm long, followed by fruit of dark purple fleshy petals around the seeds. Season does not separate them: elder flowers November to January, tutu flowers October to March and fruits November to April. Elderflowers and cooked elderberries are eaten; raw elderberries can cause stomach upsets, and elder leaves and stems are poisonous. If you are unsure which you are looking at, harvest neither.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Coriaria arborea', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriaria_arborea Corroborates the toxin and the single exception: endemic to New Zealand, growing to 7 m, and every part except the juice of the fruits contains tutin, 'which is highly poisonous to humans and livestock'. Poisoning can cause brain paralysis, convulsions, exhaustion, memory loss or death. It also records how Māori used it despite that: the petals were juiced after the poisonous seeds were filtered out through toetoe (Austroderia sp.) flower heads, making waitutu, drunk in quantity and used as a laxative, and fermented into a wine that European settlers took to as well. Leaves and young shoots treated wounds, sprains, strains and broken bones; stems of larger plants were made into flutes. Further recorded names: tāweku, tūpākihi, tāwehu, pūhou, pukou, puho, tuturakau. **The filtering is not a method to copy** — it is the context for why the warning on this page is absolute.

The honey regulation, which the warning now states precisely. New Zealand Food Safety: passion vine hoppers feeding on tutu excrete honeydew containing tutin; the resulting honey is 'chemically similar to floral honey and cannot be distinguished by taste, sight or smell' from safe honey; tutin is harmless to bees and toxic to mammals. The main risk period is January to April, over most of the North Island and the top third of the South Island. The Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code sets the maximum for tutin in honey and honeycomb at 0.7 mg/kg, and for the purposes of the Standard 'tutu' means Coriaria arborea and Coriaria sarmentosa. One compliance route is honey taken off hives by 31 December — which is where this entry's earlier 'December to April' came from, and it had the window wrong. The rules followed hospitalisations, including a family poisoned by their own honey in 2008. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.mpi.govt.nz/food-business/honey-bee-products-processing-requirements/managing-tutin-contamination-in-honey

summary.text: The most dangerous plant a New Zealand forager can meet. Learn it, then never touch it.

warnings: Every part of this plant except the fleshy petal is lethally toxic.
Contains tutin. Tutu has killed people, and historically killed a circus elephant in Whanganui. Seeds, leaves and shoots are all lethal.

Toxic honey: bees do not visit tutu, but passionvine hoppers feed on it and excrete honeydew that bees collect. This produces genuinely poisonous honey and is the reason NZ regulates honey harvesting in tutu regions between December and April.
Never make a wine, cordial or jam from any purple-black wild berry in NZ unless you have positively identified the plant.

identification.text: Lepidium didymum is an annual or biennial herb with decumbent or ascending and glabrous green stems, up to 40 centimetres long, radiating from a central position. The leaves are pinnate and alternate and can reach a length of 5 cm. It blooms between July and September. The flowers are inconspicuous, with four very short white petals or none at all, and 2 (rarely 4), stamens. The fruits consist of two rounded valves, notched at the apex, with a very short style between them. They are wrinkled and contain orange or reddish brown seeds, that are 1–5 mm long.

summary.text:
Lepidium didymum,  the lesser swine-cress, is a species of flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
Lepidium didymum is of uncertain origin, but is often cited as native to South America, mainly Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela. It has been introduced elsewhere as a weed of cultivation. It has naturalised across the globe, from Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia, North America and South America.

identification.text:
The cap is normally 4–20 cm in diameter. At first it has an involute margin and a somewhat depressed centre. The upper surface is olive brown or yellow-green and is often sticky or slimy in the middle. When young it has velvety zones and may be shaggy at the rim. Later it becomes funnel-shaped and the colour darkens to blackish. The gills are crowded, dirty white, stained olive-brown by old milk, which is initially white on contact with the air. They are somewhat decurrent. With potassium hydroxide or ammonia there is a purple reaction.
The stipe is up to about 7 cm tall by 3 cm in diameter and it is similar in colour to the cap, but much lighter. It may have shallow pits (scrobiculae). The flesh is a dirty white and tends to turn brown. The taste (especially the abundant milk) is acrid. There is little smell. The spores are about 7x6 μ and are ornamented with a pattern of ridges. The spore print is cream in colour.


Similar species
A similar species in Pacific Northwest conifer forests, as well as Sitka spruce forests, is L. olivaceoumbrinus. Usually found growing individually, it has a stronger olive-brown colour on its cap and stipe, with dark spots on the latter. Also similar is L. atroviridis.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is bright orange and slowly turns red over half an hour or more, and its gills turn orange-red and then green where bruised. Ugly milkcap's milk is white or creamy white, and old milk leaves its dirty-white gills stained olive-brown. Its cap is olive brown or yellow-green, often sticky or slimy in the middle, darkening to blackish with age. In New Zealand and Australia it grows with birch; saffron milk cap only with pine.

Season: iNaturalist NZ observations of 'Lactarius turpis' in New Zealand by month of year — 184 research-grade records, March to May carrying every month at or above a quarter of the April peak. The July–November the description gives is North American, not this one. Checked 06/10/2026. https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/382886

Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research, Virtual Mycota, 'Lactarius turpis' — the New Zealand record, with the description attributed to McNabb, R.F.R. (1971), 'The Russulaceae of New Zealand. 1. Lactarius', New Zealand Journal of Botany 9(1): 46–66. McNabb's text is in copyright, so the facts below are restated and nothing is quoted. Checked 06/10/2026. https://virtualmycota.landcareresearch.co.nz/webforms/vM_Species_Details.aspx?pk=5191 Biostatus 'Present in region - Exotic', and the entry's only New Zealand habitat statement: commonly associated with Betula pendula throughout the South Island. On New Zealand material: cap 7–23 cm, drab olive brown or dark brownish black with olive tints, paling towards an ochraceous, strongly inrolled and coarsely woolly margin; gills pale cream with dull brown edges at maturity, spotted and stained dull brown; latex copious, viscid, creamy white, unchanging; stem 3–7 cm by 2–3.5 cm, stout, often with greenish tints at the apex; spore print ochraceous buff; gills extremely acrid and flesh slightly acrid. KOH and ammonia turn the cap rapidly deep purple, which McNabb gives as characteristic. On edibility he reports it considered poisonous by European mycologists, and Pilát (1961) that it is poisonous raw or poorly cooked and edible though not recommended once the latex is soaked out.

First Nature, 'Lactarius turpis' (ugly milkcap) — © First Nature / Pat O'Reilly, all rights reserved, so facts only and nothing quoted beyond the short phrases marked. Checked 06/10/2026. https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/lactarius-turpis.php Cap dark olive brown with a paler margin, slimy when wet, 7–18 cm, convex then slightly depressed; gills cream to pale buff turning sepia-tinged when bruised, decurrent, narrow and crowded, releasing abundant white latex that dries olivaceous; stem 4–7 cm by 1–2.5 cm, no ring; spores 6.5–7.5 × 5.5–6 µm; spore print creamy white; no significant odour; taste hot and acrid. Mycorrhizal with birch in wet woodland on acid soils. Considered poisonous for its potential carcinogenic properties; the northern European practice of boiling it and using it as a seasoning is now discouraged. Lactarius blennius is the lookalike — lighter, smaller, and without the sepia-tinged gill patches.

The spore print, and why the disagreement is worth keeping. Wikipedia gives cream, First Nature creamy white, and McNabb — on New Zealand material — ochraceous buff. The spread is the point: saffron milk cap's page says a spore print cannot separate this genus because the prints run white to ochre across it, and this species runs the width of that range on its own. Checked 06/10/2026.

Which name is correct, because both are in use. McNabb sets out the dispute: Bulliard's 1791 Agaricus necator was redescribed by Persoon (1801) and revalidated by Fries (1821) against Persoon's rather than Bulliard's fungus, so most recent workers reject Bulliard's name for A. turpis Weinm., while Singer (1962) read the misinterpretation the other way and cited the species as Lactarius necator. This entry's summary already lists both, plus L. plumbeus. Checked 06/10/2026.

summary.text:
Lactarius turpis (also L. plumbeus or L. necator) is a Eurasian species of fungus, commonly known as the ugly milk-cap or green birch milk cap in English.

Lactarius turpis is found naturally in Europe and Siberia, and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. It can also be found in North America, in the northeast (July–September) and near the West Coast (September–November).

warnings: Contains the mutagenic compound necatorin. Boiling reduces it but does not eliminate it, so this is not a mushroom to eat however it is cooked — despite its use, after boiling, as a pickle in Russia and a spice in northern and eastern Europe.

identification.text: A small milk cap. Cap 1–3.5 cm across, convex when young, flattening or sinking in the centre with age, dry except in wet weather and finely powdered to the lens; Its colour is a muted salmon, sometimes closer to a grey-tinged orange or a washed-out orange-brown, and no concentric zoning is recorded on it. Gills pallid, crowded, moderately thick, up to 3 mm deep, attached to slightly or occasionally fully running down the stem. Stem 1–3 cm long and 4–7 mm thick, more or less even, coloured like the cap, solid at first and becoming chambered or hollow with age. Flesh pallid greyish orange and unchanging. The milk is white and does not change colour in the air. Gills and flesh both taste mild, and there is no distinctive smell. Found under beech.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut or nick the gills and watch the milk. Saffron milk cap's milk is carrot-orange - it stays orange or slowly turns reddish - and its gills and flesh stain green where bruised or handled. This one's milk is white and does not change, drying cream. Its cap is 1-3.5 cm across, where saffron milk cap's is 3-20 cm, so a small saffron cap can overlap. It is dull salmon, greyish orange or pale orange-brown, and unzoned, where saffron milk cap is often ringed. It grows under beech; saffron milk cap is recorded here under pine.

habitat.text: Silybum marianum establishes itself in sunny, warm ruderal meadows in regularly disturbed places such as rubble deposits, at the foot of south-exposed walls or villages and on urban fallow land or on cattle pastures. However, it does not prefer dry, stony soils.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Annual or biennial.  Stems branched above, ridged, with sparse mealy hairs at least above, 0.5–2 m tall, not winged.  Lvs elliptic to lanceolate, lyrate-pinnatifid to pinnate, sinuate, coarsely dentate, green with conspicuous white markings along veins, (10)–20–60 × (5)–10–30 cm, with sparse short mealy hairs on lamina, and sparse long tangled multicellular hairs on midrib; base amplexicaul, auriculate, with very spinous margins;  prickles marginal, yellowish, spreading, 5–12 mm long.  Capitula ovoid, erect, 4–6 × 5–7 cm, solitary, terminal and pedunculate, and also sessile in axils of uppermost lvs; peduncles with appressed cobwebby tomentum.  Involucral bracts sparsely covered with short mealy hairs;  margins with sparse cobwebby hairs.  Outer bracts leaflike, obovate with spinous apex and margins.  Middle bracts oblong; appendage ovate, subulate, with spinous margins and a long spreading to recurved apical spine.  Inner bracts lanceolate;  appendage becoming linear-lanceolate, entire.  Corolla reddish purple, 20–28 mm long;  lobes unequal, 4–6 mm long.  Anther filaments joined at margins into a tube which encloses the basal appendages of the anthers.  Style exserted 1–2 mm beyond corolla lobes.  Achenes brown or black-streaked, obovoid, weakly transversely flattened, smooth,  c. 6 × 3 mm;  outer pappus bristles scabrid,  c. 15 mm long; inner hairs very fine.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Silybum marianum is a species of thistle.
Silybum marianum is native from around the Mediterranean and much of Europe to Central Asia and India; in Africa it reaches as far south as Ethiopia. It is possibly native near the coast of southeast England. S. marianum has been widely introduced outside its natural range, for example into North America, Hawaii, Australia, New Zealand, and Colombia where it is considered an invasive weed. It also spreads invasively in almost all of Europe as a consequence of field cultivation.
Milk thistle has been potentially observed to modify fire regimes in its invasive range. Its invasion into new habitats may also be encouraged by fire.

identification.text:
Glabrous perennial.  Stem usually single, erect, not branched or branching above, finely grooved, (20)–50–100 cm tall.  Rosette and lower stem lvs petiolate, 7–20 × 3–10 cm, lyrate-pinnatifid with a large triangular or reniform ternatifid coarsely toothed terminal lobe and 1–3 pairs of small ovate-hastate coarsely toothed lateral lobes;  hydathodes prominent at tips of teeth;  lamina thin, bright green above, pale and glaucous beneath.  Upper lvs similar, with petiole becoming broadly winged and amplexicaul-auriculate at base;  uppermost lvs not divided, linear to oblong, amplexicaul.  Infl. diffusely paniculate.  Capitula numerous, narrowly cylindric.  Outer involucral bracts 2–4, very short, ovate to lanceolate, 1/10-? length of inner bracts. Inner involucral bracts linear, strictly erect, often purplish, 5–7 mm long; margins scarious.  Receptacle areoles with raised glabrous margins.  Florets 11/2× length of involucre;  corolla pale yellow.  Achenes usually 5 or fewer, dark brown to black, 10-ribbed, fusiform, flattened, very finely scabrid, shortly beaked, 3–4.5 mm long.  Pappus bristles in 2 ± unequal rows, fine, white.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

identification.text: Sprawling, hollow, ridged stems rooting at the nodes, with paired, oval, lightly toothed leaflets that smell of celery or parsley when crushed. Small white umbels sit on short stalks opposite the leaves. Watercress smells peppery, has rounded leaflets and four-petalled white flowers in a cluster, not an umbel.

lookalikes.howToTell: Watercress belongs to the cabbage family: its small white flowers have 4 petals and grow in stalked spikes (racemes) that lengthen into narrow, curved pods 8–18 mm long, and its leaves have a hot, mustardy taste. Water celery is an umbellifer: its tiny white flowers, 1–2 mm across with 5 petals, sit in small compound umbels 2–4 cm across on short stalks opposite the leaves. Watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges; water celery's are toothed, and its crushed leaves are described as smelling of carrot. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams and can be mistaken for watercress, so habitat does not separate them. Watercress from water draining grazed land can carry liver fluke and should be cooked.

summary.text: Fool's watercress. A celery-scented streamside umbellifer that grows through watercress beds and shares its water with deadly relatives. Eaten in Europe.

warnings: Pull watercress stem by stem and smell each one. Anything with a celery or parsley smell is not watercress.
Hemlock, a deadly relative, also lacks the pepper smell.

identification.text:
Almost glabrous annual herb;  stems erect or suberect, to  c. 75 cm tall, often reddish;  roots rather slender.  Lvs on main stem similar to those on branches, subsessile or shortly petiolate.  Lamina 1–12 × 0.3–2 cm, lanceolate or linear-lanceolate, bright or deep green, with small translucent glandular dots;  margins ciliolate and ± undulate;  base cuneate to attenuate;  apex obtuse to acuminate.  Ochreae to 2 cm long, reddish brown, truncate, with 0-few fringing bristles, ± flared at upper nodes.  Racemes slender, spike-like, to  c. 7 cm long, at least partly curving downwards, the lower fls often distant; pedicels short, enclosed by bracts at anthesis, later protruding.  Perianth 1.5–3 mm long, prominently dotted with brownish glands, usually pink or rose, rarely white, accrescent;  segments ± broad-elliptic, strongly imbricate.  Nut 2.5–3 mm long, trigonous or biconvex, dark brown or black, finely granular and appearing dull to moderately shining.

summary.text: Persicaria hydropiper (syn. Polygonum hydropiper), also known as water pepper, marshpepper knotweed, arse smart or tade, is a plant of the family Polygonaceae.

edibleParts.text: Leaves and tender stems.

habitat.text: Slow-moving fresh water: streams, drains, spring-fed creeks. Often in dense floating mats.

harvestEthics.text: Cut above the waterline and leave the roots so the mat regenerates.

identification.text: Rounded, glossy compound leaves with a large terminal leaflet. Hollow stems that root at the nodes. Small four-petalled white flowers. Sharp peppery taste.

lookalikes.howToTell: Water celery's leaflets are toothed, in 2–8 pairs, and its crushed leaves are described as smelling of carrot; watercress's leaflets are rounded with smooth or wavy edges and have a hot, mustardy taste. In flower, water celery has small compound umbels of tiny 5-petalled white flowers on short stalks opposite the leaves; watercress has 4-petalled white flowers in racemes followed by narrow curved pods. Water celery grows in shallow ponds, drains and the margins of slow streams, and it can be mistaken for watercress and collected and passed on as such. Water celery's young leaves and shoots are eaten in Mediterranean countries, but it is an umbellifer, and deadly hemlock — another umbellifer — also grows on damp ground in New Zealand, so be certain of the identification.

summary.text: Peppery and everywhere in NZ waterways — but the water it grows in is the whole problem.

warnings: Liver fluke risk: watercress in waterways grazed by sheep or cattle can carry Fasciola hepatica. Cooking destroys it — raw does not.
Check the waterway for agricultural runoff and toxic algae before harvesting. LAWA publishes water quality and algal bloom status for monitored sites.
Never harvest from a stream below a farm, dairy shed or urban stormwater outfall.

identification.text: This is a small flowering plant growing to a height of no more than 30 cm, usually annual or short-lived perennial, with few short, erect stems. The leaves pinnate, mostly at the base, each with about 5 pairs of rounded leaflets. Flowers very small, white, 3–4 mm across with 6 stamens. Fruits of C. flexuosa generally do not overtop the flowers, a feature distinguishing it from Cardamine hirsuta.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe weraroa' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: The species is endemic to New Zealand, and is fairly abundant in the early winter and spring months in lowland mixed rainforest near Wellington and Auckland. The mushroom can be difficult to see, often buried under leaves or eaten by slugs, and it is sometimes hard to find mature specimens that are not partially eaten. The species is typically found on decaying wood buried in forest leaf litter (either solitary or crowded), often on the rotting branches of māhoe (Melicytus ramiflorus). It has also been found fruiting on rotted cabbage trees (Cordyline australis) and associated with decaying tree-fern fronds, native to the forests of New Zealand.

harvestEthics.text: Endemic to New Zealand and a fungus of the forest. Picking it is possession of a Class A drug. Leave it standing. Photograph it, note the place, and take nothing.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Psilocybe weraroa' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text: Pileus (Peridium) 3–5 cm (1.2–2.0 in) long by 1.5–3 cm (0.59–1.18 in) wide, roundish, ovate (wider at the base and tapering towards the end, egg-shaped) or elongated and elliptic (tapered at the base and apex with a swollen mid-section), base decurrent (extending down the stem below the insertion) or rounded and blunt, margin folded and often torn, light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey, sometimes pallid green in age, longitudinally fibrillose causing a finely striated appearance, becoming smooth, polished, glabrous, tacky and leathery in age, slowly bruising blue or greenish when injured, drying yellow to dingy brown. Stipe up to 40 mm (1.6 in) long by 6 mm (0.24 in) in diameter, slender, equal in width, whitish to french-grey, bruising blue or greenish with damage, yellowish-brown at the base, initially fibrillose but becoming smooth, polished and cartilaginous in age excluding at the base, hollow, flesh yellow-orange, thickening at the internal apex. Gleba sepia-brown to chocolate-brown, cellular, coarsely shaped, often elongated, laterally compressed, sparse, chambered and gill-like. Spores 11–15(17) x 5–8 μm in size, smooth, sepia-coloured to purple-brown, elliptic-ovate or elliptical in shape, rounded at one end with a thin epispore.

lookalikes.howToTell: Colour and shape do not separate them reliably. Spindle pouch is powder blue, purplish blue or greenish, usually elongated and tapering towards the tip. Weraroa is light brown when young, becoming french-grey or pale blue-grey (sometimes pale green), and can be roundish, egg-shaped or elongated. Spindle pouch's stem is stout, solid, smooth and slippery, off-white to yellow and yellower towards the base, and widens towards the pouch. Weraroa's is slender, the same width throughout, fibrous and often hollow, whitish to french-grey with a yellowish-brown base. Weraroa slowly bruises blue or greenish where injured, on both pouch and stem. Spindle pouch is naturally blue but does not blue when damaged. Cut one lengthways. Spindle pouch's gleba is brown, reddish-brown or lighter red, rarely rust-coloured or orange, in regular cell-like chambers inside a purple-brown sack-like layer. Weraroa's is sepia or chocolate-brown to purple-brown in contorted, gill-like chambers, with no sack.

summary.text: Psilocybe weraroa, formerly Weraroa novae-zelandiae, is a secotioid fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae.

warnings: Psilocybine and psilocine are Class A controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Picking or carrying one is possession of a Class A drug.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Suillus lakei' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Suillus lakei is indigenous to the Rocky Mountains and western parts of North America. Its range extends south into Mexico. Fruit bodies grow solitarily or in groups on the ground in young conifer stands or grassy parkland. Fruiting occurs in the late summer and autumn, later on the West Coast. Suillus lakei forms ectomycorrhizae with Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), and its distribution coincides with this tree. It is one of the most common bolete species found in northwestern Montana and Idaho. In a study of host specificity in pure culture in the laboratory, S. lakei failed to form healthy ectomycorrhizas with Eucalyptus roots; the hyphae were covered in mucilage-like deposits and appeared to be collapsed.  It has also been noted to prefer poor, exposed soil such as that found on road banks and campgrounds. It can often be found with the mushroom Gomphidius subroseus, another species that associates with Douglas-fir.
Both Douglas-fir and S. lakei are non-native introduced species in Europe. The fungus has been found in several central and south European countries following the intentional introduction of Douglas-fir. These include Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. It is considered endangered in the Czech Republic. Suillus lakei has also been reported in South America (Argentina and Chile) and in the South Island of New Zealand.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Suillus lakei' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The cap of S. lakei is up to 15 cm in diameter and initially convex, but flattens out somewhat in maturity. The cap is fleshy, dry, yellowish to reddish-brown but fades with age. It is covered with pressed-down hairs or minute tufted scales in the center, with the yellowish flesh visible between the scales. Heavy rain can wash the fibrils off the cap surface, leaving a sticky, glutinous layer behind. Older specimens may be nearly smooth in age. Remnants of the partial veil sometimes hang from the edge of the cap. The cap margin is initially curved or rolled inwards, but unrolls as it grows and in maturity may be curled upward.

The tubes that comprise the pore surface on the underside of the cap are 5–12 mm deep; the angular pores are up to 2.5 mm wide and radially arranged. The pores range in color from yellow to brownish-yellow to ochre, and stain brownish or reddish-brown when bruised. They are covered by a partial veil in young specimens. The flesh is thick, yellow, and either unchanged in color when bruised or broken, or turns pinkish-red. The stem is 6 to 12 cm long and usually 1–3 cm thick, yellow, sometimes with reddish streaks (particularly below the ring zone), and solid and yellow within. The species usually lacks the glandular dots on the stem that are characteristic of some Suillus species. The stem is either equal in width throughout its length, or tapered downwards. The tissue of the stem base may weakly stain bluish-green when cut, although this reaction is not usually apparent in mature specimens. The ring is delicate and floccose (resembling woolly tufts), and soon disappears or leaves a thin whitish ring on the stem. The spore print is cinnamon to brown in color. The variety calabrus, found in Italy, has a light yellow cap and purple-red scales. Variety pseudopictus has a cap that is redder and more scaly than the more common form.
The spores are spindle-shaped to elliptical, have a smooth surface, and dimensions of 8–11 to 3–4 μm. There are both two- and four-spored basidia (spore-bearing cells), and they are club-shaped, hyaline (translucent), with dimensions of 28–36 by 10–12 μm. Cystidia are plentiful, and are found in bundles lined along the tube mouths (as cheilocystidia), or more commonly, singly along the sides of the tubes (as pleurocystidia). These structures are thin-walled, cylindrical, and measure 48–60 by 7–9 μm. The scales on the cap surface comprise more or less erect hyphae with tips that are clustered together. Clamp connections are rare in the hyphae.


Similar species

Mushrooms with an appearance similar to S. lakei can often be distinguished by their associations with trees. For example, the eastern North American species S. spraguei grows in association with Eastern White Pine. The cap of S. spraguei has red fibrils on a yellow background. S. cavipes and S. ochraceoroseus always grow with Larch. S. ponderosus, which grows in mixed coniferous forests, has a gelatinous veil. Smith and Thiers note that it is difficult to tell the difference between the two if S. ponderosus has lost its veil, since the colors of the species intergrade and cannot reliably be used to distinguish them. S. decipiens has a cap that is orangish to pink-orange with hairs or scales. S. caerulescens is a similar species in western North America; it can be distinguished by the strong blue staining that develops when the stem is injured.

identification.text:
It is a low-growing herbaceous, perennial plant. The leaves are trifoliolate, smooth, elliptic to egg-shaped, long-petioled, and usually with light or dark markings. The stems function as stolons, so white clover often forms mats, with the stems creeping as much as 18 centimetres a year, and rooting at the nodes. The leaves form the symbol known as shamrock. Almost always, a white clover will be trifoliolate (have three leaflets). However, one can, but only sometimes, possess four or more leaflets. The species includes varieties often classed as small, intermediate and large, according to height, which reflects petiole length.
It produces flowering heads of whitish florets, often with a tinge of pink or cream that may come on with the aging of the plant. The heads are generally 1.5–2 cm wide, and are at the end of 7 cm peduncles or inflorescence stalks. The flowers are mostly visited by bumblebees and often by honey bees. 
White clover spreads vegetatively through creeping above-ground stems known as stolons, which form adventitious roots at their nodes. Patches of clover can potentially double in diameter during a growing season.

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are hairless or nearly so on stem and leaf with round heads on stalks above the leaves, so separate them by habit: white clover creeps and roots at the nodes, while alsike stands erect or ascending and does not root at the nodes. White clover's leaflets often carry light or dark markings; alsike's are described as unmarked. Alsike's head is usually pink; white clover's is usually white but occasionally pink to reddish, so do not lean on colour alone. With a hand lens, alsike's calyx teeth are usually much longer than the calyx tube, white clover's shorter than it. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Alsike clover

lookalikes.howToTell: Red clover's flower head is usually stalkless, sitting directly on the leaves beneath it, and its stems (sparsely below, more densely above) and usually its leaf stalks are hairy; its stems are erect or lie along the ground at the base but do not root at the nodes. White clover's heads rise from the leaf axils on stalks longer than the leaves, its stems creep and root at the nodes, and it is more or less hairless. Colour is a guide only: red clover is pink to purple-pink, rarely cream; white clover usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Red clover's leaflets usually carry a crescent-shaped spot towards the base and white clover's often carry light or dark markings, so the mark will not separate these two. Both are edible.
lookalikes.name: Red clover

lookalikes.howToTell: If it is flowering, look at the flower: white clover packs numerous flowers, each with a corolla 8–12 mm long, usually white and occasionally pink to reddish, into a globe-shaped head, while Bermuda buttercup has separate golden flowers with petals (1.5)–2–2.8 cm long, usually 3–18 (occasionally 1) hanging together at the top of a stalk (7)–15–45 cm long. Without flowers, check how it grows: white clover's stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes; Bermuda buttercup grows upright, its leaves rising from a short vertical stem at the soil surface (or above it in shade or dense growth) over an underground bulb, and its bulbil-bearing runners are underground. Leaf shape and size do not separate them: white clover's leaflets are obovate to elliptic or nearly round with a blunt to notched tip and c. 5–25 mm long, Bermuda buttercup's are shallowly to deeply two-lobed and 10–32 mm long. Leaf markings do not separate them either — both are often marked. Season is no help: in New Zealand white clover flowers July to March and Bermuda buttercup is recorded flowering in every month. Bermuda buttercup is high in oxalic acid and is described as mildly toxic to people in larger quantities, so eat it only in modest amounts.
lookalikes.name: Bermuda buttercup

lookalikes.howToTell: Least yellow sorrel: its flowers are solitary, rarely paired, with yellow petals 4.5–9 mm long, often flushed pink outside, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Least yellow sorrel's leaflets are 1–9 mm long, white clover's 5–25 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Least yellow sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping wood sorrel: it carries 1 to 5 flowers on a stalk, with yellow petals 4.5–10 mm long, each flower open with its petals spreading from the centre, not a head of florets. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Creeping wood sorrel's leaflets are 5–18 mm long (from 2.5 mm), white clover's 5–25 mm long. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves or stems: both creep and root at the nodes, both have three leaflets that can be notched at the tip, and the leaflet sizes overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Creeping wood sorrel

lookalikes.howToTell: Pale-pink wood sorrel: each flower stalk carries a single flower, its petals 1.7–2.2 cm long, pale mauve, sometimes almost white. Its stems are spreading to sub-erect and much-branched, often with small bulbils in the branch axils, and its leaflets are 4–16 mm long and 5–22 mm wide, mostly broadly heart-shaped. White clover: its flowers come many together in a round head on a stalk above the leaves, each a pea-type floret 8–12 mm long, usually white, occasionally pink to reddish. Its stems creep along the ground and root at the nodes. Out of flower, do not rely on the leaves: white clover's leaflets are c. 5–25 mm long, can be notched at the tip and often carry light or dark markings, so leaflet size, shape and markings overlap. Both are eaten.
lookalikes.name: Pale-pink wood sorrel

preparation.text: They are not easy for humans to digest raw, however this is easily fixed by boiling the harvested plants for 5–10 minutes.

recipes.method: 225 g margarine or butter, 150 g brown sugar, 120 ml apple sauce, 30 ml milk, 375 g flour, 1 tsp baking soda, a loosely packed 120 ml of chopped white clover flowers and 150 g diced strawberries. Heat the oven to 180°C. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the apple sauce and milk, then work in the flour and baking soda. Fold the clover and strawberries through last. Bake 13–15 minutes.
recipes.title: White clover and strawberry cookies

recipes.method: About 500 ml of white clover blossoms (snip the petals from the flower heads and throw out any browned ones), 15 ml (1 tbsp, or one sheet) of unflavoured gelatine, 250 ml water, 125 ml freshly squeezed orange juice (about two large oranges), 60 ml honey, 250 ml cream whipped stiff or 250 ml full-fat Greek yoghurt, and a pinch of salt. Dissolve the gelatine in 60 ml of water. In a small saucepan, slowly bring the blossoms, water, orange juice, honey and salt to the boil. Take it off the heat, stir in the gelatine until it has completely dissolved, and leave it to stand for 10 minutes. Cover and refrigerate until it begins to set, then fold in the whipped cream or yoghurt, spoon it into a serving bowl and refrigerate until set.
recipes.title: White clover pudding

recipes.method: 500 ml–1 litre (2–4 cups) of fresh white clover blossoms, stems removed, 1 litre water, 60 ml bottled lemon juice (or 1 tsp citric acid), one 50 g box of regular powdered pectin and 1.25 kg (5 cups) sugar. Pour the water, just boiled, over the blossoms, push them under and steep for 15–20 minutes. Strain, pressing the blossoms gently, and top the tea up with water to 1 litre if it is short. Stir in the lemon juice and bring it to the boil, then whisk in the pectin until it has dissolved and boil hard for a full minute. Only then add all the sugar at once — added earlier, the jelly will not set — stir until dissolved, return to a full rolling boil for exactly 1 minute, take it off the heat and skim. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Cool undisturbed for 12–24 hours before checking the seals; refrigerate any that did not seal, and refrigerate after opening. Do not leave out the lemon juice: it helps the set and makes the jelly acidic enough to can.
recipes.title: White clover jelly

recipes.method: Pick white clover blossoms; leaves and stems can stay in, but they taste stronger, so separate them out for a milder flour. Lay the blossoms out to dry on a screen somewhere well ventilated and out of direct sun (sun dries them in a few hours, but can cost them nutrients). Grind them in batches in a small blade coffee grinder, or all at once in a food processor on high for about 5 minutes. It shrinks a lot: about 1 litre of blossoms with stems gave 500 ml of blossoms and about 125 ml of flour, so pick roughly 8 times the volume you want. It will not hold baked goods together on its own: use it for up to a quarter of the flour in a recipe. It tastes mildly sweet and green, like spring peas, and gives a spongy texture that suits biscuits and soft baking.
recipes.title: White clover flour

recipes.method: About 225 g blackberries, 225 g blueberries, 250 ml fresh white clover flowers, 125 ml orange juice and 500 ml tequila. Lightly muddle the berries in a jug, add the clover flowers, pour in the tequila and orange juice and stir. Add plenty of ice, and water to taste.
recipes.title: White clover berry punch (alcoholic)

Recipe 'White clover pudding', restated in this guide's own words, metric: Danielle Prohom Olson, 'White Clover Pudding: A Recipe for Comfort & Healing', Gather Victoria, 9 June 2015 (https://gathervictoria.com/2015/06/09/white-clover-pudding-a-recipe-for-comfort-healing/), retrieved 15/10/2026, no licence stated so all rights reserved assumed; supplied by the owner. The author adapted an old recipe written for sweet clover (Melilotus) to white clover, so this one is written for Trifolium repens. Cups and spoons converted at 250 ml a cup, 15 ml a tablespoon and 5 ml a teaspoon (the page does not say which cup it means; a US cup is about 237 ml). The page lists 1 cup of water and separately dissolves the gelatine in 1/4 cup; it does not say whether that quarter comes out of the cup, and the method keeps both as given.

Not used from the Gather Victoria page: its medicinal claims (anti-inflammatory, anti-bacterial, blood and lymph cleanser), its folklore, its claim that bees prefer white clover to red, and a reader's comment that browning clover blossoms ferment into warfarin — the author replied she believed that applies to sweet clover (Melilotus), not white clover, and neither claim was checked. The author's own instruction to discard browned petals is in the method.

Recipe 'White clover jelly', restated in this guide's own words, metric: Ashley Adamant (recipe card; the tasting notes are signed Cami), 'Clover Jelly', Creative Canning, first published 28/06/2024, updated 09/06/2026 (https://creativecanning.com/clover-jelly/), retrieved 15/10/2026, all rights reserved. Written for red, white or crimson clover. Cups converted at 250 ml (the site is American; a US cup is about 237 ml), 1.75 oz pectin as one 50 g box, 5 cups sugar as about 1.25 kg, 1/4 inch as 5 mm. Its altitude adjustment (15 minutes above 6,000 ft), low-sugar pectin variants, 'pantry shelf for 12 to 18 months' and blind-tasting flavours were not used. Found while answering the owner's question whether red and alsike clover recipes are interchangeable (15/10/2026).

summary.text:
Trifolium repens, the white clover, is a herbaceous perennial plant in the bean family, Fabaceae (also known as Leguminosae).
It is native in Europe and Central Asia, ubiquitous throughout the British Isles, introduced in North America, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and elsewhere, and globally cultivated as a forage crop.

warnings: They should not be eaten too long after picking, due to formation of cyanides.
White clover is polymorphic for cyanogenic glycosides: the leaves and flowers of certain phenotypes contain a glycoside which releases cyanide on contact with the enzyme linamarase.
