identification.text:
Liane with stout stems, or a dense, mound-like shrub of intertwining branchlets; stems terete, finely tomentose especially when young; armature of small, reddish prickles, or 0. Lvs palmate; leaflets 3–(5), glabrous or almost glabrous and rugose on upper surface, usually white- to brown-tomentose on lower surface and sometimes greyish or glaucous, sometimes glabrous to almost glabrous on lower surface also, coarsely serrate; terminal leaflet lamina usually narrow- to broad-ovate, oblong or lanceolate, rarely linear or narrow-linear, 25–70 × 4–40 mm, with petiolule 10–30–(50) mm long. Infl. a many-flowered, sometimes compact, panicle, up to 10–(25) cm long. Petals white to cream. Drupelets yellowish or orange.
R. schmidelioides is very variable in leaflet shape and indumentum. The leaflets of mature lvs are typically narrow-ovate or lanceolate and tomentose beneath, but leaflets of juvenile plants are much narrower and usually glabrous. In lowland E. South Id mature plants often retain this juvenile leaflet form in open habitats; such plants are then easily distinguished from R. cissoides and R. australis by the narrow leaflets.
[From: Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Blackberry is a scrambling, suckering shrub, usually semi-erect with arching, entangling stems that are usually angled; its leaves are palmate with (3–)5(–7) leaflets, usually hairy or felted underneath; its flowers are 15–60 mm across with white to deep pink petals; its fruit ripens through green and red to black, usually shiny, 10–15(–18) mm long. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the flowers: blackberry's are 15–60 mm across and have stamens and carpels together, while white-leaved lawyer's are 8–15 mm across, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Ripe blackberry is black and white-leaved lawyer's yellow to orange or red, but blackberry is red before it turns black, so judge colour only on ripe fruit. NZPCN adds that the native lawyers lack the long, glandular, bristly hairs some introduced brambles carry on their young stems; not every blackberry has them, so their absence does not rule blackberry out.
lookalikes.name: Blackberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Red raspberry is an erect, suckering shrub up to 1.5(–3) m tall with weak, more or less round prickles; its leaves usually have 2(–3) pairs of side leaflets along a central stalk plus one at the end (rarely only three), densely white-felted underneath; its flowers are 20–25 mm across with narrow white petals, and its fruit is of waxy red or orange drupelets, up to 15 mm long. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Both can be white-felted underneath, so the felt does not separate them: count the leaflets and see how they are attached. Raspberry's are pinnate, side leaflets in pairs along a central stalk; white-leaved lawyer's are palmate, usually three from one point. Raspberry is an erect shrub with flowers 20–25 mm across; white-leaved lawyer is a liane or a tangled mound with flowers 8–15 mm across, male and female on separate plants.
lookalikes.name: Red raspberry

lookalikes.howToTell: Bush lawyer (Rubus australis, also called swamp lawyer) is a scrambling liane armed with numerous small, slender, wide-based reddish prickles; its leaves are palmate with 3–5 leaflets, mostly hairless apart from weak hairs on the main veins and margins, usually coarsely and often unevenly toothed; the end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, 15–60 × 10–40 mm, on a stalk usually about as long as the blade or longer; its petals are white to cream, occasionally pinkish, and its fruit pale yellow to orange-red. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Flora of New Zealand's key: bush lawyer's end leaflet is elliptic to ovate or almost round, hairless except often on the veins and margins, with fewer than 10 coarse or irregular teeth on each side; white-leaved lawyer's is felted underneath or, if hairless (mostly in the lowland eastern South Island), narrow-lanceolate or linear and coarsely toothed. Juvenile white-leaved lawyer leaflets are much narrower and usually hairless. Their fruit colours overlap, so fruit does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Bush lawyer

lookalikes.howToTell: Creeping lawyer is a low shrub whose creeping stems, up to 1 m long, root at the nodes and carry small prickles only when young; each leaf is a single leathery leaflet, linear-lanceolate to linear-oblong or ovate-lanceolate, (20–)25–90 × 5–22 mm, bronze-green above, paler below and sharply toothed; its flowers are relatively large, borne singly or a few together, with white petals, and its fruit is red. White-leaved lawyer is a liane with stout stems, or a dense mound of intertwining branchlets, with small reddish prickles or none; its leaves are palmate with 3(–5) leaflets, hairless or almost so and wrinkled on top, usually white- to brown-felted underneath and sometimes greyish, though some plants are almost hairless underneath too; the end leaflet is 25–70 × 4–40 mm on a stalk 10–30(–50) mm long; its petals are white to cream and its fruit yellowish or orange. Creeping lawyer's mature leaves are a single leaflet; white-leaved lawyer's have three or more. Creeping lawyer's flowers are relatively large, with stamens and carpels together, where white-leaved lawyer's are small, male and female on separate plants. Young plants and flowering shoots of other brambles sometimes have single-leaflet leaves too, so judge by the leaves on mature stems.
lookalikes.name: Creeping lawyer

preparation.text: Noticing similarities to European wild blackberries, Early European settlers in New Zealand used tātarāmoa berries to create foods such as preserves or jams.

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. Makes 6 jars of 250 ml. Somewhere between a jam and a jelly: the juice is pressed rather than dripped through a bag, so it sets cloudy. 1 litre berry juice (fresh or thawed frozen berries put through a cold-press juicer), 300 ml cold-pressed apple juice, the juice of 3 lemons, 1.3 kg white sugar, 10 whole cloves and the zest of an orange. Wash the jars and dry them, open end up, in a 120 °C oven for about 15 minutes, leaving them in the warm oven until needed; boil the lids for 5 minutes and let them air-dry. Put the berry, apple and lemon juices and the sugar in a jam pan, dissolve the sugar over low heat, then bring to the boil. Add the cloves and orange zest, skim off foam as it rises, and boil to setting point — about 30 minutes for the author, giving a soft set. Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars and seal.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry jelly

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. 400 g berries, 500 ml white wine vinegar and 100 g white sugar. Warm the vinegar with the sugar until it has dissolved. Put the berries in a large clean jar or a non-reactive bowl, pour the warm vinegar over them and leave overnight. Strain gently through a fine sieve or muslin and pour into a sterilised bottle or jar. The author uses it to quick-pickle wafer-thin slices of raw beetroot (3 tablespoons of vinegar and ¼ teaspoon of sea salt for 2 small beetroot, soaked at least 15 minutes) served with goat's cheese.
recipes.title: Lawyer berry vinegar

recipes.method: Written for Australian native raspberry (Rubus probus), a different bramble; the author does not mention New Zealand lawyers. For one drink. Muddle a big handful of berries (fresh or frozen) in a cocktail shaker, add 60 ml tequila blanco, 30 ml Cointreau, 60 ml fresh lime juice and 60 ml sugar syrup, shake hard over ice and pour. Strain it if you don't want the seeds.
recipes.title: Lady in Red cocktail

summary.text:
Rubus schmidelioides, commonly called bush lawyer or white leaved lawyer, is a climbing plant species found commonly in New Zealand.
Rubus schmidelioides var. schmidelioides and its variant var subpauperartus are both endemic to New Zealand and the Chatham islands. It is found mainly in the South Island in eastern Canterbury but can also be found in other areas of the country and on Stewart Island.
Rubus schmidelioides grows best during the mid-stages of succession when the tree canopies have not grown high. Juveniles struggle to grow in areas of low light where the canopy is already established.

warnings: Tātaramoa, or “bush lawyer”, has hooked thorns that snag clothing and rip or prick the skin.

identification.text:
Summer-green dioecious perennial, with woody crown; roots long, cylindrical, fleshy. Stems 60–120 cm high, bright green, stiffly erect, ± woody below, branched above; shoots fleshy, edible. Scale-leaves scarious, 1–5 mm long, with short soft basal spur. Cladodes needle-like, 5–15 mm long, 2–8 at each node. Flowers axillary, 1–2–(4), greenish-yellow; pedicels drooping, 5–10 mm long; male flowers 5–6 mm long, stamens ± 3 mm long, ovary rudimentary; female flowers shorter, ± 4 mm long, stamens ± 1.5 mm long, functionless. Berry globose, ± 6–8 mm diam., red. Seeds 1–9, ± 3 mm diam., black.
[From:  Healy and Edgar (1980) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 3.]

summary.text: Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) or garden asparagus is a perennial flowering plant species in the genus Asparagus native to Eurasia.

edibleParts.text: Young roots (small and woody); flowers; seeds as a spice.

habitat.text: Roadsides, dry banks, paddock margins and waste ground — the same places as hemlock.

identification.text: Up to 1 m, with a stem that is distinctly hairy and never blotched. Leaves finely divided and feathery, smelling of carrot when crushed. Flat white umbels often with one tiny dark red flower at the very centre, and a ruff of forked green bracts beneath the umbel that hemlock lacks. Seed heads close up into a bird's-nest shape.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock's stem is hairless and hollow, up to 2 m (rarely 3 m), and usually spotted or blotched purple, but sometimes only tinged purplish or pink, so a stem without blotches does not rule hemlock out. Wild carrot's stem is bristly-hairy, more or less solid, up to 120 cm, and sometimes purple-tinged itself. Hemlock is hairless throughout; wild carrot's leaves and leaf stalks are hairy. Under the umbel, hemlock has about 4–8 narrow-triangular bracts that bend back; wild carrot's are numerous and divided into narrow linear segments. Crushed hemlock smells foetid and musty; wild carrot's root smells of carrot. Check every plant for every feature. If any one does not fit, leave it.

Wikipedia contributors. 'Daucus carota', Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. CC BY-SA 4.0. Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daucus_carota Gives the hemlock separation feature by feature, which is what this page's warning demands and did not spell out: wild carrot has tripinnate leaves, **fine hairs on solid green stems and on the leaves**, a root that smells of carrot, and often a single red flower in the centre of the umbel; poison hemlock differs in **purple mottling on stems that are also hairless**. On the parts: the root is edible while young but quickly goes too woody, the flowers are sometimes battered and fried, and the leaves and seeds are edible. The seeds and flowers have been used as a contraceptive and abortifacient for centuries, but no research confirms the effect and there is no evidence of safety. Confirms the rash too — like many Apiaceae the leaves may cause phytophotodermatitis, and contact with wet foliage especially can irritate skin. Falcarinol, the plant's own antifungal compound, is toxic to mice and to Daphnia in the laboratory; normal consumption of carrots has no toxic effect in humans.

summary.text:
Chervil (; Anthriscus cerefolium), sometimes called French parsley or garden chervil (to distinguish it from similar plants also called chervil), is a delicate annual herb related to parsley.
A member of the Apiaceae, the native distribution of chervil is uncertain due to its long history of cultivation, particularly by the Romans. The New Oxford Book of Food Plants limits its native range to the Caucasus, while Plants of the World Online cites it with a wider native range across central and southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia from Switzerland in the west, to Iran in the east.
The species is now naturalised through most of Europe and North Africa. It is also introduced and frequently grown in North America, where it is naturalised in many areas. These escapes differ from other Anthriscus species growing in North America (A. caucalis and A. sylvestris) by having lanceolate-linear bracteoles and a fruit with a relatively long beak.

identification.text: Tall (to 2 m) with feathery thread-fine leaves and flat-topped yellow flower umbels. Solid, ridged, unspotted green stem. Crushing any part releases a strong sweet aniseed smell — this is the only check that matters.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hemlock is one of New Zealand's most poisonous plants, and every part is poisonous if eaten. Its stem is usually spotted or blotched purple, especially toward the base, but not always; its flowers are white; its leaf segments are broader than fennel's — ovate to triangular and toothed or cut; it has a few narrow, down-turned bracts under each umbel; and it smells foetid or musty — also described as mousy — when crushed. Fennel has yellow flowers, thread-fine leaf segments, no bracts under the umbels, and leaves that smell of aniseed. Both are hairless with finely ridged stems, and hollow versus solid stems are not reliable, so do not use the stem surface alone. Hemlock grows on roadsides, riverbeds, forest margins, damp ground and waste areas. If it does not smell of aniseed, do not treat it as fennel — and check the flowers, leaves and bracts as well as the smell.

edibleParts.text: Leaves - raw or cooked. Rather stringy, they are used as a garlic substitute. Bulb - used as a flavouring. Rather small, with a very strong flavour and odour. Bulbils - raw or cooked. Rather small and fiddly, they have a strong garlic-like flavour. The leaves, flowers, and bulbs of Allium vineale are edible. While it has been suggested as a substitute for garlic, there is some difference of opinion as to whether there is an unpleasant aftertaste compared to that of common garlic (Allium sativum).

sources: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. III (Healy & Edgar 1980, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
habitat.text: Occasional to locally abundant in pastures and waste places. Wild onion is occasional and difficult to detect in grassy waste land and on roadsides, and is usually grazed down when growing in adjacent grassland.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Series vol. III (Healy & Edgar 1980, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
Wikipedia, 'Allium vineale' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
identification.text:
Bulb globose to ovoid, to 3 × 2.5 cm, tunic whitish, membranous, easily separated at base, with several stipitate offset bulbs. Leaves sub-cylindric, hollow, slender, < scape, upper surface ± grooved. Scape erect, slender, 30–90 cm high, sheathed for ½–⅓ its length. Umbels < 2 cm diam., with flowers and bulbils (var. vineale), or more commonly with bulbils and without flowers (var. compactum (Thuill.) Bor.); pedicels several times > flowers; spathe-valve 1, soon deciduous. Flowers c. 5 mm long, green to white, often purplish, campanulate; segments lanceolate, acute, keeled. Stamens exserted, each inner filament with 2 prominent lateral appendages > anther, outer 3 filaments simple. Capsule not seen.
A. vineale may be recognised by the garlic-like odour, the slender, cylindrical rush-like stems and stipitate offset bulbs, and by the flowers being usually all replaced by bulbils.
Of the leaves (Wikipedia): Although similar to the leaves of Allium schoenoprasum (chives), they tend to be more fibrous, have more vertical grooves, and have better defined grooves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Onion weed's leaves are solid and strongly channelled; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Onion weed carries 3–15 white flowers 10–15 mm long (up to 20) and no bulbils; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long, green to white and often purplish. Onion weed's flower stalk is three-angled and sheathed only at the base; wild garlic's is slender and rush-like, sheathed by the leaves for a third to a half of its length. The garlic smell and spring flowering do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Onion weed

lookalikes.howToTell: Naples garlic's leaves are flat, with finely toothed or hairy-edged margins; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Naples garlic carries a many-flowered umbel 5–8 cm across of white flowers 8–10 mm long; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils. Naples garlic's flower stalk has two sharp, almost winged angles; wild garlic's is slender and rush-like. The garlic smell does not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Naples garlic

lookalikes.howToTell: Rosy garlic's leaves are flat; wild garlic's are hollow, slender and roughly cylindrical. Rosy garlic carries a loose umbel 5–8 cm across of pale pink flowers 10–12 mm long; wild garlic's head is under 2 cm across and usually all bulbils, its few flowers about 5 mm long. Both carry bulbils in the flower head and both smell of garlic, so bulbils and smell do not separate them.
lookalikes.name: Rosy garlic

preparation.text:
The leaves are used as an ingredient in minestrella soup, a complex blend of wild vegetables eaten in northwest Tuscany, Italy.
The bulbils can be used fresh, or air-dried as a crunchy seasoning, or sprouted for salads (Wild Food UK).
The stems can be washed, cut like chives and frozen in bags; they keep their scent (Les Petits Plats du Prince). Cooking takes away its sharpness (Le Chemin de la Nature).

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale). Drain and rinse a 425 g tin of chickpeas and put them in a food processor with about 20 large wild garlic stems, rinsed and with any dried stems removed (more or fewer to taste). Add 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp tahini, 125 ml olive oil and 1 tbsp nutritional yeast, and process until completely smooth. Add salt, taste, and adjust any of the other ingredients. The author keeps the tahini light so it does not swamp the garlic, which is milder than a garlic bulb. Top with a little more olive oil and serve straight away, or chill.
recipes.title: Wild garlic hummus

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale), whose bulbs are each about the size of one clove of garlic. Cut 1.4 kg of broccoli into florets and simmer, covered, in 80–125 ml of water until tender, 10–15 minutes. Meanwhile peel and finely chop 8 wild garlic bulbs, and mix them with 60 ml lemon juice (from 2–4 lemons), 125 ml olive oil, and salt and pepper to taste. Toss the cooked broccoli in the dressing.
recipes.title: Broccoli with wild garlic and lemon

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale) in Gers, France. Rinse a bunch of stems in water with a little vinegar, then in clean water. Blend with 100 g pine nuts, almonds or hazelnuts, the juice of a lemon, and salt and pepper, pouring in olive oil in a thin stream until it is a soft paste. Keep in a jar in the fridge. Good with fish, pasta or on toast.
recipes.title: Wild garlic pesto

recipes.method: Written for wild garlic (Allium vineale). Serves 4. Peel and finely grate 4 potatoes. Rinse a bunch of wild garlic stems in water with a little vinegar, then in clean water, and snip them like chives. Mix the potato, the wild garlic and 1 egg, and season. Heat a film of oil in a frying pan, drop in small spoonfuls and press them down lightly. Cook about 15 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crisp, then drain on paper towel. A spoonful of flour makes them softer.
recipes.title: Potato and wild garlic galettes

recipes.method: From a French page on wild garlic (Allium vineale). Wash and cut 400 g of wild garlic and cook it in 2 tbsp olive oil, then stir in 100 g flour to thicken. Add 2 litres of water with a stock cube dissolved in it, and salt. Boil for 15 minutes. Serve with cream, croutons or cheese.
recipes.title: Wild garlic soup

summary.text:
Allium vineale (wild garlic, onion grass, crow garlic or stag's garlic) is a perennial, bulb-forming species of wild onion, native to Europe, northwestern Africa, and the Middle East.
The species was introduced in Australia and North America, where it has become an invasive species.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand), where the Flora calls it wild onion: N. North Auckland; Auckland - Auckland City, Miranda, Thames, near Hamilton; Wellington - Wanganui. S. Otago-Dunedin. It gives an unpleasant taint to meat and dairy products from animals which have grazed it.

warnings: There have been cases of poisoning caused by the consumption, in large quantities and by some mammals, of this species. Dogs seem to be particularly susceptible.

NC State Extension rates wild garlic as poisonous to eat at low severity for people, and potentially poisonous to livestock that eat a lot of it: every part may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. It advises harvesting only plants with a distinct onion smell.

habitat.text:
Found coastally in Great Britain, rarely in the north-east of Ireland. Lactuca virosa is widespread across much of central and southern Europe. It can be found locally in the south east and east of England. In the rest of Great Britain it is very rare, and in Ireland it is absent. It is also found in the Punjab region of Pakistan and India and Australia where it grows in the wild.
In North America, it has been documented as introduced in California, Alabama, Iowa, and Washington, DC, and grows wild in other parts of the continent.

Annual or biennial.  Stem erect, branching above, finely grooved, with patent pale spines up to 4 mm long, especially below, (50)–100–280 cm tall. edibleParts.text: Seed - cooked. It has a floury texture and a mild, somewhat creamy flavour. It can be used as a staple food crop in either savoury or sweet dishes. The seed can be cooked whole, though it is more commonly ground into a flour and used as a cereal in all the ways that oats are used, especially as a porridge but also to make biscuits, sourdough bread etc. The seed can also be sprouted and eaten raw or cooked in salads, stews etc. The roasted seed is a coffee substitute.

identification.text:
Tall, green or light green tufts to 1.5 m, robust, or sometimes with rather slender culms. Leaf-sheath slightly hairy, upper sheaths glabrous. Ligule 2–7 mm, truncate to oblong and obtuse, denticulate, abaxially scabrid. Leaf-blade 15–50 cm × 4–15 mm, scabrid on ribs and margins, often with scattered hairs, especially on margins. Culm erect or occasionally geniculate at base, internodes glabrous. Panicle (15)–20–38 cm, lax, equilateral, ± nodding; branches widely spreading, slender, drooping, scabrid. Spikelets 35–50 mm, 2–3-flowered, pendulous on fine unequal pedicels; disarticulation below each floret at maturity. Glumes 9–11-nerved. Lemma 15–17.5 mm, narrow-lanceolate, light brown at first becoming tough and darker brown at maturity, stiffly hairy below level of awn insertion, or sometimes glabrous, scabrid on nerves above, narrowed to bidentate scarious apex; awn 30–40 mm, geniculate, stout, column dark brown, twisted. Palea keels with one row of cilia, interkeel scabrid. Callus with horse-shoe shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs. Anthers 2.5–3.5–(4) mm. Caryopsis 6–8 × 1.8–2.2 mm, light grey, densely hairy.
[From:  Edgar and Connor (2000) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 5 (second printing).]

lookalikes.howToTell: The cultivated oat's spikelets fall intact at maturity; wild oat's break up, separating below each floret. The cultivated oat's lemma is hairless or has a few hairs near the base and is usually awnless; any awn is weak, straight or curved, not bent at a knee and scarcely twisted. Wild oat's lemma is stiffly hairy below the awn, though sometimes hairless, and its awn is stout, 30–40 mm, bent at a knee, with a twisted dark-brown lower column. Spikelet length overlaps: the cultivated oat's are usually 20–30 mm but 15–40 mm at the extremes, wild oat's 35–50 mm. None of these tests holds for fatuoids, or false wild oats — a mutant form that turns up in oat crops: their florets look like wild oat's, with a bent, twisted awn and a horseshoe-shaped callus bordered by hairs, and the spikelet breaks below every floret.
lookalikes.name: Oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Both shed below each floret and both carry a bent, twisted awn — 30–36 mm in slender oat, 30–40 mm here — so the awn will not separate them. Use the lemma tip: slender oat draws each lobe out into a fine bristle 2–3 mm long, while wild oat's narrows to a two-toothed papery tip with no bristles described. Slender oat's lemma has long, stiff, reddish hairs below the awn; wild oat's is stiffly hairy there or sometimes hairless, with no hair colour given in Flora of New Zealand. Slender oat is often very slender, with very fine panicle branches, but wild oat is sometimes slender too; the grain widths do not overlap — 0.8–1.3 mm in slender oat against 1.8–2.2 mm here.
lookalikes.name: Slender oat

lookalikes.howToTell: Winter wild oat's spikelet breaks above the glumes with its florets held together, so they fall as one unit; wild oat's breaks below each floret, so they fall one by one. At the base of each floret, winter wild oat's callus is bordered by dense short hairs; wild oat has a horseshoe-shaped scar densely bordered by long hairs. Winter wild oat's awns, on the lowest 1–2 florets, have a red-brown twisted column; wild oat's column is dark brown. Size does not separate them: in Flora of New Zealand, winter wild oat's spikelets are 3.5–6 cm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 25–50 mm in one subspecies (ludoviciana), and 6–8 cm with 3–5 florets and an awn of 60–70 mm in the other (sterilis); wild oat's spikelets are 35–50 mm with 2–3 florets and an awn of 30–40 mm.
lookalikes.name: Winter wild oat

preparation.text: Ripe florets drop from the plant one at a time, so a stand is gathered as it ripens rather than after. The seed, when harvested and dried, can store for several years. No source gives a method written for this species. Written for the cultivated oat: Harvested oats go through multiple stages of milling. The first stage is cleaning, to remove seeds of other plants, stones and any other extraneous materials. Next is dehulling to remove the indigestible hull, leaving the seed or "groat". Heating denatures enzymes in the seed that would make it go sour or rancid; the grain is then dried to minimise the risk of spoilage by bacteria and fungi. For home use such as making porridge, oats are often rolled flat to make them quicker to cook.

summary.text:
Avena fatua is a species of grass in the oat genus.
This oat is native to Eurasia (particularly the eastern Mediterranean) but it has been introduced to most of the other temperate regions of the world. It is naturalized in some areas and considered a noxious weed in others.

This species and other wild oats can become troublesome in prairie agriculture when it invades and lowers the quality of a field crop, or competes for resources with the crop plants. It takes very few wild oat plants to cause a significant reduction in the yield of a wheat or cultivated oat field.

In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: Auckland City, Bay of Plenty (Opotiki), Hawkes Bay (Takapau), more common in the Manawatu and Wairarapa, also from near Wellington City; S.: common in Canterbury, North and Central Otago, less so in Nelson, Marlborough, South Otago and Southland; Ch. Naturalised.

warnings: Claviceps purpurea is an ergot fungus that grows on the ears of rye and related cereal and forage plants. Consumption of grains or seeds contaminated with the survival structure of this fungus, the ergot sclerotium, can cause ergotism in humans and other mammals. It affects oats only rarely.

identification.text:
The parsnip is a biennial plant with a rosette of roughly hairy leaves that have a pungent odor when crushed. Parsnips are grown for their fleshy, edible, cream-colored taproots. The roots are generally smooth, although lateral roots sometimes form. Most are narrowly conical, but some cultivars have a more bulbous shape, which generally tends to be favored by food processors as it is more resistant to breakage. The plant's apical meristem produces a rosette of pinnate leaves, each with several pairs of leaflets with toothed margins. The lower leaves have short stems, the upper ones are stemless, and the terminal leaves have three lobes. The leaves are once- or twice-pinnate with broad, ovate, sometimes lobed leaflets with toothed margins; they grow up to 40 centimetres long.
The petioles are grooved and have sheathed bases. The floral stem develops in the second year and can grow to more than 150 cm tall. It is hairy, grooved, hollow (except at the nodes), and sparsely branched. It has a few stalkless, single-lobed leaves measuring 5 to 10 cm long that are arranged in opposite pairs.
The yellow flowers are in a loose, compound umbel measuring 10 to 20 cm in diameter. Six to 25 straight pedicels are present, each measuring 2 to 5 cm that support the umbellets (secondary umbels). The umbels and umbellets usually have no upper or lower bracts. The flowers have tiny sepals or lack them entirely, and measure about 3.5 millimetres. They consist of five yellow petals that are curled inward, five stamens, and one pistil. The fruits, or schizocarps, are oval and flat, with narrow wings and short, spreading styles. They are colored straw to light brown, and measure 4 to 8 mm long.
Despite the slight morphological differences between the two, wild parsnip is the same taxon as the cultivated version, and the two readily cross-pollinate. The parsnip has a chromosome number of 2n=22.

identification.text:
Annual to perennial.  Taproot swollen or slender.  Stems usually green, (10)–20–80–(100) cm tall.  Rosette and lower stem lvs lyrate-pinnate;  terminal leaflet 3–6–(10) × 3–6–(10) cm, as wide or narrower than rest of lf;  lateral leaflets in 1–8 pairs.  Stem lvs simple or with 1 pair of basal lobes, orbicular to lanceolate, 1–6 cm long.  Racemes 15–40–(60) cm long.  Pedicels 1–2 cm long, stout at fruiting.  Sepals 6–9 × 1–2 mm. Petals yellow, white, brownish, pink, or mauve, usually mauve-veined, 13–20 mm long.  Silique (1)–2–8-seeded, cylindric, constricted between seeds, breaking into segments when ripe, weakly to strongly ribbed, tapering at apex, (10)–20–60–(80) × (2)–3–8–(9) mm.  Seeds 1.5–3 mm long.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

summary.text:
Raphanus raphanistrum, also known as wild radish, white charlock or jointed charlock, is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae.
It is native to temperate regions of North Africa, Europe and parts of Western Asia.
It is found in North Africa, within Macaronesia, Madeira Islands, Canary Islands, Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia. Within Western Asia it is found in the Caucasus, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Cyprus, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Turkey. In eastern Europe, it is found within Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine. In middle Europe, it is in Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Switzerland. In northern Europe, in Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Isle of Man, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden and United Kingdom. In southeastern Europe, within Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Slovenia. Also in southwestern Europe, it is found in France, Portugal and Spain.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Spearmint' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Spearmint can readily adapt to grow in various types of soil. Spearmint tends to thrive with plenty of organic material in full sun to part shade. The plant is also known to be found in moist habitats such as swamps or creeks, where the soil is sand or clay.
Spearmint ideally thrives in soils that are deep, well-drained, moist, rich in nutrients and organic matter, and have a crumbly texture. The pH range should be between 6.0 and 7.5.

sources: Flora of New Zealand Online, Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research (CC BY 3.0 NZ)
identification.text:
Rhizomatous perennial with branched ± glandular-scaly stems ascending to c. 80 cm, glabrous, glabrate or grey-villous, often tinged red.  Lvs sessile to very shortly petiolate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, lanceolate to elliptic or ovate-elliptic to ovate or oblong, plane or rugose, either with scattered hairs on veins below, or densely hairy above and persistently grey-villous below; base cuneate to cordate;  apex obtuse to shortly acuminate.  Infl. of rather narrow, short or long, terminal spikes, the central one 4–12 cm long, usually sparsely hairy, sometimes grey-villous.  Fls pedicellate.  Calyx 1.5–2.2–(3.5) mm long, ± purple, sparsely dotted with glands;  teeth lanceolate or linear-subulate, ciliate, acuminate, slightly < to = tube.  Corolla 3–5 mm long, mauve or pinkish;  lobes dotted with oil globules outside.  Stamens included or exserted;  anthers 0.35–0.4 mm long.  Style long-exserted.  Nutlets 0.5–0.7 mm long, broad-ovoid, minutely reticulate or granular, sometimes plant sterile.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: No single character in the Flora of New Zealand separates every plant, so use several together. Apple mint's leaves are broad, usually elliptic and wrinkled, 1.5–4.5 × 0.8–3 cm; spearmint's are lanceolate to ovate, 2.5–9 × 0.7–2 cm, so leaf sizes overlap. Apple mint is densely hairy and often grey-woolly beneath; spearmint ranges from nearly hairless to densely hairy and grey-woolly beneath, so hairiness alone does not decide it. Both have stalkless or nearly stalkless leaves; apple mint's leaf base is heart-shaped or nearly so and often clasps the stem, spearmint's ranges from tapered to heart-shaped. Apple mint's calyx is more or less green and its corolla pale pink or whitish; spearmint's calyx is more or less purple, its corolla mauve or pinkish, and its stems are often tinged red. Apple mint is described as having a fruity, minty flavour, and spearmint a minty, green, cooling, spicy smell, but smell is a clue, not a test. Both are edible.

summary.text:
Spearmint (Mentha spicata), also known as garden mint, common mint, lamb mint and mackerel mint, is native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, extending from Ireland in the west to southern China in the east.
Diseases and pests

Fungal diseases
Fungal diseases are common diseases in spearmint. Two main diseases are rust and leaf spot. Puccinia menthae is a fungus that causes the disease called "rust". Rust affects the leaves of spearmint by producing pustules inducing the leaves to fall off. Leaf spot is a fungal disease that occurs when Alternaria alternata is present on the spearmint leaves. The infection looks like circular dark spot on the top side of the leaf. Other fungi that cause disease in spearmint are Rhizoctonia solani, Verticillium dahliae, Phoma strasseri, and Erysiphe cischoracearum.

Nematode diseases
Common nematode diseases known to affect spearmint are root knot, caused by various Meloidogyne species, and root lesions, caused by members of the genus Pratylenchus.

Viral and phytoplasmal diseases
Spearmint can be infected by tobacco ringspot virus. This virus can lead to stunted plant growth and deformation of the leaves in this plant. In China, spearmint have been seen with mosaic symptoms and deformed leaves. This is an indication that the plant can also be infected by the viruses, cucumber mosaic and tomato aspermy.

identification.text:
Small, hairy shrub to c. 30 cm high.  Shoots dense, erect or suberect, densely clothed in short hairs.  Lvs sessile or subsessile, 3–8 × 0.5–3 mm, elliptic but appearing linear because of revolute margins, densely hairy, with abundant oil globules, tomentose along midrib below.  Fls in dense terminal heads;  lower verticels often interrupted.  Bracts similar to lvs, often somewhat wider, green, < to > calyx.  Calyx 3–4 mm long, campanulate, green or purplish, hairy, dotted with oil globules, with tuft of white hairs in throat;  teeth of upper lip ovate, not ciliate;  teeth of lower lip linear-subulate, long-ciliate.  Corolla 4–6 mm long, white or mauve;  tube not exserted, hairy outside;  upper lip with large, broad, oblong-elliptic to obovate lobes, sparsely hairy or glabrous;  lower lip at right angles to upper. Stamens not or scarcely exserted;  anthers purplish.  Nutlets 6–8 mm diam., broad-ellipsoid to sub-spherical, dark brown.  
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

sources: Wikipedia, 'Stropharia rugosoannulata' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
The mushroom can grow to 20 centimetres high with a reddish-brown convex to flattening cap up to 30 cm across, the size leading to another colloquial name godzilla mushroom. The gills are typically adnate, initially pale, then grey and finally dark purple-brown in colour. The spore print is dark purple-brown to black.
The firm flesh is white, as is the tall stem, which bears a wrinkled ring.


Similar species
It can resemble some members of its genus, such as S. hornemannii, as well as Agaricus (the gills of which are usually more pink).

Stropharia rugosoannulata, commonly known as the wine cap, wine-red stropharia, wine cap stropharia, garden giant, burgundy mushroom, or king stropharia, is a species of agaric mushroom in the family Strophariaceae found in North America.
It is also found in Europe, and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Collybia nuda' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
The wood blewit is found in Europe and North America and is becoming more common in Australia and New Zealand, where it appears to have been introduced. In Australia it has developed a relationship with some eucalyptus species and gorse; with an entirely different growth pattern and differs slightly in appearance to its European Lepista nuda cousins. 
It is a saprotrophic species, growing on decaying leaf litter. In the United Kingdom, it appears from September through to December.
Soil analysis of soil containing mycelium from a wood blewit fairy ring under Norway spruce (Picea abies) and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) in southeast Sweden yielded fourteen halogenated low molecular weight organic compounds, three of which were brominated and the others chlorinated. It is unclear whether these were metabolites or pollutants. Brominated compounds are unknown as metabolites from terrestrial fungi.
The form glaucocana is found in mountainous environs.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Collybia nuda' (CC BY-SA 4.0) — units converted to metric
identification.text:
This mushroom can range from lilac to purple-pink. Some North American specimens are duller and tend toward tan, but usually have purplish tones on the stem and gills. Younger specimens are lighter with more convex caps, while mature specimens have a darker color and flatter cap, ranging from 4–15 cm in diameter. The gills are attached to the short, stout stem, which is about 2–6 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide, sometimes larger at the base. Wood blewits have a very distinctive odor, which has been likened by one author to that of frozen orange juice.
Wood blewits can be easily distinguished by their odor, as well as by their spore print, which is white to pale pink.


Similar species
Wood blewits can be confused with certain blue or purple species of the genus Cortinarius, including the uncommon C. camphoratus, many of which may be poisonous. Cortinarius mushrooms often have the remains of a veil under their caps and a ring-like impression on their stem. Cortinarius species produce a rusty brown spore print after several hours on white paper. Their brown spores often dust their stems and objects beneath them.
The species also resembles Collybia brunneocephala, Clitocybe tarda, Laccaria amethysteo-occidentalis, and Lepista subconnexa. It could be confused for members of the rare Texas genus Asproinocybe.

summary.text: Collybia nuda, commonly known as the blewit, wood blewit  or blue foot and previously described as Lepista nuda and Clitocybe nuda, is a species of fungi.

edibleParts.text: The whole fruiting body.

habitat.text: Dead and dying wood in damp native bush, especially māhoe and other soft-wooded trees.

harvestEthics.text: Growing on dead wood in native bush means it is usually on DOC land, where a permit is required. Cut cleanly and leave the wood intact.

identification.text: Ear-shaped rubbery brackets, brown to purplish, velvety on the outer surface and smooth within. Gelatinous and springy when fresh, shrinking to a hard flake when dry and rehydrating readily.

Retrieved 06/10/2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auricularia_cornea Corroborates the export story and adds the te reo name and the traditional preparation. In New Zealand it is known as hakeke; Māori traditionally cooked it by steaming in an earth oven and eating it with sow thistle — pūhā, which has its own entry here — and potatoes. It was collected and exported from New Zealand to China from the 1870s to the 1950s, which is the trade this entry's summary refers to. Commercially cultivated in China today, including a white unpigmented form, and used in Cantonese desserts and stir fries. Also called pepeiao ('ear') in Hawaii and taingang daga ('rat's ears') in the Philippines. A naming caution for anyone cross-checking: American authors have widely treated this species as a synonym of A. nigricans, and the misidentification persists.

Landcare Research Virtual Mycota, 'Galerina patagonica' (facts restated)
habitat.text:
It grows on rotting wood.
In New Zealand: on rotting wood — trunks, branches and heaps of leaves, mainly of mountain beech — and on the ground (Landcare Research Virtual Mycota, restated).

harvestEthics.text: This mushroom is often found in reserves, where picking is prohibited. It is not edible and has no known useful properties, so there is no reason to take one. The rotting wood it grows on is habitat in its own right — leave the log as you found it.

sources: Massee 1899, via Manaaki Whenua Virtual Mycota (public domain)
identification.text: Pileus thin, globose, then hemispherical, with a prominent elongated umbo, coarsely striate at the margin, remainder even, glabrous, 1-1.5 cm. high and broad, ochraceous-yellow ; gills emarginate, with a decurrent tooth, rather crowded, broad, ventricose, rusty-orange ; spores elliptical, 13-14 x 7-8 µ; stem about 5 cm. long and 2 mm. thick, equal, twisted, fibrillose, rusty-orange, fistulose. Distinguished by the prominent umbo.

lookalikes.howToTell: Never separate these on one character. The Galerina is deadly-suspect and both grow on rotting wood. Look for a ring. Landcare describes the common NZ Galerina as having a well-developed ring on the stem, though in the related Galerina marginata the ring may disappear. P. subaeruginosa has only a short-lived cobweb-like veil that leaves at most a raised zone on the upper stem. Check the gills: cinnamon to rusty brown in the Galerina, pale smoky brown ageing to violet-brown in P. subaeruginosa. P. subaeruginosa's cap and stem stain greenish blue with age or handling. The related Galerina marginata is described as not bruising and unchanging when cut. Cap shape and colour do not separate them. Both have yellowish to orange-brown caps, and P. subaeruginosa can also have a small pointed centre. A spore print confirms it: P. subaeruginosa purple-brown, Galerina cinnamon-brown. The Galerina's toxicity is unknown, but it sits in the group containing the deadly Galerina marginata and is thought likely to contain amatoxins.
lookalikes.name: Psilocybe subaeruginosa

lookalikes.howToTell: Both are small brown mushrooms with a bump in the centre of the cap, often more or less pointed, and both grow on fallen, rotting wood - P. makarorae on southern beech, and wood nipple fungus mainly on beech wood too - so shape and habitat do not separate them. Cap colour overlaps too: P. makarorae is yellow-brown to orange-brown, and wood nipple fungus ochre-yellow to bay or honey-coloured. Damage the cap or stem: P. makarorae stains greenish-blue, and no blue staining is recorded for wood nipple fungus. Look at the stem: wood nipple fungus has a well-developed ring, though in its close relative the ring often disappears with age. P. makarorae has only cobwebby veil remnants and never a complete ring. A spore print may help: wood nipple fungus drops cinnamon-brown, and Psilocybe prints generally run lilac-brown to dark purple-brown, though rusty-brown prints are known in at least one species. Wood nipple fungus has not been tested for toxins, but it sits in the group that includes the deadly Galerina marginata and probably carries the same amatoxins.
lookalikes.name: Psilocybe makarorae

summary.text:
Galerina patagonica is a species of agaric fungus in the family Hymenogastraceae. The toxicity of Galerina patagonica is unknown. However, it is phylogenetically nested within the Galerina marginata species complex, and thus likely contains deadly amatoxins.

It has a Gondwanan distribution, and is found in Australia, New Zealand, and Patagonia (South America).

sources: Wikipedia, 'Fragaria vesca' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
habitat.text:
Typical habitat is along trails and roadsides, embankments, hillsides, stone- and gravel-laid paths and roads, meadows, young woodlands, sparse forest, woodland edges, and clearings. Often plants can be found where they do not get sufficient light to form fruit. In the southern part of its range, it can grow only in shady areas; further north it tolerates more sun. It is tolerant of a variety of moisture levels (except very wet or dry conditions). It can survive mild fires and/or establish itself after fires.
Although F. vesca primarily propagates via runners, viable seeds are also found in soil seed banks and seem to germinate when the soil is disturbed (away from existing populations of F. vesca).
Its leaves serve as significant food source for a variety of ungulates, such as mule deer and elk, and the fruit are eaten by a variety of mammals and birds that also help to distribute the seeds in their droppings.
It is a larval host to the two-banded checkered skipper.

identification.text:
Low-growing herb with short woody stock, up to  c. 15–(25) cm high; runners greenish, pilose, bracteate, up to  c. 80 cm long and rooting at nodes and tips to form new rosettes.  Basal lvs several in rosette; petiole up to 15–(18) cm long, densely pilose;  leaflets ovate to rhombic or elliptic, obtuse to subacute, cuneate at base, ± thin, bright green above and usually sparsely to moderately silky pilose, rarely almost glabrous, paler below and usually silky pilose at least on veins, with margins coarsely serrate in upper 1/2-⅔ and pilose;  terminal leaflets (15)–30–60–(90) × (10)–18–40–(50) mm;  lateral leaflets slightly smaller;  petiolules very short or 0, silky pilose;  stipules triangular, 12–20 mm long, reddish brown, ± pilose especially along axis.  Scape (30)–60–180–(300) mm tall, ± erect and often arching in upper part, finely pilose;  infl. of 1-several fls;  pedicels 7–40 mm long;  fls 10–18 mm diam.  Epicalyx segments narrow, ± entire.  Sepals triangular, 4–6–(9) mm long, pilose, ± acuminate, connate at base, deflexed at fruiting.  Petals obovate, up to 8 mm long, sometimes only slightly > sepals, rounded, sometimes undulate, spreading, white.  Achenes uniformly scattered over and projecting from the receptacle;  receptacle usually red, occasionally white, swollen and juicy, sweet, fragrant, obconic, up to 15 × 12 mm.

habitat.text:
The plant grows from sea level to 3,500 m in elevation. Common yarrow is frequently found in the mildly disturbed soil of grasslands and open forests. Active growth occurs in the spring.

It has been introduced as a feed for livestock in New Zealand and Australia, where it is a common weed of both wet and dry areas, such as roadsides, meadows, fields and coastal places.

identification.text:
Strongly scented, rhizomatous herb, with short non-flowering rosettes often forming dense mats.  Stems usually erect, sometimes ascending, up to  c. 80 cm tall, ribbed and striate, hairy especially above, usually not branched except above to form infl.  Basal lvs petiolate, lanceolate, moderately hairy, 2-pinnate with segments again 1–2-pinnatisect, 6–15–(44) × 1–2–(4) cm; primary leaflets in 18–30–(37) pairs;  ultimate segments subulate, not all in one plane giving a feathery appearance to lf; rachis  c. 1–2 mm diam., flattened, sometimes slightly winged, not toothed.  Cauline lvs similar to basal, but above becoming apetiolate, less divided, smaller, and with fewer leaflet pairs.  Corymbs usually ± flat-topped or slightly convex, to  c. 15 cm across, with numerous, closely packed capitula.  Involucral bracts glabrous to sparsely hairy, 1.5–4–(5) mm long;  margin brown, hairy.  Capitula (3.5)–5–10 mm diam.; ray florets 4–7;  ligule and disc florets usually white, sometimes pink to deep red or purple.  Achenes grey-brown,  c. 2 mm long;  wings narrow, pale brown.

summary.text:
Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow () or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
Yarrow is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, being found in Europe, Asia, and North America.
In North America, both native and introduced genotypes, and both diploid and polyploid plants are found. It is found in every habitat throughout California except the Colorado and Mojave Deserts.

habitat.text: Exactly where field mushrooms grow: lawns, parks, pasture and under hedges, often in the same patch.

identification.text: A white Agaricus, the young cap often boxy or flat-topped rather than domed, sometimes greying with age. Gills pink, turning chocolate-brown. The test: cut or scratch the very base of the stem and watch for a few seconds — it turns bright chrome yellow almost immediately. The smell is phenolic, like ink or hospital disinfectant, and gets stronger when cooked. Field mushroom stays white or blushes faintly pink and smells of mushroom.

lookalikes.howToTell: Cut through the stem base of every mushroom in the basket. Bright chrome yellow almost at once (most marked in young, fresh mushrooms), with a smell of ink, phenol or iodine, points to yellow stainer or one of its yellow-staining relatives - discard it. Field mushroom does not turn yellow: its cut flesh reddens and it smells pleasant. Its stem narrows towards the base, where yellow stainer's is bulbous. A spore print will not help - both drop dark brown - and the white cap and pink-then-brown gills are shared.

summary.text: The field mushroom's poisonous double. Same pink-then-brown gills, same white cap — but the stem base flushes bright yellow the moment you cut it, and it smells of ink.

warnings: Causes sweating, cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea within hours. Some people tolerate it, most do not — do not use someone else's experience as a test.
Because it grows among field mushrooms, one in the pan spoils the lot. Cut every base, every time.

identification.text:
Yews are small to medium-sized trees, growing up to 10–20 metres or exceptionally 28 m tall, with a trunk up to 2 m or exceptionally 4 m in diameter. The bark is thin, scaly reddish-brown, and comes off in small flakes aligned with the stem. The leaves are flat, dark green, 1–4 centimetres long, 2–3 millimetres broad, and arranged spirally on the stem, but with the leaf bases twisted to align the leaves in two flat rows on either side of the stem, except on erect leading shoots where the spiral arrangement is more obvious.
The seed cones are modified, each cone containing a single seed, which is 4–7 mm long and almost surrounded by a fleshy scale which develops into a soft, bright red berry-like aril. The aril is 8–15 mm long and wide and open at the end. The arils mature 6 to 9 months after pollination.
The aril is gelatinous and very sweet tasting. The male cones are globose, 3–6 mm in diameter, and shed their pollen in early spring. Yews are mostly dioecious with male and female cones on separate trees, but occasional individuals can be variably monoecious, or change sex with time.

summary.text:
Taxus baccata is a species of coniferous tree in the family Taxaceae.
The yew is native to all countries of Europe (except Iceland), the Caucasus, and beyond from Turkey eastwards to northern Iran. Its range extends south to Morocco and Algeria in North Africa, and parts of Southwest and South Asia. A few populations are present in the archipelagos of the Azores and Madeira. The limit of its northern Scandinavian distribution is its sensitivity to frost, with global warming predicted to allow its spread inland. It has been introduced elsewhere, including the United States.

identification.text:
Annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb, with sprawling to suberect branched stems to c. 30 cm long, and characteristic scent. Stem base sometimes short and thick with a rosette of lvs. Petioles to c. 10 cm long, reddish where exposed to strong light, usually hairy along 1 side. Lamina very deeply palmately divided, 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, ± broad-ovate, with hairs scattered above, nearly glabrous below, often turning red with age; lobes 5, pinnatisect or less commonly pinnatifid; ultimate segments mucronate. Infl. very diffuse; fls paired; peduncles and pedicels variable, with simple and glandular hairs, often with a line of hairs along 1 side. Sepals (at anthesis) 5–8 mm long including apical awn, ovate, with mostly glandular hairs, ± reddish. Petals 6–9 mm long, ± oblanceolate, pink to rose; claw a little > limb; apex rounded. Filaments pinkish; anthers yellow. Mericarps 2.5–3 mm long, with short hairs; upper ⅔ with many, close, transverse ridges. Seed smooth.
[From:  Webb et al. (1988) Flora of New Zealand. Volume 4.]

lookalikes.howToTell: Herb robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems reach about 50 cm; its leaves reach about 9 × 10 cm, with 3–5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink or rose petals (7.5)–10–11.5 mm long; its anthers are orange; its fruit segments (mericarps) are 2.5–3 mm long, with 4–6 cross-ridges. Small herb Robert is an annual or biennial, hairy, taprooted herb with a characteristic scent; its stems are sprawling to nearly upright and reach about 30 cm; its leaves are 1.5–5–(7) × 2–6–(8) cm, cut very deeply into 5 lobes; its flowers are paired, with pink to rose petals 6–9 mm long; its anthers are yellow; its fruit segments are 2.5–3 mm long, with many close cross-ridges on their upper two-thirds. Flora of New Zealand's key separates them on the petals, usually 10–11.5 mm in herb robert and 6–9 mm in small herb Robert, and the anthers, orange in herb robert and yellow in small herb Robert. Its note on small herb Robert says the two have sometimes been confused, and gives small petals, yellow pollen and more, closer ridges on the fruit segments together as the signs of small herb Robert, which is also generally more upright, with smaller leaves. No single sign settles it: herb robert's petals can be as short as 7.5 mm, inside small herb Robert's range, and Wikipedia says both species have yellow pollen, so anther colour alone can be hard to read. Both are scented, both have paired pink flowers and deeply divided leaves that turn red, and their fruit segments are the same length. Herb robert's leaves are described as edible by two uncited websites, and two Spanish folk records call it poisonous (see its page).

summary.text:
Geranium purpureum, the little-robin, is a species of flowering plant in the geranium family Geraniaceae. It is native to Europe, Africa, and western Asia, and introduced on all continents except Antarctica. It is similar in appearance to Geranium robertianum, a close relative.
In New Zealand (Flora of New Zealand): N.: commonest in the Auckland area, but occurring at least as far north as Whangaroa (N. Auckland).
Because of the great similarity of this sp. to G. robertianum, the 2 spp. have sometimes been confused. The combination of small petals, yellow pollen, and more and closer ridges on the mericarps are diagnostic features of G. purpureum. Also, G. purpureum is generally more upright and has smaller lvs.
